# THOUSAND BLACK STAR

*A Novel of Sixty Loves Beneath One Dark Sky*

**Al Fayaz**

---

*For everyone who has kept a sentence behind their teeth.*

---

## PROLOGUE
### *Spoken by the Chorus*

In heaven's field a thousand stars lie dark,
Not dead, but dimmed by words they dared not speak;
Yet each doth bend the light about its arc
And draws the wandering heart to what they seek.
Come, then, kind friends, and lend a patient ear:
We tell of sixty loves beneath one sky,
Of some made glad, and some that drown in fear,
Of some that break mid-word and leave no why.
A boy from Dhaka, banks of river-rain,
A girl whose islands rise from Java's sea,
Shall write across the dark their long refrain,
And ask the night what yet may come to be.
Not all shall end as hearts would have them end—
Yet read: the dark hath light enough to lend.

---

---

# ACT I — THE LEDGER OPENS

## Chapter 1
### The Night the Ledger Opened

> *"I forgave you years ago and never said so."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0388

---

There is a house on the Cornish cliffs where the wind knocks at every window as though it, too, had a letter to deliver.

It is called Lantern House, and on the last night of her life it held three things worth the keeping: an old woman, a young one, and a thousand secrets in a locked oak cabinet that smelled of salt and cedar.

The old woman was Seraphine Wyndham-Rao. She was seventy-eight years old, born in Colombo under a monsoon sky, trained in London under a ceiling of lamps, and she had spent forty-five years learning that the heart is the only telescope that points both ways. She lay propped on four pillows beside a window that looked out upon nothing at all, for it was the dark of the moon, and the sea and the sky had agreed to be one colour.

The young woman was her grand-niece, Nadeesha Fernando, twenty-nine, a nurse from Galle, who had flown six thousand miles to hold a hand and had learned in four days what her profession had not taught her in seven years: that one can be perfectly competent and perfectly helpless in the same breath.

"You are doing it again," said Seraphine.

"Doing what, Aunty?"

"Counting my pulse as though it were a debt you hoped to settle." She smiled, and the smile cost her something. "Put down the wrist, child. It is not going anywhere that it has not been before."

Nadeesha put down the wrist. She did not put down the fear. Fear, like a stray cat, is not so easily dismissed once it has been fed.

"Tell me what is tonight," said Seraphine.

"The new moon."

"The new moon." The old woman closed her eyes. "The one night in the month when the sky withholds its lamp and shows you what is truly there. Do you know what an astronomer loves best, Nadeesha? Not the stars. The *dark between* them. For the dark is where the unseen things hold their court."

"Aunty, you should rest."

"I shall rest presently, and at length, and with no one to wake me." She opened her eyes, and they were bright and grey and absolutely clear. "Listen, for I will say this once, and then I shall be an inconvenience no longer."

She spoke then, not in prose, for the dying sometimes find their sentences fall into measure of their own accord, as water finds its level:

> *Beneath my bed, the cabinet; the key
> Lies in the lamp. A thousand letters keep
> Their silence there. I swore I would not share
> A single word while I had breath to guard it.
> I have no breath to guard it now. At midnight
> Unlock the doors. Let every letter speak.
> Let strangers read what strangers feared to say,
> And let them learn what I have learned too late:
> The word unspoken is no silent thing.
> It bends the course of every life it touches,
> As unseen stars bend light.*

"A thousand letters," said Nadeesha. "I thought—"

"You thought it was a few dozen love notes from sailors." Seraphine's laugh was a dry, small thing, like the rustle of a page. "A thousand people, child, over forty-five years. Each wrote me one letter, and each letter holds the one sentence its writer could never say to the person who needed to hear it. I numbered them in the order they came. I answered none. I kept every one." She paused. "The first, I confess, was not a stranger's."

"Whose was it?"

"A man's. A foolish, frightened, honourable man, who left me on a railway platform in nineteen seventy-seven because he was afraid he would love me too much." The grey eyes went somewhere very far. "He wrote it from a ship. I read it a hundred times. And then I thought: if one man has a sentence like that, how many more? And so I began a ledger. And so it became a life."

"And the thousandth?"

"Ah." Seraphine's hand moved, very slightly, toward her own breast. "The thousandth is mine. You will find it in the lamp with the key. You are not to read it until I am dead, and not aloud until the proper hour, and then only to the one it is for. He will know."

"Aunty—"

"There. I have been long enough with you. Go and open the doors."

---

She died at eleven minutes before midnight, which is to say she died exactly as she had lived: a little early for her own appointment, so as to be sure of finding a good seat.

Nadeesha sat with her for the length of one breath, and then another, and then a third, as though each might be given back. Then she wept, plainly and without shame, the way the very young and the very honest weep. Then she wiped her face with her sleeve, for she was a nurse, and nurses are trained to finish what the hour requires.

She found the key inside the lamp. She found the cabinet. She found, beneath the cabinet's loose board, a small laptop with a single file on its screen, and one button, and one line of text:

*PUBLISH THE REGISTER. — S.W.R.*

Behind her the window rattled. The clock on the mantel, which Seraphine had wound daily for forty years, said four minutes to midnight.

On the screen of a small laptop, in a house at the edge of England, a young woman put her trembling finger upon a key.

*Mark this, reader. A thousand doors, long locked, are about to open at once. And what comes through them is not wind.*

---

**Lisbon, 00:02.**

In the great grey sorting office by the river, a postwoman named Inês Carvalho was eating a custard tart over a tray of undelivered letters, which is a sin against both pastry and postage.

"They say it is the end of the world," said Pereira, the lamp-seller, who had no business in the sorting office at midnight and had come in, as he always did, to tell her that business was bad. "Not the whole world. Only the part where people keep quiet."

"What are you talking about, Pereira?"

"The Register." He held up a phone as though it were a gospel. "Some old English witch has died and given away a thousand secrets. All free. Confessions. *Love* confessions. There is a search bar, Inês. You type a city, and up come the sinners."

Inês, who read every address twice and every postcard three times (and had never, in nine years, been caught), took the phone out of his hand and typed, with the casual air of one who is merely checking the weather: *Lisbon*.

Eleven names appeared. Not names — numbers, and beneath each number a sentence.

The sixth said: **"I wrote to a woman whose face I have never seen."**

Her tart went cold in her hand.

For she, Inês Carvalho, twenty-seven, postwoman of Alfama, had delivered a letter exactly seven months ago, addressed in careful block capitals to a *Senhora, Rua da Saudade 14, Lisboa*, and the street did not exist, and she had kept it, and she had read it in the bath, and she had never been able to forget the second line.

*It is not much of a Register, Pereira,* she thought, *if it tells the truth.*

"Well?" said the lamp-seller. "What does it say?"

"It says," said Inês, closing the phone, "that the night is long, and the post is slow, and you should go home."

"That is not what it says. Your ears have gone red."

"My ears are cold."

"It is a warm night."

"Then my ears," said Inês with great dignity, "are *ambitious*."

---

**Dhaka, 06:05.** *(The same hour of the world, seen from the other side of it. The clocks, as we shall see, disagreed.)*

In a rented flat in Mirpur, where the electricity came and went like a temperamental relative, a young man sat before a laptop at the first grey of morning, with his sleeves rolled and his pride rolled up with them.

His name was Fayaz Rahman. He was twenty-six, and he looked like a man who had once been very sure of something and was now merely well-mannered about its absence. He had run a small software company for eighteen months, and the company had died as small things die: quietly, owing money. He had a father whose business had gone with it, a mother whose breathing had grown shallow, a sister named Tithi whose exams required fees, and two embassy letters, each beginning *We regret.*

He had, in short, a great many problems and no leisure in which to be unhappy about them. That, as he sometimes observed to the tea-stall boy at the corner, is how you know it is serious.

"Bhaiya," said Tithi, appearing in the doorway with a phone held out like a hot coal. "Look. There is a thing. Everyone is sharing it. *The Register of Black Stars.* You *wrote* to this, remember? Two winters ago. You said it was a stupid idea and then you did it at three in the morning."

"I never said that."

"You said it *and* you did it. Look. Your number. *Zero-seven-one-three.*"

He took the phone. The screen said, in plain white type on black:

**ENTRY 0713 — Dhaka, Bangladesh.**
***"I would tell you everything, if I were free to."***

He had written that. He remembered writing it, at a desk that was then a good desk, in a company that was then alive, to a person who was then a mere shape he hoped one day to meet. He had not expected it to be *read.* One does not write to the dark expecting an answer. It is, rather, a way of dropping a coin down a well and listening for the splash.

"It is embarrassing," said Fayaz.

"It is *poetry*," said Tithi.

"It is a sentence with a conditional."

"That is what poetry is."

He nearly smiled. Then his eyes, which were tired and honest, moved a little to the right, as eyes will, and fell upon the entry beside his own.

**ENTRY 0714 — Yogyakarta, Indonesia.**
***"I am an hour ahead of you, and I keep looking back."***

He read it. He read it again. A line, in a telescope of ten thousand words, can be the one that fits the lens.

Underneath, in the margin, in a small, steady, old-fashioned hand, someone had pencilled a note, and the note had been scanned along with the page:

*0713 posted 22:40, Dhaka. 0714 posted 23:41, Yogyakarta. One minute apart, by the stars. One hour, by the clocks. — S.W.R.*

"Bhaiya?" said Tithi. "Why are you looking at it like that?"

"No reason."

"You are *blushing*."

"The generator is on the wrong circuit."

"You do not have a generator."

"Then it is the *idea* of a generator," said Fayaz, with the dignity of a man in considerable trouble, "and I would be grateful if you went to get ready for college."

---

**Yogyakarta, 07:06.** *(An hour ahead. Always an hour ahead.)*

In a workshop that smelled of hot wax and indigo, with a copper canting in one hand and a half-drawn flower in the other, a young woman who had not been to bed was swearing at a parrot.

"Ayu," said Ermis Larasati, twenty-four, designer of batik and keeper of very large ambitions, "if you say it one more time I will give you to the cousins."

"*TOO LATE!*" said the parrot, which belonged to her grandmother, spoke only three sentences, and had learned them all from an argument. "*TOO LATE! TOO LATE! BEAUTIFUL!*"

"That is two sentences."

"*TOO LATE!*"

Ermis put down the canting. Her phone, propped against a jar of wax beads, was lit by a stream of messages from her cousin Dewi in Bali: *Have you seen it? THE REGISTER. Look at yours. Your number is next to somebody's!!!*

She had written to the old astronomer one night in her last year of design school, when she had been very tired and very sure that the thing she wanted most would be taken from her by the thing she wanted next. She had put a sentence in an envelope, because it was easier than putting it in a person, and sent it to an address in England that she had found on a foreign website. She had half-forgotten it.

Now she opened the link, and found her own sentence in the open air, and was a little annoyed at how much it sounded like truth.

*I am an hour ahead of you, and I keep looking back.*

She had meant a friend. She had meant a boy at university who had gone home to a city one time zone away, and she had never told him why she kept watching his lit window long after it went dark. It was a small sorrow, tidy as a pressed flower.

But that was not what she looked at now. She looked at the line on the *left* of her own.

*I would tell you everything, if I were free to.*

She read it aloud. The workshop was very quiet. Even the parrot, who had views on everything, said nothing.

"Dhaka," said Ermis. "Bangladesh." She looked at the clock above the door, which said 07:06. "That is an hour behind me."

She did the sum again, not because it was difficult, but because it was a pleasure to do.

Then, as sensible people do when something strange has happened, she took out a pencil and drew a small flower on the corner of the page, and wrote beneath it, in the Latin letters she used for clients and strangers:

*Hello, Dhaka. You are one hour behind. I am not sorry about it.*

She did not send it. Not yet. A message is a lamp, and one should know where one is hanging it.

"*BEAUTIFUL!*" said the parrot.

"Hush, Ayu."

"*TOO LATE!*"

"Is it?" said Ermis, to no one. And then, to the pale morning outside, and to the one window an hour behind it that seemed to hold her gaze: "Is it, though?"

---

**Cornwall, 00:00.**

At the stroke of midnight, a thousand doors opened.

They opened in Lisbon, where a postwoman sat very still over her cold tart. They opened in Accra, where a pharmacist and a taxi-fleet owner, who had not spoken in six years, each reached at the same moment for a phone. They opened in Osaka, in Cairo, in Bergen, in Kochi, in São Paulo, in Lagos, in Lyon, in Kraków, in a hundred other places where somebody was awake and ashamed.

They opened in a lighthouse in Galle, where a young man named Anil Perera watched a video call fail, and failed to know why he trembled.

They opened at dawn in a window in Dhaka, and an hour later, by the clocks, in a window in Yogyakarta: two mornings, one hour apart.

And on a cliff in Cornwall, in a house with the wind at its door, a grey-eyed old woman lay quite still, with a smile on her face that said she had never in her life been so completely on time.

---

*Margin note, in pencil, in the hand of S.W.R.:*

> *The thousand are not a thousand people. They are one people, sleeping in a thousand beds, dreaming the same dream of being known. Let them wake. Let them read. Let them, if they are brave, answer.*
>
> *— and if they are not brave, let them at least be kind.*

---

*End of Chapter 1.*


---

## Chapter 2
### The Postwoman of Alfama

> *"I wrote to a woman whose face I have never seen."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0753

---

Lisbon is built upon seven hills, and the Post has been trying to climb all of them since eighteen hundred and something.

It does not climb them well. A letter in Alfama does not travel; it is *carried*, up stairs that were laid out by a medieval drunkard, past walls tiled in blue by a hundred dead hands, beneath washing-lines strung from window to window like the bunting of a small and unwinnable war. And the carrier of the letters in that quarter, for nine years, had been a young woman named Inês Carvalho, who knew every door in it by its knock, every dog by its opinion, and every widow by the particular quality of her gratitude.

She did not sleep that night. At six, with the sky going from pewter to pearl above the river, she was already on the Rua de São Miguel with her yellow satchel and her red bicycle (which she pushed, for no bicycle born could ride that street), and in the satchel, beneath the gas bills and the pension slips, lay one envelope that was not hers.

She did not need to take it out. She had it by heart.

It had come to the sorting office seven months before, among the dead letters, which is the name the Post gives to mail that belongs to nobody: wrong addresses, vanished tenants, the tender misspellings of the very old. The envelope was cream, a little soft at the corners, addressed in careful block capitals to *SENHORA, RUA DA SAUDADE 14, LISBOA.* There is a Rua da Saudade in a number of Portuguese towns, for we are a people who name our streets after what we miss. There is none in Lisbon. Inês had held it up to the lamp, and a thing she had never before done in nine years of honest service had happened: she had opened it, and had told herself, with the ease of a woman who is lying to the one person who will believe her, that it was a matter of *procedure.*

*To the lady who writes small kindnesses on the backs of other people's envelopes:*

*I am a man who mends things that carry others, and I would like, once, to be carried.*

It was that second line. She had read the rest, a page and a half, in the bath, with the taps running to cover the sound of her own breathing, and every word of it had been courteous and clear and slightly frightened. But it was the second line that lodged in her like a fish-bone. *I would like, once, to be carried.*

She had never answered it. There was nobody to answer. It was signed with no name at all, only a drawing, a very small drawing, in pencil, of a wheel.

And now, on the screen of Pereira's cracked phone, in the night just gone, there had been a sentence beneath a number: *I wrote to a woman whose face I have never seen.*

*Entry 0753. Lisbon.*

She had let the lamp-seller go home. She had walked the wet dawn to the sorting office, and there on her own small phone, in the bright empty room with the sleeping machines, she had pressed her thumb and forefinger against the screen to enlarge the scan, as one pulls a curtain.

The Register, you understand, did not keep only the words of its confessors. It kept the *paper.* Seraphine Wyndham-Rao had been an astronomer, and astronomers do not trust a report of a star; they want the plate. So each letter had been photographed whole, cream and blue-lined and stained and creased, and the hand of 0753 was there in the open air for anyone to see: small, square, careful, upright as a row of soldiers, every letter built as if load-bearing.

Inês laid the phone upon the table, and beside it, very gently, the envelope.

The capitals were the same.

"*Ai,*" said Inês Carvalho, to the machines. And then, as a precaution, "*Ai, ai, ai.*"

---

By nine o'clock the news had gone round Alfama the way news does there: by no known channel, and faster than light.

"It is *you*," said Pereira, who had arrived at the foot of the Escadinhas with a barrow of lamps and the expression of a man who has found a truffle. "I said it last night, did I not? I said, her ears have gone red. And what does a woman do with red ears and a Register? She searches for a *man.*"

"I am not searching for a man."

"You are searching for a *handwriting*, which is a man with his clothes off."

"Pereira!"

"I am a lamp-seller, Inês. I deal in revelation." He held up a brass lamp the size of a cat. "For you, a special price, eighty euros. Read your love-letters by a better light."

"I do not have love-letters."

"Then why are you smelling envelopes?"

She was. It is a thing postwomen do. She had been going down the street with the morning's post and holding each envelope a moment to her nose, as a sommelier holds a glass, for the cheap ink of the Tax Office, the lavender of the widows, the cigarettes of the men who wrote to football clubs. She was searching, by smell and by script, for a square hand that built every letter as if it carried weight.

It was not a good method. It produced, in the course of one hour, the following events:

She delivered Senhor Matos's pension to the widow Matos's cat, which sat upon the step and refused to be signed for.

She gave the Tax Office's final demand to a young man in a bakery who had been the one *sending* it, and who took it, read it, and went quite grey.

She stopped a stranger outside the Sé Cathedral, a pale German in new walking boots, and asked him with great solemnity to write the words *BOA NOITE* on the back of her hand.

"Why?" said the German.

"It is a matter of *procedure.*"

"Is it a crime?"

"Not yet," said Inês, studying the capital B, "but I am hopeful."

It was in the Rua dos Remédios, outside a plumber's van, that she came to the first suspect.

"Inês, my *life,*" said Rui Costa, plumber, thirty-eight, in a voice like warm gravel. He had been, for eleven months at the age of twenty-six, the great sorrow of her life, and had since become a mild irritation, as great sorrows do when they are properly stored. He was wearing a vest and a look of suspicious innocence. "I saw it. I read it. The Register. And I thought to myself, Rui, you fool. She has been waiting."

"Waiting for what?"

"For the man who wrote to the woman whose face he never saw." He placed a hand upon his heart. "It was I."

"Rui."

"It was *I*, Inês. I wrote it years ago. In block capitals. I am a man of block capitals." He indicated the invoice pad on the dashboard, where indeed the numbers had been stamped in a hand of formidable squareness. "You see? The hand!"

She looked. It was a square hand, certainly. It was also a hand in which the number *four* had a small curl at the foot, like a pig's tail, and the capital *R* had a leg that kicked out at the world.

"Rui," she said gently. "You have seen my face."

"Naturally."

"You pinched my cheek at my sister's wedding."

"It was a *tender* pinch."

"You told me I looked like a boiled egg in a hat."

"It was a very *affectionate* egg."

"So you cannot have written to a woman whose face you have never seen."

Rui Costa considered this. He was not a stupid man, merely a *hopeful* one, which is the more dangerous condition.

"Then perhaps," he said, "I wrote it to another."

"Perhaps you did."

"Very likely it is *her* I meant." He stared into the middle distance. "A *mystery* woman. Hm. I will write to her again."

"Please do. Take your time."

She was walking away, with the German's *BOA NOITE* drying on her hand, when she heard behind her the long, aggrieved sigh of a man who has been wrong and will shortly be very loud about it. She did not turn round. A postwoman, like a sailor, learns not to look back at weather.

---

It was on a bench at the Miradouro de Santa Luzia, that same noon, with the whole bright shabby city laid out below her like a letter spread to dry, that her sister found her.

Rita Rocha, thirty-two, journalist, wore the face she kept for other people's scandals: bright and attentive and entirely without mercy. She sat. She unwrapped a pastry. She held it out.

"I have been wanting to say a thing," said Rita.

"Do not."

"It is about your entry."

"My *entry*?" Inês did not look round. "I have no entry."

"Entry zero-zero-fifty-three. 'I kept one letter that was never mine.' Lisbon. It is quite beautifully put."

There was a pause, in which a tram went grinding up the hill behind them, and a pigeon, which had been planning to approach the pastry, thought better of it.

"I never posted that," said Inês.

"No," said her sister. "You did not."

"I wrote it. I put it in a drawer."

"You did."

"It was in an envelope that I *sealed*, Rita, and it had no stamp on it, and it was in the drawer in the *kitchen,* under the string."

"It was," said Rita, "an excellent place for it. Very secure. I had to move the string."

"*Rita.*"

"Do not be angry. You were crying into the sink. I am your elder, and you were crying into the sink. And a person who cries into a sink about a letter should not keep the letter in a drawer; she should post it to a woman in England who will keep it for ever and tell no one." She took a bite of pastry. "As, you will observe, she did."

"She was dying!"

"She was *efficient,*" said Rita.

Inês opened her mouth, and found that all the sharp things she wished to say had melted, and that in their place was a soft, hot, helpless feeling, like a letter discovering that someone has finally read it.

"You are the worst journalist in Portugal," she said at last.

"I am the *best,*" said Rita. "I have just got you to admit it is yours."

She stood, brushing sugar from her coat. "And the man? The one who wrote to the woman with no face?"

"I have a handwriting."

"Have you a name?"

"No."

"Then find him," said Rita Rocha, "before somebody else is *found*," and she was gone down the steps in a flurry of scarf, leaving upon the bench a bitten pastry and a much-embarrassed postwoman.

*Mark this, reader.* It is a curious thing, but the people who say *I never told* are very seldom the ones who did not. The truth is a letter of its own, and it finds its post.

---

*A street in Santo Amaro. A tram depot, long and green-lit and smelling of oil and hot metal. In the pit beneath an old yellow carriage, a pair of boots, and a voice.*

"Now, Dona Conceição," said the boots. "We have discussed this. You are a lady of ninety-eight, and you have a gear-box like a general's stomach, and you will *not* seize up on me today. I have a feeling about today."

"*What* feeling?" said a second voice, above, from the platform. This was Nuno Pereira, twenty-seven, mechanic, best friend, and liar by vocation. He held his phone aloft like a priest with a relic. "Did you see it? The Register? There is a woman in Lisbon with a line like a knife. *'I kept one letter that was never mine.'* Entry zero-zero-fifty-three."

"Who keeps a letter that is not hers?"

"A thief. A romantic. A postwoman."

"Oh, come." The boots shifted. "There are three hundred postwomen in Lisbon."

"But how many kept yours?"

There was a short, hard silence in the pit, in which the cooling engine ticked like a clock.

"Mine," said the boots, "was a dead letter. It went to a nonexistent street. It was supposed to be *unfindable.* That was the *point.*"

"A man who sends a love-letter to a street that does not exist," said Nuno, with deep admiration, "is either a poet or a fool, and I have always said you were both."

Tomás Villaverde, twenty-nine, tram-mechanic, slid out upon his creeper like a man being born from an engine. He had a spanner in one hand and a smear of black grease from the temple to the jaw, and the look of a man who has been looking into the dark for a long time and has begun to see shapes there.

"I reasoned it out," he said. "I did not know her address. I know only her hand. So I wrote to *nowhere.* And the Post, if it is a decent institution, sends nowhere to somebody. I thought: the dead letters will go to the desk of the woman who writes on them. And she will either read it, or she will not." He wiped his face, and made it worse. "That is seven months, Nuno. In seven months I have had one reply. It was from the tax office, and it was about my *car.*"

"Perhaps she is shy."

"Perhaps she is sixty, with a moustache."

"She is," said Nuno, who had never seen her, "exactly sixty, and has a moustache like a Habsburg admiral."

"You are a liar."

"And a very good friend of liars," Nuno agreed. "I can recommend it."

But Tomás had slipped back beneath the carriage, and his voice, thinned by the iron above him, took on the strange musical quality of a man who is talking to himself in the one place where he is sure of no audience. He was not speaking in prose. He had not meant to. The engine had asked him, in its way, as engines do.

> *They say a man who mends the things that move
> Is moved by none. I say it is not so.
> I have been underneath this yellow thing
> A thousand nights, and listened to it ache,
> And known the very shiver in its wheel
> Before the driver felt it. That is love,
> Or else it is a trade, and I forget
> Which one I practise. Lady, if you read
> The small square words I sent into the dark,
> I do not ask you answer. Only know
> That somewhere underneath a tram, a man
> Is lying on his back, and looks at iron,
> And sees, quite plainly, through the iron, you.*

"That was very good," said Nuno, from above, after a respectful pause.

"It was the gear-box."

"It was *poetry.*"

"It was *oil,*" said Tomás, and hit the gear-box, which, as if repentant, began to hum.

---

At twenty minutes past four, at the Largo das Portas do Sol, tram twenty-eight stopped.

It had not intended to. It stopped as an elderly person stops upon a staircase: suddenly, with dignity, and with an air of having been betrayed by the stairs. A hundred tourists leaned out of the windows to photograph their own disappointment. The driver spread his hands to heaven. Up the hill, in a white cloud of ceremony, came Pereira with a barrow, selling lamps to the stranded, and behind him, shaking her head in the steady rhythm of a woman who has seen too many things go wrong in Alfama to be shocked by another, came the postwoman.

"A *call* has been made," said Pereira. "The mechanic comes."

"I don't care."

"He is said to be the best in the depot."

"I do not care *at all.*"

"And his name," said Pereira, who had a nose for it, "is *Tomás Villaverde.*"

Inês stopped.

Now it must be said, for the sake of accuracy, that she had not known the name. She had known a hand. But Rita, who is a journalist, had known someone who knew someone who had once fixed her washing machine, and Rita had sent a message at noon: *Tram depot, Santo Amaro, a Villaverde. Hands like a surgeon's, jokes like a cousin's, no wife.* There is no sorrow like being right on a hunch about a stranger, and no joy to equal it, and Inês felt both, at once, like two hot coins in a pocket.

She did not look at the tram. She looked at the pavement.

Beneath the carriage, from out of the shadow beneath it, protruded a pair of old black boots.

They did not move. A voice came from within the iron, the voice of a man engaged in an argument with a mechanism and slightly winning. "*Come on,*" it said. "Come on, my lady. Have a little courage. One more turn of the bolt and we shall both be heroes."

Inês, who had a satchel to deliver, a round to finish, and a handwriting to find, stood there with the whole city looking on and discovered, to her considerable annoyance, that her knees had gone.

The boots slid out. A body followed, in a blue boiler-suit gone black at the elbows. A face looked up from the pavement: long, serious, rather tired, with a smear of oil from temple to jaw and a pair of eyes the colour of a wet slate roof.

It was not, she thought, a face she knew. And he, for his part, looked upon the yellow satchel, and the red bicycle, and the cold-reddened ears, and the hand on which a faint blue *BOA NOITE* was running in the sun, and did not know hers either.

You will observe, reader, what is happening, for neither of them does. She has come by a hundred roads to the one man in Lisbon, and he has lain under a hundred trams for the one woman, and here, at the top of the hill, with a hundred tourists photographing the sky, the two of them stand a yard apart and do not know it. It is the cruelest of the old comedies, and the kindest.

"I am sorry," said Tomás. "I'm afraid I am in your way."

"You are not in my way. You are in the *road.*"

"A fine distinction."

"I am a postwoman," said Inês. "I am *rather* precise about roads."

"Ah." He sat up. A peculiar thing happened to his face, a tightening and a slackening together, like a man who has caught his own name called in a crowd. "A postwoman."

"Yes."

"In Alfama?"

"Nine years."

"Then you must know," said Tomás, with the elaborate lightness of the very frightened, "what becomes of a letter when it has no address."

The hundred tourists had gone quiet. Pereira, who was the soul of discretion when it paid him, put down a lamp.

"We keep it," said Inês.

"For how long?"

"Seven years. Then it is burned."

"*Seven.*"

"The Post is very patient. It is only people who are in a hurry." She was looking at the oil on his chin, and at nothing else, since she did not dare. "Seven months so far."

She saw him do the arithmetic. She saw it go through him as a current goes through a wire, and was glad of it, and alarmed, and could not in the whole world have said why, except that a man who counts months has plainly been counting them.

"And is the lady," said Tomás, very slowly, "who keeps such things... is she kind?"

"She is nosy," said Inês.

"I had heard that."

"She reads everything twice."

"I had heard *that,* too." He was getting up. He was taller than she had expected; he had to put a hand on the tram to find his balance. "She is, I am told, sixty, with a moustache."

"She is *twenty-seven,*" said Inês, with great dignity, "and has been shaving *daily.*"

For a second there was nothing in the whole hill-top. Then a tourist from Ohio began to clap, and then his wife, and then the carriage full, and Pereira, who had never missed an occasion, said in a very loud and sacred voice, "A special price on lamps!" and Tomás Villaverde, with an expression that no mechanic has ever worn in the history of the Carris, said:

"I think my name is Tomás."

"I think mine is Inês."

"The post," said Tomás, "is slow."

"But sure," said Inês, and took out of her satchel a cream envelope, soft at the corners, and held it for one moment against her chest, where he could see it, and did not give it to him. "I will have to *check* the address."

Behind them, with a long metallic sigh of relief, Dona Conceição gave up her objections and shuddered into motion.

---

*Margin note, in pencil, S.W.R.:*

> *Entry 0753 wrote to a woman he had never seen; Entry 0053 wrote to a woman who would never post it. Between them stand an envelope, a sister, and a hill. I have never known the Post to be late for a love, only careful.*
>
> *Observe, Keeper's reader: the tram has stopped. It will start again. That is all any of us may ask of a machine, or a heart.*

---

*End of Chapter 2.*


---

## Chapter 3
### Two Pharmacies, One Street

> *"I know who paid it. I was waiting for you to say."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0941

---

In Accra there is a lane called Palm Lane, though no palm has stood on it since the British left, and it is eighty yards long, and it holds two shops, one taxi yard, nine opinions, and a war.

At the northern end, in a cream building with green shutters and a red cross painted by a sign-writer who had been paid in kenkey, stood **Owusu Chemist & Dispensary**, whose proprietor, Abena Owusu, twenty-eight, wore a white coat as another woman might wear armour, and counted tablets in fives with the air of one who has caught nature cheating. At the southern end, behind a gate of corrugated iron painted the yellow of a ripe plantain, lay **Mensah Cabs**, forty-one taxis and a goat, belonging to Kwame Mensah, thirty-one, who had never in his life been seen to count anything but other people's blessings.

Between them lay eighty yards of cracked tar, which for six years neither had crossed.

"It is a *scandal,*" said Quaye.

Quaye was fifty-eight, the senior driver of Mensah Cabs, and the leader, by acclamation and by volume, of the Taxi Rank, which is what the drivers of Palm Lane called themselves when they sat upon their bonnets at dawn and considered the affairs of the world. They were a Chorus in all but name, for they spoke when the thing happened and not before, and said what everyone else was thinking a little too loudly.

"A scandal," agreed the Rank.

"Eighty yards."

"Eighty yards," said the Rank.

"I have measured it with my feet. A man could cross in a minute, with a bag of oranges. And these two" (he waved at the cream building and the yellow gate) "have not crossed in six years. What is that? Is that pride? Is that *hatred?* My friends, I have been a taxi driver for thirty-one years, and I tell you that when a man will not cross eighty yards, it is *love.*"

"It is parking," said a young driver, called Yaw, who was twenty-three and worked also as a waiter, and thus had a reputation for realism.

"Everything is parking," said Quaye. "That is how love is carried out in Accra."

For this, in fairness, was the history of the war. The Mensah taxis had begun parking, six years ago, in front of the pharmacy, and the pharmacy's queue of patients, aunties with prescriptions and boys with rashes, had begun to spread across the Mensah yard; and a notice had been affixed to the pharmacy door reading **NO TAXIS. THIS IS A PLACE OF HEALING**; and the Mensah gate had received, two days later, a reply in letters a yard tall: **AND THIS IS A PLACE OF GETTING THERE.** Since that morning the two had communicated exclusively through signs, and the signs had grown steadily in size, wit and venom, until the Ghana Standards Board, passing in a Land Cruiser, had reportedly slowed down to read.

It was against this background that, at nine minutes past six on the morning after the new moon, Kwame Mensah's phone began to play a hymn.

---

"*Chale,*" said Nii Tetteh.

He was Kwame's oldest friend, choir director of the Methodist church at Adabraka, a large devout man with the tender, theatrical face of a man who has led nine hundred Sundays of "Rock of Ages." He held the phone out at arm's length, for he had left his spectacles in the choir loft, and he read aloud in the full resonant baritone that he used for the Gospel and for football.

"*Entry six hundred and twenty-five. Accra, Ghana.* 'I paid your father's debt and let you think it was forgiven.'"

The yard went very still. A goat looked up. Under the mango tree, Akosua Tetteh, Kwame's mother, who was sixty, a brilliant cook and a hopeless remembrancer, put down the groundnut she was shelling and said, "Who has paid whose father's debt?"

"Mama," said Kwame.

"Is it a *pharmaceutical* debt?"

"Mama, it is nothing."

"It is the last line of a hymn," said Nii. "You wrote it, Kwame. Two years ago. I drove you to the post office in the rain. You said it was a *medical letter.*"

"I never said that."

"You said it was for your *back.*"

Kwame Mensah, who could discuss the carburettor of any engine ever manufactured, and who had once talked a police captain out of a bribe by asking after his mother, took the phone with a very steady hand, and read the thing that he had written. He had written it at a kitchen table, after a bad week, to a woman in England he had never met, because she had promised to tell no one. It was a sentence that had cost him eleven drafts.

He had not expected it to be read in his own yard, by a hundred strangers' eyes, at six in the morning, with a goat.

"And the next one," said Nii, who was a man of kind intentions and limited mercy, scrolling further. "Lord help us. *Entry nine hundred and forty-one. Accra, Ghana.*"

"Do not."

"'I know who paid it. I was waiting for you to say.'"

Now, there is a particular silence, in a place where thirty people have heard a thing, and the thirty are all attempting to appear deaf. It lasted perhaps four seconds. Then a voice from the mango tree, belonging to Ama Tetteh, eighty-two, retired welder, who had said nothing in the yard since Easter, remarked pleasantly:

"Well, *finally.*"

"Ma?"

"I told her six years ago, if she had eyes in her head she'd know." She shelled a groundnut. "A woman does not need a *letter* to know a taxi."

"Which taxi?" said Kwame hoarsely.

"The *one that paid,*" said Ama Tetteh, and cracked her nut.

---

At the other end of the lane, in a dispensary that smelled of menthol and clean linoleum and a faint, honest sweetness of cough syrup, Abena Owusu was reading the same two entries aloud to the same silence, and for the same reason: she had no choice.

For her friend Adwoa, who owned the kiosk beside the pharmacy and who kept everything in the world that happened within eighty yards of Palm Lane in a mental card-index, had arrived at five forty-five with her phone held aloft and her whole face lit like a church window, and had said, "You are *in* it. You are in the Register. And so is *he.*"

"Who?"

"You know *who.*"

"I do not know who," said Abena, with a pharmacist's frigid accuracy. "There are four hundred thousand people in the district. One of them is a vet who owes me eleven cedis."

"The yellow gate."

Abena had put down her pestle.

She was a small woman with a straight back and quick hands and a tongue that she kept, like the poisons cabinet, locked, labelled and open only to the properly qualified. She had run this shop for six years: ever since the spring when her father, Kojo Darko, a good, proud, hopeless man who had founded the dispensary and then remortgaged it twice on the promise of a cocoa scheme, had been told by the bank that it would be taking possession at the end of the month. She had been twenty-two. She had been counting the stock for the last time when a letter arrived, on the bank's thick white paper, to say that the debt had been *settled in full by a benefactor who wishes to remain unnamed.*

She had taken her mother's name, Owusu, over the door that very week, to see how it would look. Her father had died in June. He had been proud of her, and had told her it was nothing, in the last week of his life, in the manner of a man who finds the great things difficult to say and the small things easy. She had cried at the funeral for the shop, which was easier than crying for the man.

And she had known, in the way one knows a number before the bill arrives, who had paid.

"It is a *taxi* kind of generosity," she said now to Adwoa, who had become very quiet. "It does not leave a name. It leaves a smell of diesel and goodwill. The bank clerk said *a gentleman, tall, very polite, who laughed at his own car.* And then the landlady, Madam Naa, who said she'd had *a clerical error* with my rent, in my *favour,* for six years running. What clerical error is consistent? What clerical error pays on the first of every month, in cash, on a Tuesday?"

"A very *devoted* one," said Adwoa.

"It is a *theft,*" said Abena, her voice cracking. "It is the cruellest theft in Accra. He took from me the chance to *thank* him. I have been walking past that yellow gate for six years with a sentence in my mouth like a stone, and he is *sitting there,* and he *knows,* and I cannot say it because he never said it first."

"So say it."

"I am *waiting for him to say.*"

"Abena," said Adwoa, gently, "so is he."

---

By midday the whole Rank knew, because Quaye had put it on the radio.

It was not exactly the radio. Quaye had, in the roof of his taxi, a small loudspeaker for the announcement of fares, and he had found by experiment that any sentence addressed to it carried over eighty yards of tarmac with the clarity of a sermon. And since the Register of Black Stars had been published, he had been making use of it for the public good.

"*Attention, attention,*" said the roof of the taxi, to the lane, the cream building, the goat and the sky. "*This is your Rank. We read the Register. We have read the Register, and I can tell you the entry of Mr. Kwame is a very fine one. Wait. I will read both of them, since they are not far apart.*"

"Quaye, turn it off," said Kwame, from the yard.

"*It is for your benefit, my friend.*"

"Quaye."

"*'I paid your father's debt and let you think it was forgiven.' Good, good. That is Mr. Kwame, our employer, who is also a pharmacist of a kind, in the sense that he dispenses lifts. And the reply: 'I know who paid it. I was waiting for you to say.' That is Madam Abena, from the pharmacy. She is not here but she is perhaps listening. It is a thing I would not say if I were not an old man who has driven across Ghana nine times, and has learned that there is no eighty yards in the world like eighty yards of two proud people.*"

"*QUAYE!*"

"*I hope you will excuse the liberty.*"

Behind the green shutters, the pharmacy had gone entirely silent. Behind the yellow gate, forty-one taxis and a goat had done the same.

And then, from the northern end, there came out, quite slowly, into the white noon light, a small figure in a white coat, with a biscuit-tin held in both hands.

---

*The harmattan was early that year. A thin brown dust hung over Palm Lane, so that the sun was only a pale coin and the colours of the world were all faintly eaten. The Rank, to a man, had gone silent upon their bonnets. A woman in a white coat was walking down the middle of the lane, as if she had always done so.*

It was eighty yards, and it took her a minute, and in the course of the minute a number of things happened that nobody afterwards would be able to agree upon. Quaye maintained that he heard a clock. Yaw, the waiter, said that she smiled once, a small and terrible smile, at the goat. Adwoa, from the kiosk, said only that she saw a woman who had been very frightened for six years take a decision, as a woman takes a pill: briskly, with water, and without looking at what it was.

She stopped at the gate.

It swung open. Kwame Mensah stood there in a clean white shirt and an expression of the most profound dread, like a man who has been summoned to be thanked.

"Mr. Mensah," said Abena.

"Miss Owusu."

"I have something for you."

"I have nothing to say that—"

"I have *not* asked you to say anything." She held out the tin. It was a round blue tin, such as is used for Danish butter biscuits in every home from Aflao to Tamale, and it was held out to him with the stiff correctness of a woman presenting a summons. "This is yours."

"What is it?"

"It is the debt."

"There is no debt."

"There is a debt of forty-two thousand cedis to the Ghana Commercial Bank, settled in the spring of the year I was twenty-two, by a gentleman, tall, who laughed at his own car." She said it very fast, as one pulls a plaster. "And there is rent, paid in cash every first of the month for seventy-one months, by a clerical error. I have kept the figures. I have kept *every* figure. I have been putting aside for six years, in a tin, in the dispensary safe, behind the morphine. It is not all. I have not got interest. I do not know *what interest to charge on a kindness.* But it is the principal, and it is yours, and I should like you to take it, so that we may be *even.*"

There was a long, high, unbearable silence, with a goat in it.

"No," said Kwame.

"It is not a *request.*"

"No," said Kwame Mensah, and his voice, which was rich and easy and had never in its life been shaken, shook now, once, like a plank over a stream. "I did not want you to feel owed."

"I do not feel *owed,*" said Abena. "I feel *robbed.*"

"Robbed?"

"Of the chance to thank you! Of the whole occasion!" Her hands were trembling around the tin. "I would have done it so *well,* Kwame. I had a speech. I had it for months. It had a *beginning.* And you went and made it unnecessary, in your yellow gate, with your goat, and you said *nothing,* you let me think it was the bank, you let me think the world had been generous, and I walked around for six years being grateful to *nobody.* Do you know what that is? It is like swallowing a prayer with no God at the end."

For a moment he said nothing. Then, very quietly, and rather to his own surprise, in the language he had been taught at his mother's knee, Kwame said something in Twi that the Rank had no business hearing, and which will not be set down here. It was brief. It was a proverb, about water, and the person who carries it to the thirsty without being asked.

She replied, in the same tongue, with another.

It was shorter.

Quaye, who understood both, took off his cap.

"So," said Abena, in English, recovering herself with an effort that the entire lane could hear, "will you take it?"

"No."

"Then I will leave it."

"Where?"

She looked about her with sudden decision, and set the tin, with a small dry click, upon the bonnet of the nearest cab, which was a very old green Corolla known to the Rank as *Auntie Beatrice,* and then folded her arms and said, to nobody, with sublime scrupulousness: "You may count it."

"I will not count it."

"Then you may *not count it,* but I have left it."

"And I will not open it."

"Then it will sit."

"Then it will *sit,*" said Kwame, "on Auntie Beatrice, in the sun, for ever."

"So be it," said Abena.

They stood a yard apart, in the white dust, with the tin between them like a small round moon. And it seemed to every driver watching that this was a quarrel of such perfect and symmetrical courtesy that it could not be settled by any further word; that it would simply be carried over, like a debt, to the next day and the day after, a perfectly balanced sorrow, in which each held the other's gift and refused it, and each was glad.

"The generator on your roof," said Abena abruptly, looking away. "It is too loud. It disturbs my patients."

"The queue outside your door," said Kwame, "disturbs my *taxis.*"

"Then it is war."

"It is a great pity."

"It is *thoroughly* a pity," said Abena, and turned, with her back straight and her coat flapping and her whole slim body radiating dignity, and walked the eighty yards home.

She did not look back. A pharmacist does not.

But at the green shutters, she paused, with her hand upon the door, and a long, shy, secret curl came into the corner of her mouth, which Adwoa, from the kiosk, would swear to on any Bible you cared to name.

---

*And here the Rank, who had held its breath through the whole of it, let it out together, and since a Chorus must say something, said it in the only measure it knew, which is the rhythm of a taxi on a bad road:*

> *Eighty yards of tar, and neither one would take it;
> A tin upon a bonnet, and neither one would break it.
> She said, I owe thee. He said, Thou owest not.
> The sun went down on two proud hearts, both caught.
> Oh, who will count the cedis? None of us, we think.
> The debt is made of kindness, and kindness has no ink.*

"That is not bad," said Quaye, wiping his eyes. "Who wrote it?"

"You did," said Yaw, "just now."

"Then I am a poet, and I demand a rise."

---

That night, when the Rank had gone home and the dust had settled and the lane was as dark as a good conscience, Kwame Mensah went out to the green Corolla alone, and took the tin from the bonnet, and carried it to his office, and sat before it for a very long time.

He did not count the money.

He had promised.

But he turned the tin over once, as a man turns a stone, and under the lid, in neat violet pharmacist's ink, on a white sticky label of the kind that she used for the dosage on every bottle in her shop, was a line in her small straight hand:

**TAKE AS DIRECTED. MAY CAUSE DROWSINESS, DIZZINESS AND UNEXPECTED FEELINGS. DO NOT OPERATE HEAVY MACHINERY UNTIL YOU HAVE CALLED.**

And, beneath that, smaller, as if she had changed her mind and been too stubborn to cross it out:

*(Eighty yards. I counted.)*

Kwame Mensah, who had never been seen to cry, sat in the harmattan dark with a biscuit-tin on his knee, and laughed like a man released from a long sentence, till the goat in the yard woke and complained.

---

*Margin note, in pencil, S.W.R.:*

> *Entry 0625 and Entry 0941. Between them eighty yards of Accra, a tin, and six years of arithmetic. They think they are settling accounts. They are doing the opposite. A debt, rightly held, is the surest bond that two people can share: it is a thing each has promised the other never to forget.*
>
> *I once lent a man a book. I never asked for it back. Reader, I am still waiting for the return.*

---

*End of Chapter 3.*


---

## Chapter 4
### The Critic Who Would Not Taste

> *"I cook one bowl each night for the woman who never returned."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0510

---

The people of Osaka are said to eat until they fall down. The expression is *kuidaore*, and the city is proud of it, as other cities are proud of their cathedrals.

On the night of the new moon, in the narrow alley behind the Tenma canal where the lanterns hang so close together that they gossip, there was a shop with eight stools, one counter, a curtain the colour of old tea, and a single man. The curtain bore, in letters faded by many winters, the words **TANABE-YA**. The man bore a white towel about his head, a pair of forearms scarred with small honest burns, and a silence so complete that his regulars had been known to lose money betting on it.

"Seven words," said Daichi Ito, setting his phone upon the counter. "My calculation. Since opening at six. *Irasshai. Hai. Mō ippai? Arigatō.* That is four. And a *nn*, which I count as a half, and a cough, which I do not."

"Cough counts," said Rin Hayashi, from the third stool.

"A cough is not a *word.*"

"It is when *he* does it."

Daichi, thirty-four, a historian from Kobe who was said to be writing a history of the noodle and was believed by his friends to have been writing it since the Meiji era, folded his hands. He was a superstitious man. He would not sit at a table of four, nor whistle at night, nor begin a chapter on a Friday, and for the past fourteen months he had also declined, with a small shudder, to look at stool number eight.

For stool number eight was empty. It was always empty. Though the shop was full, though salarymen stood in the alley in the November chill with their collars up and their breath standing before them, stool eight stayed bare, and at the end of the counter, in front of it, a place was laid: lacquered chopsticks upon a rest, a glass of water, and a small blue towel, folded in thirds.

At eleven-forty, Hiroshi Tanabe would make one bowl.

He made it exactly as he made all the others: the clear brown broth, fourteen hours in the pot, kombu and pork bone and dried bonito and a hundred small secrets; the noodles, thin and straight and springy, lowered into the water for exactly the time that it takes to say a short prayer; the pale slice of pork, the half-egg gone soft as a thought, the green onion cut so fine that it looked like a rumour. He set it upon the counter before the empty stool. He stood back, and bowed to the air.

And for twenty minutes, while the room went quiet, the bowl sat, and steamed, and cooled.

"It is a *ghost,*" whispered Daichi. "I have told you. It is a ghost, and it eats."

"It does not eat," said Rin. "I have watched."

"That is *because* it is a ghost."

"Daichi. The man gives it a bowl. At midnight he pours it into the sink."

"Into the *sink?*"

"And then he washes the bowl, by hand, and dries it, and puts it on the shelf with the others, and does not use it again." Rin looked at the broad, silent back at the stove. "Four hundred and twenty-six nights."

"He is counting?"

"He is a man who has counted since he was a boy. I think he counts the way other men pray."

At the stove, without turning round, Hiroshi lifted one finger from the ladle, lightly, as a conductor does. It meant: *you are speaking of what is mine.*

Daichi shrank. Rin laughed. In the corner a very old woman in a quilted jacket, who had been shelling pickles for an hour into a steel bowl, said briskly, in the high dry voice of Kyoto, "*Honma, you boys are noisy. My son hears everything. He has been hearing everything since he was four years old. He just does not say.*"

"Obā-san," said Rin, with deep respect. "You know the story?"

Nanami Shimizu, seventy, retired welder, gossip, and Hiroshi's mother, placed a pickle in her mouth, looked at the ceiling, and said, with a profound air of withholding:

"I know *some* of it."

---

Across the canal, five floors up, in an apartment of white walls and exactly three plants, a woman sat in the dark with her phone, and did not weep. She had learned not to. Weeping, since the illness, had a flavour of nothing, which is the worst flavour of all.

Her name was Mei Sato. She was thirty-three, and for six years she had been the most feared and most loved restaurant critic in Osaka: author of the Sunday column *A Hundred Bowls,* in the *Naniwa Shimbun,* wherein she had once reduced a three-star kaiseki master to tears with the single sentence *"The soup is afraid of its own salt."* People said that Mei Sato could taste the sorrow in a sauce. They said she could name the hand that held the ladle. They said, in the tone of men who fear for their trade, that if you wished to be remembered, you should be eaten by Mei Sato.

Fourteen months ago she had had a fever, a common one, of the sort that arrives on a Tuesday and is forgotten by Friday. On Saturday she had sat down before a bowl of her favourite *tamagoyaki,* and had tasted nothing.

Not weak. *Nothing.* A warm softness, as of wet cloth. Salt, a ghost of salt, there and then not. She had put down her chopsticks and had looked at the egg, which was yellow, and glistening, and perfectly made, and had understood that she was standing at the edge of a country from which she would not be permitted to return.

"I'm *telling* you," said Nanami Yamamoto, from the sofa, with the severity of a woman who works the Tempozan ferry in all weathers and does not take back a word. "You are going to the doctor."

"I have been to six doctors."

"Go to a seventh."

"They say it is the nerve. They say it may return. They say it may not." Mei's voice was flat. "They say, *Miss Sato, you are very lucky; you can still smell lemon.* I can smell lemon, Nanami. I cannot taste a lemon. A lemon is a shape and a cold."

"So what do you do? With the *column?*"

There it was. The question that her friend had waited fourteen months to ask, and had asked only on the night when the whole country was reading its own heart in a stranger's ledger.

Mei said nothing for a long while.

"I write from memory," she said at last. "Every Sunday, I go to a shop. I sit. I order. I watch the faces of the people eating. I hear the sound the noodles make, I feel the heat, I watch the way a man closes his eyes when the broth goes down. And I write what I *remember* it would taste like, if it were good. Or bad." She put down the phone. "I have been right, Nanami. Mostly I have been right. That is the shame of it. I am a counterfeit whose forgeries are better than the originals."

"Your editor knows?"

"Mr. Kato suspects. He has begun sending me to places that cannot lie. Tofu shops. Plain noodles." She smiled. It was a dreadful smile. "And Sakura at the news-stand, who thinks she can do my job better than I, has begun to read my column aloud with a very peculiar voice."

"Sakura Takahashi is a *snake.*"

"She is a newsagent. It is the same thing, with more weather."

Nanami laughed, in spite of herself. Then she took the phone from the table, thumbed it alight, and without speaking held the screen out, as a nurse holds out a cup.

*ENTRY 0510 — Osaka, Japan.*
*"I cook one bowl each night for the woman who never returned."*

Mei looked at it.

She looked at it for a time that was a good deal longer than it takes to read eleven words.

*Entry 0810 — Osaka, Japan. "I can no longer taste a thing, and I am ashamed."* That one was hers; she had written it three nights after the fever, to a woman in England who would never tell. It stood two columns to the right. They did not touch. They did not need to.

"You know him," said Nanami.

"I have not seen him in fourteen months."

"But you know who he is."

"He is the best cook in Osaka," said Mei Sato, in a voice she did not recognise as her own. "He was my Thursday for two years. Seat eight. He never asked me what I thought. He did not need to. I would eat, and I would put down my chopsticks, and he would look at the bowl, and I would nod, and that was the whole of the review. And then the fever came. And I could not go back to the one man who would know, in a *glance,* that the nod was a lie."

"So you did not go."

"So I did not go."

"For fourteen months."

"I am a very *disciplined* coward," said Mei.

She rose and went to the window. Below, in the long black ribbon of the canal, the lights of the city lay broken and trembling. A boat went by, with a small red lantern at its prow, and a man singing.

It was then, as she stood against the glass, that she spoke, not to Nanami, and not to the night, but to the thing in between that is called the heart's ear, and she did not do so in prose:

> *They say the tongue remembers what it loved.
> They lie. The tongue forgets. It is the mind
> That holds the sweetness, and the mind grows thin.
> I have a hundred bowls inside my head,
> And every one is cold. I taste them still
> The way a blind man tastes the sun: by heat,
> By the soft weight of light upon the skin.
> He cooked for me four hundred nights and six,
> And I was not there to be disappointed.
> Oh, cruel kindness, to forgive so hard
> A woman who has nothing left to judge!
> I will go down. I will not eat. I will sit
> And let him see me not taste, and be shamed,
> And then at last be free.*

"That," said Nanami Yamamoto, wiping her eyes, "was extremely *bad* for a woman with no sense of taste."

"I had a metaphor."

"You had a *sword.* Go. Go before you think of a better one."

---

It is a fact little known to those who have not suffered it that the world, when stripped of flavour, grows louder.

Mei Sato walked the six minutes to the alley and was astonished by it. She could not smell the sweet-sour breath of the *takoyaki* stall, with its octopus and its bonito flakes dancing in the steam. She could not smell the grilled eel, nor the fried batter, nor the sea-reek of the canal. But she could *hear* it all: the clack of a tin spatula; the hiss of oil; the laughter, the high laughter, of three girls in rain-capes; a vendor calling "*Atsui, atsui!*" in the cracked tenor of a man who has sold hot things for forty years. She could *see* it. She could feel the warmth of every shop-front as she passed, on one cheek and then the other, like a series of small hands.

She came to the curtain at eleven-thirty-eight.

She did not go in. She stood at the gap between the cloth and the post, and looked.

He was there. Of course he was there. He was in the white towel, with his back to the room and his hands upon the pot, a heavy, still, unhurried man, and she saw the shoulders that she had watched for two years, and a thing happened inside her that she had not been prepared for; a feeling like homesickness for a house she was standing in front of.

The regulars were silent. The old woman at the end had stopped shelling pickles. The historian, with the wide eyes of a man who has seen the dead, was holding his phone aloft as though to capture a miracle.

And then, at the exact stroke of eleven-forty, Hiroshi Tanabe lowered noodles into the water.

She watched him make it. She had always wished to watch him make it, and had never done so, for a critic does not stare at the cook; it is a breach of the contract. But now she was no critic. She was a woman in a doorway. She saw him lift the noodles with the long chopsticks in one smooth turn of the wrist and shake them, twice, with a motion like a bell-ringer's. She saw the broth go in, the colour of dark amber. She saw the egg laid down, the onion scattered, the pale pork fanned like a hand of cards.

She saw him set the bowl before the empty stool, and stand, and bow.

And then she did the one thing she had not told Nanami she would do.

She pushed aside the curtain.

---

There is a particular noise, in a small room full of people, when a sound that has been expected for fourteen months finally arrives. It is not a gasp. It is much quieter than that. It is the sound of eight strangers deciding, simultaneously, to hold their breath.

"*Irasshai,*" said Hiroshi Tanabe.

He had not turned. He had known her footstep, as he might have known the footstep of weather.

"I am sorry," said Mei. "I am late."

He said nothing. His mother, at the far end, said "*Ara,*" very softly, and put down a pickle.

Mei crossed the floor. It was a short floor, four steps, and she took each of them as one crosses ice. She sat on stool number eight. It was warm. It was warmer than the room. And it took her a moment to understand why, and when she did, she nearly stood up again: it was *kept* warm. He had placed upon it, earlier that evening, a small heated cushion, such as the old use in winter, and had plugged it in at the wall, and had done so for four hundred and twenty-six nights.

She put her hands in her lap.

"It is still hot," said Hiroshi.

It was the first thing he had said, in her hearing, in three years that was not *irasshai* or *arigatō.* His voice was low, and very slow, like a bell struck in a distant temple. "It has been on the counter two minutes. The broth holds."

"Hiroshi-san," said Mei.

"Eat."

"I *cannot.*"

She had meant to say it better. She had meant to say it with the whole of her critic's armoury of syntax and irony. What came instead was five words, flat on the counter like a dropped plate, and she heard them, and did not take them back.

"I cannot taste," said Mei Sato. "Since last September. A fever. It has not come back. I am a woman who writes about food and cannot taste it, and I am so ashamed that I have not been able to walk down your street." Her eyes were stinging, which she found, in an odd detached way, to be very interesting. "I wrote a column every Sunday from *memory.* I am a fraud. I do not deserve a bowl. I do not deserve a *stool.* You should pour it down the sink."

She waited for the blow.

In the shop, you could have heard a noodle fall.

"I know," said Hiroshi.

"You—?"

"Your column." He wiped his hands upon the towel, slowly, one finger at a time. "Eleven weeks ago. The shop at Namba. You wrote that the broth was *a clear autumn pond.* Their broth is thick. It is a pig's bath. A person who had *tasted* it would not say *pond.*" He paused. "You do not make mistakes by being wrong. You make them by being *beautiful.* I knew."

"And you cooked for me *anyway?*"

"I did not cook for the critic," said Hiroshi Tanabe. "I cooked for the woman who ate my noodles with her eyes closed."

He set down the chopsticks on their rest. Then, because he was a man for whom great events could only be expressed in small adjustments, he turned the bowl, a quarter-turn, so that the handle of the spoon lay toward her right hand.

"Eat," he said. "Not to taste. To be *fed.*"

---

The old woman at the end of the counter had her hand upon her mouth. The historian had lowered the phone. Rin Hayashi, who had been a lifeguard for eight years and had pulled four swimmers from the Osaka surf, now found himself with a lump in the throat, and addressed it to the ceiling.

Mei took up the chopsticks. They were light, and made of some pale wood, and they were warm from his hand.

She lifted the noodles. She was astonished to find that she knew them; that her whole arm remembered the weight, the long smooth resistance, the little spring of them against the lips. They went into her mouth, and she tasted nothing, a hot softness, an oil, a coolness of onion that was only cold. She drank the broth. It was heat, and the memory of heat, and a faint richness upon the lip.

She closed her eyes.

She was a critic. She had been trained for a decade to name what she ate. And so she sat in the dark of her own eyelids, with the steam against her chin, and listened to a room full of people not speaking, and attempted for the first time in fourteen months to say not what was *in* the bowl, but what the bowl was *for.*

"It is warm," said Mei.

"Yes."

"It is the warmest thing I have been given in a year."

He did not answer. She heard the faint scrape of a ladle. When she opened her eyes, he was standing over her with the pot, and was, with a gentle, almost shy movement, filling the bowl again to the brim, as a man tops up the lamp of a vigil he has kept too long.

"Kaedama," said Hiroshi. "Second noodles. Free."

"Hiroshi."

"I have been told," said the cook, "I am too quiet."

He bowed. It was the smallest bow she had ever seen, no more than a lowering of the eyes, but the whole shop saw it, and the old woman at the end rose, and so did Rin, and so did the salarymen from the alley in their damp coats, and the girls in rain-capes, and Daichi Ito, historian, who had begun to cry, and who had to be given a pickle.

Behind them all, from the corner, a high excited voice said, quite clearly: "*It worked! Look! Look at the picture! The ghost bowl! Eight thousand likes!*"

This was Daichi's young cousin, aged sixteen, who had been sitting very still beside the pickle-jar for an hour with her phone held steady, and who had, in the confusion of the great moment, taken an excellent photograph of an empty stool, a perfect bowl, and, in the foreground, out of focus and unmistakable, the back of a woman's head.

Nobody had heard her. Nobody ever does, at the beginning.

"Hush," said Hiroshi's mother, taking the phone away and putting it among the pickles. "Let her eat."

---

*Margin note, in pencil, S.W.R.:*

> *Entry 0510 cooked four hundred and twenty-six bowls for a woman who could not taste them. Entry 0810 hid for fourteen months from a man who would not have minded. Reader, I have known critics, and I have known cooks. The former tell you what is wrong with the world; the latter feed it.*
>
> *She thinks that she has lost the thing she was. She has only mislaid the part that could be fooled.*
>
> *(And somebody, I note, has taken a photograph. Never trust the cousins.)*

---

*End of Chapter 4.*


---

## Chapter 5
### The Pianist's Silence

> *"I wrote a waltz for you and never asked you to dance."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0234

---

In St Petersburg the first snow does not fall. It is *issued,* like an order, from a sky the colour of an old spoon, and the whole city, which has been waiting for it with the stoicism of a very long marriage, pulls up its collar and carries on.

It was issued that Thursday at four in the afternoon, upon the Fontanka, upon the bronze horses, upon the green roof of the Nevsky Chamber Theatre, which on this night, of all nights in its hundred and twenty years, was giving a gala.

"A *gala,*" said Sergei Orlov, with the reverent contempt of one who has to sew it. "Eleven hundred sequins on the soprano alone. She has asked for a train. I said, Madam, there is no room on the stage for a train; she said, then we shall move the stage."

"And have you?" said Dmitri Volkov, from the piano.

"I have moved the *soprano.*"

The theatre at that hour was a cavern of dust and half-light, full of ladders and the smell of size and varnish and hot lamps. In the pit, at a black Bechstein with a cracked lid and a candle-stub on the music-desk (against all regulations, and by common consent of the fire-marshal, who was a patron), sat the pianist, in the stiff dark jacket he had worn to every rehearsal for sixteen years, and he was running through the programme, which he had printed on a single sheet and pinned to the wall like a bill of indictment.

He was forty. He had a long grave face with a good deal of forehead in it, a pair of hands that looked as though they had been borrowed from a much taller man, and a manner of courtesy so rigid that it could have been used for scaffolding. He rose when women entered rooms. He apologised to doors. He had accompanied, in his time, four hundred performances of the repertory and one funeral, and had never once been heard to say what he thought of any of them.

"Number nine," said Sergei, reading the sheet over his shoulder, for he read everything over everybody's shoulder; it was a vice, and a devout one, for he said that God had given him two eyes so that one might guard the other. "*Waltz.* Composer: *Anonymous.* Dmitri Andreyevich, you cannot do this. A gala is for the *famous* dead. Nobody will know whose it is."

"That is the idea."

"It is a very strange idea."

"It is a very *short* waltz," said Dmitri, "and I should like it to be heard without being explained."

"And who is the dedicatee?"

"There is no dedicatee."

"I did not say *dedicatee,*" said Sergei Orlov, who was fifty-seven, a dressmaker, a deacon's cousin and a man of subtle instruments. "I said *who is it for?* A tune like that is never for *no one.* I have heard you at night, Dmitri. Every night when the house is dark you play it, twenty-four bars, very soft, as if you were arguing with a ghost. The whole fourth floor knows it. The boy who sweeps the stairs whistles it."

"Sergei."

"The ballet mistress hums it."

"*Sergei.*"

"Madam Petrova's students have been heard to *dance* to it," said Sergei, and then, with the instinct of a good tailor who knows exactly when to put down the shears, stopped.

Dmitri did not turn his head. He did not stiffen. He did not do any of the things that a man does when a nerve has been touched, because for sixteen years he had practised not doing them. He merely placed one hand flat on the closed lid of the Bechstein, as one steadies a horse, and said in his most perfectly courteous voice:

"The snow will be heavy by seven. I should like the stage-door lamp to be lit."

"It will be lit."

"Thank you."

"It is no trouble," said Sergei. And, thoughtfully, after a long moment, to the empty house: "It is *all* trouble."

---

Above the theatre, on the fourth floor, in a studio with a bare wooden floor and a long barre and a window from which one may see, on a clear night, the whole slow shining curve of the river, a woman of thirty-eight stood with her hand on a child's back.

"*Longer,*" said Anya Petrova. "The neck is a swan, not a *goose.* Yuri, are you listening? You are standing like a man waiting for a bus."

"I'm waiting for you to say stop, Anna Sergeyevna."

"I shall say stop when you have *earned* it."

The boy was twelve, thin as a blade of grass, with a cough he had had since October and a determination to conceal it that touched her more than she would allow. His name was Yuri Orlov. He was the best pupil in the school and the worst liar, and she did not mention the cough. She had her reasons. She was a woman who had been told by doctors, when she was thirty-two, that a knee is a hinge and a dancer's knee a hinge made of glass, and she had learned in the long winter afterward which truths to press and which to leave, like a sheet, folded.

She had been, for ten years, the first dancer of the Nevsky. They had written about her in four languages. They had compared her to a candle, to a bird, to a thing seen once in a childhood dream; and then one night in the second act of a ballet she had danced two hundred times, the left knee had gone out beneath her, quietly, like a lamp in the next room, and she had finished the act on one leg and sat down in the wings, and had not stood on a stage since.

That was six years ago.

She walked now with the slightest hitch, a faint hesitation upon the left foot as it landed, so small that strangers took it for a mannerism and friends for a courage. She had a bad temper, a good sister, and a flat above a theatre in which every night, after the last curtain, a man sat down at a piano in the dark and played twenty-four bars of waltz.

"It is a very *beautiful* waltz," said the boy shyly, and the sentence went through her like a fork.

"What waltz?"

"The one he plays. Upstairs. Downstairs. I do not know where. I hear it through the floor." He coloured. "Seryozha says it is yours."

"Seryozha is a *rumour* in a cardigan."

"But is it?"

"Plié," said Anya Petrova. "*Now.*"

---

She had known it, of course, from the first night.

She had known it as a woman knows her own footfall upon an empty stair. It had come up through the old planks of the studio, one night in the first winter after her fall, a small clear waltz in three-quarter time, very simple, very sad; twenty-four bars, and then silence; and then the same twenty-four again. At first she had thought it a student's piece. By the third night she had stopped doing her exercises and sat upon the floor with her back against the barre, in her stockinged feet, with her good leg tucked under her and the bad one stretched out, and counted.

In the seventh bar, upon the third beat, there was a rest. A small one. An eighth-note's silence, no more; a hitch, like a breath caught on a stair.

She had *limped* there.

Not on the stage, where she had never limped; in the corridor. In the back stair. She had gone up and down it every evening for six years, and somebody, lying in the dark beneath her, had listened, and had put it in the music.

She had told no one. Not Natalia, her sister, who kept an inn on Kronstadt and cried at weddings. Not Oleg Popov, the policeman, her oldest friend, a thin wry man who had stood guard over her pride for twenty years and had never once been asked to. She had gone on listening. She had gone on being too proud to knock on the door of a man who was too proud to knock on hers.

And on Monday of that week, a niece of Sergei's had put a telephone in her hands and said, "Anna Sergeyevna, you must look; it is the *Register*—" and she had looked.

*Entry 0234 — St Petersburg, Russia. "I wrote a waltz for you and never asked you to dance."*

And there, in the same column, on the other side of the night:

*Entry 0017 — St Petersburg, Russia. "I heard the waltz and knew it was mine."*

She had written that one herself. She had sat up on a winter night six months before, and had written it, and had posted it to an address on the English coast; and had never, until that Monday, understood that somewhere in the same city, on the same night, a man had been writing the other half of her sentence.

"You are not going," said her sister on the telephone, in the voice of an innkeeper who has lost a patience contest.

"I am not."

"They have sent you the card. *Madam Petrova is invited as guest of honour.* Anechka, you have refused six times. You are a woman of principle."

"I am a woman with a *knee.*"

"Then sit down in a box."

"I will not be looked at, Natasha. I will not be *observed* by eleven hundred people to see if I weep."

"Then do not be *in* the box." Natalia Lebedev, thirty-five, innkeeper, sister, had a quick brutal mind that she hid inside a soft round face. "Go to the wings. Go where you used to stand. Stand in the dark behind the black cloth, where nobody can see you and you can hear every note. And if you do not like it, you can go home. And if you do—" She stopped.

"If I do?"

"Then you shall have heard it," said Natalia, "without having to decide anything."

It was, Anya thought afterward, the wisest thing that had been said to her in six years, and she hated it with a fervour she kept for what was true.

---

By half past seven the Nevsky was full.

It was full to the roof: a sea of black and gold, of furs steaming in the warmth, of jewelled throats and old men with medals, and in the pit the musicians were tuning like birds in a dispute. Dr. Oleg Morozov, the chairman of the board, who was also, by one of those arrangements that history makes when it is bored, the theatre's dentist, rose upon the stage to deliver his speech. He had a toothache. He had had it for three days. Every sentence, therefore, came out with a certain compressed fury, like a man reading the Gospel through a hot coal.

"*Ladies and gentlemen!* One hundred and twenty years! A *great* theatre! A theatre of tradition! Of *courage!* Of—" he put a hand to his jaw "—*molars.*"

A rustle went through the house.

"Of *moral* fibre," said Dr. Morozov, recovering, and sat down, and was seen, in the dark, to be offered a clove by the soprano.

The gala went on.
