A tenor sang, and a girl of sixteen played Prokofiev with her whole face; a mezzo wept in an aria and was forgiven; a chorus of fifty old men from the Naval Choir sang a song about a river, and no one in the house, not the Chairman, nor the Minister's wife, nor the deaf man in the tenth row, was dry-eyed at the end. And in the wings, in a corner so black that the stage-hands had learned never to look at it, a woman in a plain grey dress, with one hand upon the cold brick wall and the other gripping her own wrist, stood and waited.

She had not been seen. Sergei, who saw everything, had seen it, and had put his thumb to his lips, and gone to hide in a basket of wigs.

At twenty to ten, the stage emptied. The lights fell to a single warm pool at the centre. And out of the dark at the left walked a man in a stiff jacket, with his long hands at his sides, who crossed to a piano, and bowed to the house with the rigid exactness of a mourner at a public funeral, and sat.

The programme said: *9. Waltz. Anonymous.*

Eleven hundred people coughed, rustled and settled. A woman in the third row said, in a whisper that carried: "Who is *he?*"

"The pianist," said her husband.

"But who is the *composer?*"

"Anonymous."

"I never heard of him."

"Nobody has," said the husband, with an air of finality, and was, for once in his marriage, entirely correct.

Dmitri Volkov raised his hands.

He did not look at the house. He looked, as he always did before the first note, at nothing, at a point a little above the music-desk, where, a pianist will tell you, the first note is waiting. And in the wings, in the dark, with her hand upon the wall, Anya Petrova heard him breathe in.

And the waltz began.

---

How shall the page say it? Music is the one confession that cannot be forged and cannot be translated. Let it be told, therefore, as the thing was done: plainly, and in three-quarter time.

It began in the left hand: a low, quiet, rocking figure, *one*, two, three, *one*, two, three, like a child being walked to sleep by a mother who is herself too tired to sleep. Over it, the right hand laid down a melody, small and clear, that went up a little way and came down again, as one goes up the stair of a house one has loved. It was not a grand waltz. It was not made for ballrooms. It was a waltz for a corridor: for a lamp at the end of a passage, and a person walking toward it who did not yet know that she was being watched.

And in the seventh bar, upon the third beat, the pianist let go his breath, and the music stopped.

One eighth-note. Barely more.

It was not a hesitation. It was an *attention.* It was the sound of a man standing at the foot of a stair, listening to a footstep that he has loved so long he knows each place where it falters, and *waiting for it,* as one waits for a friend who is always slightly late; holding the whole bar open like a door.

Then the melody went on.

In the wings, Anya Petrova made a sound.

It was not a sob. She would have been the first to say that she was not a woman who sobbed. It was a short, sharp, dry intake of breath, as of someone dipping their hand in cold water, and she pressed the heel of her hand against her mouth, and stood perfectly still; and the whole of her face, which had been for six years a face she held, was for the first time unguarded in the dark.

> *So that is how it sounds, to be forgiven.
> The thing I limped upon, and hid, and cursed,
> He took and made a rest in. I had thought
> The hinge was broken. He has made it music.
> Oh, you have listened to me going home,
> Alone, up all those stairs, and said not one
> Word of it, not one word, in six long years,
> But set it in the middle of a waltz
> Where all the city hears and no one knows.
> I should be angry. I am proud, I know it;
> I am a woman with a temper, and a knee.
> I should go out and strike him for his courage.
> I cannot move. I cannot, for I am
> Dancing. Here, in the dark, against the wall,
> My foot is keeping time.*

It was true. She had not noticed. Under the long grey skirt, upon the bare boards of the wings, her left foot, her bad foot, had begun to move: a little, a very little, a small and obedient step, *one*, two, three, *one*, two, three: and upon the third beat of the seventh bar it paused, like a breath, and took the music up again.

The waltz ended as it had begun: quietly, with the left hand last, a single low chord that hung in the air like a held coat.

There was silence.

Eleven hundred people sat in it. They did not know why. A man in the front row, a retired admiral with a chestful of ribbons, was found afterward to have taken off his glasses and to be unable to find them. A woman in a green dress said, loudly, "*Well!*" and was hushed. And then somebody began to clap, a single pair of hands, high in the gods, and then the house.

Dmitri Volkov rose. He bowed, rigidly, to the dark. He did not look into the wings, because he did not know that anyone was in them. He turned, with his formal and perfect exactness, and walked off the opposite side, and the lights went up on an elderly baritone, who looked at the pianist's departing back with the deep and venomous envy of a man who has been following an act he cannot follow.

By the time the pianist had reached the stage-door, and stood there in the cold, with the snow on his shoulders and his long hands trembling, and the whole of the river dark beyond the lamp, the gala was nearly over; and the woman in the wings had gone.

---

"Dmitri Andreyevich," said a voice at his elbow.

It was the voice of a man who has been doing something he is ashamed of for some time and now wishes to be congratulated upon it. Sergei Orlov, in his shirt-sleeves and with a wig on his arm, was standing at the foot of the iron stair, holding a small cream envelope.

"This," said Sergei, "has been left for you."

"By whom?"

"By *nobody.*" He cleared his throat. "Under the stage-door lamp. In the snow. By a person with a slight hesitation on the left foot, who did not wait. And I should tell you, as an honest Christian, that I have read it, because it was folded, and an unfolded letter is an invitation, and I am a man of weak will."

"Sergei."

"I have *read it.* It is four lines. I want you to know, Dmitri Andreyevich, that I wept like a calf."

Dmitri took the envelope. His hands were not steady, and he disliked the fact, and looked at it. Then, with the tact of a man who had, for forty years, been apologising to doors, he drew out a single sheet, white as the snow, and unfolded it beneath the lamp.

There were four lines. They were written in a quick, proud, upright hand, with a pen pressed hard.

*Seventh bar. Third beat. I limp there.*
*How long have you been listening?*
*Six years is a very long time to hold a door.*
*— A.P.*

He read it.

He read it again.

The snow fell, issued by the sky, upon the bronze horses and the green roof and the long black river. A tram went by, in a rattle of yellow light. On the fourth floor, in the window of a studio above the theatre, a lamp, which had not been lit in half an hour, came on.

"Well?" said Sergei Orlov, in a hushed and sacred voice, with the wig clutched to his bosom like a lamb. "What will you do?"

And Dmitri Volkov, who had played four hundred performances and one funeral, and who had never once been heard to say what he thought, folded the letter very carefully along its crease, put it in the inner pocket of his jacket, over his heart, and said, with an expression that no one in the whole Nevsky Chamber Theatre had seen on his face in sixteen years:

"I think I shall need to go upstairs."

"*Now?*"

"It is only four flights."

"It is *six years,*" said Sergei. "But go. Go, go. Take the lamp."

---

*Margin note, in pencil, S.W.R.:*

> *Entry 0234 wrote a waltz for a woman he never asked to dance. Entry 0017 heard it through a floor for six years. Neither has knocked. Both, I observe, have lived in the same building the whole while.*
>
> *Reader, a man may stand at the foot of a stair for half his life, and call it patience. It is not patience. It is only that he has not yet been given the first step.*
>
> *(Four flights. I was a cautious woman, too. It is a long way to go for a thing that is only up.)*

---

*End of Chapter 5.*


---

## Chapter 6
### Walls of Color

> *"Your face is on a hundred walls and you do not know."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0299

---

The week after the dead have been fed, Mexico City smells of marigolds.

They are everywhere: heaped in the Jamaica market in orange mountains, crushed in the gutters of the Roma, caught in the grilles of tram-stops and the hair of small girls, and long after the last candle has guttered on the last altar, their bitter gold perfume goes on hanging in the thin high air, as if the city were not yet quite sure that the visitors had gone home.

It was in this week, upon a scaffold of rusted pipe on the Calle Zacatecas, at ten minutes before dawn, that a young man named Rafael Ortega stood with a bucket of cobalt blue in his left hand, a radio blasting a ranchera into the whole sleeping neighbourhood, and the end of a very large nose upon his right.

It was the nose of a woman. It was thirty feet high. It was one of a hundred and three.

"She has the *worst* nose," said Marisol García, holding the ladder, from the street. "It's too long, Rafa. She looks like a heron who has read a lot."

"It is the nose of a *lawyer.* A woman who reads like that is going to be a lawyer or a saint. She had a book as thick as a loaf. She was frowning at it as though it had insulted her mother." He leaned back, with one foot on a plank and the other on empty air. "And she was *right.* Whatever the book had said."

"You saw her once, at the Parque México, in the rain, two Novembers ago. And once in a dream."

"The dream," said Rafael, "was more *detailed.*"

He was twenty-six, loud, broad in the shoulder and long in the leg, with a mop of black hair stiff with a decade of paint and a pair of eyes in which every emotion arrived at once and nobody was ever in charge. He painted as other men argue: with his whole body, at the top of his lungs. In two years he had covered, without a permit, without a sponsor, and without, as far as anyone could tell, any plan, a hundred and three walls of the capital with a single face.

It was always the same. A young woman on a bench, reading. Her hair fell forward over one shoulder; her mouth was set in a line of ferocious concentration; her head was bowed, and her eyes, upon every one of the hundred and three, were *closed.* The critics called it *La Lectora.* The children called it *La Señorita Que No Se Cansa.* The city, which will make a saint of anyone who stays in one place long enough, had begun to leave small offerings at the foot of her bigger walls: a marigold; a pencil; once, on the Calle Chihuahua, a copy of the Civil Code.

"And why," said Marisol, who was forty-five, and a painter, and had known him since he was a boy with chalk on his knees, "are the *eyes* shut?"

Rafael did not answer for a moment. A truck went past. On the radio, a man sang of a girl who had broken his heart in Guadalajara.

"Because I do not know," he said at last, "what colour they are."

---

At the end of the block, in the thin first light, there was a policeman.

He was a very fine policeman. He had a moustache of formidable architecture, a belt that creaked with importance, and a profile that he turned, wherever he stood, slightly to the left, so that the world might benefit from its better side. His name was Alejandro Hernández. He was forty-five and had been making Rafael Ortega's life a misery for two years, with that peculiar tenderness that exists between a man and the thing he is obliged to fine.

"*Ortega!*" called the officer. "Article forty-one of the Civic Culture Law! Unauthorised alteration of a building!"

"It is a *wall,* Commandante!"

"It is the property of a private citizen!"

"The private citizen has asked me to do it. He is eighty. He is weeping with joy. He has given me a plate of *tamales.*"

"The tamales will be taken into evidence."

"They are in my stomach."

"Then your stomach will be taken into evidence." But the policeman's eye had strayed up to the wall, as it always did, as it had done on the hundred and two previous walls; and as always he found himself regarding the great painted face with an expression in which severity and something else contended. He cocked his head. He turned his profile. He regarded the line of the painted jaw.

"That *jaw,*" said Alejandro Hernández, slowly.

"What of it?"

"It is a very strong jaw."

"It is a woman's jaw, Commandante."

"I have been told," said the policeman, "I have a similar jaw. I have been told that by a number of people, including the *barber.*" He folded his arms. "I have the impression, Ortega, over two years, that you have been painting a *portrait.* And I do not wish to say that I believe it is *me.* I only wish to observe that the resemblance is *close.*"

"Commandante. It is a *girl.*"

"A girl with my jaw."

"She is twenty-five."

"A *young* girl," said Alejandro Hernández, with a shiver of indignant satisfaction, "with *my* jaw." He took out his citation book. He wrote, for a long time. Then he tore the sheet out and handed it up on the end of his baton, which was long enough, and said gruffly, in the manner of a man who has had a lot to bear and a very little to say: "That is a fine for the scaffold. For the *painting,* I make no comment."

"Thank you."

"I am saving money to disappear, you know," said the Commandante, staring into the middle distance. "To a small village in Oaxaca. To keep goats. I tell this to no one."

"You have just told it to a street."

"It is a *private* street," said the policeman, and walked away down it, with a tread that was faintly unsteady, and his profile turned to the left.

---

Eleven kilometres to the south, in an apartment in the Colonia Narvarte with a map of the capital pinned to the kitchen wall, a young woman was losing an argument with her best friend, and enjoying it.

"It is *circumstantial,*" said Camila Reyes.

"It is a hundred and three walls," said Lupita Hernández, who was a chef at a restaurant in Xochimilco, twenty-five, round-faced, unalarmable, and had arrived at six in the morning with a pan of *chilaquiles* and a phone. "You have been to ninety-one. You keep the list in a *drawer.*"

"I keep the list *for research.*"

"On what?"

"On the phenomenon of *public portraiture.*"

"Cami. The woman has your nose."

"A nose is not evidence of identity."

"Show me a heron," said Lupita, "who reads the Constitution, in a coat, with *that* chin."

Camila Reyes, twenty-five, fourth-year student of law at the National University, and the most disciplined human being in the south of the city, shut her eyes. She was a small, plain, intense young woman with her hair twisted up in a pencil, a flat voice that she used on judges, and a heart that she kept, by long habit, in the same drawer as the list. She had lived all her life by the principle that a fact is a fact and a feeling is an *allegation.* She had noticed the first wall two Decembers ago, on the Avenida Álvaro Obregón, when she was walking home with her books, and had stopped dead in the middle of the pavement, and had stood there for twenty minutes with a bag of oranges, because a thirty-foot woman with her own mouth was reading her own case-book, in the rain, with her eyes shut.

She had been very *angry.* It had taken her a month to understand why. It is an uncomfortable thing to be seen by a stranger, and to be seen *accurately.*

"Read me his," said Lupita softly.

Camila took the phone.

*Entry 0299 — Mexico City, Mexico.*
*"Your face is on a hundred walls and you do not know."*

"He's wrong," said Camila.

"Is he?"

"I *do* know."

"I know you know. *He* doesn't."

"And mine?" said Camila, very low. "Show me mine."

*Entry 0121 — Mexico City, Mexico.*
*"I have walked to every wall to find the hand that painted me."*

She had written it at three in the morning, after the eighty-ninth wall, and posted it to England in a general despair. It was a very unlawyerly sentence. It contained no conditionals, no reservations, and no precedent. It was the single honest line in her entire body of written work.

"There is a new wall," said Lupita, scrolling, with the finger of a conspirator. "On Zacatecas, in the Roma. It went up *last night.* The one that was at the top of the page. Everyone says it is the biggest. Everyone says—" she paused "—it has a *tag.*"

"A *what?*"

"A line at the bottom. Hand-lettered. It says, *To the one who reads: I have not finished your eyes.*"

Camila Reyes stood perfectly still, in her kitchen, with a map on the wall behind her and a hundred and three pins in it, and a plate of chilaquiles going cold.

"What time," she said, "is the light?"

"Six," said Lupita, who was a chef and knew about mornings. "He paints at six."

"It is five-twenty."

"I know."

"I am going to need a coat."

"I have brought you," said Lupita, with the dignity of one who has been right in advance, "*two.*"

---

**Dhaka, 22:41. Yogyakarta, 23:41.**

*(Between the two cities and the two walls: a small thing, a pulse of light. Let us listen.)*

In the corner of a lane in Mirpur, under a tin awning loud with the late rain, a tea-stall boy named Bunny, thirteen, was explaining the art of the *cha* to a customer who had not asked.

"The secret," said Bunny, "is not the leaf. The secret is the *wait.* You must let it sit exactly as long as it takes a man to decide whether he is going to be a coward. And then you pour. Here, Bhaiya."

Fayaz Rahman, twenty-six, took the glass with the weary courtesy of a man who has just worked a fourteen-hour day on a contract in a currency that was not his own. He had walked here from his flat with a laptop that smelled of hot dust, and he was sitting on a bench with his sleeves down and his shoes wet, looking at his phone without looking at it, as men do who have been waiting for a week without admitting it.

For eight nights he had read the Register on his phone. He had read the line beside his own, and then he had read it again. He had not written to the girl who had written it. He had begun, perhaps forty times. He had typed *Dear* and deleted it; he had typed *Hello* and deleted it; he had once typed *I don't wish to intrude* and had deleted that so hard the whole screen went white. It is an unfortunate thing to be polite in an hour of need: one has so many ways of not saying it.

And then the phone, in his hand, in the lane, under the tin and the rain, gave a small pale shiver.

It was not a ring. It was only the tiniest of lights, an envelope, a name.

> **Ermis Larasati:** Hello, Dhaka. You are one hour behind. I am not sorry about it.

He read it.

He read it a second time, which is to say, he went on reading it, though the sentence had long since ended, as a man goes on holding a door after the guest has come in.

Behind his shoulder, in the steam of the stall, Bunny, who was a boy of the most spotless discretion and no manners whatsoever, had planted his chin.

"*Bhaiya,*" said Bunny, in a hushed and terrible voice.

"Do not read it."

"I was not reading it. I was *visiting.*"

"She is a *stranger.*"

"She is a stranger," said Bunny, "who has an hour to *spare* and has *sent* it to you. That is not an ordinary thing. Say *hello* with *dignity.*"

"I am a man," said Fayaz, with a faint despairing smile, "who apologises to a vending machine."

He did not say that. He typed, in the end, a thing that took him three minutes and cost him a pound of nerves and read, when it was done, exactly like the work of a man who had spent three minutes on it, which is to say, honestly:

> **Fayaz Rahman:** Sorry. (Reflex. It was not about the hour.) Hello, Yogyakarta. I would tell you everything, if I were free to. May I tell you a little?

He looked at it. His thumb hovered. A bead of rain ran off the awning and down his wrist.

He sent it.

The word *delivered* appeared. The word *seen* appeared beneath it, almost at once, small and grey and merciless.

And now it was her turn. She sat, in her workshop, an hour ahead of him, at the exact minute a week since the old astronomer's margin had pencilled them side by side; at 23:41, by the clock above the door, with the stove burnt down and the wax gone cold and a copper pen lying idle in its dish; and beside her, on the rail of the window, eyeing her with a cold and bottomless suspicion, a large green bird.

"*TOO LATE,*" said Ayu.

"Hush."

"*TOO LATE. BEAUTIFUL.*"

"I said hush!" said Ermis, and laughed, once, with her hand to her mouth, like a girl caught at a keyhole. The phone was shaking in her hand. She looked at what he had written. *Sorry. Reflex.* She looked at it again.

It was not what she had expected. She had expected something cool: a *Thank you for your message.* She had not expected an apology for a thing he had not done, nor that it would feel so *exactly* like the thing she had been listening for.

She typed. She deleted. She typed.

She did not draw a flower on the corner this time. She simply wrote, in the Latin letters she used for clients and for strangers, and sent it before she could think better of her own hand:

> **Ermis Larasati:** A little is how every pattern starts. Begin.

And then, because it was a night in which courage was in the air like a smell of marigolds, and nobody was watching but a parrot, she put down the phone and laid her forehead for a moment against the cold edge of the table, and said, very softly, in Javanese, a word that was only a name.

*Three lines,* the reader will say. *That is all?* It is the whole of the matter: a lamp lit, a hand raised, a small, stiff, honourable reply. The great speeches are seldom long. They fit upon a telephone, and are said at night, across an hour.

---

**Calle Zacatecas, Colonia Roma. Six o'clock.**

The light came up over the Roma as it comes up over every Mexican morning: not as a dawn, but as an *announcement,* the whole east flushing from lemon to rose to a gold so fierce it seemed to have been purchased. The pigeons rose off the roofs in a clatter.

And on the pavement, below the longest and newest of the hundred and three walls, in a borrowed coat, with her hair coming out of its pencil and her heart, which she had kept in a drawer, now beating in her ears like a fist, stood a young woman looking up.

It was *her.* It was, without any possibility of doubt, her. There was the nose; there was the dreadful chin. There was the exact way her hair fell forward over her left shoulder; the way her mouth was set; the little frown, between the brows, of a woman who reads as though the page might be taken away. And all thirty feet of it was alive with colour: rust and violet and a blue like the first hour of the night; and the whole face, for the first time, was not looking down, but *up*; the book was lowered; the head was lifted, as if at some sound; and the eyes were still shut, and were *waiting.*

Beneath, in a long ragged line of yellow capitals, a man had written:

**TO THE ONE WHO READS: I HAVE NOT FINISHED YOUR EYES.**

Up on the scaffold, thirty feet above the traffic, with a brush in his hand and a bucket of ochre in the crook of his elbow, a young man with a mop of paint-stiff hair had stopped in the middle of a stroke. He had seen a woman come into the street. He did not know her. He knew only that she was standing exactly where the wall was best seen from; that she had put her hands in her pockets; that she was looking up at his work as though it had said something *libellous* about her mother.

"*Hey,*" said Rafael Ortega, from the sky.

"You've given me a nose like a *heron,*" said Camila.

For a moment nothing moved upon the Calle Zacatecas. The ranchera on the radio had gone on to its second verse. A dog barked. A bus went by, with a grinding of gears, and was gone.

Then the scaffolding, which had been designed by an optimist, creaked; and Rafael Ortega began, with a haste that put every regulation in the country to shame, to come down it.

He came down three ladders and a pipe. He came down the last six feet by a means known only to painters and the fallen. He landed in the street, with paint to the elbows and a smear of ochre across his forehead, and stood before her with his arms at his sides and his mouth open, for once with nothing in it.

"I—" said Rafael.

"Camila Reyes."

"I—"

"Fourth year of law. Narvarte. I have been to ninety-one of your walls." She said it as one reads a charge. "I have eaten bad *tortas* at six in the morning in eleven different colonias. I have been *stared at* by a man in a moustache. I have stood beneath my own face in the rain for two years, and I would like to know, Mr. Ortega, *why you never finished the eyes.*"

He opened his mouth. He closed it. Something went across his face that was too large for it, like a weather.

> *Because I would not guess. A hundred times
> I stood before a wall with that same brush
> And could have made them brown, or black, or grey,
> Or any colour that would make a pleasing
> Picture; and each time I could not lie.
> I saw you once. You looked up once. You were
> Not looking at me, but you looked, and it
> Was gone, a second, a grey-green, a ring
> Of something. I do not know. I would not make
> The thing I did not know. I'd rather paint
> A hundred closed doors than one false window.*

"Brown," said Camila.

"What?"

"They are brown. With a ring of green round the pupil. It is called *hazel,* and it's a very ordinary colour, and I am rather ashamed of it." Her voice was almost steady. "I have never liked them. You will find them very *dull.*"

"Dull?"

"They do not *do* anything."

"Camila Reyes," said Rafael, staring at her eyes with the unashamed devouring attention of a man who has been hungry for two years, "I have been looking at them for four seconds, and I would like it to be known that they have *already* done *everything.*"

It is unseemly to burst into tears in the Colonia Roma at six in the morning, in front of a stranger, a pigeon and a hundred and fifty gallons of paint. She did it nonetheless: a short, furious sob, like a flood out of a locked cellar, and then another, and then she laughed, and put both hands over her face.

He held out a brush.

She looked at it through her fingers. It was a thick, soft, fat-bellied brush, wet with ochre-brown and a little green.

"You do it," said Rafael.

"I cannot paint."

"You cannot be *wrong* about your own eyes."

"It is thirty feet up."

"There is a scaffold."

"It was built by an optimist."

"I am an optimist," said Rafael. "I will hold the ladder."

She climbed. It took her eleven minutes, and the ladder swayed, and a bus-driver, passing, sounded his horn in the manner of a Greek chorus; and at the top, in the cold sweet gold of the morning, with the whole slumbering city spread below her like a quilt, a small woman in a borrowed coat stood on a plank at the level of her own face and laid, with a hand that shook only a little, a single brown arc beneath the lid.

And the painted woman opened her eyes.

Far down in the street, a policeman, who had returned for the *tamales,* stopped dead, with a half-written citation in his hand. He looked up at the wall. He looked at the two small figures on the plank, the girl and the boy, with the great closed face blooming between them into sight.

"*Unauthorised alteration,*" said Alejandro Hernández, faintly, to the empty street.

Then he put the citation book in his pocket, took off his cap, and, turning his profile for once away from the light, stood with his hand to his heart like a man at an anthem.

"Article forty-one," said the Commandante, "is *suspended.*"

---

*Margin note, in pencil, S.W.R.:*

> *Entry 0299 painted a face a hundred times without once daring to guess its eyes. Entry 0121 walked to every wall and was too proud to ask. Between them: one hundred and three portraits, a heron's nose, and the one thing a painter will not do, which is lie.*
>
> *And elsewhere, at 22:41 and 23:41, in two lit windows an hour apart, a few words crossed an ocean. The Keeper remarks that she has seldom seen so small a letter carry so great a weight.*
>
> *Entries 0713 and 0714 — three lines. The pattern has begun. I shall be watching the wax.*

---

*End of Chapter 6.*


---

## Chapter 7
### The Restorer's Seal

> *"I knew it was false. I kept it because it was yours."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0666

---

In Cairo it is said that everything is for sale, and that the only question is whether it is the thing you were told it was.

Nowhere is the saying put to the test more cheerfully than in the Khan el-Khalili, that warren of brass and perfume and patient bargaining where for six hundred years the same lanes have sold the same lamps to the same astonished strangers. A man may buy there a coffee-pot that belonged to a pasha or a perfectly good tray that belongs to nobody at all, and he will leave happy in either case, which is the true miracle of the place.

And in the narrowest, crookedest, most hospitable of its alleys, between a spice-seller's pyramids of red and gold and a boy who sold hibiscus in dripping glasses, stood a little shop with a green door and a sign painted in two languages: **HADDAD & SONS, ANTIQUITIES AND CURIOSITIES. EST. WHEN GOD WAS YOUNG.**

It had no sons. This was a matter on which the proprietor was sensitive, and on which the neighbours were not.

"Sons," said Karim Fouad, potter, thirty-nine, fearless, who had known the proprietor since they were nine years old and had once been sold, by him, a scarab, a camel and a share in the Suez Canal. "The sign says *sons.* How many do you have, Omar?"

"I have *potential.*"

They were sitting in the long, mirrored, noisy room of Fishawi's café, where the glass has hung since the days of Napoleon's cousins and every gilt-framed reflection holds a different century. It was the hour of the afternoon prayer, and the air was thick with apple smoke and with mint. At the next table, upon a velvet cushion, in a suit that had been fashionable in nineteen-sixty, a very old man was holding court to nobody.

"I am the greatest novelist in Egypt," announced Sherif Sabry, seventy-two, retired writer, vain as a peacock in a fountain, "whom nobody has read. This is the whole secret of my genius. Had I been *read,* I should have been *contradicted.* But what is *this?* This Register! A thousand confessions, and every one of them *better* than my novels, and all of them *under* one hundred words. It is an insult to a profession."

"Read us one," said Omar Haddad, and his voice, which had been light, went very quiet. "Read us *six hundred and forty.*"

He was thirty-five, and he was beautiful in the way that a very good counterfeit is beautiful: so smooth, so apt, so exactly what one hoped to find, that it took a careful eye and a bad experience to look for the seam. He had a gold tooth he did not need, a ring he had not paid for, and the manner of a man who has never in his life been refused a table. He had once sold a tourist the same Fatimid door twice in a single afternoon.

Sherif scrolled. "*Entry six hundred and forty. Cairo, Egypt.* 'I sold you a forgery and have never confessed.'" He lowered the phone. "Well, that's a *confession.* That's a very lazy one. Where are the details? Where is the *crime?*"

"The crime," said Omar, "was a cat."

---

It was a small cat.

It was eleven centimetres tall, and made of bronze, and it sat upright upon a base inscribed with a line of hieroglyphs in a style that was not quite right and not quite wrong; and it had been sold, three years before, in a back room of the Khan, by a young dealer with a gold tooth, to a young woman with a very straight back, for exactly three thousand Egyptian pounds.

*A Ptolemaic Bastet,* he had said. *Late period. From a private collection in Alexandria. It has been in the family since the days of the Khedive.*

*It is lovely,* she had said, turning it in the light. *It is very, very lovely.*

And she had paid. And had carried it home in a handkerchief, as one carries a bird.

"It was a good one for the tourists," said Omar, rubbing his eyes. "I had it made by a man in Giza who had made six. I added the patina myself: vinegar, tea, a little cat-litter, a month in a drawer. I asked her name three times, because I wanted to *know* it. And she turned it in her hand, and looked at the base, and I thought: *she knows.* And I waited for her to say. And she said it was *lovely.* And she *paid.* I have been sixteen years in this trade, Karim, and I have never been paid for a thing by someone who knew it was a lie. So I assumed she did not know. What else is there to assume? She has kept my cat three years on the shelf over her lamp, and I have not been able to *sleep.*"

"Why do you not simply tell her?"

"Because she would look at me," said Omar Haddad, in a voice that none of them had ever heard him use, "as a restorer looks at a thing which has been made to deceive; with perfect attention and no hope."

There was a long, smoky silence, in which three centuries peered from the mirrors.

"So what will you do?" said Sherif, entirely sober.

Omar rose. He stood a moment, with his hands upon the marble and his reflection standing behind him, at his shoulder, in a gilt frame, looking suddenly much older, and he spoke, not as he usually did, in the brisk glittering patter of the sales-floor, but slowly, as a man says a thing he has not yet decided to believe:

> *I will confess in the one grammar she respects.
> She does not read men's words. She reads their hands,
> The tool-mark in the metal, the small slip
> Of a chisel that will not lie. She reads
> How long a man has loved a thing, by how
> The edges soften. So I'll make her one.
> I'll make a piece, a perfect piece, in brass,
> A forgery so exact, so obviously false
> To any eye that has an eye to see,
> That she shall turn it over, once, and find
> Beneath the hinge, in letters smaller than
> A grain of rice, the thing that I have never said.
> And if she throws it from the window, well.
> At least I'll be the first man in the Khan
> To tell the truth in brass.*

"That," said Sherif Sabry, after a considerable pause, wiping his eye with the tip of a silk handkerchief, "was an *extremely* good speech."

"Thank you, Ammu."

"I should like to have written it."

"You may," said Omar. "I will give you the credit, in the obituary."

---

**The Conservation Laboratory of the Museum of Islamic Art stands behind a green iron gate in a quiet street, and within it a very clean silence is kept.**

It smelled of acetone and warm dust and old paper; it had white walls, a skylight, six benches, and on each bench a lamp. At the farthest bench, under the best of the lamps, a woman of thirty-two sat, with a loupe screwed into her right eye, a lacquered brush in her left hand, and a fragment of fourteenth-century glass held in a pair of tweezers to the light.

Her name was Layla Mansour. She was exacting, dry, small, and immaculate; she wore a grey linen apron, with the sleeves rolled to exactly the same height, and she spoke to objects in the voice that other people use to speak to a nervous child. She had been called, in the journals, *the finest eye in North Africa.* She had been called, in the corridors, *the Ice Pharaoh.* She had once told a German professor to his face that a Mamluk lamp he had proudly authenticated was *twelve years old and from Marseille,* and had been proved right in eleven days.

On the shelf above her lamp, as it had sat for three years, sat a small bronze cat.

"It is looking at you again," said Dina Shaker.

Dina, fourteen, was the granddaughter of the only woman cab-driver in Heliopolis; she had arrived at the Museum two years ago on a school trip, refused to leave, and had since been appointed, by a process nobody could reconstruct, Official Sweeper and Unofficial Witness. She had enormous round spectacles and an inability to let a silence lie.

"It is a *cat,* Dina."

"It is a cat that *looks.* I think it knows you've read the Register. You read it on Monday, at your bench, with your lips, and went the colour of a boiled egg. Doctor Karim said, *Is something wrong, Madam Layla?* and you said, *It is the acetone.* But the acetone was in the cupboard."

"Then say it to the *floor.*"

"The floor is not interested," said Dina Shaker, with dignity, and swept.

It is true that Layla had read it. She had read the whole of it, in her kitchen, on the Monday night, on a small cracked tablet, with a glass of hibiscus at her elbow and the call to prayer coming across the roofs; and she had found, beside the Register's long ribbon of Cairo, two entries she had known she would find. The first: *I sold you a forgery and have never confessed.* The second, which was her own, written on a night she did not wish to remember, to a stranger in England: *I knew it was false. I kept it because it was yours.*

"Madam Layla," said a voice in the doorway, with a trembling deference. "Forgive me. Did I come at a bad time?"

The speaker was a thin, anxious man in an enormous overcoat, carrying a battered satchel with both arms, as a man holds a baby he is afraid to put down. This was Tarek Hassan, forty-one, librarian of Alexandria, who had come to Cairo for the week to consult with the Museum on a catalogue and who had not slept properly since the night of the new moon, because he remembered, with perfect clarity, the exact day on which every dreadful thing had ever happened to him.

"Not at all, Mr. Hassan."

"It is only that I was *told*—" he lowered his voice "—that there is *a certain dealer,* with *a package,* coming *here,* to be *authenticated.*"

"Many packages come here."

"But *this* package," said Tarek, with the glassy fixity of a man who recalls the Twelfth of March nineteen-ninety-eight, a Thursday, rain, a dropped ink-pot, "is *cursed.*"

"By whom?"

"By *love,*" said the librarian, and put down the satchel, and sat upon it, and was not seen to stand up again for some time.

---

He came at four o'clock.

He came in his best suit, a pale cream linen that had been, in its day, an act of financial violence; with a hat, a stick, a gold tooth and a wooden box. And he came in at the green iron gate with the swagger of a man who is trying very hard to walk as if he were not afraid of a woman in an apron.

"Madam Layla," said Omar Haddad. "May the day be blessed."

"May it be blessed twice, Mr. Haddad."

"I have something," he said, "for you to look at."

"I assumed you had. You have not been to this laboratory in three years. I take it it is not a social call."

"I have not been *invited.*"

"You have not been *willing.*" She did not look up from the glass. "Put it on the bench."

It was a small box of brass, inlaid with silver. He set it down upon the white cloth with both hands. It was a pen-box, such as scribes had carried in the belt in the days of the Mamluks: long, narrow, with a hinged lid, and upon the lid in lines of beaten silver an ornament of looping vines and stars, and about the rim a band of inscription in a firm, flowing, practised hand.

"A *qalamdan,*" said Omar. "Fourteenth century. Syrian work, I think; possibly Damascene; brought to Cairo in the time of Sultan Hasan. From a house in Giza. I believe it to be extremely fine."

"Thank you, Mr. Haddad. I will see."

"I should like your seal," said Omar, "upon it. If it is, as I hope, sound."

There was a silence. Dina, in the corner, had forgotten her broom. Tarek Hassan, on his satchel, had gone the colour of the wall.

Layla Mansour put down the glass, and screwed in the loupe.

She did it as she always did: in order, in silence, by the book. She looked first at the whole, the proportion, the weight in the hand. She looked at the brass under the lamp, and then under the ultraviolet, where an old patina glows a dull amber and a young one flares like a cheat. She tapped the rim and listened for the ring. And then she did what the great forgers have always feared more than any machine: she *smelled* it.

"It is modern," said Layla.

"Is it?" said Omar, faintly.

"Brass sheet, rolled in the last ten years. The patina is vinegar and tea, with a little *tobacco.* You have used cigarette-ash to dull the rim." Her voice was quite level. "The vines are good. The stars are better. The inscription is a stock verse of blessing, in a thuluth that is nearly right but for the *alif,* which the Mamluk scribes never drew with a serif. It is a very beautiful forgery, Mr. Haddad. I should say it is the best that I have seen this year."

"I am so very sorry to have wasted your time."

"You have not."

She had not looked up. She held the box in the lamp-light, close to her eye, and her fingers, which were small and square and as steady as a surgeon's, were turning it over slowly, as one turns a sleeping child.

"Because there is something *wrong* with it," said Layla.

"Wrong?"

"It is *too good.* A forger who makes a thing to deceive makes it to be *admired.* He makes the hinge as fine as he can. He makes the silver as bright as he dares. But this—" She stopped.

It was a very small repair. A hairline crack, in the brass at the pivot, such as comes of a hundred years of opening and shutting a lid; and over it, in place of the usual neat invisible mend, a mend made *visibly:* a single thread of soft yellow gold, laid in with a fine tool along the length of the crack, so that the flaw was not hidden but *shown,* made a thing of beauty, a seam of light.

Layla Mansour did not move.

It was a mend she knew. It was a mend she had made. She had made it, in that very manner, on forty-one objects in the Museum of Islamic Art, over the course of nine years, against the advice of three directors and the horror of a German professor. It was her habit. It was her *signature.* She had never said so; she had never written about it; she had never, to her knowledge, told another living soul.

"Who did this?" said Layla.

"I do not know," said Omar, in a voice that was trying very hard to be a salesman's.

"It is my *mend.*"

"Is it?"

"It is not a *copy* of my mend. A copy would be neat. This is *crooked,* in just the place that mine goes crooked: *there,* at the third turn, where my wrist catches. It is a copy of my *mistake.*" She put down the box. "Mr. Haddad. You have forged not the piece, but the *restoration.* You have made a box that was found, broken, and mended by *me.*"

Her voice, which had never in thirteen years wavered upon a bench, now did, very slightly, as a thread does when it takes a strain. "That is not a forgery of an antique. It is a forgery of my *taste.*"

"Layla—"

"Under the hinge."

He did not answer.

"There is something under the hinge. I can feel it. There is an engraving." She had taken up the loupe again, and bent, and the long clean lamp lay over her face and over the little box, with its stars and its seam of gold. For a time there was only the sound of her breathing and a distant mutter of the muezzin from a minaret across the roofs.

Then she read it.

It was in letters smaller than a grain of rice, in a perfect, delicate, beautifully formed thuluth, cut with the point of a needle on the underside of the lid:

*Made by the hand of Omar Haddad, in the year of the Register, in a house in the Khan, with a good deal of vinegar. He sold you a cat three years ago and has been sorry every day since. He would like to be forgiven, and cannot see how.*

---

She sat for a long time with the loupe in her eye, which made it impossible for anybody to tell whether she was reading or weeping, and a woman in an apron is under no obligation to explain which. She put it down at last, and reached up to the shelf above the lamp, and took down the little bronze cat.

She set it beside the box.

"It was sold to me," said Layla Mansour, "as a Ptolemaic Bastet. Late period. From a private collection in Alexandria."

"I know what I said."

"It has the left ear of a reproduction cast in Brooklyn in nineteen-ninety-one. The base was recut in the last decade by a competent man with an electric tool. The patina is vinegar, tea and *cat-litter,* Mr. Haddad. *Cat-litter.* I could smell it from across the Khan."

"You *knew?*" said Omar.

His voice cracked in the middle of the word like a plate.

"Of course I knew."

"From the *first moment?*"

"From the moment you put it in my hand."

"But you *paid!*"

"I paid three thousand pounds," said Layla, "which was a *fair price,* for the hours of work, and the value of the lie." She did not look at him. She was looking at the cat, with a face of such formidable composure that it could only have been held up by a very great weight. "I had never in my life been *sold* anything with so much hope. You stood there with your gold tooth and your ring, and you said it had been in the family since the Khedive, and I looked at your face, and I thought: *he is lying to me, and he is not enjoying it.* And I had never seen that before."

"Layla."

"So I kept it."

"Why?"

"Because it was yours," said Layla Mansour.

There are silences in this world that are made of nothing, and there are silences that are made of everything, and in the Conservation Laboratory at that moment there was the second kind. Tarek Hassan, who had been sitting on his satchel in a state of spiritual collapse, took out a large clean handkerchief and blew his nose like a trumpet. Dina Shaker said, very loudly and to nobody: "I *knew* it."

"So," said Omar, and sat down upon the nearest stool, which was Dina's, as though his strings had been cut, "I have been confessing for three years to a person who was *waiting for me to start.*"

"I would not put it so."

"How *would* you put it?"

"I would say," said Layla, drawing a clean sheet of paper from the drawer and uncapping a pen, "that you are, Mr. Haddad, a very bad forger and a very fine craftsman, and that the two have never before been found in one man."

She wrote. She wrote for some time, in her small upright hand, upon the Museum's cream paper with the crescent at the head; and when she had written, she took from the inside of her apron a small brass seal on a ribbon, which she had worn for nine years and used on five thousand pieces of the heritage of Egypt, and breathed upon it, and pressed it, hard, in red, at the foot of the page.

She turned the paper round.

*CERTIFICATE OF EXAMINATION. Object: one pen-box, brass inlaid with silver, of modern manufacture. Opinion: not a work of the fourteenth century. A work of the twenty-first, wholly and honestly made. Authentic — as to the hand that made it.*

*— L. Mansour, Conservator.*

Omar Haddad read it three times. He had the look of a man who has been given a kingdom, and is looking about him for the forgery.

"It is not for sale," said Layla.

"I know."

"Doctor Karim will wish to buy it. He will offer forty thousand pounds. I shall decline. It is not a museum piece; it is evidence."

"Of what?"

"That," said the Ice Pharaoh, and for the first time in three years the corner of her mouth moved, which Dina Shaker would afterwards swear was a *smile,* "is for the court to decide. Dina. Mr. Hassan. I think the laboratory will be closing early."

"Mr. Hassan," said Dina, hauling the librarian to his feet by one sleeve with the strength of a very small and determined crane, "I think it is time for a *tea.*"

---

The door closed behind them. The skylight had turned a deep and dusty rose. The muezzin of the nearest mosque began, in a high clear thread of sound, to call the faithful to prayer; and outside, over the green iron gate, the whole of Old Cairo lay in the last long gold of the afternoon, like a city under glass.

Omar stood up. He did not know what to do with his hands.

"I should like," he said carefully, "to ask whether I might—"

"You may take me to dinner," said Layla.

"I was going to say *apologise.*"

"You have apologised. In brass. It is in the record." She took off the apron, folded it exactly in three, and laid it on the bench. Without the apron she seemed younger, and a good deal less formidable, and a great deal more frightened. "But you may take me to dinner. On the condition that you will tell me nothing that is not true."

"Madam Layla, I am a *dealer.*"

"Then I shall require provenance," said Layla Mansour, "for every word."

---

*Margin note, in pencil, S.W.R.:*

> *Entry 0640 forged a cat. Entry 0666 knew, and paid. Between them hang three years, a shelf, and a seam of gold. Reader, there is a school of thought that holds that a forgery is a lie told in metal. I hold otherwise. A forgery that is made for one person, and fits her to the grain, is the nearest thing that metal has ever come to a love-letter.*
>
> *I have had a thousand confessions. I have seldom had one so well mended.*

---

*End of Chapter 7.*


---

## Chapter 8
### Nets and Numbers

> *"My boat is failing and so am I."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0443

---

### SCENE I
*Bergen harbour, a Tuesday in late November, before dawn.*

In Bergen it rains two hundred and forty days of the year, and on the remaining one hundred and twenty it is merely considering it.

The Bergensers do not complain of this. To complain would be to admit that the weather had an opinion, and they prefer to think of it as a lodger: noisy, always behind with the rent, and, in the end, part of the household.

On a Tuesday in the last week of November, at ten minutes past seven, with the sun still some hours from its brief and grudging appearance, a man named Lars Eriksen stood on the deck of a boat and spoke to it as one speaks to an aged and expensive relation.

"You will start," said Lars.

The boat, whose name was *Ragnhild*, did not reply. She was eleven metres of tarred oak and old paint, built in the year his grandfather had been young and his grandfather's opinions had been newer. She had a wheelhouse the size of a confessional, a winch that groaned like a bad conscience, and a diesel engine that, in the spring, had begun to cough as a smoker coughs, politely at first and then without apology.

"I have been patient," said Lars.

The engine considered this, and coughed.

Lars Eriksen was thirty years old. He was tall and square and weathered beyond his years, with hands like folded oars and eyes the grey of the fjord at its least forthcoming. He was the third of his name to fish out of Bergen, and he would, it was generally agreed, be the last, since the *Ragnhild* owed the bank four hundred and twelve thousand kroner, the quota for his class of vessel had been trimmed twice in three years, and the sea, which had once been a sort of savings account, had become a sort of overdraft.

He was a man of very few words. These he spent as a poor man spends his coins, one at a time, with a look of faint regret afterward.

"Ikke bra," said a voice from the quay.

---

It was the voice of Kristian Strand, who was seventy-eight, and who had been for fifty-one years a waiter at the finest restaurant on the Bryggen wharf, and who had never, in his retirement, put down his napkin. It hung over his left forearm even now, in the rain, in the dark, at a fishing dock. In his right hand he carried two paper cups of coffee on an imaginary silver tray.

He had married Lars's mother late in both their lives, and had buried her six winters since, and in the grief of it had simply gone on being a father, in the way a clock goes on ticking after the room has emptied. Lars called him *Far*, which is father. Kristian called Lars *the young master*, which was a joke that had stopped being a joke in about the year two thousand and twelve.

"That engine," said Kristian, passing down a cup, "sounds like a man trying to remember a name."

"She will start."

"Of course she will start. Everything starts. It is the question of what happens next." He examined the *Ragnhild* with the cold eye of one who has seen ten thousand dishes sent back to the kitchen.

"You are carrying passengers today."

"The institute. The woman with the nets."

"The biologist." Kristian's eyebrows rose by about one millimetre, which in a waiter of his school was the equivalent of a flourish of trumpets. "The one who talks."

"She is not so bad."

"Lars Eriksen," said the old man. "That is the longest sentence you have said in praise of any human being since your confirmation."

"It was *four words*."

"In this house, young master," said Kristian, "four words is a sonnet."

---

### SCENE II
*The Fish Market, Bergen. Eleven o'clock. The light has arrived, in the manner of an inspector: late, grey, and with no intention of staying.*

There is a woman at the corner of the Fisketorget who sells umbrellas, and she is not popular.

Her name was Solveig Dahl. She was thirty-six, an umbrella maker from Ålesund, who had come south to Bergen on the theory that if one has to sell umbrellas it is wise to sell them in the one city on earth that requires them. Her stall carried a hand-lettered sign that said, in two languages, *UNBREAKABLE*.

"Excuse me," said a tourist, a large and aggrieved gentleman from Ohio, holding up a skeletal wreck that had, a few moments before, been an umbrella. "Your sign says unbreakable."

"Yes."

"It broke."

"It did not break," said Solveig. "The *wind* broke."

"The wind broke my umbrella."

"The wind," said Solveig, with the patience of a great teacher, "was not covered by the guarantee."

"Ma'am, I'd like a refund."

"I do not give refunds. I give *advice*. The advice is: do not stand in the wind."

The gentleman went away muttering. Solveig watched him go with a very faint and secret satisfaction, and turned to find that a tall young woman in a yellow oilskin had stopped at her stall, and was examining the stock with the frown of one who solves problems for a living.

This was Sigrid Haugen.

She was twenty-nine, a marine biologist at the Institute of Marine Research on the Nordnes peninsula, with the look of one who has had a great many ideas in the last ten minutes and is trying to finish all of them at once. Her hair, the colour of dark honey, was escaping from three separate clips. When she stood, she bounced very slightly, as though the ground were a little too slow for her.

"Is it really unbreakable?" said Sigrid.

"No."

"Then why does the sign—"

"A sign is not a *promise*," said Solveig. "A sign is a hope with a frame around it." She looked Sigrid up and down. "You are restless."

"I am *not*."

"Your left foot is going. You have been tapping it since you arrived." Solveig produced a small umbrella the colour of a ripe plum and held it out like a gift. "Take it. You cannot go through the world with a hood. A hood makes you look at your feet. An umbrella makes you look *up*, to see what is the matter."

"What would I owe you?"

"Two hundred and ten kroner."

"That is a great deal for a thing that is not unbreakable."

"I am saving money," said Solveig Dahl, and for a moment something very small and naked looked out of her face, and then went back inside, "to disappear."

Sigrid blinked. "I beg your pardon?"

"I said, to *dis*count it. Two hundred, then." Solveig looked away at the grey water. "Take the umbrella."

Sigrid took the umbrella. She paid the two hundred. It was not until she was halfway back to the institute, and the rain had begun in earnest, that she opened it and found, stitched into the lining in tiny, furious, red thread, a line that Solveig Dahl had embroidered for no customer in particular, and perhaps for herself:

*Look up. It is only weather.*

Which is, as the reader may have noticed, the whole philosophy of the Norwegian people in six words, and the reason that they are, on the whole, rather cheerful.

---

At the institute, a thing was waiting on Sigrid's desk, and it was not an email.

The foundations that give money to scientists send their good news by electronic mail and their bad news in the post. A thick cream envelope, with a window and a crest, is the equivalent of a surgeon's face when he steps out of the theatre.

Sigrid sat down on her chair without taking off her oilskin. She did not tear the envelope; she was a scientist; she slit it with the tip of a pipette, as though the letter might have fingerprints.

*Dear Dr. Haugen,*

*We are delighted to confirm that the Foundation will continue to support work in your field. We regret, however, that the present grant for the coastal cod study cannot be renewed beyond the thirty-first of March. Funding for the successor programme has been allocated to the Arctic station at Ny-Ålesund, Svalbard, where a post of fourteen months is offered to the present holder of the grant, subject to acceptance by the fifteenth of January…*

She read the paragraph twice, as one reads a map one hopes to be wrong.

*Fourteen months.* In Ny-Ålesund, in the high Arctic, where the sun does not rise for four months of the year, and the nearest city is a thousand kilometres of black water away. A post of a lifetime. Everything she had ever wished for; everything she had spent her twenties writing grant applications to be offered; and, laid on a desk in the rain in a cream envelope, it had the exact weight of a stone.

*And if I take it,* thought Sigrid, who could do such sums in her head faster than she could control her feelings, *I will not be back for a year and a quarter. And if the programme grows, as such programmes do, I may not be back at all.*

"Sigrid."

She turned. A man stood in the door of her office, a slender, dry, dark-haired man in a surgeon's green scrubs with a raincoat over them, holding a sheet of paper in one hand and a coffee in the other. He did not enter. He did not speak again. He held up the paper.

The paper said, in black marker: **HOW ARE YOU?**

"Henrik," said Sigrid. "You are standing in my doorway with a sign."

He shrugged and held up a second sheet, which he had evidently prepared for the occasion: **I TRIED TO TELEPHONE. I CANNOT. I CAME IN PERSON.**

"It is three hundred metres from the hospital."

**IT IS A LONG WAY WHEN YOU ARE AFRAID.**

Henrik Strand was thirty-one, a surgeon of real skill, who had held human hearts in his hands and could not bring himself to lift a telephone to his ear and hear a voice come out of it. He had been her best friend since the age of nine. He wrote everything down.

She handed him the letter.

He read it standing, which is how a surgeon reads bad news. Then he took a third sheet from his pocket, uncapped his marker, and wrote, with his usual neat and merciless hand:

**YOU ARE GOING TO TAKE IT.**

"I have not decided."

**YOU ARE GOING TO TAKE IT. AND YOU ARE GOING TO WISH SOMEONE WOULD ASK YOU NOT TO.**

"Henrik—"

**WHO WOULD YOU LIKE TO ASK YOU?**

She opened her mouth. She closed it. A small unbidden image rose before her: grey eyes under a wet cap, a square jaw, a man who had said, in six months of weekly voyages, not four hundred words in all.

"No one," said Sigrid.

Henrik regarded her for a long moment. Then he wrote one more sheet, and put it carefully on her desk, and went away down the corridor, a figure in green, with his coffee going cold.

The sheet said: **YOUR LEFT FOOT IS GOING.**

---

### SCENE III
*The Byfjorden. Two in the afternoon. The sun, having made its inspection, has begun to leave. A fog is coming down the water like a slow white curtain at the end of a very long play.*

"One more station," said Sigrid. "Just one more. I need the dip at ninety fathoms, and then I swear on my mother's good name that we go home."

"Your mother's good name is not at risk," said Lars.

"That was a joke."

"I know. I am being *supportive.*"

She laughed. It was a surprised, delighted, startled laugh, the laugh of a person who has been told a joke by a wall. She sat on an upturned crate on the foredeck, in her yellow oilskin, with her plum umbrella furled between her knees (it was not raining, and she held it nonetheless, as a man will hold his hat in church), and wrote numbers in a little notebook with a pencil on a string.

They had done eleven stations. They had netted, tagged, measured, and returned to the sea some forty cod, each of them looking at her, as cod do, with an expression of profound moral surprise. They had spoken, between them, perhaps sixty words, of which Sigrid had supplied fifty-four.

It was the best day of her week. She knew it; she was a scientist, and had at last learned to count the things that were not on her list.

And then the engine coughed.

It coughed once, with a sound like an old man being asked to climb a stair. Lars, at the wheel, did not move. Sigrid, who was watching him, saw that his shoulders had gone very still, in the way a horse's will when it hears something the rider does not.

It coughed again.

And then the *Ragnhild* made a sound that was not a cough, but a long, descending, apologetic sigh, like a great beast lying down, and the engine, which had borne them across forty thousand miles of grey water, went silent.

The silence that followed was enormous. The water lapped. A gull remarked upon the situation and flew away. Somewhere behind them the fog slid over the city, which went out like a candle.

"Lars," said Sigrid.

"I know."

"Is it—"

"It is nothing." He turned the key. Nothing. He turned it again. A small, wretched click. "It is flooded. It will clear."

He went below.

For eleven minutes she listened to the sounds of a proud man talking to a machine: a clank, a murmur, a muttered Norwegian syllable of a kind not found in the hymnbook. She did not go down. She did not offer to help, which was the kindest thing she could have done, for a man who is ashamed will bear almost any burden but a witness.

*Reader, let us go below, since it is permitted, and since the lady cannot.*

The engine room of the *Ragnhild* was the size of a coffin and about as cheerful. Lars Eriksen knelt before the engine with a wrench in his hand and a lamp in his teeth. He took the lamp out. He spoke, and because he thought himself alone, he spoke in the only form a taciturn man will trust: in measure, slow and low, with the pauses where a man swallows.

> *Old girl, I have nursed you since the spring,
> And bought you parts I could not well afford,
> And lied to the bank, and lied to my own father,
> And told myself the sea would give me back
> The thing I put in. And she does not give.
> She takes. She is the one great creditor
> Who does not send a letter. Nor will I.
> I have not told a living soul how far
> Behind I am. I have not told the woman
> Who sits above me with her careful numbers,
> And laughs, and does not know she is the light
> Upon this deck. I would not tell her. No.
> What could a man like me say? That I fish
> For cod that are not there? That I am tired?
> That I would sooner drown than ask for help,
> And that the drowning is the cheaper course?
> Start, damn you. Start. If you are all I have,
> At least be something. Be a boat. Be warm.
> Be a thing that does what it was built to do,
> And I will be a man. We'll go together.*

The engine, which had been listening with every appearance of sympathy, did nothing at all.

Lars put his forehead against its cold green flank. He stayed there some time. Then he took a breath, and straightened his shoulders, and returned the lamp to his teeth.

*Mark this, reader.* He did not weep. There is a species of courage that consists wholly in carrying on with a wrench. It is not much admired in poems. It should be.

---

By the time he came up, the dark had come down.

The dark comes early in the north: a short grey afternoon, a long blue dusk, and then the black, with only the lights of the far shore laid out along the water like beads on a thread. They drifted in a pocket of clear air, with the whole city shining three miles off, and seven hundred feet of water beneath them.

Sigrid had turned on the cabin lamp. She had put the kettle on the little stove. She had found, in a locker, a bag of *skolebrød*, the sweet custard buns of Bergen, rather stale, and set two of them on a saucer, with that particular dignity people give to a meal when everything else has gone wrong.

"We could call," she said.

"No."

"The rescue boats are volunteers. They would come in half an hour. It is what they are *for*."

"We are not in danger."

"We are adrift in a fjord in the dark, Lars."

"We are in a *fjord*," he said. "That is not a danger. That is an address."

She looked at him. He sat on the locker opposite, in the glow of the lamp, with engine-grease on his cheek, holding a stale bun as though it were a document he had been asked to sign. He did not look at her. He looked, with great concentration, at the bun.

"It is the money," said Sigrid.

He said nothing.

"You do not want to call because the rescue society asks a donation, and the tow, and the engineer, and you do not have—" She stopped. "I am sorry. That was not mine to say."

"No," said Lars. "It was not."

"But it is true."

He was silent for a long time. The kettle began to mutter. Out on the black water something moved, a seal, perhaps, or the tide.

"Four hundred and twelve thousand," he said at last, to the bun. "It is what I owe. It is not so very much. My father had more, once. I think about the number at night, you understand. It has a shape."

"What shape?"

"A *hook*." He very nearly smiled. "It is a stupid thing to say."

"It is not."

"I have not said it to anyone."

"Then," said Sigrid, softly, "I will not either."

It was the most they had said to one another in six months. The kettle sang. She poured two cups of tea, and handed one across; and for a moment their fingers touched on the warm china, and withdrew, each with the air of a party that has been formally introduced.

And Sigrid Haugen, who could not keep a foot still, who had never in her life kept a secret for longer than a week, felt the cream envelope lie in her pocket like a sleeping coal. *Fourteen months. By the fifteenth of January.* She opened her mouth to tell him. She had always told everyone everything. It was a fault.

"Lars—"

"Yes?"

*Say it,* thought Sigrid. *Say: I have been offered the sun at the top of the world, and I do not want it, and I cannot say why.*

"Your tea is going cold," said Sigrid.

*Ah, reader.* Two people on a small boat in a large dark, each with a letter against the breast, and both of them, in the great Norwegian manner, discussing the temperature of tea. There is an art to missing the moment by exactly the width of a cup. The whole nation practises it daily.

---

### SCENE IV
*Half past nine. The lights of the rescue boat come over the water like two kind and slightly officious stars.*

They were found by a boat from the Sea Rescue, crewed by six volunteers in orange suits, among whom was a retired poet.

His name was Espen Lund, he was forty-nine, he wrote the weather-poems that were chalked each morning on the board outside the harbour café ("Today: wet, with rising hope"), and he served as a rescue volunteer for the excellent reason that it gave him something to rhyme. He leaned from the bow and caught the line Lars threw.

"Eriksen!" he called. "I have written a poem about you."

"I am not yet dead."

"It is a *preventive* poem. It is hard to rhyme with 'diesel'."

"Then throw the rope."

On the quay a small crowd had assembled, for in Bergen a breakdown is a public entertainment. Marit Strand was there, Kristian's daughter and Lars's friend since the cradle, a train guard of thirty-eight in a very good coat, who arrived in the middle of a sentence she had evidently been conducting alone for some time.

"—and I said to the stationmaster, a woman of my position cannot be told that the eight-fifteen is *philosophically late*. Lars! You have grease on your face, it is very *attractive*—who is this? Oh, you are the *biologist.* Lars says nothing but I can read it in his eyebrows. Is that a plum umbrella? How *sensible*—"

"Marit," said Lars.

"Yes?"

"Breathe."

"I *am* breathing, I am breathing *through* it, it is an art—"

And the young woman in the yellow oilskin, who had a letter in her pocket and a stale bun in her satchel and a left foot which, she noticed with surprise, had at last stopped tapping, looked once across the black water at a tall, silent man being hugged by a talking train guard, and thought, with a clarity that astonished her:

*I would like to be on that boat again on Tuesday.*

And then, a second later, with the dread of the scientist at the moment the data refuse to fit:

*And I have until the fifteenth of January.*

---

*Margin note, in pencil, in the hand of S.W.R.:*

> *Entry 0443: "My boat is failing and so am I." Entry 0610: "My grant ends in spring and I may not return."*
>
> *They were posted on different nights, one winter and two postboxes apart, by two people who did not know that each had written the other's reply. A boat is a promise made of wood. A grant is a promise made of paper. I have been an astronomer for forty-five years, and I will tell you which of them floats: neither. It is the one who stays on board who keeps the boat afloat.*
>
> *They will have to decide which of the two of them is the boat.*

---

*End of Chapter 8.*


---

## Chapter 9
### The Bookshop at Kochi's Edge

> *"I hid a poem in a book I knew you would buy."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0699

---

### SCENE I
*Fort Kochi, Kerala. The small hours of the twenty-sixth of November. The north-east monsoon, which the Malayalis call* thulavarsham, *is leaning on the roof like a tired guest who has no intention of leaving.*

At two in the morning, in a room above a bookshop, a man was copying a poem for the seventh time, and had not yet got it right.

His name was Arjun Nair, he was twenty-seven, and he possessed the three gifts of the shy: a neat hand, a good memory, and a talent for being found out by nobody. He had a long, grave, kind face, spectacles mended at the hinge with a thread, and a way of standing in his own shop as though apologising to the shelves for the intrusion. The shop below him was called Karayil Books, which is to say *On the Shore*, and it stood at the very edge of Fort Kochi, where the old Dutch lanes run out of ideas and become the sea.

He wrote with a pencil, on onion-skin paper, in Malayalam script, with its great loops and curls like waves seen from above. He had written it first when he was twenty, on the afternoon a girl in a green churidar had come into the shop, and asked for a copy of a certain children's annual, and said "Thank you" so exactly, with such a plain bright courtesy, that he had gone upstairs afterward and sat on the stairs for an hour.

He had not told her. He had done the other thing, which is cheaper and takes longer. He had folded the poem very small and slipped it between pages forty-one and forty-two of the book she was carrying away, and then stood in his doorway while she walked down the lane with it, saying to himself, with the unreason of the very young, *If she finds it, she will know; and if she does not, I shall be spared.*

She had found it. He knew that, because the following November she had come back and asked for the same annual, and the November after that, and every November since, with the unfailing punctuality of the tides. And every November he had copied the poem out afresh, in new pencil, on new paper, and tucked it between forty-one and forty-two.

Neither had said a word of it. Seven years. It is the longest conversation in the history of Fort Kochi, and not a syllable has been spoken.

Here, since it is the thing itself and the reader is owed it, is the poem. It does not sound so well in English. Poems seldom do. They are like fish carried inland.

> *You do not know my name; I do not mind.
> The ink is small, the paper thin as air.
> I put it where I knew that you would find,
> And then I turned away, and was not there.
>
> I am the shelf you pass and do not see;
> The shop-bell that announces who has come;
> I am the hour between your tea and me,
> The word a shy man keeps beneath his tongue.
>
> And if one year the page should come out blank,
> Know that the pencil failed, and not the hand;
> Know that the book, the sea, the year are thanks
> To one who could not say it. Understand.*

"Seven years," said Arjun aloud, to the lamp. "And I still cannot rhyme *hand* with anything."

A voice from the doorway, brittle and anxious, made him jump.

"You are *talking* again," said his father.

---

Hari Panicker, seventy-six, was a retired butcher, a large, anxious, soft-eyed man in a lungi and an undershirt, who had spent forty years in the confident trade of carving and the last seven in the unconfident one of worrying about a son who read. (He was a Panicker who had married into a Nair house, and been absorbed by it as a small stream is absorbed by a larger river; the boy had taken the river's name.) He stood at the top of the stairs holding the old brass scale that had hung in his shop for four decades, which he had brought to the bookshop and which now sat on the counter below, where it weighed, with great solemnity, the cheaper kind of paperback.

"Appa," said Arjun. "It is two in the morning."

"I could not sleep. The rain is coming in at the back wall. I have been listening to it. It says something."

"What does it say?"

"It says, *Hari, move the books.* Every year the tide comes up the lane. What do you intend to do about the poetry?"

"Put it on a high shelf."

"And the thing you are writing?"

Arjun put his hand, very lightly, over the onion-skin paper.

"That," said Hari, with a sigh that carried forty years of fathers, "is the *only* part of the shop that is not insured."

---

### SCENE II
*Mattancherry. A schoolroom. Nine in the morning. Rain.*

"Class Six," said Meera Menon, "who can tell me what a metaphor is?"

Thirty hands went up, which was a lie, because eleven of the children had been told by their mothers to put their hands up, and nineteen had no idea. Meera Menon was twenty-six, a schoolteacher, with a long braid, a green sari the colour of a parrot's wing, and the straight bold look of a woman who has never been afraid of a classroom. She taught English at the old Jewish quarter's school, in a room with four fans, two of which worked, and a view of the spice-merchants' lane, where on a dry day the whole air tasted of ginger and pepper and the dried-fish smell that is the real perfume of Kochi.

"A metaphor," volunteered a small boy in the front, "is when you say a thing is a different thing, and it is *not*."

"Very good, Anoop. Example?"

"The rain is a teacher."

"And why is it a teacher?"

"Because it comes every day," said Anoop, "and it is always wet."

A little girl at the back, fourteen years old and the oldest of the class by the grace of a long illness, lifted her hand, and Meera nodded. This was Sreeja Nambiar, the school's unofficial librarian, a solemn child with a plait to her waist who saw everything and reported nothing, which is the whole equipment of the born novelist.

"Teacher," said Sreeja. "You are going to the bookshop today."

"Whatever makes you say that?"

"It is the twenty-sixth."

There was a delicate pause.

"Every year on the twenty-sixth," said Sreeja, "you wear the green sari, and you go to Mr. Arjun's shop, and you come back with *The Schoolchild's Annual*, and for the rest of the day you smile at it like a person who has been told a very good secret." The solemn eyes did not blink. "That is a simile, Teacher."

"It is an *impertinence*," said Meera. "Sit down."

"I *am* sitting."

"Then be quiet in a sitting position." But she was laughing, and she coloured to the roots of her braid, and thirty children, who had not the faintest idea what was going on, applauded.

---

The rain, by noon, had stopped being weather and become geography.

It poured on the harbour and the ferries, which crossed from Ernakulam with the dazed look of ducks in a bath. It came down on the Chinese fishing nets, those great wooden cantilevers that rise like the skeletons of enormous insects, with a roar that drowned the church bells and the muezzin and the temple drums alike.

"Madam!" shouted Vishnu Kurup, from the front of his auto-rickshaw. "I cannot take you down the lane! There is a river!"

Vishnu Kurup was forty-five, a rickshaw puller, a large grave man with a moustache like a wet broom, who had been Meera's friend since she was a student and who had adopted, on that basis, a severe and total authority over her life. He stopped the rickshaw at the mouth of Princess Street. Before them lay a thing that had been a road.

"Ten centimetres of water," he announced, "and rising. It is the high tide and the rain agreeing with each other. In my experience, madam, nothing worse can happen than two things agreeing."

"I must go to the bookshop."

"The bookshop is *drowning*."

"Then," said Meera, taking off her sandals and tucking them into her bag, "I had better go and help it drown *with dignity.*"

"You are going for the book."

"I am going for the *shop*."

"You are wearing the green sari," said Vishnu, gravely. "Everyone in Kochi knows what the green sari is."

She tucked up the border of the sari, which in Kerala is a thing a woman does the way a soldier slings a rifle, and stepped into the brown water with her chin up.

---

### SCENE III
*Karayil Books. A quarter to one. The tide in the lane has reached the doorstep, considered it, and come in.*

There is a particular silence that falls over a bookshop when water enters it, and it is the silence of a very large congregation holding its breath.

Arjun stood in water to his shins with a stack of Malayalam poetry in his arms and an expression of calm despair. The lower shelves were already gone: the cookbooks, the maps, the volumes of Marxist theory that nobody had ever bought and nobody had ever sold. They stood in the brown flood like a row of drowned gentlemen. Somewhere at the back, with a wet slap, a shelf of Agatha Christie gave way, and forty murders were solved all at once, with no detective present.

"Appa, take the dictionaries to the loft!"

"I am *carrying* the dictionaries!"

"You are *weighing* them!"

"A man must know what he is losing!" shouted Hari, with his scale in his arm and a Concise Oxford under it.

The door banged open. A woman in an oilskin poncho and rubber boots strode in, carrying a large red toolbox in each hand and followed by a short wet man with a sack of sand.

"Where is the problem?" said Sreeja Iyer.

She was fifty-five, a plumber from Alappuzha, who had been called out for a quite different job in the next street, and had seen the shop's door standing open in a drowning lane with the instinct of her calling. She was a woman of the school of Kerala that regards a crisis as a personal compliment. Her hair was iron grey, her forearms were a mason's, and she had a way of saying "problem" that made the problem feel it had been *found out*.

"The problem," said Arjun, "is the *sea.*"

"The sea is not a problem. The sea is a customer." She slung a tool-bag across the doorway. "Sand-bag the threshold. Sreenath! Raise the lower shelves onto the bricks. Who is in charge of this establishment?"

"I am," said Arjun, and Hari, simultaneously: "I am."

"Then you are both useless. Where is the pump?"

"We do not *have* a pump."

"Then you have a *bucket.* Madam—" this to a green-saried figure that had come through the door with a whoosh and a splash, and was already wading to the nearest shelf "—you, yes, are you family?"

"I am a customer," said Meera.

"Good. Customers carry things."

---

It was a very Kochi sort of rescue, which is to say it involved everybody.
