Word went down the lane by that mysterious route by which news travels in the rain: through the café, the chai-shop, the fishermen mending their nets under the tarpaulin. A line of people formed, thirty, forty, then sixty, from the shop's back door up the narrow stairs to the loft. Fishermen in dripping lungis. Two nuns from the convent school. A Jewish antiques dealer from Jew Town, with a face like a kindly walnut, who announced that he had survived the great flood of 2018 on a single prayerbook and was happy to attempt another. A pair of Gujarati sweet-makers, a troop of Class Six children who had walked out of school without permission and were not, strictly, supposed to be there, and Sreeja Nambiar at their head with her plait tied round her head like a general.

They passed the books from hand to hand, hand over hand, up the stair, in the dark and the wet, in four languages and one rhythm:

*"Take it. Pass it. Take it. Pass it."*

And in the café next door, a young woman in a white apron watched through the window with her arms folded, delivering a commentary to a customer who had not asked for one.

Lakshmi Panicker was twenty-seven, a waitress, and the café's principal asset. She was a woman of enormous good humour and no discretion whatsoever. She had been standing in the doorway since eleven, ostensibly serving banana fritters, in practice conducting a running broadcast to the lane.

"Look at that," said Lakshmi, to the customer. "Look at Arjun Chetta. The man has lifted four hundred books in the last half-hour, and he has not once looked at the one he is *afraid* of losing."

"Which one is that?" said the customer, a sleepy tourist from Hamburg.

"The one with the *poem*." She dropped her voice to a stage whisper that could have been heard in Ernakulam. "I do not know what it says. I know only that every November, a woman in a green sari comes, and the shop goes quiet, and he cannot look at her and I cannot look at him, and there is a banana fritter growing cold in my hand for *seven years*."

"I see," said the tourist, who did not.

"It is the greatest tragedy in Kerala," said Lakshmi, with deep satisfaction. "And nobody will do anything. *I* would, but I am a waitress. I only bring tea to history."

"What a lot of rain," said the tourist, politely.

"That," said Lakshmi, "is also a metaphor."

---

Arjun, at the head of the line, had not looked at Meera for seven minutes.

This was not because he had not seen her. He had seen her at the instant she entered, as a man sees lightning before he hears the thunder, in the green sari with its hem tucked up and her braid coming loose and her face fierce with purpose. He had seen her seize a box of cookbooks and wade away with it as though it were a baby. He had seen her fall into step beside the great Sreeja Iyer and, in thirty seconds, be given the tone of command. He had thought, quite clearly: *I will never be able to speak to her again, because I have seen her in my shop, in a flood, and a man cannot be expected to survive that.*

So he gave her wide berth, in a foot of brown water, with a stack of Tagore.

"Arjun," said Meera, from behind him.

He dropped the Tagore. It floated.

"Oh," said Meera. "I am so sorry. *Gitanjali* is going."

"It is—it is all right, it is—" He plunged for it, and surfaced with a damp, sodden, reproachful volume. "It is a very forgiving book."

"It is *dripping.*"

"It was always a little *emotional.*"

She laughed. It was, he thought, the sound of a very bright coin on a stone floor. He felt his ears go hot, and prayed, in the way of the bookish, that the dark of the shop would hide it.

"It is the twenty-sixth," said Meera.

"Is it?"

"You know it is."

"I—the Annual. It came last night. It is on the top shelf. It is quite safe. It is—" He stopped, with a face of the purest panic. "I have not *looked* at it."

"Good," said Meera, very gravely, and a little pink. "I should not like you to have looked."

"No?"

"I would like to find it," she said, "as it is."

There was a silence. It was the silence of a very large number of things not being said, and it had room in it for the whole flood.

"I will fetch it," said Arjun, and fled up the stairs.

---

He found the crate at the top, safe and dry. He found the copy on the top, the best, with its cover unbent, and he opened it, and there between pages forty-one and forty-two lay the folded square of onion-skin, which he had slipped in at dawn.

*She asked to find it as it is,* thought Arjun. *Does she know? Has she known all along, and been waiting seven years for the shop-boy to say one word?*

He had a pencil in his pocket. It would take only a moment, and a half-sentence, in the margin: *It is I.*

And a voice from below, unmistakable, shouted: "Arjun! The dictionaries have gone! The Oxford is *floating!*"

He put the pencil back.

*Reader, I do not blame him. A man with one hand on a poem and the other on the Oxford English Dictionary is a man pulled by both ends of language. Many have been torn so. Few have recovered.*

---

By dusk the water had begun, grudgingly, to retreat.

It left behind a thin brown shine on the floor, a smell of wet paper that would last a month, and a shop that was, by some miracle of human arms, almost entirely intact. The Marxist theory was ruined. The cookbooks were a complete loss. But upstairs in the loft, in tall dry stacks, with the dictionaries on top and the poetry at the summit, were four thousand books, and in the lane below were two hundred people who had saved them and who were now being fed by Lakshmi's café on the house.

"I wish to record," announced Sreeja Iyer, wiping her hands on her poncho, "that this is the best flood I have been in. Normally the shop is *grateful.* Here everybody is *talking.* Gopal-sir! Come and look at the tide."

This was Gopal Varma, fifty-eight, a village vet from Alappuzha and the most unstoppable matchmaker in three districts. He had come that morning to propose to Hari Panicker a girl from Kottayam with a chemistry degree and a *jathakam* that matched Arjun's on nine points out of ten; he had been trapped in the loft since one o'clock, holding the Concise Oxford over his head, and had formed, in the interval, a different opinion.

"I have been looking at the stars," said Gopal, with a thoughtful frown.

"You cannot see stars. It is raining."

"I have been looking at them *internally.*" He examined his folder. "The Kottayam girl's chart matches Arjun's on nine points. But I have also been observing this *other* young lady, in the green sari. I do not have her chart. But I have observed, in three hours, that when the boy drops a book, she picks it up, and when she drops a book, he picks it up, and neither has dropped a book at the same time. In forty years of horoscopes, I have never seen so *perfect* a synchrony." He closed the folder with a snap. "Hari-sir. I withdraw the girl from Kottayam. The stars have had an internal revision."

"What do the stars say?" said Hari, anxiously.

"They say," said Gopal Varma, "it is a *great deal of rain.*"

---

At the shop door, in the blue light of the end of the day, Arjun put the book into Meera's hands.

He said, "It is a little damp."

"It is a very good book."

"It was always a little damp," said Arjun. "In a way."

"I know," said Meera. She held it a moment, against her chest, and looked at him; and in the look was seven Novembers, and a green sari, and the flood. "Thank you, Arjun. For the…" She stopped. "For the shop. For everything. I will see you next—"

"Yes."

"—*soon.*"

"Yes."

She went down the lane in the failing light, barefoot, her sandals in her bag, with the book wrapped in the end of her sari to shelter it from the last of the rain; and Vishnu Kurup, with his rickshaw bobbing at the corner like a small steamship, took one look at her face, and did not say a word, which for Vishnu Kurup was an act of heroism.

On the back seat, in the light of a dim bulb and the ticking of the rain, Meera Menon opened the book to pages forty-one and forty-two.

It was there: folded small, on onion-skin paper, in pencil.

She read it by the light of passing shop-windows, as she had read it seven times, with her heart doing its usual absurd gymnastics. She came to the last verse, which she knew by heart, and which she read, nonetheless, with the old fresh shock of gladness.

*And if one year the page should come out blank…*

And then she stopped.

For the paper had been caught, in the loft, in a single drop that must have fallen from the leaking roof, and it had run: and where the last line of the poem had been, the single line that said *Understand*, there was now a faint grey smear, the pencil dissolved into a cloud.

She stared at it. She turned it to the light. She could not read it.

"Madam?" said Vishnu from the front. "Madam. Are you well?"

"I am very well," said Meera, in a voice that was unusually small. "The rain has taken the last word."

"That is a great pity."

"Yes." She folded the paper. She kept it against her heart, damp as it was. "But I know what it was."

"Do you?"

"I have *always* known what it was," said Meera Menon, and looked out of the little window at the drowned and glittering town, "and I think, Vishnu, that it is time somebody said it out loud."

"Who?" said Vishnu.

She did not answer. She was smiling at the rain, as one smiles at an old friend with whom one has at last made up one's mind.

---

*Margin note, in pencil, in the hand of S.W.R.:*

> *Entry 0699 (Kochi): "I hid a poem in a book I knew you would buy." Entry 0153 (Kochi): "I buy that book every year to read the poem again."*
>
> *Mark that the Register places them five hundred and forty-six entries apart. It is not far. It is, in the matter of love, the width of a bookshelf, and I have known men to spend a lifetime in the aisle.*
>
> *I will say this for the rain. It takes the last word, as it takes everything. But it cannot take what is already known. And the one thing a flood cannot wash from paper is the shape of the hand that wrote it.*

---

*End of Chapter 9.*


---

## Chapter 10
### Surgeon's Hands

> *"I lost the patient you taught to walk."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0818

---

### SCENE I
*São Paulo, Brazil. The rehabilitation wing of the Hospital Santa Aurora. Seven in the morning. The city outside is already honking, in a dozen million keys.*

São Paulo does not sleep; it merely lowers its voice from a roar to a mutter, and by seven in the morning it has remembered its mistake.

Carlos Mendes, thirty-three, sports physiotherapist, stood at the end of a set of parallel bars and said, in the voice of a man coaxing a nervous horse over a stream: "Dona Cida. One more. It is only a step. A step is the smallest unit of heroism."

"I am seventy-one," said Dona Cida, "and it is a *very large* step."

She took it. The little ward, which contained a dozen patients, six physiotherapists, and one television tuned to a soap opera in which somebody's twin had just returned from the dead, burst into applause. Carlos bowed. He had a warm, crooked, handsome face, brown eyes that crinkled at the outer corners, and the easy manner of a man who has made it his life's work to be useful to people in pain, and has found that if one is sufficiently useful, no one inquires after one's own.

On the fourth finger of his left hand, a plain gold ring caught the light of the fluorescent tube.

He wore it, as he had worn it for three years, with the unselfconscious ease of a thing that is part of the body. His patients assumed that he had a wife. His colleagues, who knew that she had died of a long and slow illness two Marches ago, did not mention it, in the delicate Brazilian way, by mentioning everything else at great length. His friend Pedro Souza, the pharmacist across the street, who never answered telephones but sent voice messages of eleven minutes' duration, had once said: "Carlos, one does not have to take it off. But one might *polish* it less."

He polished it, in fact, on the hem of his white coat, whenever he thought himself unwatched.

*I am a widower,* he had written to an old woman in England, one night, with a bottle of cachaça and a bad conscience, *pretending to be a free man.*

It was a good sentence. It was a true sentence. It had never been spoken.

"Seu Carlos," said a young voice. "Excuse me."

---

He turned.

A boy stood at the entrance to the ward, sixteen, in school uniform, a thin, serious, wide-eyed boy holding a paper bag against his chest, and in his face, at once, Carlos knew the family.

"Leandro," he said, very quietly. "Raimundo's grandson."

"Yes, senhor."

"You came all the way from Santos?"

"The bus is two hours, senhor. My grandmother sends this." The boy held out the bag, which was warm and smelled of cheese. "It is *pão de queijo.* She says, thank you for the fourteen months. She says that you made him a man who could curse you on his own two feet."

It was the exact and only epitaph that Raimundo Teles would have wished.

He had been fifty-eight, a bus driver, a vast and furious man who had fallen from a scaffold while painting his daughter's house and had woken in a hospital with a spine like a broken broomstick, and a verdict that he would never again walk to his own front door. Carlos had spent fourteen months proving the verdict wrong. It had been a long war. Raimundo had insulted his mother, his methods, and the football team he supported, and on the last day, panting between the bars with sweat on his forehead, three hundred steps and not one of them pretty, he had said: "Doutor, I will walk to my own funeral."

Which, three weeks ago, in the narrow and ironic geometry of life, he had very nearly done.

"My grandmother also wants to thank the doctor," said Leandro.

"Which doctor?"

"The one who tried." The boy swallowed. "The lady surgeon. She says the lady cried."

The ward, which was full of noise, became for Carlos Mendes a very long and quiet corridor.

---

### SCENE II
*The same day. The staff cafeteria, 9 p.m. Rain, in great loud sheets, as it comes in São Paulo: not falling so much as arriving.*

Beatriz Lima had been awake for thirty-one hours, and was eating a bowl of beans with the expression of a woman reading a final demand.

She was thirty-one. She was the youngest vascular surgeon in the hospital's history, and she looked it only in one respect, which was that she had not yet learned to stop proving it. She was tall, straight-backed, in green scrubs, with black hair pulled back so tightly it seemed an act of discipline, and eyes that were large and dark and rimmed with the grey of a person who has forgotten the use of sleep. Among the nurses she was called *a Doutora*, in a tone that contained admiration, fear, and an undertone of pity that they never let her hear.

Her mother's name was Lima. She had kept it, after the funeral, as one keeps the key to a house that no longer exists.

"Eat," said her father, from across the table.

"I *am* eating."

"You are pushing a bean from the left side of the bowl to the right. It is a sad little pilgrimage."

Pedro Rocha was sixty, a retired chef, a huge, bald, talkative, gossipy man with the forearms of a blacksmith and the soul of a tabloid. He had arrived at the hospital at eight-thirty with a thermos of feijoada the size of a fire extinguisher, in defiance of every regulation concerning outside food, and had distributed it among the nursing staff with the air of a man dispensing sacraments. He was immensely proud of his daughter, so proud that it had never occurred to him to say so, since to say so would have been a vulgar attempt to describe the sun.

"Papai, I lost a patient."

"You lose patients. It is your profession. You are a surgeon."

"I *lose* them very rarely."

"Then it is the more astonishing that it should have happened to you." He leaned forward. "Who was he?"

"A bus driver."

"A *bus driver!* A man of the road! Salt of the earth! What was his name?"

"Raimundo Teles. He was fifty-eight, and he had been paralysed from the waist, and a physiotherapist taught him to walk. And then on the morning of the surgery, Papai, he *walked in.* Three hundred metres, from the front doors. He refused the stretcher. He told the porters, 'A man who has walked for Carlos Mendes can walk into any hospital in Brazil.' And I stood at the end of the corridor and watched him come." She put down the spoon. "And the aneurysm gave way at four minutes past ten, on the table, and there was nothing, *nothing*, not a thing I could do."

Pedro Rocha said nothing. For a talkative man, it was a feat of love.

"I have never met the physiotherapist," said Beatriz. "I have only seen his name on charts. But I think about it every night. I think: a man spent fourteen months, and made a man whole, and then I—" Her voice caught. "I could not hold him a *morning.*"

"Daughter." Her father reached across the table and put a hand like a spade over hers. "It is not your fault. Do you think the Lord, who is not a fool, would send a man a physiotherapist for fourteen months and a surgeon for ten minutes if He did not know how to count?"

She laughed. It was a small, startled, wet laugh, and she covered her face with her free hand.

"Ah," said Pedro. "There she is. Now let me show you something that will cheer you up." He took out his phone with the pride of one displaying a grandchild. "You know, of course, that I have a *blog.*"

"Papai, nobody reads your—"

"A hundred and forty thousand people have read *this.*"

---

The photograph showed an empty counter: a long counter of pale wood, in a very small shop; eight stools, a red-and-white curtain, a steam-clouded window. In the foreground a bowl of ramen stood at the third stool from the left: perfect, golden, steaming, with a single sheet of seaweed and an egg cut in half, and no one before it.

Under it, in Portuguese and in a clumsy English translation, Pedro had written:

*Osaka, spring. The chef told me, through the interpreter, that he makes one bowl every night for a woman who stopped coming. He sets it at her stool. He does not eat it. At closing he pours it away, and in the morning, he begins again. I asked, "How long?" The chef did not answer. He only wiped the counter.*

Her father wiped his eyes with a napkin. "It is *very* popular," he said. "A man in Curitiba has proposed to his girlfriend. And nobody has said a word about the *ramen.*"

Beatriz looked at the photograph for a long time.

A single bowl, steaming, before an empty stool. A thing made every night for one who is not there. She did not know why her throat had closed; she was a doctor, and wished to blame the beans.

*I know that bowl,* she thought, and could not have said why.

---

### SCENE III
*A lift, in the old wing, at a quarter past ten. The storm has taken the lights. The elevator, one of those great brass antiques that the Hospital Santa Aurora refuses to retire on grounds of sentiment, has stopped between the second and third floors.*

It was, of course, a conspiracy.

The reader should not be surprised. A hospital contains choirs, locksmiths, and matchmakers in roughly equal proportions, and when all three are present, the result is inevitable.

The choir was that of Fábio Santos, a thirty-year-old choir director from Campinas, who conducted the hospital's Christmas ensemble every Thursday in the ground-floor atrium and who, being of an artistic nature, had a great many old letters in his bag and a great many opinions in his head. The locksmith was Thiago Oliveira, forty-one, a vain and glittering man with a waxed moustache, who had been summoned by the hospital porters to rescue the elevator, and who, being a matchmaker by vocation and a locksmith by trade, regarded the entire building as a lock with a very obvious solution.

"Who is in the lift?" he asked the porter.

"The Doutora Beatriz. And the physiotherapist. Seu Carlos."

"Both?"

"Both, Seu Thiago."

"Hm." Thiago Oliveira put down his bag, and looked at the ceiling with an expression of great professional delicacy. "It will take," he said, "approximately forty minutes."

"Forty? It is a simple fault. A child could—"

"A *good* lock," said Thiago, "is a slow lock."

And he sat down, and began, with a flourish, to lay out his tools in order of size.

*Mark this, reader. In forty minutes of a stuck lift, more things have been said than in forty years of dinner.*

---

It was dark. It was warm. There was a crack of emergency light along the floor, thin and amber, and by it they could see each other's shoes.

"I am sorry," said Carlos. "I was on my way to the pharmacy."

"I was on my way to a bed." She was standing with her back to the wall, arms crossed, in the gloom. "You are Mendes."

"I am."

"Lima. Beatriz Lima." There was a pause. "I was Raimundo Teles's surgeon."

"I know."

"I should have come to find you."

"I should have come to find *you*," said Carlos.

The elevator creaked. Somewhere beneath them, down in the atrium, a thin sound began, a choir with its hymn-book open, and the notes crept up the shaft like a faint, sweet smoke.

"He walked in," said Beatriz. "You must know that. He walked into my hospital, three hundred metres, in front of the whole ward, and he said your name. He said it to the porters, to the nurse, to the lift. I stood there, and I thought, *This is a man who has been given his life back. And I am about to—*" She stopped. "I have not been able to put it down."

"Doutora."

"Do not tell me it was not my fault. Everyone says so, and it is a kindness, and I cannot *use* it."

"I was not going to say that," said Carlos.

There was a silence, thick as velvet.

"I was going to say," he said, "that I have thought about that morning every day. Not about the aneurysm. About the three hundred metres. Do you know what I realised? Fourteen months. And in all that time, he never once walked for *me.* He walked to spite me, to prove me wrong, to see my face. But that morning he walked for *himself.* To a hospital. Into the hands of a woman he had never met. It was the whole point." His voice roughened. "I taught him to walk, Doutora. You gave him a place to walk *to.* There are not many surgeons who could say that."

She was silent. In the thin light he saw her put a hand to her mouth.

"That," said Beatriz, at last, unsteadily, "is the first thing anyone has said to me in three weeks that I can bear."

"I will say more if you want. I am a physiotherapist. I can say things for hours in a very reassuring voice."

She laughed. It broke out of her like water out of a cracked jug, and she slid down the wall of the lift to sit upon the floor, laughing and weeping at once, in her crumpled scrubs. Carlos, after a moment, sat down on the other side, at a safe and gentlemanly distance of about a metre, and found a clean handkerchief in his pocket, and extended it across the gap.

She took it. Their hands touched.

And in the amber glimmer, she saw it: a plain gold band on the fourth finger of a warm brown hand.

It is a curious thing, the speed of the heart. It can fall four floors in a quarter of a second.

"Your wife," said Beatriz, drawing her hand back with great composure, "must be very patient, to have a husband who sits on floors with strangers."

Carlos looked at the ring.

For a moment he opened his mouth. *Not what you think,* he thought. *It is exactly what you think. It is neither.* Words stood in his throat like men in a doorway, each waving the others past.

"She—" he said. "It is—a difficult matter."

"I am sure it is," said Beatriz, with the clipped kindness of a surgeon closing a wound. "Thank you for the handkerchief. I am very sorry for keeping you from the pharmacy."

*Ah,* says the Keeper, quietly, from the dark between the floors. *There it is. He might have said: I am a widower. A word of four syllables, and a world of difference. And she might have said: I should like to know. And neither did, and the lift did not move.*

---

> *O small gold circle, three years on my hand,
> You are the thing that says a thing is so
> When I cannot. You are my grammar. You
> Stand where a verb should stand. I never said,
> "She's gone." I said, "My wife." The tense is wrong,
> And no one corrects me, for they are kind.
> I wear you as a man might wear a bandage,
> Long past the time the wound has closed. And yet,
> If I should take you off, I fear I'd find
> The skin beneath is pale, and strange, and mine.*

---

The lights came on at ten fifty-two.

They came on with a great shudder, like a house waking. The lift gave a sob, and a lurch, and began to rise; the doors opened on the third floor, and a golden wedge of light fell in upon two people sitting very straight on opposite sides of the floor, each studying the ceiling.

And from the stair below, in four-part harmony, with great conviction, came Fábio Santos's choir, singing a carol which had been chosen, apparently, in the belief that it was Christmas in November.

"*Thiago!*" shouted a nurse. "What took so long?"

"A very old lock," said Thiago Oliveira, rising from his tool-box and brushing his moustache. He glanced at the elevator, in which a surgeon was standing up with great dignity and a physiotherapist was handing her a lost shoe, and in his face there was something that in any other man would have been tenderness and in Thiago was merely vanity. "They do not make them like that any more. I should say they were *made* for each other."

"Which lock?" said Fábio, a little confused.

"*Any* of them," said Thiago, and sailed off in search of his fee.

Beatriz stepped out first. She turned, in the doorway, and said, with perfect composure: "Seu Carlos. Thank you. I think we shall not need to speak of this again."

"No?"

"No." And then, a little more softly: "But I shall be at the rehab wing on Thursday, for a follow-up. A patient I am concerned about. If that is... not an imposition."

"It will be," said Carlos, "an honour."

"It is a *follow-up*," said Beatriz Lima, very sternly, and walked away down the corridor with her chin up, and her hand, which she did not know she was doing, pressed to the pocket where she had put his handkerchief.

---

### SCENE IV
*Osaka, Japan. Twelve hours ahead. It is the next morning, and has been, here, all along. Six a.m. in the ward of Fukushima, where the ramen shops put out their curtains in the dawn like flags.*

There is an old joke, among those who live between time zones, that it is always tomorrow somewhere. The people in São Paulo, who were wiping the last of the storm from their windows at four in the afternoon, had been preceded to the day by a good twelve hours, in a city on the other side of the world; and in that city, in a narrow apartment above a stationer's, a woman of thirty-three stood in her kitchen at six in the morning, with a cup of tea she could not taste, looking at a phone.

Mei Sato had been a food critic for eleven years. She had written, for a great Osaka newspaper, the best reviews in the history of the city: a cadence of salt and smoke, sweetness and acid, that readers had called *a hymn in a bowl.* And in the spring, one morning, without warning, with no pain and no fever and no dignity, she had put a spoonful of miso soup into her mouth, and tasted nothing at all. It had been, she thought, like hearing the world's last piano go quiet.

She had told no one. She wrote now from memory. She was good at it. She was a clever woman, and could construct a review of any bowl in Osaka from the vocabulary of her past, and no one, so far, had known the difference. But she had stopped going out. And she had stopped, in particular, going to a very small ramen shop in an alley in Fukushima ward, eight stools, run by a taciturn man called Tanabe, where she had eaten, on the third stool from the left, near the pipe where the steam rose, every Tuesday for six years.

She had not been back since March. *A critic who cannot taste is a liar with a pen,* she thought. *And a woman who cannot taste cannot sit at his counter. He would know. He would look at me and know.*

On her phone, a friend had sent a link, with a single line: *Is this your Tanabe?*

She opened it.

A photograph. A counter. A bowl. An empty stool, the third from the left, near the pipe.

The caption was in Portuguese, which she did not read. But beneath it ran an English translation, and she read that, very slowly, with her hand on the cold kitchen counter.

*He makes one bowl every night for a woman who stopped coming.*

She put the phone down.

Across the city, at that hour, she knew, a man of thirty-four sat alone behind a counter before opening, in the clean quiet of a closed shop, skimming a pot he had begun at three in the morning. And between that man and a stranger's photograph, in a kitchen, with a cup of tea that tasted of nothing, stood the one woman for whom it had been made.

"Daichi," said a voice, in a shop an hour's walk away, to a bewildered historian who had arrived at dawn with a mobile phone and the news. "You are telling me that I am famous in *Brazil.*"

"A hundred and forty thousand hearts, Tanabe-san! A woman in Recife says you have ruined her mother's soup!"

Hiroshi Tanabe did not look at the phone. He did not look at the empty stool. He lifted the ladle, tasted the broth, adjusted nothing, and said, with the economy of a man who had spent one sentence a day for six months:

"Eat."

At the kitchen window of a flat above a stationer's, Mei Sato put on her coat.

She stood in the hall. She took it off.

She put it on again.

*Tuesday,* she thought. *It is only Tuesday. I will go on Tuesday. And I will tell him the truth, or I will tell him a lie, and either way I shall have been there.*

Far away, a boy called Leandro sat on a bus back to Santos with an empty paper bag on his knee, a surgeon sat in her car in a hospital garage with a man's handkerchief in her pocket, and a physiotherapist polished a ring on the hem of his coat.

And at a small shop on a narrow street, a bowl was set on the counter, as every night, and every morning, at the third stool from the left, and steamed, as though it knew.

---

*Margin note, in pencil, in the hand of S.W.R.:*

> *Entry 0016 and Entry 0818, São Paulo. A ring and a scalpel. He is afraid to take off the one; she is afraid to put down the other. They are two hands, each trying to hold the same grief and each convinced that the other has the better grip.*
>
> *Entry 0510 and Entry 0810, Osaka. A bowl and a tongue. Do you see how the world is made? The one cooks for the guest who cannot taste. The other cannot taste, and will not sit at the bowl. It is the oldest comedy and it is, as always, a tragedy by Thursday.*
>
> *And I notice that the lift, which is a kind of room, stopped between two floors. That is the whole state of the human heart. It is always between two floors. It is always waiting for a locksmith with a sense of occasion.*

---

*End of Chapter 10.*


---

## Chapter 11
### The Founder and the Dressmaker

> *"I only design clothes for the woman I am afraid to become."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0954

---

### SCENE I
*Yaba, Lagos, Nigeria. Adeniran Court, a five-storey building that was once a bank, then a church, and is now a cluster of ambitions with a shared generator. Six in the morning. The generator has begun.*

In Lagos, the sun does not rise. It is *switched on*, by a large and unseen hand, at an hour when everybody has already been awake for three hours, and the first sound of the day is not a bird but a generator.

It is a sound of enormous character. It is a cough, a clearing of the throat, a long grinding grievance, and then a steady and defiant drone, as of a man determined to have the last word in an argument that began in nineteen-eighty. Under the drone, in a city of twenty million, the danfo minibuses begin to hoot, the *okada* motorbikes weave like needles through the go-slow, a woman at the corner begins to fry *puff-puff* in a pan the size of a cartwheel, and from the Third Mainland Bridge there rises the roar of a metropolis that has never in its history been asked to wait.

On the fourth floor of Adeniran Court, in an office with a whiteboard, nine desks, and a very handsome neon sign that said **AJO**, a young man sat alone before a laptop, and read the same bank notification for the eleventh time.

*Your balance is insufficient for the scheduled transfer.*

"It is not *insufficient*," said Emeka Okafor, aloud, to nobody. "It is *shy.*"

He was twenty-eight, the founder of a company named for the *ajo*, the old Yoruba savings circle in which a dozen neighbours each put a little money in a pot every week and take the whole pot in turn, so that a market woman can buy a freezer and a tailor can buy a machine, with no bank and no interest and nothing at all but trust. He had built a phone application to do the same thing on a grand scale. For two years it had been the most promising thing in the building. It had been featured in a magazine. It had won a prize in Nairobi, and a lunch in London, and the heart of an investor who had said, with tears in his eyes, that Emeka was *going to change Africa.*

And then, in March, the investor had changed *his mind.*

It had gone quickly, as a good building goes: first the funding, then the clients, then the app store ranking, and finally, in the quiet of a Thursday, the last of the sense that anyone would ever want to talk to him about it again. The company was dead. It was simply that nobody had told its heart.

He had nine employees. He paid them, on the twenty-fifth of each month, from his own account: from his savings, from his car, from the sale of a good watch, from a loan against a flat in Surulere, from the last of his father's gift. He had not told them. He had not told his sister. He had not told the neon sign, which went on, every morning, with its hopeful buzz, and which he had begun to hate.

*My company is dead,* he had written to an old woman in England, on a night in which the generator had failed, *and I keep paying salaries from my own pocket.*

He had meant it as a confession. He had not realised it was also a budget.

---

### SCENE II
*Mama Put Joint, behind the building. Noon. A tin roof, long benches, and enormous steaming pots. A woman of sixty in a sailor's cap is eating* amala *with the manner of a captain taking a ship.*

"You are looking," said Ifeoma Bello, "like a man who has swallowed an anchor."

She was sixty, a tiny, wiry, mahogany woman from Ibadan, who had gone to sea at nineteen as the only woman on a Lagos-registered freighter, and had spent thirty-one years on the oceans of the world, rising to a ship's first mate and acquiring a vocabulary that could blister a bulkhead. She had retired with a pension, a parrot-handled cane, and a very large number of opinions, and she now invested small sums of money in the young, on the condition that they take her to lunch.

"I am well, Auntie."

"You are lying, and it is the first thing a young man learns, and the last thing he learns to do *well*." She tore a morsel of *amala*, dipped it in *ewedu* and gbegiri, and chewed with great deliberation. "What is the number?"

"Which number?"

"The number you are not saying."

He looked at his plate. "Four million, one hundred thousand naira. Outstanding. After the payroll."

"And the company?"

"It has—" He stopped. "Auntie, it has three customers. They are all my cousins."

"Hm." Ifeoma Bello put down her morsel, and wiped her fingers on a napkin with an air of solemn purpose. "I will tell you a thing from the sea. There is a story of the captain who goes down with his ship. It is a very fine story and you will find it in every poem. In thirty-one years, young man, I met three captains who went down with their ships. They were all *very* dead." She raised an eyebrow. "The captain who lives is the one who writes the lifeboat list on the *first* night of the leak, and lets his crew read it."

"They will blame me."

"Naturally. They will blame you for a week. And then they will remember that you paid them for nine months from your own pocket, and they will blame you for being a fool, which is a different thing, and keeps better."

"How do you know I—"

"Emeka," said Ifeoma gently, "you have sold your watch. You have a pale line on your wrist like a very sad bracelet."

He looked at his wrist. He put his hand under the table.

"Pride," said the old sailor, "is a heavy ballast. A ship needs some. Not so much that it cannot rise." She pushed the pot of *ewedu* towards him. "Eat. And go and look at the third floor. I am told that there is a young woman there who is making something you could learn from."

"A woman?"

"A *dress*," said Ifeoma Bello, with great dignity, "is also a company. It also dies if nobody pays. Go."

---

### SCENE III
*The third floor. A workroom, gold with afternoon. Bolts of cloth in every colour of the earth: adire in indigo, aso-oke in rust and wheat, ankara in a hundred voices. A long table. A mannequin in the corner.*

Now we must make the acquaintance of a young woman who lives in her own opera.

Chidinma Eze was twenty-seven, a fashion designer from Enugu, who had come to Lagos at twenty with a suitcase, a sewing machine, and a conviction that the whole city was a stage on which she had been unaccountably cast as the maid. She was small, quick, and brilliant, with a short crop of black hair, a mouth that could convey eleven emotions per sentence, and a way of entering a room as though she had been announced. She wore her own designs always: that day a gold-and-indigo wrap with sleeves like a pair of wings, and a headscarf that made her look like the figurehead of a very expensive ship.

She was at that moment kneeling at the feet of a mannequin, with a mouth full of pins.

"No," she was saying, round them. "*No.* The shoulder must be sharper. Sharper, my dear. You are a woman who walks into a boardroom and *causes it to be silent.* You do not have a *gentle* shoulder."

The mannequin did not argue.

It stood in the corner, headless, in a jacket of heavy indigo adire with hand-pleated sleeves, and beside it, on a hook, hung eight garments in different states of completion. It was the strangest thing in the studio, and the most beautiful, and Chidinma, who confided in it as other women confide in their mothers, called it *Her.*

"Excuse me," said a voice from the door. "I am told that the sea requires me to go and look at a dress."

She did not turn. "Who is there?"

"Emeka Okafor. Fourth floor. The, ah, *Ajo* people."

"The neon people."

"The neon people."

"You are the ones who have been stealing my diesel."

"We pay our levy."

"You have *not* paid your levy for two months. The generator committee has a list. You are number three. I am number one, because I am saintly." She took the pins from her mouth and turned, at last, on her knees, and looked up at the tall, tired, handsome, creased young man in the doorway, with a lock of hair falling into his eyes and a pale line on his wrist. And, because she was a designer, she saw the whole of him in a glance, as a tailor does: the slope of the shoulder, the tension in the jaw, the shirt that had been ironed with great care and a failing hope.

*That man,* she thought, *has not slept in a month.*

"I will pay the levy," said Emeka.

"You will not," said Chidinma. "I paid it. For both of us."

There was a short and terrible silence.

"I did not ask you to."

"No. You did not ask anyone for anything. It is a *remarkable* condition." She stood and brushed off her knees with a theatrical flourish. "Do not worry. It is four thousand naira. I charged it to the ministry of nobody."

"Why?"

"Because the generator is a *commons,*" said Chidinma, "and the whole of the building is a *tragedy* of it, and I am an actress at heart. If I see a man with a grave face and a fine shirt and a company that is making the sound of a deflating tyre, I do what any decent woman does. I pay his diesel and say nothing, and then I wait for the opening to say it *very* loudly." She smiled. "Welcome to the third floor."

He looked at the mannequin.

"Who is she?"

"Nobody." The smile went out. "It is a dress form."

"It has a name."

"Everything has a name." She went rather pink. "It is a thing I do. Do not mind it."

"May I—" He came into the room. He stood before the jacket, and he looked at it in silence, for rather a long time, with his hands in his pockets, the way one looks at a diagram that one does not understand but cannot bear to leave. It was the most extraordinary garment he had ever seen. It was powerful. It had a collar like a drawn bow. It looked like the coat of a woman who had decided, at last, to be *looked at.*

"It is not a *design,*" said Emeka. "It is an *argument.*"

Chidinma looked at him for a moment in a manner she had not looked at anyone for a long time.

"Yes," she said, very quietly. "That is exactly what it is."

---

*In her workroom, that night, with the machines asleep, she speaks to the empty room, and to the headless guest, in the only manner a designer can trust; which is to say, in the language of the thing she cannot afford to say in daylight.*

> *I have been sewing thee these seven years,
> My silent lady of the sharp-cut sleeve.
> I never gave thee eyes, for fear of finding
> Thou lookedst somehow like myself. Thou art
> The woman I am frightened of: unbowed,
> Unasking, tall, and not apologetic;
> The woman who has never said, "I'm sorry
> To take up room." I dress thee every season.
> I say, "She is a fiction. She is cloth."
> And then I stand before thee, in the dark,
> And measure: here the shoulder; there the waist;
> And find that every inch of thee is mine.
> It is a mortal thing to make a woman
> Whom thou wouldst love, and tremble to become.*

She stood in the dim, with a pin in her hand, until the generator coughed and went out. Then she laughed, once, at herself, and said, "You see, *Her*, this is the problem with being theatrical. The cure is worse than the complaint."

---

### SCENE IV
*The next evening. The lobby of Adeniran Court. The light has gone. It has not merely gone: it has been taken by the State, with a smile, and without notice, and a crowd of forty people stands in the dark with their mobile phones lit, like a congregation in a cathedral of small blue candles.*

It was the night of the show.

It had been meant to take place in a great ballroom on Victoria Island, with a runway, a sponsor, and a DJ. Eight weeks ago the venue had been booked. Three weeks ago the sponsor had withdrawn. A week ago the venue had demanded a deposit of two million, three hundred thousand naira, which Chidinma had not got and could not borrow. And yesterday she had called her father in Enugu, a retired tailor, a devout and silver-haired man with a stern face and a very tender conscience, who had said, over a faint line, in the voice of a man who has said the thing many times: "Nnem, a coat is a coat, whether it is hung in a palace or a lobby. The woman who wears it will not ask."

So the show was in the lobby.

The tenants of Adeniran Court had made themselves its audience: the lawyers from the second floor, the three young men who ran an app for hailing motorcycles, the woman with the dental practice, a pack of children from the compound, Mama Ngozi from the stairwell. There were no seats but plastic chairs. The runway was a strip of ankara cloth laid down the length of the tile. There were eight models, all friends. There was a single working speaker, and a cousin of Chidinma's in a bow tie with a laptop; and there was an enormous silence, black as an inkwell, in the middle of which, with great ceremony, the power failed.

"*Abeg,*" said somebody in the audience. "Not again."

"It is a *design feature,*" said somebody else.

Chidinma, in the wings, in gold, closed her eyes.

"Chineke," she whispered. "It is a joke. It is a very bad joke, and God is the comedian."

"Madam?"

She opened them. On the stair, with the lights of eleven phones behind him like a very small constellation, stood Emeka Okafor in his ironed shirt, flanked by a short, powerful young woman in coveralls with a spanner in her belt and a face of divine patience.

"This is Ngozi," said Emeka. "She is a mechanic."

"I am her *best friend,*" said Ngozi Afolabi, who was thirty-three and had been, for six years, the sole person on earth to whom Chidinma Eze did not play. "And I have been downstairs for twenty minutes, and your generator has the soul of a man who has been told it is Monday. It needs a *belt.*"

"We do not have a belt!"

"*I* have a belt," said Emeka, "and it is in the car, and I will go and fetch it, and I will also bring the cables from the office, and the nine laptops, which will be the light." He paused. "It is a thing we know about. We are a company that has been running on very little for some time."

Chidinma stared at him.

"You are a founder," said Ngozi Afolabi, wiping a spanner on her coverall, "and a man of *infrastructure.* This is a rare thing. Do not waste him."

"I am not wasting—" said Chidinma. "I am only—"

"Go on," said Emeka, quietly. "Get ready. It will be lit."

*Reader, it was.*

For in fifteen minutes the nine desks of AJO had been emptied, and nine staff members, whom their employer had supposed to be ignorant of the entire state of his finances, filed down the stair in a solemn procession, each carrying a laptop, an extension cable, and an expression of great composure. Tobi, the youngest, a twenty-four-year-old with spectacles and a ferocious talent for code, set down his machine on the lobby floor and opened it with a click. It lit a small circle of tile in a pale electric blue. Beside it, another. And another.

They arranged the nine screens in a long line along the sides of the ankara runway, like the lamps along a harbour. Each of them, on a white background, burned a single word, which Tobi had typed in thirty seconds, with the dry humour of the very young.

*WELCOME.*

*ENTER.*

*PAY.*

*(Support available.)*

"Oga," said Tobi, to his employer, as the crowd laughed and the light settled over the tile like warm water. "We have been reading your bank alerts on the office printer for two months. We thought you would tell us when you were ready."

Emeka did not speak.

"We are not stupid, oga," said Tobi, very gently. "We are *nine.* We have been quietly agreeing, in the toilet, that we shall keep coming to work until the building falls."

---

The show began in the glow of nine screens, and it was the best thing that had ever happened in Adeniran Court.

The first model came down the cloth in a skirt of golden aso-oke that moved like a lit bell. The second, in an adire wrap the colour of the deep Atlantic. The third, the fourth, the fifth: coats and gowns and caftans cut from the old loom-cloths of three peoples, remade as armour, as laughter, as a woman who knows her price. The audience went quiet; then, as the sleeves went by, it began to murmur; and by the sixth garment they were on their feet.

And at the back, by the stair, a very old woman in a purple wrapper and white head-tie, who had been standing in the stairwell of the building for eleven years, offering to any who would listen the word of the Lord, said, in a voice that carried: "*I have seen it!*"

"Mama Ngozi?" said Emeka, beside her.

"I saw it in a dream, my son." She was fifty-nine, the leader of a small chapel in Yaba, a woman of true and unwavering faith and no sense of direction whatsoever; and she gripped his sleeve with a hand like a bird's. "I saw that a man in this building would lose everything on a Thursday and gain it on a Friday. I did not know what it meant. I thought it was the stock market."

"It is *Wednesday,* Mama."

"Then," said Mama Ngozi, with perfect serenity, "I am early." She looked at the runway, and the lit faces, and the nine screens glimmering, and the girl in gold at the end of the cloth with her hands clasped before her in a posture that no one had ever seen on her. "But I do not think the Lord *minds.*"

And there was a hush, because the last model had not come out.

---

She had not come.

There was a gap. The whole room felt it. There was a silent beat at the end of the runway, where the eighth garment should have come: the jacket, the indigo, the sharp-shouldered one, the armoured one that cost her eleven weeks. Beneath it in the dark, with a hand on her mouth, stood a young woman in gold who had expected to see it lifted down from its hook by a friend who had that morning been called away to a funeral in Anambra.

"Where is *Her?*" whispered Chidinma. "Ngozi, where is the eighth?"

"The model—her train—"

"She is not coming?"

"She will not come."

She looked at the jacket on its hook. She looked at the dark. She looked, for the first time in seven years, directly at the woman she had been making.

*It is a jacket. It is cloth.*

*It is not cloth.*

She took it down.

*Mark this, reader.* A person does not walk into the thing she fears with a flourish. She walks into it with one foot and a bad heartbeat, in the wrong shoes. Chidinma Eze put on the coat in the dark, and it fitted as if it had been cut against her bones, and she stepped onto the ankara cloth between two lines of glowing screens, with forty people in the dark before her, and the whole tall frightening woman she had stitched, shoulder by shoulder, for seven years, walked into the light.

No one spoke.

At the end of the runway, in the nine small blue lights, a young man in an ironed shirt stood up out of his chair, without knowing that he had, with his hands at his sides and a pale line on his wrist, and thought, with absolute clarity, in the middle of the end of a company:

*I know that woman. I will do anything not to lose her.*

And then, from somewhere at the back, the generator, with a long shuddering gasp, caught.

The lights came on.

It is a curious fact about the people of Lagos that they will applaud a thing for any reason at all, but they applaud a thing that is *true* as though it were a goal.

---

*Margin note, in pencil, in the hand of S.W.R.:*

> *Entry 0051 and Entry 0954. A company that is dead and keeps its payroll; a woman who wears her fear and dresses it as courage. It is the same condition. Each is performing an act of faith in a thing no longer visible.*
>
> *I would like it noted that nine young people sat in a toilet and agreed to go on working for a man who had not told them the truth. It is the closest thing to a ledger I have seen in forty-five years. There is a kind of love that doesn't go in the register of love at all. It goes in the payroll.*
>
> *The woman will have to learn to be seen. The man will have to learn to be helped. I do not know which is harder. I only know that the generator coughed first, and the lights came on after.*

---

*End of Chapter 11.*

## Chapter 12
### Flour and Violets

> *"I still bake my wife's bread every Sunday."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0844

---

### SCENE I
*Lyon, France. The Croix-Rousse, the steep hill of the silk-weavers. Sunday, a quarter to four in the morning. A fog from the two rivers has climbed the hill and is looking in at the windows.*

At the hour when the honest are asleep and the dishonest are, for once, at a loss, a baker was talking to a lump of dough.

"You are too wet," said Pierre Dubois. "It is the weather. Do not take it personally."

He was forty-five, large and stooped and flour-white to the elbow, with a nose that had been broken at rugby and a pair of hands that had never in their lives been idle. He had inherited the shop from his father and the habit of silence from his mother, and had added, by his own labour, a reputation for the best *pain de campagne* on the hill and the worst temper. He kneaded with his whole back, in the yellow light of the oven, in the warm, sweet, living dark of a bakery before dawn, which is the nearest thing on earth to the inside of a heart.

It was Sunday. On Sundays he made *the other bread.*

It was a round loaf, dark-crusted, with walnuts and a little rye and a pinch of cumin that no one else in Lyon would have dared, and it had been invented in the kitchen of a small flat in the Rue Imbert-Colomès by a woman called Odile, who had died four years ago in the spring of a thing that had taken eleven months to say its name. She had baked it every Sunday of their marriage. He had never in his life made it until the first Sunday after she was gone, when he had woken at four, and found his hands in the flour, and understood that they had decided without him.

He had never sold it. He gave it away. Every Sunday at six a boy of thirteen came on a bicycle, and took twelve loaves in a basket, and delivered them to the old and the lonely of the hill, who had no idea who sent them, and who ate them in silence, with butter, as if they were an answer to a prayer.

*I still bake my wife's bread every Sunday,* he had written, to a stranger, in the dark. *I do not know how to stop. I do not think I want to.*

"Pierre."

He turned. The boy was in the doorway: Baptiste Lefèvre, thirteen, a thin, severe child in an oversized anorak, with a school satchel, a bicycle helmet, and the expression of a very small and uncompromising judge.

"You are early."

"I am never early. *You* are late."

"It is four o'clock."

"It is *five to,*" said Baptiste, "and you have flour on your face. It is the look of a man who has been thinking."

"Go and sit down."

"I do not sit. I *witness.*" He looked about the shop with narrowed eyes. "Has it come yet?"

Pierre's hands stopped in the dough.

"Has what come?"

"The thing," said Baptiste, with the impatience of the young explaining the obvious to the old, "that is on your step every Sunday. At half-past three. I am a boy who gets up. I have *seen.*"

---

For eleven weeks, on Sunday mornings, a small bunch of violets had been laid at the baker's door.

They were Parma violets, the sweet-scented double kind that Lyon's gardeners coax into bloom under glass in the cold months: a dozen blooms, tight as a clenched fist, tied with a grey ribbon, in a twist of brown paper. They had no card. They had no name. They lay on the worn stone step in the first light, damp with the fog and smelling of a spring that was months away, and Pierre, who found them each week when he opened the shutter, had begun, to his own annoyance, to look forward to the finding.

He did not know who. He had asked. He had put it, in his gruff and wounded manner, to every female customer who had come in that month: "Madame, did you leave some flowers?" and had been given, in return, a series of long stares of the kind that a woman gives a man who has just asked whether she is in love with him.

Now he put down the dough and went to the door.

He opened it a crack, as one opens the door on a stranger, and the fog came in, white and cold, and with it, curling through the cold, faint as a note from a distant room: *violets.*

On the step lay a small twist of brown paper.

He looked up. Down the steep hill, at the corner, in the lamplight, for a single moment, a figure in a long grey coat was walking away, quickly, with its head down, past the shuttered bank and the tobacconist's, toward the river and the flower market. A woman. He saw the line of her shoulder, and a scarf the colour of a pigeon's wing, and then the fog closed round her like a hand.

He did not call out. His throat had forgotten how.

"It is the florist," said Baptiste, at his elbow.

Pierre turned. "*What?*"

"Madame Laurent. From the Rue de la Martinière. The one with the sad shop." The boy shrugged, with magnificent indifference. "I do not know why. I have simply seen her. She leaves them and she looks at the window and she goes. I did not tell you, because I was not asked, and I am not good at apologising when I am wrong."

"You were not *wrong.*"

"I might have been. It is a risk."

*Mark this, reader.* There is a great deal of wisdom in thirteen-year-olds, and nearly all of it is used to avoid being embarrassed.

Pierre stood a long moment with the violets in his hand. Then he went back inside, and wiped his palms, and took from the cooling rack the last loaf of the morning, the dark round one with the walnuts, and wrapped it in a clean cloth.

"I have always baked twelve," he said gruffly. "Today you will take thirteen."

"To whom?"

"To the Rue de la Martinière. Say nothing."

"I never do," said Baptiste, with dignity, "unless I am not asked."

---

*At the other end of the hill, in a very small shop, a woman in a long grey coat had just come in out of the fog, and was hanging up her scarf with a hand that was not quite steady.*

Margaux Laurent was forty-two, a florist, a widow of three years' standing, with soft brown hair going silver at the temple, and a way of pausing before she spoke as though she were arranging the sentence in a vase. Her husband Luc had been a violin-maker and had died quickly, in the middle of a Tuesday, and she had been left with a shop called *Les Violettes,* an unpaid lease, and a house that was too quiet by half. She was gentle and humorous and exceedingly shy, and had, eleven weeks ago, done the most daring thing of her life.

She had been walking to the flower market in the dark. She had passed the bakery on the Croix-Rousse, where the lamp was lit; and she had looked, for no reason, through the window, and seen a large man with his arms in a trough of dough, and his shoulders shaking.

It is a thing we are not supposed to see. She had stood there for a full minute in the fog, with a bunch of violets in her basket meant for the market. And then she had done what a florist does, which is to know when a thing is not a bunch of flowers, but a sentence.

She laid them on the step. She walked away.

*I left the flowers at your door,* she had written, afterwards, to an old woman in England, with the kettle going cold. *It was always me.*

Now she stood in her little shop among the zinc buckets and the paper cones and the smell of wet green stalks, and said to her assistant, who happened to be her twenty-year-old brother (the hill, it must be said, had an inordinate number of Baptistes) and who was at that moment arranging chrysanthemums in a manner she found personally offensive: "He saw me."

"Who?"

"The baker."

"Did he *speak* to you?"

"He did not speak. He *stood.*" She sank onto a stool. "He looked at me through a fog. I have not been looked at through a fog since nineteen-ninety-nine."

"What do you intend?"

"To go on," said Margaux, with a gentle and appalled dignity, "and to be a coward at the same time. It is a skill. I have been practising it for three years."

The shop bell rang. A thin boy in an oversized anorak stood in the door with a basket, and in it, wrapped in a clean cloth, one round dark loaf, warm still, and smelling of walnuts and a pinch of something that no one else in Lyon would have dared.

"From a witness," said Baptiste Lefèvre, and set it on the counter, and fled.

Margaux Laurent looked at the loaf. She broke it. The steam rose, and she put her face into it, as one puts one's face into a flower.

---

### SCENE II
*Kraków, Poland. The workshop of a clockmaker on Floriańska Street, a long dark room that ticks, as a forest breathes, with a hundred small lives. Noon. The great bugle of St. Mary's Church is about to sound from the tower.*

In Kraków, at every hour, a trumpeter climbs to the window of the tallest tower in the square, and plays a short, old, sad tune to the four corners of the earth; and at the exact moment the tune would reach its end, it stops.

It is cut in the middle of a note, by tradition, because on one afternoon seven hundred years ago the player on the tower was shot in the throat by a Tatar arrow while sounding the alarm, and the city has kept the tune unfinished ever since, in his honour. So that every hour, in the chill clear air above the square, from the clock tower of a medieval church, a stranger may hear a thing that stops mid-sentence. *Mark this, reader. The people of Kraków have been trained for seven centuries to bear a sentence that stops.*

"It is noon," said Jakub Nowak, without lifting his eyes from the movement before him.

"I know," said Zofia Kowalska. "I heard it."

*She had not.*

The reader may keep that, with the rest of the day's secrets, for later.

Jakub was twenty-four, the apprentice of the oldest clockmaker in the street, a precise and gentle young man, fair-haired and long-fingered, with a loupe pushed up into his hair and the habit of holding his breath when he worked, as though the watch under his hands might wake. He had learned in four years that a clock is only a promise to go on, and that everything in the trade follows from the discovery that one must not hurry a promise.

Zofia was twenty-three, a violinist in her last year at the Academy of Music, a slight, luminous girl with a mass of dark hair and a face of such fine and shadowed attention that people, on meeting her, tended to lower their voices. Six weeks ago she had left in the shop a silver pocket-watch wrapped in a handkerchief, with a worn look about the eyes, and said: "It stopped four years ago, at eleven fifty-two. It was my grandfather's." The master had given the job to his apprentice. And Jakub had opened the case, and read, engraved inside in a tiny copperplate hand: *Zofia, for her birth.*

He had mended it. It was a *minute repeater,* a rare thing, the kind of watch that chimes the hour and the quarter and the minute on two tiny silver gongs at the touch of a slide; and he had sat for six weeks of evenings, with a light and a loupe, restoring it, and when it was done, on the last night of October, he had thought, with no reason at all: *Zofia. It is the name of the girl who plays the violin under the tower.* For he had heard her. Every Thursday at dusk, at the foot of the church, in a thin red scarf, she played for coins. He had stood across the square every Thursday for a year with his hands in his pockets, and had never once put a coin in her case, because he could not trust his face.

And now she had come to collect it, at noon, and was holding out his own work as though it were only hers.

"It is ready," said Jakub. "It is a repeater. It will chime. Listen."

He pressed the slide.

*Hear it, reader, if you can.* The tiny silver chime, bright as a drop of water on glass: three high notes for the hour, then two for the quarters, then four more, as precise as a heartbeat. It filled the shop; it was the sweetest sound a clockmaker knows; and he watched her face as it rang, and saw it do a thing he did not understand.

It went very still. It went, for one moment, the stillness of a person listening to a door that is not opening. And then she smiled, a bright, composed, practised smile, and said:

"It is perfect."

He frowned. "You heard all of it?"

"*Of course.*"

"The last four notes? They are very high."

"They are very beautiful," said Zofia, with the smile fixed, and he did not press her; for he was twenty-four, and a gentleman, and a man who had learned that a person who says a thing very quickly is generally not asking to be examined.

*She had heard the first three notes. She had not heard the rest.*

*It is a small matter, the top of a scale, in a young woman's left ear. She had noticed it in September. She had told no one. She had told herself that it was the damp.*

---

"You play," said Jakub, a little later, after he had named a price she could pay and she had pretended to argue.

"How do you know?"

"You hold your hands like a person carrying a bowl."

"I am a violinist."

"I know. I have heard you." He went red from the collar upward. "I mean, I have *heard of* you. At the tower. On Thursdays."

"You have *heard* me?"

"I have a window," said Jakub, desperately.

She laughed. It was a clear, surprised, delighted sound, and for a moment the clocks seemed to quiet to hear it. "You are a very strange man," said Zofia. "You mend a watch that is not yours and you listen to a girl from a window. Is that a profession?"

"It is *horology.*"

"I am sure it is." She stood up, glancing about the long ticking room, and her eyes fell on the back wall. "Is that a piano?"

It was. It stood in the corner, an old upright pianino of walnut with a missing candle-bracket, which had belonged to the master's wife, and on which Jakub, in the long dull afternoons, with the door shut, played the songs his grandmother had sung to him in Nowy Targ.

"It is out of tune."

"Everything is out of tune. Play me something."

"I do not—I am not—"

"Play me *anything,*" said Zofia, "and I will do the rest."

---

*So it was that on the twenty-ninth day of November, at a quarter past noon, in a clockmaker's shop in the most beautiful medieval city in Europe, with a hundred clocks ticking and a very old piano missing its candle, a boy and a girl played the first duet of their lives.*

It was a simple tune: an old Polish lullaby, four bars and a turn. He played the chords, in his careful, even, gentle way, as a man lays bricks. She took the violin from its worn case and tucked it under her chin and closed her eyes, and drew the bow, and the shop was *filled.*

Reader, I cannot describe it. I am a mere narrator and I have only words. It was as though a window had been opened in a closed room, and a bird had flown in. She played the way a river runs. And he, bent over the keys, looking for the first time in his life at nothing but the notes, felt his chest do a thing that was not on any list of the diseases of the heart.

She did not once look at him. She played with her eyes shut, her whole body bent toward the piano, her head a little turned.

*Turned. He saw it, in the end, with the unforgiving eye of a man who takes engines apart: she had turned her right ear toward the piano, and her left away.*

*She was following his hands.*

He did not know what it meant. He knew only that when he slowed, a hair, in the second bar, because he had caught his breath, she slowed an instant before him, as though she had *seen* the beat, rather than heard it; and that in the high register, in the turn, when she should have lifted the line, her bow dipped, ever so slightly, and found the note by the width of a hair.

*A clock does not lie,* thought Jakub. *Nor does a person who plays by sight.*

And the bugle sounded from the tower of St. Mary's, a quarter past noon, the thin brave tune breaking at its end in the air, and *she did not hear it.*

---

### SCENE III
*Lisbon, Portugal. A tram, the 28, climbing the great hill of Alfama in the rain. Evening. The tiles shine like the sides of fishes.*

The old yellow tram ground up the Rua da Graça with a noise like a bad conscience, and in the cab, behind the driver, on a folding seat, an engaged man was telling an engine that he loved it.

"Not *you,*" Tomás Villaverde hastened to explain, patting the great brass controller. "You are a friend. I mean *her.* I have asked her. She has said yes. It is a matter of the postal service."

"You have said so four times," said Nuno Pereira, his friend and fellow mechanic, from the other end of the cab.

"It is a matter of the *postal service,* Nuno. I proposed, as everything between us has happened, by *post.* I wrote it in a very good letter, in the correct format, I sent it to *Senhora Inês Carvalho, Rua das Flores* (a street I have never seen), and the post, in the person of Inês, with her own hands, delivered it to *herself.*"

"And she said?"

"She said she had read it twice. She reads everything twice. And then she took out a pen and signed the back, and *returned* it to the sender." He took out a creased, much-handled sheet. On the bottom, in a small round hand, it said: *Yes. Delivered. — I.C.*

It was the best receipt he had ever been issued.

At the bottom of the hill, in the rain, a lamp-seller named Pereira was holding forth to a captive passenger. "I sold her a lamp, you know. A small one, for the table. She said it was for her mother. It was for the *letter.* To read it by. A person must have good light for a thing like that. It is the principal duty of my trade, and no one has ever thanked me."

Inês Carvalho, at that moment, was in her tiny flat above the sorting-office, with a small lamp on the table, and a ring that was not a ring, because he could not afford one yet, but a small loop of copper wire from a tram's motor, that he had bent into a circle with his own pliers and slipped on her finger with the solemnity of a bishop. She sat with it before her in the light. Across the table, her sister Rita, thirty-two, a journalist, was looking at her with an expression of the most complete and unrepentant smugness.

"You *sent* it," said Inês. "The first letter. To the street that did not exist. It was *you.*"

"I was the one who sent the letter," said Rita. "Yes. I am the author of this entire romance. I put a letter in a postbox. I would like some credit." She poured the wine. "I will accept a toast."

"Rita."

"I will accept *two.*"

Inês laughed. She turned the copper ring in the light, as a postwoman turns a letter, looking for the postmark, and found it, in the shine of the wire: the small bright mark of a man who could not rhyme, and had mended it with his hands.

*It is a good ring,* thought Inês, who read everything twice. *I shall read it for a lifetime.*

---

*Margin note, in pencil, in the hand of S.W.R.:*

> *Entry 0844 and Entry 0908. A loaf and a bunch of violets, a step and a street. It is the gentlest of the comedies, and I have saved it for the last of the autumn because it is the one that shows how little a person needs: one gift, left at a door, and the courage not to knock.*
>
> *Entry 0471 and Entry 0609. A watch that chimes, and a girl who cannot hear it. I have not the heart to tell you what comes after. I will only say that I have read the whole of the Register, and a good clockmaker is a better friend than a good doctor, since he will wait.*
>
> *Entry 0753 and Entry 0053. They are engaged. It is very sweet. It is copper wire and a receipt. Let them have it. Let them have every hour of it.*
>
> *The winter will ask for payment.*

---

*End of Chapter 12.*
