# ACT II — THE HOUSES AT WAR

### *The Chorus*

When frost has closed the harbours of the heart,
Old quarrels wake, like wolves behind a wall;
And house on house, with envy set apart,
Will stake the young upon the pride of all.
Two ferries cross one strait with hostile prow;
Two shops divide one street with hostile eyes;
Yet love, that knows no feud, nor flag, nor vow,
Slips through the fence beneath the winter skies.
Some shall be saved by what their fathers spurned;
Some shall be lost to what their fathers swore;
And some shall wait where all their letters burned,
And hear the tide knock softly at the door.
Then mark the cold; it tests what will not fail,
And what is true outlives the winter's gale.

---


## Chapter 13
### Two Ferries

> *"I write poems to the boy on the other ferry."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0732

---

### SCENE I
*Istanbul, Türkiye. The Üsküdar pier, on the Asian shore. Early December, a quarter to seven. A fog has settled on the Bosphorus like a sheet on a sleeping giant, and out of it, one after another, come the ferries.*

There is a city that stands with one foot in Europe and the other in Asia, and washes both in the same water, and the water has never been able to decide which of them to belong to.

It is called the Bosphorus, and it is a river only in the way that a lion is a cat. It runs for thirty kilometres between the Black Sea and the Marmara, under the old stone fortresses and the red roofs of the wooden houses, and every morning, in the grey before the call to prayer has finished echoing from the minarets, it is crossed by a thousand ferries carrying a million people to their jobs. The gulls follow them in screaming flocks. The tea-sellers move down the aisles with tulip glasses on brass trays. A boy of fourteen with a flat basket on his head sings out the price of *simit,* the sesame bread-rings of the city: "*Simit, sıcak simit!*"

Two of those ferries, on this particular morning, were red and blue.

The red was the *Hızır,* of the Yılmaz Line, which had run between Üsküdar and Karaköy since 1956, with a tall black funnel and a crew who would have drowned for the captain and for each other, in that order. The blue was the *Nilüfer,* of the Kaya Line, with a white-and-blue band round her funnel like a bandage, and the same crossing, the same hour, the same passengers, and the same quiet and ancient hatred.

For thirty years the two houses had sailed the same water. For twenty-two of them they had not spoken.

It had begun, like most great quarrels, in a very small place. A fog. A grounding on a sandbar in the winter of 1996. A ferry that was damaged, a passenger who was hurt, two partners who had each been at the wheel of a different boat and each remembered, quite sincerely, that the other had been at fault. Captain Süleyman Yılmaz had stood on a pier in front of three hundred people and sworn, with his hand on his heart, *by my mother's grave, I will see the Kaya flag go under.* Recep Kaya, who was not a man to be outdone in an oath, had sworn the same, and the two had gone their ways, and built their separate fleets, and the Bosphorus had been in a state of cold war ever since.

And now, in the Council hall in Fatih, a ten-year licence for the crossing was up for award, and both families had bid.

---

*At the window of the Kaya Line ticket office, on the pier, twenty paces from the Yılmaz window, a young woman has lifted the blind.*

Elif Kaya was twenty-six, a ticket clerk, small and quick and dark-eyed, with her hair pinned up under a navy cap and a pencil behind her ear, and she was, in the unanimous opinion of the pier, the fastest hand with a ticket machine on the Bosphorus. She was also, in the unanimous ignorance of the pier, a poet.

She wrote on the backs of old tickets, on the margins of the timetable, on the inside of the paper bag of her morning *simit.* She wrote in the old manner, in rhymed couplets with a repeated refrain, which her grandmother had taught her, and she put them, from the age of fifteen, in a biscuit tin under her bed.

For six months she had been writing them to somebody.

He stood, every morning, on the bow of the *Hızır* when she came alongside: a tall young man in a navy jersey, with a coil of rope on his shoulder and a face she could have drawn with her eyes closed. He was the captain's son. His name was Ahmed Yılmaz. He was twenty-eight, broad of shoulder and quick of temper and kind to a degree that infuriated the people around him, and he stood, every morning, with his back to the dock, looking at the water, and whistling.

It was an old tune. It belonged to the shepherds of the Black Sea coast, and had no words, and rose and fell like a boat on a swell. He whistled it very softly, every day, as the *Nilüfer* came alongside; and every day, in the ticket office, with her hand on the machine, Elif Kaya pretended she could not hear it.

*Reader, I will tell you what was in the paper bag.*

It was, that morning, a poem. She folded it small. She put it inside a *simit* wrapper, and she held it up to the little window, and a boy of fourteen with a flat basket on his head, who stood among the hawkers on the pier with an expression of bookish and entirely unwarranted innocence, took it from her hand without a word.

"For the tall one on the red boat," said Elif.

"I know."

"You are not to read it."

"I have read it," said Burak Aydın. "I read all of them. I need to know what I am carrying. It is a matter of professional ethics."

"You are fourteen."

"It is the age of *discretion,*" said Burak. "And you owe me four books."

He walked away across the pier with his basket, calling "*Simit, sıcak simit!*" and, in a lull between calls, lifting the paper to his nose with a look of profound and satisfied connoisseurship.

---

> *O wind, who crossest water east and west,
> Tell him: the other ferry carries me.
> The boat is blue, the boy is on the red;
> Tell him: the other ferry carries me.
>
> The fog has swallowed both our lamps, and yet
> I know the tune he whistles in the mist.
> I fold my silence small, and send it out:
> Tell him: the other ferry carries me.
>
> The fathers wage a war across the strait.
> The daughters read the tide and say no word.
> If drowning is the price of knowing him,
> Tell him: the other ferry carries me.*

---

### SCENE II
*The ferry café at the Eminönü landing. The cook's kitchen is a counter, two gas rings, and an enormous brass samovar. A crowd of sailors, porters, and clerks. It is the only ground on the Bosphorus on which, by an ancient custom, no quarrel may be fought.*

Sema was fifty-one, wide, fierce, and floury, with her sleeves rolled to the shoulder, a headscarf of orange silk, and the strongest forearms in Eminönü. She had cooked at the landing for twenty-eight years, had fed three generations of both houses off the same chipped plates, and had made it a law that whoever brought a quarrel in at the door left it on a hook, along with the coat.

"Tea has no flag," she was fond of announcing, to the room at large.

"It is the *truth,*" said her husband Kerem. "I read it in a paper."

Kerem Arslan was forty-four, a grocer, thin and gloomy, with a moustache like a question mark, and he believed everything he read, which was a great sorrow to the newspapers.

"What did it say?"

"That on the day of the Council vote, the sea will be lowered by three centimetres. It is something with the moon."

"Kerem. You have never been to sea in your life."

"I have seen it from the *bus,*" said Kerem, wounded.

Sema ladled out two plates of *menemen,* the creamy eggs and tomatoes of the Turkish breakfast, and slid them across the counter in opposite directions, toward two tables, one red and one blue, where two groups of men were drinking tea with their backs to one another, in the cold dignity of ancient enemies. At the red table sat the crew of the *Hızır,* and at their head the old engineer, Kerem Aydın, seventy-three, retired in name and never in fact, who had kept the Yılmaz boats running for half a century and who had raised the captain's son with a spanner in one hand and a string of prayer beads in the other. At the blue table sat the crew of the *Nilüfer,* and at their head a short, sunburnt man with a pair of headphones round his neck: Mehmet Şahin, sixty-three, radio-man of the Kaya Line, the uncle who had raised Elif after her father's death, and who ran the fleet from a small glass room full of crackling dials, trusting, as a man must who spends his life listening, almost everything he was told.

"I will tell you the whole matter," said Sema to her tea-glasses, in an under-voice that carried the width of the room. "They quarrel because they are the same. Both want the crossing. Both want the other to go under. And neither can sail without the other, because a man with no one to be angry at will go quite *mad.* It is a great cruelty that God made the sea a *single sea,* and that the fools have given it so many names."

"It has three," said Kerem. "The Bosphorus, the Strait, and *Boğaz.*"

"It has *one.* The rest is labels."

*Mark this, reader. She was talking about eggs. She was, as the wise often are when they think themselves at a stove, entirely correct.*

At the red table, a voice rose.

"I will see it done by Christmas," said Captain Süleyman Yılmaz.

---

He had come in at the door. He was fifty-eight, a tall, magnificent, scowling man with a white moustache and a captain's cap and a voice that had been trained over thirty years to carry across a gale. He stood at the end of the red table, in the doorway, like a statue of the sea, and spoke to the room.

"The Council will award the crossing to the family that has run it longest. That is *us.* And I tell you, on the head of the Prophet, that I will see the Kaya flag lowered on that mast if I have to haul it down myself."

Across the room, at the blue table, a chair scraped.

"You will do *nothing* of the kind," said Mehmet Şahin. He had risen: a small man, but he stood now with his headphones round his neck like a noose, and a ferocity in his sunburnt face that a stranger would never have suspected in a man who listened for a living. "My brother-in-law Recep, God rest his soul, built that line with his two hands. I will not see his name washed off a funnel by a man who cannot tell a sandbar from a mirror."

"*Gentlemen,*" said Sema.

She did not shout. She lifted a ladle, an enormous brass ladle, the kind that serves forty, and brought it down on the counter with a crack like a pistol. The two tables froze.

"My café," said Sema, "has a rule. Leave the quarrel on the hook with the coat. And *eat.* I have made two hundred plates of menemen this morning and I will not have them go cold for the sake of a sandbar."

There was a very long silence.

Then, to the astonishment of the pier, Captain Yılmaz sat; and Mehmet Şahin sat; and a hundred men began, gingerly, to eat.

"Better," said Sema, and went back to her pan. "Kerem. The sea has not gone down by three centimetres."

"It is not the day *yet,*" said Kerem.

*At the red table, between two mouthfuls, the old engineer Kerem Aydın met the eyes of the captain's son, who had said nothing throughout, and who sat with his fork motionless in the eggs and his gaze fixed on a point across the room where, for an instant, a pair of dark eyes in a blue cap had appeared in the café's open door, and as quickly gone.*

---

### SCENE III
*Dusk. The pier. The last ferry of the day has gone. The water is the colour of a plum, and the minarets of the old city stand against it like a row of pens.*

They did not speak. They had never spoken.

They stood on the two piers, the Yılmaz and the Kaya, twenty paces apart, in the failing light, with the water between them and a white gull sitting on the rail, and she was in her cap and he was in his jersey, and in the lap of the tide, with the passing of the last ferry, was a long, soft, speaking silence.

It had been six months, and one hundred and seventy-three poems carried across by a boy in a basket, with four books outstanding. It had been, in return, a whistle, to which she had never replied, because there is no reply to a whistle that does not itself contain a promise.

And at last, that evening, the boy had come back with the paper bag, and on the inside of it, in a large, square, careful, unaccustomed hand, a line.

It said: *I cannot write as you do. I can only say that I hear it. — A.*

She read it twice. Then she went down onto the pier in the failing light, in the blue cap, and stood at the very edge, where the stone met the water, and looked across.

He was there.

He stood at the end of the Yılmaz landing, twenty paces off, with his hands at his sides, very large and very still, and she could not see his face. He lifted one hand. He did not wave. He only held it out, palm open, to the water.

She lifted hers.

Between them the Bosphorus slid by, black and silver and indifferent, with the lights of Europe coming on along the farther shore like a thousand small intentions. Behind her, in the glass room at the end of the pier, her uncle sat at his radio, listening to the wrong stations. Behind Ahmed, up the other hill, his father was cleaning a cap he meant to wear to the Council on the day the Kaya flag went down.

*There are two oaths in this scene, reader, and neither is the one you think. One is the oath of the fathers. The other has not yet been sworn.*

He began, very softly, to whistle.

She stood at the edge of the pier with her hand still lifted and the tune coming over the water to her in the dusk, thin and sweet and brave, like a thread drawn through a needle; and Elif Kaya, who had a poem for everything, who had a couplet for the sea and a refrain for the night, found that she had no words at all.

She put her hand to her mouth.

And from the pier behind her, from a flat basket, a boy's voice, low and pleased and a little aggrieved, said: "That is a *very* good poem, and you have not even written it yet."

---

### SCENE IV
*Accra, Ghana. Osu, on Oxford Street. The same evening, which is, at that longitude, the same hour. The air is the gold of the harmattan: that dry, dust-laden wind that comes down from the Sahara every December and turns the sunsets to copper.*

On a certain street in Accra, in the wake of the great, bright, honking river of the evening traffic, there stood two shops.

One was a pharmacy, in whose window a very bright green cross shone through the dust; the other was a taxi depot, with a hand-lettered sign over the door, reading *MENSAH CABS — YOU CALL, WE ARRIVE (EVENTUALLY).* Between them there lay twelve metres of pavement, a gutter, and, in the hearts of the people on either side, an ocean.

On the night of the ninth of December the pharmacy was dressed in garlands, and a banner hung across its door.

**OWUSU PHARMACY — GREATER ACCRA PHARMACY OF THE YEAR.**

"*Ei!* The woman has done it," said an old driver, leaning on the bonnet of a yellow cab across the road with a bottle of malt in his hand. "She has won the prize. Who is surprised? *Quaye* is not surprised."

Quaye was seventy, the oldest driver in the fleet, a small, bright, bandy-legged man in a flat cap and a faded football shirt, with a gold tooth and a commentary on everything. He kept court on the bonnet of his taxi each evening like a parliament of one, and had been known to announce the weather, the football scores, and the secret feelings of his employer in the same breath. Around him, as ever, the drivers had formed a loose half-circle, like a Greek chorus in a state of great leisure.

"She worked for it," said one.

"She has the best-kept shop in Osu," said Quaye. "She has the honestest scales. She has a *brain.* And she has a debt that someone paid."

There was a silence.

"Who paid it?" said a young driver, who was new.

"Someone who lives twelve metres to the east and is *very* bad at hiding," said Quaye. "If a man does a kindness, and then goes and sits at the back of every ceremony with a face like a church door, in my profession we call him a man with a problem. It is called *pride.* It is the worst passenger there is. It sits in the front, and it has no fare."

*Behind him, across twelve metres of dusty pavement, in the lit doorway of the Owusu Pharmacy, a young woman in a kente stole was standing with her award in her hands.*

---

Abena Owusu was twenty-eight, a pharmacist, with a sharp tongue and a straight back and a grave, watchful face, and she was holding a glass trophy in the shape of a mortar and pestle as though it were a very hot dish. Beside her stood her friend Adwoa Tetteh, forty-four, the kiosk-owner from the next street, a tall, restless woman who never forgot an insult and had been enumerating them, at length, to the guests.

"You must say a word," said Adwoa. "The Minister is coming."

"I do not make speeches."

"You make *prescriptions.* It is the same. You tell people what they need and they do not like it."

Abena laughed in spite of herself. And then, as the guests began to gather on the pavement in the dust-gold light, and a choir of twenty began to sing in the lively, rolling, many-voiced harmonies of the Ghanaian Methodist hymn, led by Nii Tetteh, forty-three, choir-master, devout, and a man who told lies for amusement and never in church, she turned to look across the road.

He was there.

He was standing, as he always stood, at the back, by the door of his own depot, a tall, broad, quiet man of thirty-one in a plain white shirt, with his hands behind him and a face that had been carved from a very hard wood and then left out in the rain. Kwame Mensah. Taxi-fleet owner. A man who would lend money to a stranger at a lamp-post and then give a lecture on his reasons, and who could not, to save his life, pay a woman a compliment.

He caught her eye.

He nodded, once, formally, as a man nods to a landlord.

She nodded back.

And then, because the Minister was late, and the choir had run out of verses, and the whole street had gone quiet, and a hundred people were looking at her, Abena Owusu stepped forward to the pavement, with the trophy in her hand, and the gold dust in the air, and said, in a clear, low, startling voice:

"Thank you. I will be brief, since the Minister is not here.

"Everything good in this shop was given to me. The floors by my mother. The scales by my father, who is not here to see them. The stock by a bank that has been very patient. And the rest—" She paused. "The rest I owe to a neighbour."

A ripple went through the crowd. On the bonnet of the taxi, Quaye took off his cap.

"There is a debt," said Abena, in the stillness, "that was once mine. It was paid. I was told it was *forgiven.* And I accepted it, because it was kind." She looked across the road, and her voice did not shake, but it did slow. "But I am a pharmacist. In my profession we do not give a person medicine without telling them what it is. It is a matter of respect.

"So I will say this, and then I will sit. I know. I have known for some time. I am not angry. I am only waiting. I have always been very good at waiting. It is the only skill my profession allows."

There was a silence.

Then the choir, which had no idea what had just occurred, and was led by a man who told lies for amusement, struck up a very loud and cheerful hymn, and the whole street began to clap; and Abena Owusu went in, with her glass mortar, and set it on a shelf between the aspirin and the ointments, and put her hand over her face.

At the back of the depot, Kwame Mensah did not move.

"*Oga,*" said Quaye, quietly, from his bonnet, "I have been your driver for nineteen years, and I have never asked you for anything but the day off for funerals. I am asking now. Go and say *something.* A man does not have to say the whole of a thing. He only has to say the first word. The road is very long, but it starts at the gate."

Kwame looked across twelve metres of dusty street, at a lit doorway where a woman in kente had set down her prize and was straightening a row of tablets that did not need straightening.

He took one step.

He stopped.

"It is a very long road," said Kwame Mensah, in a low, hard, hopeless voice, "and I have never been good at the gate."

"Then it is a good thing," said Quaye, "that tomorrow is also a day."

---

*Margin note, in pencil, in the hand of S.W.R.:*

> *Entry 0211 and Entry 0732, two ferries, one strait. Entry 0625 and Entry 0941, two shops, one street. In the first, an oath was sworn by fathers, and the children will have to find which of them is bound by it. In the second, a debt was paid, and the debtor has had the sense to know it, and the payer has not yet the sense to be known.*
>
> *I have always said that the Register is a book about distances, and that the most dangerous distance is not an ocean. It is twenty paces of pier. It is twelve metres of pavement. A man can cross an ocean in nine hours. A pier may take him all his life.*
>
> *I notice that Sema is right. It is a single sea.*

---

*End of Chapter 13.*


---

## Chapter 14
### The Heiress and the Guide

> *"I am the heir of a haveli with no roof."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0626

---

*Enter the Chorus, with a pocket watch in each hand and a third in his hat.*

> At midnight, Dhaka; Jaipur, late
> By half an hour; Bergen, early yet,
> Where dusk is dinner; and, a step ahead,
> Yogyakarta, one o'clock, and set
> To sleep, and not asleep. Observe, good friends:
> The world keeps seven clocks and one true hour,
> And lovers are the only horologists
> Who read them all at once. Attend. The tower
> Of Babel was a scheme to stop the clocks;
> We merely ask you not to break the locks.

---

### SCENE I
*Jaipur. The boardroom of Sharma Textile House, above a lane of block-printers' shops. A long table, nine uncles, one tea tray, and a young woman holding a roll of cloth as though it were a sleeping child.*

There are two ways to be an heiress. The first is to inherit. The second is to be *told* you will inherit, at every wedding, by every aunt, until the word becomes a coat sewn so exactly to your shoulders that you cannot lift your arms. Priya Sharma, twenty-seven, had worn the second kind since she was nine.

"Beta," said her father, Mahendra Sharma, who sat at the head of the table with the patience of a man who had lost an argument to his daughter in 1998 and had been preparing his revenge ever since. "We are a house that *sells* cloth. We have sold cloth to three maharajas and one Hollywood film. We do not make poems."

"It is not a poem, Papa. It is a collection."

"A collection of what?"

"Of roofs," said Priya.

Nine uncles looked at nine cups of tea.

She unrolled the cloth. It ran down the length of the table like a river that had been told a secret: dabu, the old mud-resist print of Bagru, dipped and dipped again in indigo until the blue went down into black, and across that black, in gaps where the clay had held back the dye, there were small shapes the colour of milk. They were not flowers, as every uncle in the room expected. They were the little arched windows of old Jaipur, and above each window, where a roof should have been, the cloth was left open: bare, pale, and utterly without a lid.

"Sky," said Priya, and her voice shook only once. "I want to print the houses of this city as they are when the roof has gone and the sky has moved in. People do not want another peacock, Papa. They want to be told that a thing may fall and still be beautiful."

"Who told you this?"

"A man with no roof."

At that precise moment, with a sense of timing that no stage-manager could have invented and no stage-manager would have dared, the door of the boardroom was thrown open, and into it swept a figure in a saffron safa, a waistcoat embroidered with peacocks (which Priya's uncles regarded as a personal insult), and a moustache that had been oiled, curled, and, one suspected, individually named.

"*Namaste, esteemed gentlemen!*" cried Vikram Rathore, thirty, heritage guide, and the sole surviving heir of a house in the Chandpole bazaar whose roof had been carried off by the monsoon of 1998 and never replaced. "I am *late*. This is a deliberate strategy. A man who is early is a clerk; a man who is late is an *arrival*."

"Who," said Mahendra Sharma, "is this?"

"My consultant," said Priya, with great firmness and no authority whatever.

"Her *humble witness*," said Vikram, bowing so low that his moustache brushed the tea tray.

He had met her five weeks before. She had come to the old city with a camera and a ruinous idea: that somewhere behind some stone gate where the paint had given up, the printing-houses of her great-grandmother's time still kept their wooden blocks, forgotten, unsold. The guild had sent a man in a peacock waistcoat who announced, in the first minute, that he had once been mistaken for a maharaja by a Dutch tourist and had not corrected her.

He had led her, in the end, to his own front door: a tall carved door in a lane that smelled of marigold and diesel, and behind it a courtyard with a neem tree, a broken swing, a staircase that ascended to nothing, and, in a cathedral of light that fell straight down through the place where the roof had been, three hundred blocks of seasoned teak, stacked like the pages of a closed book.

"My great-grandfather's," Vikram had said, and for the first time in her hearing he did not perform. "The family printed for the court. Then the court was gone, and the printing was gone, and then the roof. I give tours of it on Thursdays. I call it *The House That Chose the Sky.* Tourists weep." He had shrugged, a small, unlovely shrug with no peacock in it. "Mostly the Dutch."

She had stood in the column of daylight, with dust turning in it like slow gold, and she had thought: *There it is. There is the whole collection. A thing that lost its lid and let in the stars.*

It is a dangerous thing, reader, to be shown a ruin by a vain man who is, for one minute, not vain. Engagements are made of less.

Back in the boardroom, the humble witness cleared his throat.

"Gentlemen," said Vikram, in the voice of a man who had once read the Ramayana at a wedding and been asked to stop. "A house without a roof is still a house, if the sky consents to be its ceiling. Your daughter—" a dreadful pause "—your daughter has seen what nine gentlemen with nine calculators have not. People do not buy cloth. They buy the *reason* the cloth was made. Give her fifty pieces. If they do not sell, I will personally eat my safa."

"I would do it *slowly*, with chutney, and in public."

It was the first time the Sharma boardroom had laughed since the Gulf War. In the corridor, a writer named Pooja Tiwari, twenty-seven, who had come for the gossip and stayed for the odds, passed a folded note to the clerk who kept the tea ledger: *Ten rupees says Papa Sharma says yes. Twenty says the guide proposes by Diwali.*

Papa Sharma said: "Fifty pieces. Not fifty-one."

And Priya Sharma, who had held her breath since the age of nine, let it out quietly, in the boardroom, in front of nine uncles, in the shape of her name.

*She did not look at Vikram. This is how you may know she was looking at nothing else.*

---

### SCENE II
*Bergen. The sea off Askøy, 3:40 in the afternoon, which in a Norwegian December is the evening. A wooden boat, a gale, and a woman with a clipboard.*

If Jaipur's trouble was a roof that had gone, Bergen's was a hull that was going.

The boat was the *Ragnhild,* eleven metres of tarred oak and old paint, and Lars Eriksen, who was thirty and as talkative as a granite step, called her *her* when she behaved and *it* when she did not. She was held together, as the old men of the Fisketorget liked to say, by habit and the Lord's low opinion of insurance.

The woman with the clipboard was Sigrid Haugen, twenty-nine, marine biologist, who chartered the *Ragnhild* every Tuesday for a cod-tagging study, because her owner would take her to the deep water at six in the morning without asking why. She had not stopped moving since she came aboard. She tapped. She measured. She sighed at the water temperature, and at the plankton count, and, with some warmth, at a cormorant.

"The fresh water is coming off the mountain too fast," said Sigrid. "It means the whole top layer is—Lars, are you listening?"

"Mm."

"You say *mm* as though it were a complete sentence."

"It is," said Lars, "in Norwegian."

"It is not a language. It is a *noise*."

"It carries more than most." He did not look up from the engine hatch, where a spanner and a very small prayer were doing their best. "Sigrid. How long does the sample take?"

"Another forty minutes."

"We do not have forty minutes."

He did not say it loudly. Lars Eriksen did not say anything loudly; he said things the way a fjord says them, by being already full. But she heard the thing under it, and she looked up at last, past the clipboard, past the grey-green slope of the water, and saw what he had been watching for an hour with the stoic's dreadful patience: the western sky going the colour of a bruise, and a line of white, low and quick and moving, coming toward them over the sound.

"Oh," said Sigrid.

"Yes."

"How long?"

"Ten minutes. Perhaps eight."

The first wave struck her quarter like a hand slapping a table. There was a sound below the deck: not a crash but a long, wet *sigh*, as of an elderly person sitting down. Lars was in the hold before the spray had settled. He came up the colour of porridge.

"A plank's sprung. By the keel."

"How bad?"

"Bad enough that I am going to teach you to steer."

"I have never steered!"

"Then it will be your first. Both hands, there. Bow to the lighthouse. Do not look at the water; it will only upset you." He pulled the bilge handle, which squealed like a pig at a christening, and then, when that failed, took up a bucket, because in the end every seaman is a man with a bucket and a great deal of faith. "If the engine dies—"

"What happens if the engine dies?"

"We will have a very interesting conversation," said Lars, "while I bail."

---

They did not die. But for forty minutes it was neither comedy nor anything else; it was cold water, and wet wool, and the red lamp at Marstein, and a bucket going out and coming in, out and in, in the hands of a man who did not once ask for help and a woman who did not once let go of the wheel.

At the end of it, at ten minutes to five, in the black, with the harbour lights of Vågen swimming up out of the rain like a festival, the engine coughed, and the old boat limped into the fish market quay and sat down in the water with the weary dignity of a horse that has finished its last race.

Lars cut the motor. In the silence the water ran out of the scuppers and clacked against the stones.

"I should not have taken you out," he said.

"I hired you."

"You hired a boat. I knew what the boat was."

"I—" Sigrid let go of the wheel and found that her hands would not at first unclench. "I came out today because I thought that if I counted every plankton in this fjord, I would not have to think about what happens when I have counted them all. And you let me. For a month, you let me. You said *mm*."

"It was the right thing to say."

"It was not *anything*."

"Sometimes," said Lars Eriksen, to the harbour, to the rain, to the lamp at Marstein, to the whole unlit shore of everything he could not say, "it is the only thing the boat will carry."

There was a movement on the quay. It was a woman in a yellow slicker, with a stall of bright umbrellas lashed in tarpaulin under a lamp, who had been selling them to the ferry queue since morning with, so far, one customer.

"Ha!" said Solveig Dahl, thirty-six, formerly of Ålesund and lately, by her own account, a refugee from a city where it sometimes stopped raining. "You are wet! The sea has done my selling for me. Four hundred kroner."

"For an umbrella?"

"For the *idea.* One does not buy shelter. One buys the pretence of it." She regarded Lars, and the bucket, and the boat's low and sorry waterline, and Sigrid's hands. "The boat will sink next week," she said, quite kindly, "and you will both pretend not to mind. I do not charge for the truth. Only for the umbrellas."

Neither of them bought one (Sigrid owned a plum-coloured one already). She walked to the end of the quay and was sick, over the rail, with great discretion; and when she turned back, Lars was standing with his bucket, looking at the boat as at a friend who has been faithful for a very long time and does not deserve to be put down.

*I am afraid,* thought Sigrid, *that I will not come back.*

*I am afraid,* thought Lars, *that I will never ask her to.*

They stood twelve feet apart in the rain, each with a whole unwritten letter in the mouth, and neither of them mended the silence with a single word.

*Mark this, reader. A silence is not nothing. It is a boat that has not yet gone under.*

---

### SCENE III
*Mirpur, Dhaka. A tea stall at eleven at night. Then a third-floor flat, a laptop, and the first of many nights.*

"Bhaiya," said Bunny, "you are checking your phone."

"I am not."

"You are *glaring* at it, which is checking with a bad character." The boy slid the glass across the counter. He was thirteen, thin as a ruler, and ran the corner stall with an air of having done so since the Mughals. "Who has not answered?"

"It is a client."

"At eleven at night. On a *Friday.* The client has a first name, Bhaiya, and it has a *flower* in it." (Bunny saw everything, forgave nothing, and billed for neither.)

Fayaz Rahman, twenty-six, whose company had died in the spring and whose debts had not, put the phone face down on the counter, like a man laying down a card he did not wish to explain.

"She is a designer," he said. "From Yogyakarta. We have exchanged, I think, nine messages. Her website does not load properly. I am helping."

"Nine messages."

"In five weeks."

"And how long does she take to answer?"

"Never more than an hour."

"And you?"

"Four minutes."

Bunny closed his eyes in physical pain. "Bhaiya. A man who answers in four minutes is a man who is *waiting.* Rule one: you wait four minutes *before* you answer. Not three: that is eager. Not five: that is cruel. Four. It is a medical fact."

"You have invented that."

"I have *observed* it." He wiped the counter with a rag the colour of old weather. "And you have a face like a closed shop. Open it a little. Otherwise she will think there is nobody home."

Fayaz paid for the tea, and for two biscuits he did not want, and climbed the three flights to the flat, where his mother's breathing came faintly through the wall, in and out, like a long thread being drawn over a small rough stone; and where, on the balcony in the dark, his father sat on a plastic chair with a green ledger on his knee and a pencil he did not use.

"Abbu," said Fayaz softly. "You should sleep."

"I am counting."

"It is the same number as yesterday."

"Yes," said his father. "I wished to be sure." Then, after a moment, in a voice so careful that it nearly was not a voice: "Fourteen lakh is not so much. Is it? Other people owe more."

"It is not so much, Abbu."

"No." The pencil moved a little in the old man's hand, and made no mark. "Go on. Go to your work. You have a client."

---

At 12:07 by the clock above his desk (the clock was seven minutes slow; he had never fixed it, because to fix it would have meant admitting he was always going to be somewhere between two times) Fayaz opened the chat window.

There was one new line.

> **Ermis:** *Are you awake? Stupid question. I can see the green dot. I am sorry. I am panicking in a very small and well-organised way.*

He waited four minutes. He had never in his life waited four minutes so badly.

> **Fayaz:** *I am awake. What is wrong with the website?*

> **Ermis:** *The portfolio will not upload. It says "file too large." I have made it smaller three times. I think it is a personal attack.*

> **Fayaz:** *Send me the folder name. Do not tell me what it is for.*

> **Ermis:** *Why not?*

> **Fayaz:** *Because you have not told me, and I would like to deserve being told.*

There was a pause, long enough for a dog to bark twice in the lane below and for the power to flicker and, mercifully, hold.

> **Ermis:** *That is the most irritating nice thing anyone has said to me this year.*

> **Ermis:** *It is an application. That is all I can say. It is due at 2 a.m. my time.*

> **Fayaz:** *It is 12:14 a.m. mine. You are an hour ahead of me.*

> **Ermis:** *I know. I have been aware of it for five weeks. I am always ahead of everyone and they always say "slow down."*

> **Fayaz:** *I have never once said "slow down."*

> **Ermis:** *No. You have said "the file is in the wrong format." Which is the same thing, but more helpful.*

It took him eleven minutes. The problem was a single photograph of an indigo vat at dawn, saved as a file the size of a small country, hidden among thirty others like a bear in a sheep-pen. He compressed it, and wrote a four-line script to resize the rest; and in the intervals, through a voice note she had left running by mistake, he heard all the sounds of a night he could not see: a stove, a tap, a pencil, and a distant, bad-tempered voice shrieking *"TOO LATE!"*

> **Ermis:** *That is Ayu. My grandmother's parrot. She has three sentences and has never used them correctly.*

> **Fayaz:** *She seems well informed.*

> **Ermis:** *She is a lunatic and I love her.*

He looked at that for a little. He did not remark upon it. A man with fourteen lakh taka to find does not remark upon the word *love,* even where it is attached to a parrot.

> **Ermis:** *Uploaded. Oh, it works. It says "received." Fayaz, it says RECEIVED. I feel like I jumped off a very high thing and was told, after, that there was a net.*

> **Fayaz:** *There is always a net. It is simply very far down, with a clock that is seven minutes slow.*

> **Ermis:** *How do you know about the clock?*

> **Fayaz:** *I did not say that. Did I?*

> **Ermis:** *You told me in your second message. You said you had never fixed it, on principle. I keep your messages the way other people keep receipts.*

He laughed aloud, alone, in the dark, for the first time that week. Through the wall his mother stirred and settled. He lowered his voice, as if the words themselves might wake her.

> **Fayaz:** *What time is it there?*

> **Ermis:** *1:23 a.m. I am sitting on the floor of my workshop with my feet in a tray of cold water, because I am a fool. Everything is blue. What time is it there?*

> **Fayaz:** *Sixteen minutes past twelve by my clock, which is seven minutes slow. So really 12:23.*

> **Ermis:** *So you are an hour behind me.*

> **Fayaz:** *I prefer "in your past."*

> **Ermis:** *No. Not the past. The past is finished. You are not finished. You are only a little way down the road.*

> **Fayaz:** *Then what are you?*

There were three dots. They pulsed and sank. They pulsed again. In a workshop that smelled of hot wax, a girl with a pencil in her hair looked at the ceiling beams, and at the cold blue water, and at a green bird that had gone, for once, to sleep; and then she typed the line that she would, in the spring, repeat in a different voice, to a screen going dark.

> **Ermis:** *I am in your future.*

> **Ermis:** *Ask me anything about tomorrow. I have seen it. It is only an hour away.*

Fayaz sat quite still. In the lane below, a rickshaw bell rang and was swallowed. 
> **Fayaz:** *Will the electricity come back?*

> **Ermis:** *I can only tell you that in the future, everyone has had dinner.*

> **Fayaz:** *That is not an answer.*

> **Ermis:** *It is the most important answer I know.*

> **Fayaz:** *Will it be a good tomorrow?*

> **Ermis:** *It is only an hour old, Fayaz. I cannot say yet. Ask me again in an hour.*

He did. He asked her an hour later, at 1:16 by his slow clock, which was truly 1:23 and therefore 2:23 in Yogyakarta, while the first rooster went up from some courtyard in the sleeping city and the first grey came into the window of a flat in Mirpur like water into a basin.

> **Fayaz:** *It is an hour later. What does tomorrow look like?*

> **Ermis:** *Grey, a little. A very early rooster. A man who is up too late being kind to a stranger with a website.*

> **Fayaz:** *That sounds like a good tomorrow.*

> **Ermis:** *It is a good start. I will tell you if it holds.*

> **Fayaz:** *You will have to. You are the only one who has seen it.*

> **Ermis:** *Yes,* she wrote; and then, after a pause so small only the machine measured it: *I am quite happy to be, for now.*

> **Ermis:** *Good night. Or good morning. Whichever of us is right.*

She went offline, and the little green dot beside her name went grey. It was nearly three in the morning in her city and nearly two in his, and the neighbourhood roosters were beginning to quarrel. Fayaz Rahman closed the laptop, and sat, in the beginning of a day that was already a day old somewhere else, and discovered with some alarm that he was smiling at a wall. On the other side of it, his mother breathed, in and out, steady as a thread.

*An hour,* he thought. *She is an hour ahead. Then whatever comes, she will see it first.*

It did not occur to him, until he was nearly asleep, that this might be a comfort.

---

*Margin note, in pencil, in the hand of S.W.R., against Entries 0626, 0443 and 0713:*

> *Three clocks, three silences, and one bucket. A man who showed a stranger his own ruin; a man who said* mm *to the sea; a man asked, in the dark, to name tomorrow. The first two fell in love by the hour. The third by the minute, and he waited four.*
>
> *Nothing in the Register hurries. It is the clocks that do.*

---

*End of Chapter 14.*

## Chapter 15
### Fiddle and Fever

> *"There is a song I cannot finish, and it is about you."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0025

---

### SCENE I
*Galway. A flat above a closed bakery, on a Thursday in December, with the Atlantic doing what it does to windows. A suitcase, open on a bed. A woman who has been packing for nine days and has not yet put in a single thing she means to take.*

Aoife Brennan, thirty, veterinary surgeon, was a woman of great directness, and she had never been less direct in her life.

"Socks," she said to the room. "Two weeks of socks. Why do I own so many socks, when I have only two feet?"

The room, which was small, damp, and loyal, made no reply. On the dresser stood a framed certificate, a jar of coins from the pockets of farmers who paid in kind, and a hoof-pick shaped like a small silver oar. On the bed lay a letter of acceptance from a large-animal practice outside Antigonish, in Nova Scotia, a county that, as she had discovered on the internet at four in the morning, held a Highland games, kept a great many horses, and was short of a vet who would shout. On the pillow lay a ticket: *Shannon to Toronto. Toronto to Halifax. Sunday, 6:40 a.m.*

She had told no one. Not the clinic, where her resignation lay in her bag, signed and sealed and heavy as a stone. Not her mother, who would say *Canada!* in the voice used for *cancer.* Not Niamh, her oldest friend, who sold fish on the Long Walk and could not say goodbye to a bus.

And not, God help her, the fiddler.

She sat down on the bed, among the socks, and, since there was nobody in the room to be direct to, she was direct to the dark:

> *I have been brave with bulls. I have put my arm
> Into the throat of weather, to the shoulder,
> And turned a calf that did not wish to come.
> I have said "Hold him" to a hundred men
> Who held, because I said so. I am not
> A woman who has ever been afraid
> Of anything with hooves, or fangs, or horns.
> And yet there is a man on Dominick Street
> With a bad fiddle and a worse coat, who has
> Not asked me anything in six years' time
> Except to stay for the last tune, and I
> Have never stayed. I leave before the reel.
> I tell myself it is the early rounds.
> It is not early rounds. It is that if I stayed
> To hear the last tune, I would hear its end;
> And if I heard its end, I would not go.*

She laughed, once, at herself. Then she laid her hands flat on her knees, like a woman who has delivered a verdict, and took out of the suitcase a pair of socks and replaced them in the drawer, and took out of the drawer a different pair and put them in the suitcase, which is the sort of thing a person does when she is leaving and wishes not to be.

On the pillow, beside the ticket, lay her phone, and on the phone, where she had left it open for three days, lay a page of the Register of Black Stars.

*ENTRY 0025 — Galway, Ireland.*
*"There is a song I cannot finish, and it is about you."*

She knew the hand. She did not need the name. Nobody else in the west of Ireland would have written a thing in which the second clause was a promise and the first was a lie.

The doorbell rang like a fire alarm.

"*AOIFE!*" cried a voice from the street. "I have a *hake!*"

---

Niamh Quinn, forty-one, fishmonger, stood on the step in a coat the colour of a wet gull with a hake under one arm and a bottle of something under the other. She had the face of a woman who spends her life in the cold being gentle to dead things, which is to say, a face that had never in its whole career managed to hide a feeling.

"It's Thursday," she said. "I know what Thursday is. Thursday is session, and you've a face on you like the last cow at the mart, and I thought: I'll bring her a fish."

"I do not need a fish."

"Nobody needs a fish. That's the *beauty* of the fish." She pushed past into the hall with the confidence of the long-acquainted. "I'll put him in the sink. Don't look at his eyes, they follow you. What's that you're hiding?"

"I'm not hiding anything."

"You're standing in front of the bedroom door with your arms out, like an unconvincing Christ."

"It's a... it's a *draught excluder.*"

"Aoife."

"It's *laundry,* Niamh."

And at that moment, with the timing of a thing that has been waiting nine days, the suitcase on the bed, which had been shut with a hasty hand and a prayer, burst its clasps and sent forth upon the carpet a shower of socks, a hoof-pick, a rolled-up map of Nova Scotia, and a small framed photograph of the sea at Blackrock, which Aoife had not known she had packed.

There was a silence in which a hake, in the sink, seemed to take an interest.

Niamh looked at the map. She looked at the socks. She looked at her oldest friend, who stood in the doorway holding the doorframe with both hands as though the building had begun to move.

"Ah, *Aoife,*" said Niamh.

"It's not what it looks like."

"It's a map of *Canada.*"

"It's a map of Nova Scotia, which is *part* of—" Aoife stopped. She had not cried in front of another person since the funeral of a Labrador in 2009. She did not cry now. She merely sat down rather quickly upon the edge of the bed. "I've not told anyone. I was going to tell you. I was going to tell you on Saturday."

"Saturday?"

"Sunday's the flight."

"*Sunday.*" Niamh sat beside her, still holding the bottle. It did not seem to be a bottle in which either of them had any further interest. After a time she said, in the small flat voice of a person who has never learned to say what the next sentence is for: "I'm no good at this."

"I know."

"I'll cry in the airport."

"You'll not come to the airport."

"I'll cry in the *car park.*" She wiped her face with the sleeve of the wet-gull coat, which smelled of ice and mackerel. "Does he know?"

"Who?"

"Don't be thick."

"He doesn't."

"He's going to finish it tonight, you know. The song. He told me on Monday over the haddock. He said, 'Niamh, I've a fever, and I've a last verse, and I think God has decided the two should be sung together.' And I said to him, 'Liam, that is a *flu.*'"

"It's a flu?"

"He's thirty-nine degrees. He took it himself with a thermometer from the chemist, and then he asked the chemist if it was *romantic.*" She turned her wet and honest face on her friend. "Come tonight. You never stay for the last tune. Come, and stay."

"I'll come," said Aoife slowly. "I'll stay for the last one. And then—"

"And then?"

"And then I'll see," said Aoife Brennan, who had never in her life said such a thing, and meant it, as she had meant everything: with her whole hand.

---

### SCENE II
*Mulroy's of Dominick Street. A long low room, a turf fire, a ceiling of black beams, and a Thursday-night session already three tunes deep. Rain on the windows. Steam on the rain.*

Mulroy's pub held, on a good night, sixty souls; on a Thursday in December, with the Christmas market packed into Eyre Square and half of the west of Ireland looking for a roof, it held eighty-four and a dog.

By the fire, on a stool that had been shaped over decades to the exact curve of his grievance, sat Fergal Walsh, forty-five, who sold roast chestnuts from a cart on Shop Street by day and by night, for the love of God and a free pint, told stories, which he called *the real news*. He had coveted the Thursday slot for eleven years. He had fourteen stories, each with at least six endings, and a nose that had been broken in one of them.

"Ladies and gentlemen," said Fergal, rising, and the room, which had learned over many winters that it was easier to let him than to argue, turned its eighty-four faces toward the fire. "A story. An old one. I had it from my grandmother, who had it from a man in Inis Meáin, who had it from the sea, which is *notoriously* unreliable."

"Is it the one with the donkey?" someone called.

"It is not the one with the donkey. The donkey is *separate.* This is the story of the two fiddlers."

"Here we go," said a voice.

"In the old time," said Fergal, "there were two fiddlers on the Aran Islands who played a tune between them that had no end. The first would play a phrase and the second would answer, and the first would answer the answer, and on they went, for forty years, through weddings and wakes and one very bad christening. And everyone said: *Isn't it marvellous, the tune that has no end.* And it was. Until the day a stranger came off the boat, a man with a clever face and a leather case, and he said: *That's a grand tune. But where does it finish?*"

He paused, with an expert's cruelty, and sipped his pint.

"And the first fiddler, who was a decent man, said: *It doesn't. That's the point of it.* And the stranger said: *Ah, but the best tunes have a last note, and until you play it, you've never really said anything.* And the second fiddler—who was a woman, and sharper than the pair of them—looked at the first and said: *He's right.* And the first said: *But if we play the last note, we'll have to stop.* And she said: *Yes.* And do you know what he said?"

"What?" said eighty-four voices.

"He said," said Fergal, "*I'll tell you tomorrow.* And he never did, because the next day she took the boat. And that—" he spread his hands "—is why, to this very hour, there's a tune on Inis Meáin that has no ending, and a boat that never comes back, and a man who has nothing but his own two hands, and that, ladies and gentlemen, is why you should never, *ever,* buy a chestnut from a man who's had a drink."

There was a roar. It is the peculiarity of a fool, reader, that he says the wise thing by accident and the foolish thing on purpose, and so is never forgiven for the first.

But in the corner, near the door, where she had come in out of the rain with her coat on and her hair dripping and a hake's worth of resolve in her chest, Aoife Brennan did not laugh. She had been listening for a long time, and she stood against the wall with the very particular stillness of a woman who has heard a story that was not about her, and found her own name in it.

---

On the low stage, which was a platform of three planks and a tablecloth, a thin man with a worse coat than any she had imagined was tuning a fiddle that he had played, by his own account, since the age of eight and fixed, by his own account, with nine different sorts of glue.

Liam O'Connor, thirty-two, pub musician, was ill.

It was visible to anyone with eyes. His face had the high, bright, dreadful colour of a man lit from within by the wrong lamp. He wore two jumpers. His hands, which on a sound day could make a reel sound as though it had been born in a thunderstorm, trembled slightly on the neck of the instrument, and from time to time, between phrases, he coughed into his elbow with a fine sense of drama.

"He's *dying,*" said a woman at the bar.

"He's *thirty-nine degrees,*" said Niamh Quinn, from the corner, with the authority of a woman who has taken his temperature through a haddock. "It's different."

Beside him sat Maeve Ryan, seventy-two, retired guard on the Galway–Athenry line, with a bodhrán across her knee and a ticket-punch on a string around her neck, which she clicked in time with the reels, because for forty years she had never known a rhythm that was not a timetable. It was Maeve who had taught him his first tunes, in a front room in Spiddal, smacking his knuckles with a ruler for sloppiness. She was a woman of few words and many coughs, and she watched him now with an expression that people took for sternness, and was in fact the face of a person counting something she did not wish to lose.

Next to her, on a low stool, Sinéad Murphy, twenty-four, electrician, who had rewired the pub's lighting in October and could not be persuaded to stop looking at it, held a tin whistle in one hand and, in the other, a small screwdriver for emergencies.

"Right," said Liam, into a microphone he did not need. His voice cracked on the *R* and he swallowed. "That's a set of reels. Thanks, now. Thanks to Maeve, who's been punching my ticket since I was six. And to Sinéad, who has rewired the room, so if the lights go, that's *her.*"

"It'll not be me!" said Sinéad.

"And I've one more tonight. A new one. Well, not *new.* It's been the same one for six years, and I've never finished it. I'll tell you now, folks, I've been *saying* it was nearly finished since the Famine." A little laughter. "But I've a fever, and a last verse, and I thought, *God sent me the one, so he should have the other.* So if I fall off the stage, somebody throw a coat on me."

He took a breath. The fiddle came up under his chin.

He did not look at the door. He had known she was there since the first note of the first reel: a man who has played to a room for ten years knows who has come in, as a sailor knows weather. He played the first notes, and the room, which had been loud, went still.

> *The tide goes out at Blackrock Pier,
> It leaves the weed, it leaves the stone,
> It leaves me standing, year on year,
> With a tune I cannot call my own.
>
> You set the leg of my old collie
> And told me he was fed too well,
> And I went home with a sort of folly
> That no vet's bill could ever tell.
>
> You'd stand at the back with your coat still on,
> And leave before the last reel's done,
> And I'd play on till the lamps were gone
> For the one who never stays for one.*

He was not a great singer. His voice was low and rough and slightly flat on the long notes, and in the third line of the third verse it nearly gave out, so that for half a bar there was only the fiddle, speaking on its own, and in the corner by the door a woman in a wet coat put her hand flat against the wall, as if the building had moved.

He opened his eyes. He looked straight down the long smoky room, over eighty-four heads, over the turf-smoke and the faces and a dog, and found her.

"And this," said Liam O'Connor, very quietly, so that the room had to lean in, "is the last verse. It's the one I've never had. Hold on to your hats."

He bowed the fiddle. He sang:

> *So here is the end, and I'll sing it plain,
> For I've the fever and I've the nerve:
> If you are going, Aoife, go on the morning tide,
> I'll not be the one to say you've to stay,
> But before you go, I'll say what I should have said
> At the back of the bar, on the first wet night,
> When you took off your gloves to look at my dog:
> I have loved you since the winter that you*

*Here the page is torn.*

---

### SCENE III
*Lantern House, Cornwall. A little before midnight, in the same hour. A gale. A laptop. A postman's bag, empty at last.*

Nadeesha Fernando had answered four thousand, one hundred and twelve messages in fourteen days, and she had come to understand that grief and clerical work have a great deal in common: both are done by lamp, in the dark, until they are done.

"*Is Entry 0388 me?*" said the first. "*I think Entry 0388 is my husband. Is it possible to find him?*" said the second. "*Please remove Entry 0219. It is true, and I would like it not to be.*" The Register, she had learned, could be opened by anyone but could not be closed by her; and she sat at the oak table in the library of Lantern House, in a blanket, with a pot of tea gone cold at her elbow and the wind trying every door in the house in turn, and typed, to each of them, the same four lines that Seraphine had once said she should say: *Thank you for writing. I cannot tell you whose words are whose. I can tell you that they were true. Be kind, and be brave in that order.*

The laptop chimed.

A small square opened. A man, in a white shirt with the sleeves rolled, in a room full of grey dawn and brass fittings and a great wheel of glass, looked out of the screen and smiled at her with the diffident honesty of one who has not yet decided whether he is allowed.

"You are awake," said Anil Perera.

"It is midnight."

"It is five in the morning. The lamp is going off. I have been keeping the Galle light since four, and I thought: I will call. I will not say anything important. I will say good morning, and ask whether the Register is well."

Nadeesha looked at him for a while. She had been looking at strangers' confessions for fourteen days, and she found that the plainest face in the world was rather a rest.

"It is a thing like a tide," she said. "It does not stop. I thought the thousand would be quiet when they were read. They are not. They are *loud.*"

"And you? Have you read your own?"

"I have not written one."

"You did. You wrote, *I opened the Register and now I cannot close it.* It is Entry 0223. I read it before I read mine." He said this all at once, and then looked appalled. "I am sorry. That was private."

"It was *published,*" said Nadeesha, "by me."

"Even so."

The wind knocked once, politely, at the shutter. She laughed, which she had not done in fourteen days, and the sound surprised both of them.

"Tell me about the weather," she said. "At the lamp. I should like to hear someone say a fact."

"Calm," said Anil. "Southerly, five knots. A tanker off the Fort. A woman in the market selling king coconut who has argued with me every dawn for twenty years about a mango, and I have not once conceded." He leaned his chin on one hand, in the pale light, and his eyes, steady and dark as a harbour, held hers across six thousand miles of sleeping water. "I have been reading a Galway entry, Nadeesha. A man who cannot finish a song. I have been thinking that he will, tonight. It is a thing I know, as I know the tides, without being able to say how."

"You have never been wrong about the weather."

"No."

"And about people?"

He thought about it, honestly, for the whole of a long moment, with the great glass wheel turning behind him, and the first light of a tropical morning gathering on the water.

"I have never been asked," said Anil, "by anyone who wanted to know."

Nadeesha turned the laptop's small lamp down, and the room filled with the sea's dark noise, and a gale, and a thousand voices waiting to be answered; and, in the centre of it, with her tea cold and her blanket slipping, a nurse from Galle sat in the house of a woman she had loved and found that there was, in the middle of the long night, a light that had come on at the far end of the world, and that she had not put it there, and that it did not mind.

---

*Margin note, in pencil, in the hand of S.W.R., against Entries 0025 and 0956:*

> *A song is a promise made in public. This is why men are afraid of finishing one.*
>
> *Entry 0956 wrote that she had told no one. By Thursday night she had told a fishmonger, a hake, and a wall.*
>
> *I do not know the last line. I have never known it. Some tunes are only given the Keeper in pieces.*

---

*End of Chapter 15.*

## Chapter 16
### Hanbok Hours

> *"I have measured everyone in this city but you."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0351

---

### SCENE I
*Seoul. The bank of the Han River at one in the morning, minus eleven degrees. A convenience store with a ramyeon machine, two plastic stools, and a man with a spreadsheet.*

Daniel Cho, twenty-seven, head coach of the esports team called Hanul, which means *Sky,* believed that every difficulty in life could be reduced to a table, and he had brought his table to the river.

"Column one," he said, holding up his phone, "is *Reasons to Stay.* The salary. The trophy. The nineteen boys who think I am their father. Column two is *Reasons to Go.*"

"How long is column two?" said Joon-ho.

"It has one entry."

"What is it?"

"It is in a *foreign* format," said Daniel, with dignity, and turned the phone face down upon his knee.

Joon-ho Yoon, forty-one, umbrella-maker, sat beside him on the other stool with a paper cup of noodles steaming into his moustache. He kept a repair stall in Euljiro that had survived three landlords, two recessions, and a fashion for folding umbrellas he regarded as a moral failure. He was Daniel's oldest friend, if one can use *oldest* of a man who had only been a friend since Daniel was nineteen and had brought him a broken umbrella and a broken heart in the same week; and he had a vice, which was that he read anything that was lying open. Letters. Menus. Phones.

He had read the resignation before Daniel had finished writing it.

"*Dear Mr. Kang,*" Joon-ho recited, around a mouthful of noodles. "*It is with a heavy heart, and following extensive consideration, that I tender my resignation as Head Coach, effective at the close of the winter split, in order to pursue—*" He paused. "Hyung. Pursue *what?*"

"A quiet life."

"That is not an activity. That is a *sound.*"

"It is a lifestyle choice."

"It is a coward's way of saying you have found a woman." Joon-ho put down his cup with great finality. "I have known you eight years. You do not, as a rule, leave a trophy for a *lifestyle.* You leave a trophy for a *person.* Who is she?"

"I cannot say."

"Cannot, or have not got her name in a *cell*?"

Daniel did not answer. Across the black river, past the ice floes turning slow in the lamplight and the lit bridges stitched across the water like seams, the city went on shining and not looking at him, as cities do. He had spent six years teaching nineteen-year-olds to read a screen in ninety seconds. He had spent the same six years failing, by a gap of exactly four steps, to walk into a shop in an alley off Jongno and say a sentence he had drafted one hundred and forty times.

"There is a tailor," he said at last.

"*Ah,*" said Joon-ho.

"She makes hanbok. I take my mother, for the new year. For the autumn festival. For her birthday, for the... I have been in her shop fourteen times in three years."

"You have a mother with fourteen birthdays?"

"My mother is theatrical," said Daniel. "She regards the lunar calendar as a series of *opportunities.*" He rubbed his eyes. "Every time I go, the tailor measures my mother. She measures my mother's shoulders and my mother's wrists and the span from my mother's neck to her heel. She measures the neighbours. She measured a Japanese tourist once, who had come in to buy a hat. I stand at the edge with my hands in my pockets and I think: *I should say something.* And I say: *Is the silk imported?*"

"And is it?"

"It is, apparently, *always imported.*"

Joon-ho, who was not a man of unusual delicacy, said nothing for a long minute. A tram of wind went up the river bank, and the plastic sign above the shop door clapped like a thin applause.

"Hyung," he said, "you could say a better thing than *quiet life.*"

"Such as?"

"Anything. Something with her in it." He wiped his moustache and, with a tenderness that astonished them both, laid a hand on the younger man's shoulder. "I mend umbrellas. Do you know what a broken one has in common with a man? The *frame* is fine. It is only that nobody ever opened it in the rain."

"That," said Daniel, "is nearly a good sentence."

"I know. I read it on a postcard."

He sent the letter in the morning, at 9:02, a minute after the building opened. He did not use *pursue.* He used six words, and the president of Hanul Esports read them twice, and then, for reasons of his own, closed his office door and did not come out until noon.

---

### SCENE II
*Osaka. The Fukushima ward, under the railway arches, at ten minutes before midnight. A ramen shop with eight stools. Steam, trains, a paper lantern that has lost the argument with the weather.*

There is a particular kind of Osaka night, in winter, when the trains go over the arches every four minutes and each one shakes a little salt out of the sky, and every shop beneath the tracks keeps its door half open so that you can smell the broth from the next street.

The shop of Hiroshi Tanabe had a curtain, a ticket machine that dispensed a single choice, and a counter with eight stools; and beside the steam pipe, on the stool where the heat rose best, nobody ever sat. In front of it, every night, stood a bowl.

It was a bowl like any other. White glaze, a blue ring at the lip. A clear brown broth fourteen hours in the pot, with a shaving of leek and three slices of pork laid in a fan. He made it at twenty to midnight, after the last customer, and set it before the empty stool, with the chopsticks on their rest and a small blue towel folded in thirds; and then he stood on the other side of the wood with his arms folded and waited, as one waits for a train that is late, but not very late. At midnight he poured it into the sink. He washed the bowl by hand.

"Tonight," said Rin Hayashi, from the third stool, "has an air of *event.*" He was thirty-three, a retired lifeguard, who had pulled four swimmers from Osaka Bay and had spent six years of nights watching a man pour a bowl down a drain, which he considered the harder rescue.

"You say that every night."

"I mean it more tonight. Look at the lantern."

"It is the same lantern."

"It is *swaying,*" said Rin, "in an expectant manner."

At the end of the counter, among her pickle-jars, an old woman in a quilted jacket went on shelling cucumbers with the serenity of one who has outlived most omens. At the counter nearest the stove sat Daichi Ito, thirty-four, historian, who had come in from Kobe with a bag of books and had been eating one bowl of noodles for forty minutes in order to be present for the atmosphere. He had written six hundred pages on the history of the noodle in the Kansai region and could not cook water. He read every portent aloud and apologised for none of them, which is the secret of his trade.

"I will say," said Daichi, to nobody, "that in the Heian period it was believed that the last customer of the night was a visitor from a better world."

"It's eleven fifty," said Hiroshi.

"A better world with its own timetable. I merely *note.*"

Hiroshi, thirty-four, perfectionist, said very little and was said to say it in the order of importance. His hands were large, scarred, steady, with a burn along one thumb, and they moved across a clean board with the rhythm of a man who has found in repetition the only mercy of the world. Since the spring he had been saying one sentence a day. Last week a boy from Recife had put his counter on the internet, and the sentence had been *Eat.*

He did not look at the door. He had learned a long time ago that to look at a door is to ask it for something.

The curtain moved.

There are people who come into a room like a stone into a pond, and people who come in like a drop of ink, and there are people who come in like a held breath. The woman who stepped under the noren, in a grey coat the colour of an old photograph, with her face half-hidden in a scarf and her hand still on the edge of the cloth as though she had not decided whether to let go of it, was the third kind.

She was thirty-three. She had hair cut at the jaw, and tired eyes, and the straight, careful posture of a person who has spent eleven years looking closely at things and has lately been afraid of what she might see. For six years, on the same night every week, she had sat beside the steam pipe and eaten with her eyes closed and said almost nothing. Since March she had said nothing at all.

"Welcome," said Hiroshi. It came out of him as a thing is said by a man who has said it fifty thousand times and has never meant it as he meant it now.

"*Irasshai,*" said Rin, instantly, and then, in a stage whisper that could have been heard in Kyoto: "*Look at the lantern.*"

The woman stood in the doorway. She looked at the bowl, the white glaze, the fan of pork, the steam, which went up into the lamplight in a single thin rope and was cut, from time to time, by the roar of a train.

"The photograph," she said. "A friend sent it. A bowl at the end of a counter, in Portuguese. The caption said: *He makes one bowl every night for a woman who stopped coming.*" Her fingers tightened on the noren. "I recognised the glaze."

"Mei-san," said Hiroshi.

It was the first time he had said her name aloud since March. It broke a little in the middle, like a stick of kelp.

"I was not sure you would remember."

"I know your order. I have known it for six years." He did not say what else he knew. "Sit. Please. It was made for you."

"It is *cold,*" said Rin, kindly. "I'll make a new—"

"It is not cold," said Hiroshi, without turning. "It is nine minutes old. It was made at eleven-forty. It has been waiting."

Daichi Ito had stopped chewing. Rin Hayashi had risen halfway off his stool, a lifeguard at the edge of a deep and difficult water. At the end of the counter the old woman, who was Hiroshi's mother, had put down her cucumber. And above them, at that exact second, the last train of the night went over the arches and shook the whole shop, so that the lantern swung, and the pot lids sang, and the bowl shivered once, and was still.

Mei crossed the room. It was a short floor, four steps, and she took each of them as one crosses ice. She sat. The stool was warm; it had been warmed, she understood, on purpose. Her hands, bare and unsteady, came to the lip of the bowl and rested there, as if she were warming them at a fire. She lifted the spoon. She did not drink.

"Hiroshi-san," she said. Her voice was very quiet. "Before I eat this, I must tell you the real reason I stopped coming. It is not the one you think. It was not that I disliked the soup, and it was not that I—" Her eyes went to the broth, to the clear gold of it, and a thing crossed her face that was not quite shame, and not quite grief, but the look of a woman about to read out a verdict against herself. "It was that one morning in the spring, when I woke, and put a spoonful of miso soup into my mouth, I found that I could no longer—"

*Here the page is torn.*

---

### SCENE III
*Seoul. An alley off Jongno, between the bindaetteok stall and the stationer's. The shop of Han Ji-woo, on a Thursday, three weeks before the lunar new year. A bell on the door. A kettle on the ondol. The wild light of a winter afternoon.*

The shop was so full of colour that it seemed less a room than an argument that silk had won. Along the walls hung jeogori jackets in jade and ember and plum, their ribbons unknotted like the fringe of some great beast; chima skirts in a hundred pinks; the white collars called *dongjeong* stacked in rows, sharp as new paper. In the back a sewing machine hummed like a bee in a bottle, and in the middle of everything, at a long cutting-table scored by thirty years of chalk, stood Ji-woo.

She was twenty-six. She was small, and exact, and she moved as a good needle moves: neither fast nor slow, but exactly as fast as the thread. Round her neck, for good reason, she wore a yellow tape measure, and she had worn it so long that her friends, when they spoke of her, said *the tape,* as in: *Is the tape in?*

At the counter, in her third-best cardigan, sat a nine-year-old called Tae-yang, who had been left there by an aunt for the afternoon, and was reading a book about volcanoes with the grave air of a magistrate.

"Ji-woo noona," he said, without looking up. "Who measures you?"

"I measure myself."

"No. Who *else.* You said you cannot measure your own back. Nobody can. You said a tailor has the worst-fitting coat in the city."

"It is a proverb."

"It is a *problem,*" said Tae-yang, turning a page. "I read that, in a volcano, the thing at the centre is the one you cannot see."

At the door, the bell gave its small bronze cough.

"*Ji-woo-ya!*" cried a woman of fifty-eight in a gold quilted jacket, entering like weather. This was Yoon Ji-ah, goldsmith, who made the tiny knotted ornaments called *norigae* that hang from the ribbons, and who had never in her life been on time for anything, owing to the fact that she made every promise a little faster than she could keep it. "I have them! I have your *norigae!* I brought them myself. I said *tomorrow* on Tuesday and *tomorrow* on Wednesday, and I said *tomorrow* on Thursday, so it is a statistical triumph that it is only Friday."

"They were due three days ago."

"They were due *in spirit.*" She dropped a small silk bag on the counter, and out of it spilled a clutch of gold and coral: butterflies, little bottles, a fish with eyes of jade. "And for the *old lady*—for the mother of that nice boy with the face—I have made the peach. The big one. With the tassel. Where is he? Is he coming? He came last Thursday. He asked about the *silk.* I said to my husband, that boy has not once asked about the *silk*—"

"Aunty," said Ji-woo.

"I am only saying. A man who asks about silk four times in three years is not asking about silk."

The bell rang again.

Daniel Cho came in with snow on his shoulders and no coat, having left it, in a state of what he later described to Joon-ho as *procedural collapse,* on the number 6 bus. He had resigned at 9:02 that morning. He had been told, at ten, that the president of Hanul wished to see him. He had been told, at noon, that the president wished him to reconsider. He had been told, at one, in a corridor, by a nineteen-year-old with a stunning mouse-hand and an unexpectedly wet face, *Coach, you can't go.* And he had come here, because it was his mother's turn.

"It's for the new year," said Daniel. "My mother's outfit. She has requested... a *peach.*"

"A jealous peach," said Ji-ah the goldsmith, "with a tassel."

"She was quite specific."

"Of course she was. She is a lady of discernment." Ji-woo came out from behind the table with the yellow tape hung round her neck, and with an air so composed that only a person who has practised could have achieved it. "Mr. Cho. How is your mother's height? Last time I had the measurement but I have mislaid the paper."

It was not true. She had never mislaid a paper in her life. She had the number in her head and in two notebooks and, on a good night, in her sleep.

"I—" said Daniel. "She is— I think she comes to my ear. Here."

"Here?"

"Or here. Perhaps lower. She wears shoes of an *ambitious* heel."

"Then," said Ji-woo, "you had better stand there."

"Where?"

"There. By the post. I will use you."

"As a *mannequin*?"

"As a *reference,*" said Ji-woo, who found, to her great surprise, that her own voice had gone a little high at the end, like a thread under strain. "Stand straight. Look at the wall. Do not talk."

He stood by the post. He looked at the wall, where a calendar hung of a tiger in a hat. He did not talk. This, for him, was a feat of discipline on the level of Olympic sport, and it was compounded by the fact that somewhere behind him a woman was walking slowly round him, once, and then again, with her head a little on one side, saying nothing, and not touching him at all.

"Shoulder to shoulder," she murmured, to herself. "Neck to heel. The set of the arm." She had her pencil out. "Your mother is smaller. You are... that is the proportion I will take."

"I am taller than my mother."

"Yes."

"Considerably."

"Yes. I will adjust."

"By how much?"

"By a *standard* amount," said Ji-woo, and her pencil moved, not on the large white pad on the counter where her customers' numbers were written, but on the small blue notebook she kept in the pocket of her apron. She had not taken the tape from her neck. She did not need to. She had been measuring this man by eye since the first Thursday, and the tape, which she had worn for twelve years like a stole, hung at her collarbone as unused as a bell with its tongue tied.

"That's not the number for his *mother,*" said Tae-yang, from the counter, without moving his eyes from the volcano.

"Tae-yang."

"It's the one for a man. A *tall* man. You wrote the sleeve in a different pencil." He turned a page. "Also you haven't touched the tape, which you always do, and you are blushing, and you've dropped it twice."

"I have *not* dropped the—"

The tape was on the floor. It lay in a loose yellow coil at her feet like a thing that had given up on discretion.

There was a silence. Ji-ah the goldsmith, who had never in her life let a silence go unfilled, opened her mouth, and then, with a delicacy that surprised everyone, including herself, shut it again and began, with great interest, to reorganise the butterflies.

"Mr. Cho," said Ji-woo at last, in the voice of a person lifting a heavy thing and finding it, to her horror, lighter than she had feared. "How is the team?"

"I have resigned," said Daniel.

"From what?"

"From being a coach. I... would like a quiet life." He turned from the wall, at last, with snow melting in his hair and a face as bare as a field, and looked at her with the whole of his analytical, awkward, honest heart. "I have a table. I mean, I had one. It had a column with one entry. I am here to say that I think I have... that I would like to learn something that is not a game."

"What?"

"I do not know. A button. How to sew on a button."

"That," said Ji-woo Han, slowly, and picked up the tape, and found that her hand did not shake at all, "I can teach you."

"When?"

"The new year is in nineteen days. Come back for the fitting. Your mother's. And—" She did not say *and what.* "Thursdays are quiet. You may fold silk."

"For how long?"

"For as long as it takes the silk."

"That is a great many hours," said Daniel Cho, who had never in his life said so, and heard it, and found, to his surprise, that he did not mind.

Outside, in the alley, the snow came down in thick, slow flakes over the bindaetteok stall and the stationer and the little brass bell, and Yoon Ji-ah the goldsmith, who had slipped out to give them privacy and had been standing for ten minutes with her ear against the door, said to the street at large, with the most reliable promise she had ever made:

"*Tomorrow,* I will tell the whole of Suwon."

---

*Margin note, in pencil, in the hand of S.W.R., against Entries 0351 and 0254; and beside Entries 0510 and 0810, a single short line, like a stitch that has been cut:*

> *A tailor who has measured a city and not the man who stands in her doorway. A coach who has made a column and left it blank.*
>
> *Of the other two, the cook and the critic, I will say only that the bowl was not cold.*

*End of Chapter 16.*
