Chaminda Abeywardena, forty-seven, proprietor of the newsagent's by the clock tower, was a devout man in the same sense that a sponge is a wet one. He carried in his arms, with the care of a procession, six king coconuts, a flask of tea, a bundle of white thread, and the front page of a newspaper dated the fourth of February 1989. "I have kept every paper since the day I started," he declared, "and today I thought: what is a lighthouse but a very old newspaper? It tells the news, and warns of danger. It is the same trade."

"Chaminda," said Anil, from the floor, "why have you brought the *paper*?"

"For the pirith! I will bless the lamp. I have brought the sacred thread. And for the *luck* I have brought the paper of the day the lamp was last repaired." He unfolded it. "This," he said, with great tenderness, "is Wimbledon."

"Chaminda, the lamp was last repaired in 1994."

"Then I have brought the *wrong* Wimbledon," said the newsagent, calmly, and sat down on the floor and began, in a noble baritone, to chant.

It was in the eleventh minute of this blessing, with Anil swearing quietly in two languages at a seized housing, and the sea behind the great curved glass the colour of a very old coin, that Nadeesha, who had been lying on her stomach holding a torch into the cavity behind the lens pedestal, said, in an entirely different voice:

"Anil. There is a tin."

---

It was an old biscuit tin, with a faded painting of a coach and four on its lid, and it had been placed in the hollow behind the brickwork so long ago that the rust had bonded it to the wall. They had to cut it out. Anil did it with a chisel, as gently as a man delivers a calf, and when it came free, he carried it to the window as one carries a sleeping child.

Inside lay the letters.

There were seventy-one. They were thin and blue and weightless, the old airmail kind that folds into its own envelope, bundled in the faded string of an age that tied bundles. The earliest were addressed in a girl's looping hand to *Mr. D. Perera, Keeper, Galle Light, CEYLON.* The later ones said *SRI LANKA.* On the back, in the corner, each carried the same return: *Miss S. Wyndham-Rao, Mrs. Alder's rooms, Kentish Town, London.*

Nadeesha did not touch them. She sat on the bottom step of the gallery stair, with her hands pressed between her knees, and a sound came out of her that was not a word.

"My grandfather," said Anil, very quietly, "was the keeper in those years. He never told us. I thought he had *no* letters." He turned the first envelope over, with a care that cost him. "It is your aunt's hand."

"I know it is," said Nadeesha. "She wrote *every list in her life* in that hand. She wrote my birthday card in it. She wrote *Wash your hands* on the kitchen door."

It was she who opened the first. It had been written in the summer of 1964, by a girl of eighteen about to go to London to study the stars:

*Dear Mr. Perera. Thank you for letting me stand in your lamp-room last August, and for not laughing when I asked what the light was for. You said, "for the ships." I have been thinking since. I think it is for the ones who do not know they need it. I am going to London. I shall write to you. You need not answer. A keeper is not expected to. A light does not reply, it only goes on being there. — Seraphine W.-R.*

She read it aloud. Chaminda had stopped chanting, which, in an age of miracles, was perhaps the whole miracle. When she had finished she held it against her chest.

"There is one more," said Anil. "At the bottom. It is the last. It is dated 1979."

---

The afternoon went. The bearing went in, a new bronze one that had come up from Colombo on a bus, on the knee of Nadeesha's brother Sampath, who had sold tea to the driver all the way. Anil set it with a tenderness that was almost indecent. The brass housing was oiled; the lens, which was the size of a small room and held all its glass in the exact attitude in which it had been set by a foundry long ago, was released.

At half past six, with the tropical dusk coming down like a cloth on a table, a girl of fifteen with a basket of jasmine appeared at the foot of the stair and shrieked something up the well of the tower. This was Kumari Senanayake, who had been telling the whole of the Fort for a month that the lighthouse keeper looked at the sea when the nurse was not there, and at the nurse when she was not looking.

"What did she say?" said Nadeesha.

"I did not hear it," said Anil, who had. He went to the switch. His father, who had kept the Galle Light for thirty-eight years and whose eyes were now two milk-white moons, stood in the doorway of the lamp-room in his old white jacket, with one hand on the rail and his head tilted, as a man listens to a thing he has heard ten thousand times. Nobody had asked him to come up the stairs. Nobody had been able to stop him.

"Throw it, putha," said Mr. Perera.

Anil threw it.

For a moment there was nothing but the light, white and round and enormous in the glass. Then, with a faint sigh, like a deep breath let out after a long swim, the lens began to turn. The beam swung out across the sea, a hard bright road laid down on the water, and went round, and found the horizon, and went on. Far below, on the ramparts, on the beach, on the road of the fort, people looked up, as a congregation looks up when the bell is finally rung.

"Twelve seconds," said Mr. Perera, listening. He had counted it by ear. "Twelve. Same as always." His blind face turned, with great accuracy, toward the nurse. "Madam. Your aunt used to stand at the rail where you are standing. She was twelve, I think. My father allowed it. She never once said thank you. She only looked."

"Mr. Perera," said Nadeesha, "I am going to cry."

"Do it on the rampart, madam," said the old man gently. "The glass is expensive."

---

She went down. It seemed the only thing to do. She went out through the old iron door at the tower's foot and along the rampart to the place the fort-people call Flag Rock, where the stone drops sheer to the surf, and there, with the wet wind blowing the first of the cool evening against her face, she stood and let herself weep for the first time since a night in November.

Behind her, high up, the beam went round.

It found her, as it passed. It left her. It came back. Twelve seconds, a circle of light, a long turn of dark, and again the light on her wet face, and again the dark, a pulse like the beat of a slow heart. She could not have said why this should comfort her. Perhaps because something in the world had been turned, at last, in the right direction and was going on being turned whether or not she could stand it.

Above her, in the gallery, with a spanner still hanging forgotten from his belt and his father humming softly beside him, Anil stood at the rail and watched the small figure on the rock. Each time the light passed over her, he saw her face for the length of a breath. Then the dark. Then, twelve seconds on, the face. He found he had begun to count. He found that it was the longest he had ever waited for anything, and the shortest.

He spoke then, quietly, as men do who have kept silent for a very long time and find that the night is not listening, and are mistaken:

> *The lamp goes round. I never see the ship.
> I send the light to find a thing it cannot see,
> And trust it will be found. This is my trade.
> For ships, I keep the lamp. For her, I keep…
> I have no word. The beam goes round again,
> And finds her face, and leaves it, and returns.
> There is no kindness like a thing that turns
> And passes you in the dark, and comes again.
> I'll turn like this, if she will let me. Slow.
> For twelve long seconds, and for as many years
> As there are stairs. I'll come round. I'll come round.*

"It is for the ships," said Anil, to nobody, to the glass.

"*Putha*," said his father, who had very good ears, "it is for the ships *and* for the stairs."

---

She came up when it was dark. It was a hundred and thirty-six steps, and she took them one at a time, with the last letter in her fist. She stood in the doorway of the lamp-room with her face still wet, and the beam went over her like a hand.

"I found the one from 1979," said Nadeesha. "I read it on the way up."

"What does it say?"

"I'll read it."

She read it in the doorway of the lamp-room, by the light that went round:

*Dear Mr. Perera. A man wrote to me from a ship in the autumn of '77, and I have kept his letter, and I find that I want to keep others. I have placed a notice in three foreign papers: if there is a thing you cannot say, write it to me. I will keep it. I will number it. I will say nothing. I do not know why I tell you, except that you taught me what it is to keep a light for someone who may never come to harbour.*

*P.S. If any of my blood should come to your door one day, needing to see further than she can, let her up the stairs. — S.*

She folded it.

"You let me up," said Nadeesha.

"Of course," said Anil.

"She asked you to."

"She asked my grandfather."

"You were not *asked*," said Nadeesha. "You came with a spanner and a torch and a king coconut." And then, because there are limits to what a person can carry in one evening, she laughed, and wiped her face with the heel of her hand, and walked across the room and put her hand on the brass rail of the lens beside his own.

They did not speak. The great glass turned above them, and every twelve seconds the room flashed white and dark and white again, and in each flash the two of them were standing a little closer, as in a flickering reel of film, until at the last their hands lay together on the rail, which was warm from the lamp, and neither one said anything at all.

In the corner, Chaminda Abeywardena, who had been present throughout and had been entirely forgotten, took out the front page of the fourth of February 1989 and, with the greatest delicacy, laid it over his face.

---

**Kyoto. The same evening, by a different light.**

The workshop of Kenji Watanabe smelled of cypress and glue and the old sweet dust of shell. It stood at the end of a lane in the north of the city, in a wooden house the colour of strong tea, and it contained, on shelves, in baskets, hanging from nails, some two hundred faces.

They were all of one family: the long pale women of the Noh stage, with brows high-painted and mouths like closed leaves; the old men with beards of horsehair; the demons with gold eyes; the girl called *ko-omote*, whose face is neither smiling nor weeping and has been copied, by carver after carver, for six hundred years. They watched the room with the patience of the dead.

"You may not touch the chisel today," said Daichi Kobayashi, twenty-five, apprentice, drinker of too much tea at night, and a young man of strong superstitions, to a figure bent over a workbench in the corner. "It is *Butsumetsu*. It is a day of ill omen. A man who carves on Butsumetsu will make a face that will not look at him."

"I am not carving," said Kenji. "I am finishing."

"It is a different *kind* of bad luck."

Kenji Watanabe was twenty-seven, quiet to the point of furniture, a man whose hands were far more fluent than his tongue. He had been apprenticed at fifteen, and had learned in twelve years that a mask is a face with its mind removed: it holds a feeling as an empty cup holds the shape of water. He was very good at it. It was perhaps because he could not show his own.

On the bench before him, wrapped in a square of purple silk, lay the thing that had taken him four months.

"Master," said a voice at the door, "the wood you ordered has come."

It was Yuto Shimizu, the river-boatman from Arashiyama, a hot-tempered man of twenty-nine who believed what he was told by anyone who looked sure of themselves, and who had brought with him, on a handcart, an enormous slab of timber with the air of a man presenting a firstborn. "Genuine three-hundred-year-old cypress. From a temple that burned down. My cousin's friend got it. Look at the *grain.*"

Kenji looked at the grain. He tapped the slab. He bent and smelled it.

"Yuto-san," he said, with great gentleness. "This is the top of a chopping board from a sushi shop in Osaka."

"No!"

"There is a small fish-scale in the corner."

"It is a mark of *age!*" said Yuto, and sat down on the handcart, abruptly, with the expression of a man betrayed by a cousin and a cousin's friend. "I paid four hundred thousand yen."

"You were robbed," said Daichi, with delight.

"I was *educated*," said Yuto, with dignity.

The door slid, and there was a hush, because there is always a hush when a certain kind of person comes into a room. She came in as she always came, without sound. She was twenty-six. She wore a plain grey kimono and her hair up, and there was a small, correct, immovable smile on her face that she wore through the streets, and the station, and her mother's table, and the green-room of every theatre in the city, like a mask she'd never learned to remove.

Haruka Mori was a Noh actress, and a very fine one, in a tradition that had not been built for her. On the stage she could, in the turn of a head, be a ghost of a thousand years. Off it she was a woman with a polished smile, who said *Yes, of course,* and *It was nothing,* and *Please don't trouble,* and who had told no one in six years what it cost.

"Watanabe-san," she said. "Your boy said you wished to see me."

"Mori-san," said Kenji.

He said nothing for some time. It is a method of speech, in certain trades. Daichi, with an almost audible click of the brain, took Yuto by the elbow and removed him, protesting, along with his chopping board, to the lane.

When they were alone, Kenji took up the silk bundle and placed it, with both hands, on the bench between them.

"It is not for the stage," he said. "I did not make it for the stage. It will not be good on the stage. It is for you."

She unwrapped it.

It lay in the purple silk, a young woman's face of pale cypress, finished with a thin pearl of shell-powder; and it was *wrong*. It was perfectly formed, and entirely correct in every curve, and it was wrong in that it had no expression whatever. The brow did not lift. The mouth did not close. There was no sorrow in it and no joy. It looked, in its blank, restful, patient beauty, like a face before it has been told what to be.

"It has no face," said Haruka.

"It has *all* of them," said Kenji. He took it, and tilted it a little upward, so that the lamp fell across the brow, and the face seemed to lighten, as if on the edge of a laugh. He turned it down, and the shadow ran into the eye-sockets, and the same face, without a mark altered, held a grief as quiet as a pond. "It is called *terasu* and *kumorasu*: to brighten and to cloud. All the masks do it. But this one has no mind of its own to get in the way." He set it down. His fingers were not quite steady. "I make faces because I cannot show my own. You wear one because you will not set yours down. I thought: if you had a face that was permitted to be nothing, you could rest. You could put it on in the evening, in the dark, and not have to choose."

The workshop was very quiet. The two hundred faces on the walls seemed, with great delicacy, to look elsewhere.

Haruka lifted the mask. She held it before her own face, not yet touching, and for a moment he saw the little perfect smile she wore, and the blank cypress one, side by side, and he understood, as a carver does, which was the hollow.

She put it on.

She did not tilt it up. She did not tilt it down. She stood, with a young woman's blank face over her own, in the lamplit shop of a quiet man, and said nothing at all; and from behind the wood a very small sound came, such as a person makes who has been holding her breath for six years and has been given leave to let it go.

When she took it off, there was no smile on her face. There was only a wet, tired, entirely honest face, which was, he thought, the most beautiful thing that he had ever carved or ever would.

"It is the first one," said Haruka Mori, "that lets me stop."

On the inside of the silk, in a hand so small that it might have been a worm's, Kenji had written, in the old five-line form of the court:

> *Carved from one block,
> a face that has no country.
> Tilt it to the lamp:
> spring. Tilt it from the lamp: rain.
> Whichever you are, be it.*

She read it. She folded the silk. She said, in a voice quite without the smile, "Watanabe-san. You will have to teach me to be *sorry* in front of people."

"I do not know how," said Kenji. "I have never done it."

"Then we will be bad at it together," said Haruka. And at that, in the lamplight of a Kyoto evening, with a blank mask between them and two hundred painted faces turned politely to the wall, the carver and the actress did, for the first time in either of their lives, the same thing at once: they laughed.

---

*Margin note, in pencil, in the hand of S.W.R.:*

> *I am told I should be embarrassed that my girlhood was found in a biscuit tin. I am not. A lighthouse does not choose the ship it saves. A face does not choose the weather it must wear. But both, if they are wise, will agree to be turned toward the light that is coming.*
>
> *I wrote to a keeper once, and he did not answer, and it was the kindest thing that anyone has done for me.*

## Chapter 36
### Cycling Through Cloud

> *"I crashed because I was thinking of you."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0586

---

**Antioquia, Colombia. Stage Six of the Vuelta. A quarter to eight in the morning, on the climb of Las Palmas, inside a cloud.**

In the Colombian Andes the cloud does not drift; it sits down on the mountain, like a hen on an egg, and stays until it has been sufficiently admired.

On this particular morning it had been sitting for six hours, and the road up from Medellín, which climbs a thousand metres in eleven kilometres by way of hairpins and prayer, had been swallowed to the knee. Along its edges the people of the mountain stood in their ponchos with their transistor radios held to their ears like the wounded holding hearts. They sold empanadas and sweet *aguapanela* from steaming pots. They shouted the names of men they could not see. And over every radio, from a motorbike somewhere in the white, boomed the voice of the most beloved commentator in the south-west of the Republic, a gentle, nervous, cardiganed man from Cali named Esteban Ortiz, who became, the moment a microphone came near, a thunderstorm.

*"Amigos del ciclismo, GOOD MORNING! Nobody can see anything, which is the finest thing that can happen to a radio man! I am inside a cloud, I am inside a legend! Here come the leaders, I think. I hear them. It sounds like a swarm of very expensive bees! And behind them, forty seconds behind, comes the story of the day, ladies and gentlemen: Sebastián Torres of Bogotá! Eleven months ago, a crash on the descent at Letras. A collarbone, a hip, ten months of hospital and rehabilitation. And today, the comeback! I have lost a bet on this man four times, and I would lose it again for the pleasure!"*

The man in question was at that moment climbing at the speed of a determined snail, in a group of six, with the white wall closing before his front wheel and his own breath loud as a bellows in his ears. Sebastián Torres, twenty-nine, professional cyclist, stubborn by trade and humorous by reflex, could not see his handlebar. He could see a foot of grey tarmac, and a rival's rear tyre, and now and then a yellow leg like a drowned man's.

*It is a strange thing,* he thought, *to ride for a year toward a day, and have it arrive in a cloud.*

He knew the road. He had ridden it a hundred times in training. And he knew what lay a kilometre ahead, behind a green gate on the left, where a hillside of glass had been hung out of the cloud like washing.

A year before, he had punctured at that gate, on a Tuesday, cursing in two registers; and a young woman in rubber boots had come out of a greenhouse with a roll of tape, a spoon, and a face like an indignant sunrise. *You climb,* she had said, kneeling to his wheel, *like a man running away from something.* *I climb,* he had said, *like a man who is late.* She had mended it with a teaspoon and a temper. She had given him a rose for his mother. It was a Tuesday, and nothing had occurred.

Two weeks later, descending a mountain in the Tour of the Andes at eighty kilometres an hour, he had seen, at the corner of his eye, a flower stall, a bucket of red roses, and thought of a teaspoon; and the road had turned, and he had not.

He thought it now, in the white, in the only prose the lungs allow at that gradient, which is verse:

> *White, and a white beyond the white, and breath.
> I cannot see the road. I know the road.
> The legs are maps that need no light to read,
> And I have ridden blind since one small spoon
> Mended one wheel. So let me climb in cloud
> And trust the grade, as some men trust in prayer
> Who never saw the One they pray to. Let
> There be, somewhere on the left, a gate. A boot.*

The cloud thinned.

---

**The same morning, at a green gate on the left.**

The farm was called La Nube: The Cloud. That spring it had been living up to its name.

Daniela Ruiz, twenty-eight, flower farmer, bright and proud and out of money, had stood in her greenhouses before dawn, among forty thousand roses that nobody would now buy. A Miami buyer had cancelled by e-mail on Thursday, with a pleasant apology, and the apology had arrived at the precise moment that the letter from the bank had arrived with an unpleasant one. A rose, once cut, keeps for nine days. These had been cut on Wednesday. By Friday they would be a very expensive compost.

"I could *give* them away," she had said at four in the morning, to her foreman, to the radio, to the stripped benches. "Or I could put them on the road."

It was not a plan. A plan has a bottom line. It was the thing that proud people do when they cannot afford to be seen losing, which is to lose magnificently.

Now, with sixty of her workers and every cousin in the *vereda* and a ten-year-old named Paola Ramírez who was supervising with a hand-lettered sign, she laid them out, stem to stem, in a long red ribbon along the grass on the left verge of the road, for eight hundred metres, from her gate to the top of the rise. Forty thousand roses. They lay in the white like a thread of blood on a bandage, and nobody who came up that road, if he looked to his left, could fail to follow it.

She did not know if he would see it. She did not know if he was even riding. She had read **ENTRY 0586** in a cloud of her own, in November, in her kitchen, at three in the morning, and had said nothing to anyone, and had put the phone in the flour jar.

*"I can hear them!"* howled the radio, in the hands of eleven people. *"Here they come! A blur of colour! A tremble in the air! And—wait. Wait. Friends of Colombia, I do not believe it. There is a road of roses on the left. Forty thousand red roses, the whole verge, a carpet! The leaders are riding on the right of the road, they are going past in a kind of astonishment—"*

On the right of the road the leaders went by like a gust. They did not look to the left. Cyclists do not. They are busy, and in pain. Then the second group, and the third.

And then, out of the white, with his head down and his jersey the grey of old ash, came a single rider on the left-hand edge of the tarmac, so close to the verge that his tyres hissed in the petals.

*"It is Torres!"* cried Esteban Ortiz, and his voice cracked in half. *"He has seen it! He is riding the roses! He is following them as a blind man follows a rail! Señoras y señores, a man who crashed because of a flower is climbing through a cloud on a red road. I am a professional. I am not supposed to cry. I am crying."*

She saw him pass. It was a second, no more. His face was streaked and grey and grimly absurd. His eyes went sideways, once, to a girl in rubber boots standing at a gate with her hands clasped under her chin, and held there, as you hold a hot plate you have no intention of putting down. And then he was gone into the white, and the sound of his freewheel faded up the hill like a thing that goes on being sung.

He did not win. It should be said at once, since the reader is an honest person and will want to know. He came over the summit in eleventh, with a time that Esteban Ortiz described to the Republic, in a voice quite gone, as *the best eleventh place in the entire history of cycling, and I have the figures.*

---

**Kraków, Poland. The old hall of the Collegium Maius. The same week, as the evening bells began.**

There is a hall in Kraków, up a stair where Copernicus is said to have set his boot, and in it, on this night, three hundred people held their breath for a girl who could not hear them.

Zofia Kowalska, twenty-three, violinist, stood alone in a pool of light, in a blue dress, with her instrument under her chin. She had not heard a note for nine weeks. She had not told her teacher until the day the sound went; she had not told her mother until the day after; and she had told only one other person the whole of it, in a stairwell, in March, in the voice of one reading a will. There was a name for what lay on her nerves, a Latin name, which Jakub Nowak, clockmaker's apprentice, had written on his palm that day in biro and spent three weeks learning to pronounce.

She was to play the great *Chaconne*, the long dark mountain at the end of Bach's second partita, fourteen minutes without a note of accompaniment. Nobody could play it without hearing it. This was a well-known fact. It was why the hall was full.

She lifted the bow.

Nobody saw that the floor of the stage had a trapdoor. Nobody knew that beneath it, on his back among old cables and the dust of two centuries, in his one black suit, lay a thin young man with a clockmaker's mallet in his right hand, tapping, on a seasoned oak beam, with the precision of the finest escapement in Poland, the pulse of the *Chaconne*.

It was a thing he had worked out over six weeks, with a stopwatch, a stethoscope borrowed from a cousin, and a length of rubber hose. The boards of the stage were old and resonant. A tap on the beam went up through the joists, through the planks, through the soles of a violinist's shoes, and into her bones; and she, who had stood and played with her whole body since she was five, could take the pulse of the music in her feet.

She began. And the thing she could not hear came out of her instrument, and out of her, and went into three hundred listeners as a river goes into a sea.

He could not see her. He could only hear it, from below, through the planks, as the people in a cellar hear the church above them: the great chords like beams falling, the long ascents, the slow descent into the minor, the dark opened and opened again. He tapped. His arm went numb, and he went on. Somewhere in the ninth minute he found that he was weeping, flat on his back in the dust, quite soundlessly, and that he had not missed a beat.

At the end she stood in the silence with the bow lifted, as the old players do, to hold the last chord in the air. She did not know whether it had ended. She felt, through the soles of her shoes, three taps, soft, final, like a clock saying *there*. And so she lowered the bow.

The hall rose. She felt it as one feels a ship's deck begin to move: three hundred pairs of feet, a shudder in the boards, a roar in the floor, a gladness that she could not hear and did not need to.

Afterwards, in the arcaded courtyard, in the half-dark, with the old clock above them preparing to strike, Jakub came out with dust in his hair, and she saw it, and began to laugh.

"You have been under the stage."

"Fourteen minutes. I was very comfortable."

"Liar." She put out her hand and brushed the grey from his fringe with great tenderness. She read his lips by the lantern. "Jakub. I have to tell you the date."

"I know the date."

"It is on the ninth. They say that if all is well, I may hear again, a little. They say that if all is not well—" She did not finish. The Latin name lay between them like a coin. She took from her bag a small silver pocket watch with a faded engraving on its case: *Z.K.*, her grandfather's, which had stopped three summers ago, and which had, in January, been left on her doorstep, going. She had never asked who had mended it. "Keep it wound," said Zofia, "will you? At nine every night. Do not let it stop."

"I will."

"I want to ask you one thing. The last bar." Her eyes did not leave his lips. "Did I get the last bar?"

"Every note," said Jakub.

"Liar," said Zofia, tenderly.

"Yes," said Jakub.

And she smiled, and put her forehead against his shoulder, and they stood in the arcade of the oldest university in Poland while above them the little mechanical figures of the great clock began to turn, and the hour was struck, and she did not hear it, and he did, and neither of them said so. It was the kindest transaction in Kraków that night.

*Reader, you were told this was a tragedy, and it is. The Keeper's pencil is not a cruel one, and so here is the fact, plainly: the operation was on the ninth of June. She did not wake. The surgeon wrote that it was quiet. And Jakub Nowak wound the silver watch at nine every night for the rest of his life.*

---

**Bucharest, Romania. The Circus of the Silver Mare, on the night of the new programme.**

Elena Stanciu, seventy-seven, retired hotelier, had sat in the third row of every circus performance in Bucharest since 1962, and was therefore in a position to inform the young woman beside her that nothing, in the entire history of the circus, had ever been as dangerous as it looked, or as safe.

"My husband was a trapeze man," said old Elena, sucking a lemon sweet, "and he fell eleven times, and he was never so hurt as when he did not fall."

"That is not comforting, doamnă," said Ioana Dumitrescu.

She was twenty-eight, a nurse, and she was sitting bolt upright, with her hands knotted in her lap and her coat still on. She had read the scans. She could have drawn the hairline in the third lumbar vertebra of Andrei Popescu with her eyes shut, and had told him that if he went up without a net, she would not watch. And here she was, with her eyes open, as the lights died on the ring and the owner of the circus, Ionuț Radu, forty-three, a dentist who had inherited the big top and pulled teeth on Mondays, made his announcement in the voice of a man who has bitten on something and decided to enjoy it.

"Ladies and gentlemen! Without nets, without harness, without insurance, and with my *deepest regrets*—the man who has walked the wire for eleven years! *Andrei Popescu!*"

The drums began.

He came out in white. He was thirty-one, lean, quiet-faced, fearless in the air and timid on the ground, a man who in the ordinary world could not ask a woman to dinner without rehearsing it, and who now climbed a rope ladder as though it were a staircase in his own house. At the top he stood on the little platform, twelve metres above the sawdust. He lifted his pole. He looked down, once, over the rows, until he found the third seat in the third row, and a woman with her hands in her lap.

He smiled. And he set his foot on the wire.

It was nothing. It was eighteen metres of steel cable, thin as a pencil, and he walked it as a man walks a pavement, with the pole sinking and rising, sinking and rising, like the bar of a scale. The drums hushed. The trumpets held a single sustained note. In the third row Ioana counted his steps, as she counted a pulse, one, two, three, four, and found that her own had slowed to match.

Halfway across, the wire sang a note she had never heard it sing. It was high, and short, like a kettle just before the lid. And she saw his left foot come down a little to the side of where it should have, and in the same moment saw him smile, which was not what he did when a step was good, it was what he did when

*Here the page is torn.*

---

**Antioquia. Six in the evening.**

At six, in the first clear light of the day, when the cloud had gone up the mountain like a congregation going home, a figure on a racing bicycle came down the Las Palmas road without his team, without his jersey zipped, and with a lamp clipped crooked to his handlebar.

The roses were still there. The road had been opened, the vehicles had passed, the whole circus of the Vuelta had flowed on to Rionegro in a river of horns. But on the left verge, in the dusk, a long red ribbon still lay along the grass, half trampled, half untouched, an eight-hundred-metre testimony.

Daniela was at her gate, in her boots, with the end of a broom. She had sent her workers home. She had told Paola to go and tell her mother. She stood alone at the entrance of a farm, with a letter from a bank folded in her back pocket, and watched a man ride toward her through a field of her own pride.

"You are supposed to be in a hotel with a physiotherapist," said Daniela.

"I am supposed to be where I crashed."

"You did not crash *here.*"

"I did, a little," said Sebastián, and put his foot down.

He was shaking. It was not the effort. He leaned the bicycle against her gate, with the care that he gave nothing else in the world, and he stood with his helmet in his hand and his hair plastered and his knees going, a man of twenty-nine who could not remember the first line of what he had rehearsed up a mountain.

"I came eleventh," he said.

"I know. I heard. It was on every radio in the valley. They are going to name a *sandwich*."

"I crashed because I was thinking of you."

"I know. It is on the Register." She did not smile. She held the broom as a bishop holds a crook. "Sebastián. They were going to rot. It was not a gesture. It was a Tuesday decision. I could not sell them. I have a bank that wants ninety million pesos by the end of the harvest, or it will take the farm, and I will not stand in my own greenhouse and tell a man who has just climbed a mountain on a carpet of my roses that I need to be rescued. I am *not* a rose in a bucket."

"I did not say that you were."

"No. You were too kind."

"I have a prize of four hundred thousand pesos," said Sebastián, "for the eleventh place."

She laughed. It was a startled, offended laugh, the laugh of a person who has been caught in the middle of being proud, and it went on a good deal longer than she meant, and left her eyes bright and wet. He, who had made a career of timing, did not say a word.

"If I asked you now," he said, after a while.

"Then I would say, *not now.*" She looked at him, straight and clear and tired. "It is not the same as *no.* I have found that the two are very different animals. One of them is a door shut. The other is a door that wants to be a better door."

"How long does it take to build a better door?"

"I think," said Daniela, "until the end of the harvest."

He nodded, slowly, in a ragged dusk, like a man who has been told the length of a mountain and will take the hairpins as they come. From the edge of the verge she took, out of a bucket, one single rose, the last one, stem and thorns and all, and held it out to him, across the gate.

"For your mother," said Daniela Ruiz.

"She will be insufferable," said Sebastián.

"I am counting on it."

---

*Margin note, in pencil, in the hand of S.W.R.:*

> *Entry 0586, Sebastián Torres. Entry 0360, Daniela Ruiz. Entry 0609, Zofia Kowalska. Entry 0471, Jakub Nowak. Entry 0697, Andrei Popescu. Entry 0137, Ioana Dumitrescu.*
>
> *Three stories, and the weather in each of them was the same: not knowing. A cloud, a silence, a wire in the lights. I have noticed that we ask of the unknown the one thing it cannot give, which is its name; and that the brave among us go on, regardless, in the white.*
>
> *Of the page that stops in the middle of a sentence, reader, I will say nothing. Some silences are the author's and some are the paper's. I have never been certain which of them is the more merciful.*

---

*End of Chapter 36.*

# ACT IV — WHAT TIME TAKES

### *The Chorus*

Time, that devours the child and feeds the old,
Walks softly through the summer's heavy hours;
He steals the voice, the hearing, and the gold,
And leaves instead a handful of dry flowers.
Yet mark how time restores what time hath torn,
Not in the shape it left, but changed and grown;
The seed laid down in winter greets the morn,
The wandering heart returns to claim its own.
But some shall wait, and wait, and not be paid;
And some shall sing their last in empty halls;
For summer's wage is kind, but long delayed,
And every light at last to dark must fall.
So bear with Time: he steals, but he is just;
And what he spares was meant to outlast dust.

---


## Chapter 37
### Exile Poems

> *"I am writing your story before you have lived it."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0198

---

*Enter the Chorus, in the heat of noon, carrying a fan.*

> The summer comes. It does not ask permission.
> It sits upon the roofs of Cairo, Baghdad,
> And presses, like a palm, on every forehead:
> "Remember what you left. Consider what you carry."

---

**Giza, Cairo. A clinic on the second floor above a pharmacy, in the street where the Sudanese had opened, in nine months, three restaurants, two tailors, and this.**

It was forty-one degrees at ten in the morning, and the ceiling fan of the waiting room had been turning for eleven years in the belief that it was doing something.

Dr. Hassan Idris, thirty-five, courteous to the point of illness, bent over the chest of a four-year-old girl with a stethoscope, and said to it, under his breath, as he said to everything, "Please." He said it to the child, to the instrument, to the door, and once, on a bad night, to a generator. He had been a surgeon's registrar in Khartoum. He was now a doctor of no licence in a city of twenty million, practising under the signature of a kind Egyptian colleague and the discretion of a landlord, and he had learned, in nine months, that the first medicine for a man who has lost everything is to be called *doctor* by somebody.

"Breathe in, habibti," he said.

"It is hot," said the child.

"Yes. It is very hot. That is why you are coughing. It is also why I am asking you to breathe in."

On his phone, which lay on the desk face-up, a voice note had come in from Omdurman. It had been arriving in pieces since seven, in a staccato of dropped syllables, like a man running over stepping-stones. *Hassan... Mama... the fever... the pharmacy is... no, the road to... Hassan, I cannot... do you hear...* His brother Osman, who made umbrellas and was therefore, in that country, a prophet. He had said it nine times, this morning, in nine different broken ways, and it came to the same thing: *Mother is not well. Come. Or do not come, and send the money, and say nothing.*

He had not said anything. He had gone on listening to the child's chest, which was clear.

"Doctor," said a voice from the doorway, "your feet."

It belonged to Old Zuhura, who had been the cleaner of this building since it was a dentist's, and who would, in the opinion of everybody, be mopping its corridors when it was a mosque, a bank, and a ruin. She was seventy, from Aswan, as dark as a good coffee and as wide as a doorway, and she could not read a letter of any alphabet; but she had learned the whole building by heart, as a blind man learns a house, and she did not trust any person who was not standing on a dry floor.

"I am not wet," said Hassan.

"You are *always* wet, ya doctor. It is something in the walk." She took a few swipes at the tiles round his shoes, and straightened, one hand on her back. "I have been watching you since January. You walk like a man carrying two sacks of flour, one in each hand. One is the clinic. The other is Omdurman." She nodded to herself. "A man cannot carry two sacks and open a door."

"Zuhura—"

"It is not wisdom," said Zuhura. "It is flour. We had a delivery on Monday and the boy dropped it." And she moved off down the corridor, trailing wet, singing something in Nubian that sounded like a very long apology to a very large river.

It was her idea, too, that the walls of the waiting room should wear poems.

She had had it in January, when a young Egyptian woman named Amal Yusuf had come, with an enormous bag and a face like a lit match, to ask whether the clinic would allow her to read verse to the patients on Thursday afternoons, *as waiting rooms are the only churches without sermons.* Hatim Babiker, the manager, a nurse of sixty-two from Omdurman who was superstitious and could not keep time, and who arrived every day at noon with a fresh omen to account for it, had consulted a cat, and said yes.

Since then the poems had begun, like moss, to appear. They were taped to the wall beside *WASH YOUR HANDS*; they were stuck up with plasters; and Zuhura, who could not read them, had decided, with great confidence, that they were *the prescriptions of the clinic's second doctor, the better one,* and had begun to dispense them by instinct.

"Take this," she would say, peeling one from the wall and pressing it into the hands of a man with a bad back. "Three times a day. With bread."

"It is a poem about the sea," said the man.

"It is *medicine*," said Zuhura.

It must be recorded that the man's back got better.

---

**Baghdad. The Dijla, which the foreigners call the Tigris, at the east end of a bridge that did not yet reach the west.**

On the other side of a desert, at a quarter to twelve, in a heat of forty-six degrees, the most obstinate stonemason in the Republic of Iraq was refusing to answer her telephone.

"It is the butcher," said Shaimaa Al-Obaidi, twenty-eight, wiping her chisel on her thigh, with the voice of a woman who knows what she is looking at. "He has rung eleven times."

"Then answer it," said the engineer.

"Never. A telephone is a leash. A man at the other end of it wants something."

The bridge was a footbridge, six hundred metres of steel and pale stone, from the old book-market at the bottom of Mutanabbi Street across the brown water to the Karkh shore, and it was due to open in the autumn, and was, at the moment, exactly two metres of air short of the far bank. A gap, like the gap in a child's smile. The two halves stood in the river, each reaching, and in the middle the Dijla went through, as slow as a thought.

"*Habibti!*" came a roar from the quay, and up the steps, with a steaming foil parcel the size of a baby, came a short wide man in a stained apron, perspiring with the indignity of a fortune-teller whose predictions have been publicly mislaid. This was Zaid Jabbar, thirty-five, a butcher of Basra, who had driven eight hours with the lunch, and who made promises faster than he could keep them, a habit that had made him, at once, the best matchmaker in the south and its most unpopular. "I promised the kebabs by noon!"

"It is three minutes past," said Shaimaa.

"Then I am a liar and a butcher."

"It is the same thing, but the second one is on a skewer."

"Mustafa, my friend, *tell her!* I have not slept! I have been driving since the *dawn* prayer, and I have good news, I have news of the woman—"

"Zaid," said Mustafa Karim, civil engineer, thirty-four, hopeful, practical, with a safety helmet on the back of his head like a halo that had slipped, "not here."

"But the Basra gossip is *excellent*. Her father is coming on the bus!"

The engineer put down his drawings.

"Her father," he repeated.

"On the five o'clock! He will not telephone, because he fears the telephone, he is seventy-eight, he was a lifeguard on the Shatt al-Arab for forty years and he has never in his life been willing to say a thing to a machine that he could say to a face! I have it from the cousin of the baker's wife. He is coming up to Baghdad, to see his daughter, for the *answer*." The butcher put down the kebabs. His voice dropped by an octave, which for him was a collapse. "She has until tomorrow midnight. The Italians, I am told, are impatient."

Nobody spoke. Down on the water a boy in a very small boat passed under the gap, singing to himself, and a pair of pigeons crossed the open air above the Dijla in a short, scornful line, unimpeded by engineering.

For the past five months, Mustafa Karim had built a bridge. He had stood in the river at dawn with a surveyor's staff. He had drawn the piers and checked the tolerances and argued with a committee of sixteen. And on every one of those mornings, he had been joined, at six, with two glasses of sweet black tea, by the architect who had designed the lamps, the railings, and the little pavilion at the Rusafa end, in which a man could sit and read; Noor Hashim, thirty, ambitious, eloquent, with a pencil in her hair and a way of looking at a half-finished span as though it owed her an explanation.

He had built the whole of it so that she should have somewhere to come back to. It was a sentence he had written to a stranger in a ledger, and not once said aloud.

"Eat the kebab," said Shaimaa Al-Obaidi, unexpectedly, in the voice of a woman who, for all her war against the telephone, was a good deal kinder than she let on. "It will get cold. The rest is the river's business."

---

**Giza, Cairo. Thursday afternoon.**

At three, by the clock above the pharmacy, nineteen people sat in the waiting room in the heat, with their bad backs and their children's coughs and their ration of silence, and a young woman stood at the front in a long grey dress, with a notebook open in one hand like a hymn-book, and began to read.

Amal Yusuf was thirty-one. She was fierce and lyrical, and wrote, as she lived, at the edge of a thing; and her father, a retired railway guard of sixty-nine who believed in timetables and had never forgiven poetry for being late, said that she would starve for it, as other men's daughters did for love. She had a great deal of black hair and an inability to be dull. She read in a plain, hard, steady voice, with no performance in it, as one reads a ration card, and in the third row, with a tin of salt crackers on her lap, sat a girl of fifteen named Nahid Osman, who had come from Khartoum with her aunt and a battered book of Arabic grammar, and who drank in every poem as other girls drink fizzy orange.

> *He will not go home this year. The roads
> Have learned a new geography of fear.
> He will stand at a window in a borrowed city
> And carry, in two hands, a river and a house.
> He will heal the stranger's fever, and forget
> To eat; he will say "please" to the stethoscope;
> His mother's number will be busy, busy, busy,
> And then one morning, like a bird, it rings.
> He will not say what he has left behind.
> That is the whole of it. The leaving. And the doctor
> Who leaves to save, and lives in what he saves,
> And does not know that he is already home.*

A silence settled over the waiting room, the kind that comes after a thing has touched the right bone. Somebody blew her nose.

At the back, against the wall, with a clipboard he was not reading and a stethoscope that he had forgotten to take off, a man had gone entirely still.

"Is it about someone real?" said Nahid, from the third row, who had no talent for tact. "The doctor?"

"It is about a man I have not met yet," said Amal, which was true; and then, because she was honest, "or whom I met in January, and have been writing for five months, in the future tense, to see if he would arrive."

A ripple went through the room. Old Zuhura, who had been mopping a corner in an attitude of the deepest disinterest for the past twenty minutes, stopped, and put her mop upright against the wall.

"I wrote it," said Amal, "in November. In the dark. On the night the Register opened. I read a sentence there from a doctor in Cairo, whom I did not know. It said: *I left my family behind to save strangers.* And I thought: *somebody should write that man a country to walk into.*" She closed the notebook. "I wrote him a country. It is a poem. It is a rather bad one. It is only a poem. Thank you for coming."

She went out. She went out quickly, with the big bag and the lit-match face, down the stair into the white glare of the street.

Hassan Idris did not move. His stethoscope hung from his neck like a rope.

"Doctor," said Zuhura, at his elbow.

"I am not... I did not..." He took off the stethoscope with unaccustomed violence. "It is a coincidence."

"It is an *accident*," said Zuhura, with the stern gentleness of the old for the foolish, "and an accident is only a coincidence in a hurry." She reached into the bandage cupboard, which no one but herself ever opened, and took out an enormous brown envelope, softened with handling. "She leaves them here. Every Thursday. All of them. Not for the wall: for you. She did not know I knew. *I* did not know I knew, until the second month, when the knees told me." She put it in his hands. "Read it tonight. I will lock the door."

"Zuhura, I cannot read the private—"

"*Ya doctor,*" said Zuhura. "In forty years I have mopped every secret in this building. They are all very small. You will be quite all right."

---

**The clinic, ten at night.**

It was the hour at which the building ceased to be a clinic and became a place of old tiles and good silence. The fan had stopped turning. The street below was a long yellow sleep of lamps. In the empty waiting room, in the chair by the window where the mothers sat, with a single bulb on, Dr. Hassan Idris sat with a brown envelope open on his knee, and read.

There were thirty-one poems. They were written in a quick, black, impatient hand, as of one who writes at a kitchen table with a cigarette she is trying to give up. They told, in the future tense, the whole of a man's life, and he knew, from the first, that it was his. The long flight; the stairs; the room above the pharmacy. The sack in each hand. The sister-in-law's weeping in the voice note; the way he could not bear a woman's name said in a certain way. His mother's door. In the nineteenth poem, he found the bread; in the twenty-second, the wall; and in the twenty-seventh, with a clean stab of shock, a line about a boy of nine on a bad road, whom Hassan had never mentioned to a living soul.

*She could not have known.*

*She wrote it,* said another part of him, with weary logic, *before I lived it.*

He turned the thirty-first page. It was the last, and the shortest. It was not in the future tense. It was untitled, and the hand had changed, was smaller and less sure, as of a woman who had written it on her knee in a doorway:

> *I wrote you in the future tense because
> The present was too small to hold the thing.
> But here's one line that cannot wait: it's now.
> The door is open. I am standing here.*

He read it. He read it twice. He was a man who had spent a lifetime reading the faces of those in pain, and he read, without being able to say how, that the person who had written this had put down the pen at that moment and was, at this moment, in the building.

There was a sound behind him: a small, deliberate, human sound, the sound of a breath being taken by someone who has decided on a course.

Beneath the last line, in a hand grown so small that he had to tilt the page to the lamp, there was one more sentence, written, evidently, an instant before the poet had walked in from the stair. It was the only line in the whole of the cycle that had no verse in it, and the only one that spoke of the very moment in which it was being read, and it said that she was standing in the doorway behind him now, that she had been for some time, and that when he turned round she would

*Here the page is torn.*

---

**Baghdad. Five in the morning, on the bridge.**

The call to prayer came up out of the old city in a long, rising thread, and was answered by another, and another, until the whole of the Dijla seemed hung with sound. The sky over the Karkh shore was the grey of a pigeon's back. On the unfinished bridge, a girl with a pencil in her hair stood on the stone of the east half, with her toes at the edge of two metres of air, holding a telephone, and, on the opposite lip of steel, with his helmet in his hand, a man stood and looked at her across the gap.

Her father had come on the five o'clock bus. He had not telephoned. He had sat for an hour in Noor Hashim's kitchen with a glass of tea in his old gnarled lifeguard's hands, and had said, at the end of it, in the voice of one who has said all the prayers he knows and has only the plain ones left: *In forty years on the Shatt I pulled nine people out of the water. And I will tell you the one thing I know. You cannot save anyone by standing beside them. At some moment you have to go in.* And then, since he was a man who feared the telephone and the sea in about equal measure, and had conquered only one, he had gone to bed.

"I have written it," said Noor. "I am going to press the button."

"I know," said Mustafa.

"You do not know what I have written."

"I know what it *says.* I have known since the winter. I have never been able to say what I would have said, and so I built six hundred metres of it." His voice was quite steady. It cost him a great deal. "It will be a good bridge, Noor. It will be the best thing I ever do. I will not ask you to stay for it."

"You have not *asked* me anything," said Noor. "You never have. It is the most infuriating quality in a man."

"It is the only one I inherited."

She laughed, in the dawn, on the lip of the stone. And then the laugh went, and she said, very low, across the gap: "I am going, Mustafa. In September. Copenhagen. Two years. They want me to learn how a city should live beside its water. And I want to. I want it so badly that it frightens me. And I want *this*," and she lifted her hand, with a small, hopeless gesture, toward the bridge, the river, the shore, the man, "and I have never in my life wanted two things that were the same size."

"That is why one builds a bridge," said Mustafa. "Two shores. One road."

"Do not be an engineer at me. Not now."

"I am not being an engineer. I am being a man who will leave one bolt out."

She looked at him.

"The last one," said Mustafa. "In the centre of the last span. The bridge will be finished, and sound, and safe, and open, and in the very middle there will be one bolt that I do not tighten. For you. And I will not tighten it until you come and stand on it, and say it may be done."

"That is *unsafe*."

"It is a very small bolt."

"Mustafa Karim," said Noor Hashim, with her eyes quite bright and her voice shaking at the seams, "you are a terrible engineer."

"I am an excellent one," said Mustafa. "I know exactly how much a bridge can bear."

Behind her, over the old city, the sun came up over the minarets, a clean white coin. She raised the phone. She pressed the button: a small sound; a tiny whoosh; *sent*. Then she did a thing she had never done in her life. She took the pencil out of her hair and threw it, underarm, across two metres of air, and he caught it, in both hands, like a man catching a bird.

"Keep it," said Noor. "For the drawings."

They stood, the two of them, one on each lip of the unfinished span, with the Dijla going by below, and neither crossed, since it was not yet a bridge, and both knew it; and the pigeons passed over, and did not care.

---

*Margin note, in pencil, in the hand of S.W.R.:*

> *Entry 0181, Hassan Idris. Entry 0198, Amal Yusuf. Entry 0076, Mustafa Karim. Entry 0165, Noor Hashim.*
>
> *Summer, they say, is the season of fruit. I find that it is the season of distances. A river between two halves of a bridge. A thousand miles of dust between a son and a mother's door. A whole life in the future tense.*
>
> *I am old enough to know that a gap is not an absence. It is a place where something is being decided.*

---

*End of Chapter 37.*


---

## Chapter 38
### The 5:40 to Lucknow

> *"I drive past your platform twice a day and never stop."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0363

---

**Delhi. Seventeen-fifty-eight, by the clock on platform six of Shanti Nagar Junction, where the great expresses do not stop.**

There are stations at which trains arrive, and stations at which trains are merely seen to pass, and the second sort are the more romantic, since a thing that does not stop must be, by definition, on its way to something.

Shanti Nagar was the second sort. It sat on the eastern edge of the city, in a haze of brick-dust and marigold, with six platforms, a footbridge, a signal cabin the colour of a tired mango, and a tea-stall; and the Lucknow express went through it every evening at 5:58 at a speed that made the pigeons rise in a single grey sheet. It had never slowed. It had been going through Shanti Nagar for eleven years as a very important person goes through a room full of people he is not going to speak to.

On the sixth platform, at the very end, under the one working lamp, a woman had been standing every evening at half past five for four years.

Her name was Sunita Verma. She was thirty-nine, a teacher of Hindi to the eighth class at a government school two stops down, a woman wry and resolute, in cotton saris the colour of old tea, with a leather satchel of exercise books and a steel flask. She stood at the same spot. She stood with her left hand on the strap of her satchel and her right hand free. And at 5:58, when the great blue engine came round the curve with its headlamp burning like a decision, she raised that hand, with a yellow handkerchief in it.

And the horn spoke: two short, one long.

That was all. It had been all for four years. But the biscuit-seller had a view.

"You are a very *odd* woman, Madam," said Pooja Singh, thirty-four, baker by origin, platform vendor by misfortune, who hid behind her jokes as other people hide behind newspapers. "For four years I have sold you a biscuit every evening, and you have not eaten one. A platform is not a temple. A train is not a god. It does not hear you."

"It is a *horn*," said Sunita. "It speaks."

"A horn says what the driver tells it."

"Then he is a man of very few words."

"*Hai Ram*," said the vendor. "She admits it. That it is a *he*."

Sunita Verma, who had faced forty children a day for sixteen years and had never once been seen to blush, adjusted her satchel strap and said with the greatest composure, "It is a figure of speech."

"So is love," said Pooja.

On the footbridge's lowest step, with a stopwatch and the pinched, concentrated face of a sixteen-year-old with a theory, sat Shweta Bansal, the eighth class's sharpest pupil and its worst for minding other people's business. She was Madam Sunita's student. She was, by a coincidence she had not arranged, the niece of an assistant loco pilot of Northern Railways. And she had spent the past month, in her free time, at the signal cabin's small shrine to Hanuman, in a state of the most devoted prayer.

---

**The cab of the 5:40 to Lucknow, doing eighty-five kilometres an hour.**

"Ravi sahab," said Rohit Bansal, forty-three, assistant loco pilot, bookish, an Agra man who read other people's mail whenever he could, and who was at the moment reading a magazine of Urdu poetry propped on the control desk, "the signal at Shanti Nagar was green at 5:54."

"It is always green at 5:54."

"I am only saying it is a *good* green."

The driver did not reply. Ravi Chaudhary, forty-one, loco pilot, punctual, patient, had a long, grave, handsome face, a moustache of unvarying length, and a hand on the regulator that had never, in nineteen years, been known to shake. He drove the 5:40 out of New Delhi to Lucknow six days a week and had never been late except for fog, floods, and, on one occasion, a cow of such obstinate holiness that the Divisional Manager had written a letter to a temple.

In the long dark between stations, with the lamps of the villages swimming past the window like a slow shoal, he had a habit which his assistant had learned to tolerate, and which he did without knowing, as another man hums. He recited the stations. It was not poetry. It was a list. But a list, said often enough, in the right voice, can carry a man across the night:

> *Ghaziabad. Khurja. Aligarh. Tundla.
> Etawah. Kanpur. Unnao. Lucknow.
> A rosary of stations; every bead
> A halt where I am wanted, and I halt.
> But one, the first, the small one, which is hers,
> I pass at eighty with my hand upon the horn,
> And what I say to her is two short, one long:
> The only sentence that I know by heart.*

"You did not say Shanti Nagar," said Rohit, not looking up from the page.

"I said *hers*."

"Hers has a name. It is Shanti Nagar. It means *the town of peace*."

"I have never been able to afford it."

The curve was coming up. Beyond it, the lamp.

"It is only that I do not know why she is there," said Ravi, to the windscreen, in the smallest voice the cab had heard from him in eleven years. "A woman does not stand on a platform in the heat for four years to wave at a driver. She is waiting for a train that stops. There is some man, Rohit, for whom the evening halts at six, and she is polite enough to wave to the one that doesn't."

"It is also possible," said Rohit Bansal, turning a page, "that you are an idiot."

Ahead of them, with a clean, bright, mathematical suddenness, the colour on the signal over the curve changed from green to red.

"That," said Ravi, "is not right. It has never been red."

"It is a *very* red red," said the assistant, with reverence, and closed the poetry.

---

**Vienna, Austria. A bus on the Ring, on an afternoon of the same week.**

It was the last bus in Vienna with a conductor, a fact which the municipality had overlooked, as it overlooks the odd great tree, and which a man named Lukas Bauer, thirty-seven, took as a personal charge.

"*Frau Maestra*," said Lukas, taking her coin with a clip of his punch, "you are late."

"I know that I am late," said Clara Weber. She was thirty-two, a conductor at the Musikverein, five feet five of Prussian-blue coat and absolutely nothing out of place, and she was holding a score as another woman holds an infant that has begun to scream. "I am *conducting* in an hour."

"So am I," said Lukas.

"You are not conducting. You sell tickets."

"I conduct people from one place to another. I do it with a clip and a bell. You do it with a stick and sixty violinists. We are colleagues." He leaned on the pole. He was blunt, and could not apologise, and had, in nine years, acquired the biography of every regular on the line. "And you are on my bus at a quarter to five on a Thursday, going the wrong way. The Musikverein is *behind* you. Where is it that you are *really* going?"

"That is none of your—"

"A violin maker."

The bus rocked round the Opera, and the conductress, a woman who could silence the whole of the second violins with the lifting of an eyebrow, visibly considered whether to murder a man in public service.

"Since February," said Lukas. "You get on very tense. You get off at the Albertina very *less* tense. Frau Weber, I am a simple man, and I know that there are only two things which make a person walk that fast to a door. One is a debt. And the other…"

"If you say it, I will have you removed from the municipal register."

"The other," said Lukas Bauer, with immense tenderness, ringing the bell for the Albertina, "is a *flat note.*"

She got off. The door hissed. She stood on the pavement of the Albertina in her coat, in the late sun, with the knowledge that a bus-conductor had just played her better than the second violins ever had.

---

It was a small shop in a narrow street, with a bell over the door and one window lined with the pale amber bodies of unfinished violins. It smelled of spruce and maple and varnish and hide glue. At a bench at the back, with a magnifying lens in one eye, a man of thirty-six was bending over a scroll, and an apprentice of forty-nine named Theresa Hofer, wry and unstoppable, who talked over everyone, including herself, was telling the entire shop about her cousin's wedding.

"—and the *cake*, Herr Müller, three tiers and a *gondola*, I told her, Gretl, it is Salzburg, not Venice, and she said, *It is a symbol*, and I said—*oh*."

Her voice died. Clara Weber had stood in the doorway for some time, with her score in her arms and her face composed, and Jonas Müller, who had not looked up, had known it, as a man knows that the weather has changed.

"Frau Weber," he said.

"Herr Müller."

"The violin is on the wall."

It was. It hung alone, in a case of glass at the back, made over the winter from a piece of maple he had been keeping for ten years, with a dark red-gold varnish and a faint wavering flame in the grain of the back. He had made it so carefully that it was perfect; and he had made it, secretly, with a flaw. For every violin has, at some place on its fingerboard, a note that growls: a wolf, the old makers call it. Every maker spends his life driving the wolf out. Jonas had built his in. He had tuned it, to the last hair, so that the wolf lived on one note only, the flat one, the one that sounded, in a house of pure tone, like a human being.

"I have not touched one since I was twelve," said Clara. "I conduct. One must stop one's hands from doing anything, and let sixty people do it instead."

"I know," said Jonas.

She set down the score. She took the violin from its case, with fingers that had forgotten, and that remembered, and that were not entirely able to be steady. She lifted it to her chin as to a face. She drew the bow, once, along the lowest string, and it spoke, rich and round and deep, and then she found the place where her hand knew to go, and put down a finger, and drew.

It was flat.

It was not the flatness of error. It was flat as a voice is flat when someone has stopped pretending. It filled the little shop and rang in the glass cases of the unfinished violins, and it went on, a single note, a little off the world, and she let it ring until it died.

"That is me," said Clara.

"That is you," said Jonas.

"No." She lowered the bow. Her eyes, which were grey and very exact, were wet, and she did not trouble to hide it. "That is *you*. I have conducted four hundred concerts and never had one flat note. And you came into my life on a Tuesday, with a screwdriver, and everything has been very slightly off ever since, in the most beautiful way."

"I can fix it," said Jonas, in a terrified voice. "If you do not like it—"

"Herr Müller."

"Yes."

"If you ever fix it," said Clara Weber, "I will never forgive you. I have enough perfect violins."

At the bench, Theresa Hofer, for the first time in her entire life, had nothing to say, and said it very loudly.

---

**Sofia, Bulgaria. The Palace of Justice, between two stone lions, at eleven in the morning.**

The judge was a tired woman of sixty in a black gown, with the look of one who has read a great many sentences and written every one of them in her sleep, and she asked the question in Bulgarian, gently, because she had read the file and was not a cruel woman.

"Nikolai Ivanov. Do you admit that on the night of the fourteenth of November, nine years ago, at the post on the mountain road, while on duty as an officer of the Border Police, you did see a child of about six years old cross the line, and did not stop her?"

Nikolai, thirty-eight, in the grey suit of a man who has not been in a suit since a funeral, shook his head from side to side.

It should be said that in Bulgaria this means *yes*. It is one of the glories of the nation, that its people nod for no and shake for yes, and the foreign newspaperman at the back of the court, who had been told this twice and forgotten it twice, wrote on his pad, with great decision, *DENIES.*

"Yes," said Nikolai, aloud, to avoid all doubt. "I admit it."

It was the Register that had done it. The Keeper's ledger, which had opened a thousand doors, had opened one more than anyone intended. *I once looked away and let a child cross.* Entry 0032, posted in a different life; a thing a man had written in the dark, to be rid of it. A colleague had read it in a canteen on his phone. There are no secrets in a canteen. By Christmas there had been an inquiry; by March, a charge. And on the third of June, in a courtroom that smelled of floor-wax and old coats, the dutiful, haunted, honest man had stood up and said that it was true.

"The court has heard a witness," said the judge.

The witness was fifteen. She was small and straight and wore her school blouse. She had come from Plovdiv by the early train, with a foster mother, and a notebook, and when she stood in the box she did not look at the judge. She looked at Nikolai.

"My name is Tsvetana Dimitrov," she said. "It was not always. I do not remember the first name. I remember the night. It was very cold, and the man in the booth looked at his boots. He had very clean boots. I thought, as a child will: *that is a man who polishes the things he is afraid of.* And then he looked at the other side of the road. And I went across." She swallowed. "I do not think it is right to send him to prison for looking at his boots. But I understand that the law is not an ear. It is a ruler."

The courtroom was very still.

The sentence, when it came, was two years. The judge said it with her eyes on the file, and it was said in the voice in which grief is read from a card. *As the law, which has no ear for children, requires.* And then, because she was human, she added something that was not in the law, and was not recorded: "Mr. Ivanov. For what it is worth to you. Thank you."

On the steps, between the stone lions, with a policeman standing at a decent distance and looking at the sky, a woman in a long coat was waiting. It was a very warm day for a coat. In its lining she had carried for six months a document with the photograph of a man she loved and a name that was not his; she had been to a border and back with it, and had not used it, which was luck, and had not been able to burn it, which was love.

Elena Georgieva was thirty-four, a translator in four languages, discreet, precise, and entirely out of words.

"The train for Thessaloniki is at one," she said, in a flat, quick, unnatural voice. "I have the tickets. I have the passport. They have not looked at the coat. Nikolai, they have not put the cuffs on. You can be on the platform in nineteen minutes."

"Elena," said Nikolai, very gently, and took her two hands, coat-cuffs and all, in his. "I looked away once. It was the only wrong thing I ever did, and I have not been able to put it down in nine years. I cannot do it a second time. I will not look away from my own account." He smiled; it was a terrible, tender smile. "It is only two years. I shall learn to read the old poets. You will write to me in four languages."

"I will not be able to *bear* it."

"You will do it very well. You do everything very well. It is the most infuriating thing about you."

She was crying now, quite openly, in a way that made the policeman study a pigeon. He did not let go of her hands. He spoke, then, in the older and plainer language of two people standing in sunlight:

> *A border is a line drawn by a man
> Who never had to walk it with a child.
> I crossed it once by looking at the ground.
> I'll cross it back by looking at your face.
> Keep the false passport. Put it in the fire
> The day I'm out, and make me a new one:
> A true one. We shall take a train at noon
> To any country where the guards are kind.*

She laughed, through everything, a wet cracked laugh, and kissed him once, on the forehead, as one signs a document of which one is proud. The policeman, with the delicacy of a man who has seen a great many partings and has never got used to one, stepped forward, and said that it was time.

---

**Delhi. Seventeen-fifty-eight, and four minutes, at platform six.**

The blue engine of the 5:40 to Lucknow came to a stop at Shanti Nagar Junction at 5:58 and eleven seconds, with a long, enormous, trembling sigh of brakes, directly opposite a woman with a yellow handkerchief, in a silence so total that the pigeons did not know what to do with their wings.

Nobody on the platform spoke. The biscuit-seller had dropped a tray. On the footbridge, a girl of sixteen with a stopwatch, who had asked of a mango-coloured shrine only that *the signal be red for a very short time, not enough to hurt anyone,* put her hand over her mouth and sat down suddenly on the step.

Sunita Verma did not move.

The cab door above her opened. A man leaned out of it, a tall man in a blue cotton uniform with a smear of engine-grease on the sleeve, holding the rail as though it were the rail of a ship. He had looked at her for four years from a distance of eighty kilometres an hour. He had never before seen the colour of her eyes. They were dark brown, and she was looking at him with an expression of the most perfect and ferocious composure, which was, he recognised with sudden horror, the face of a woman working very hard at not crying.

"The signal," said Ravi Chaudhary. "It is red."

"I see that," said Sunita.

"It will change in a minute. Perhaps four."

"Then you will drink tea."

She had a steel flask in her satchel, which she had carried every evening for four years and not once opened. She unscrewed it. She poured into its steel cup, with hands that were very steady and a face that was not. The tea was cold. It had been made at seven that morning. She held it up, to the open door, to the cab, to the man.

He leaned down. He took it. His fingers touched hers for one second, and in that second, on the sixth platform of Shanti Nagar, among the shoes and the pigeons and the stunned vendors, a great many people discovered that they had been holding their breath.

He drank. It was dreadful. It was the best tea he had ever had.

"Madam," said Ravi. "I have always wished to stop."

"Then," said Sunita, "you should have stopped."

"I did not know," he said, in a voice quite unlike a driver's, "whom you were waiting for."

She looked at him. Something went across her face that was not a smile, but was the shadow of one, travelling a long way. "Mr. Chaudhary," she said, "I teach the eighth class. I have forty pupils. Not one of them is as slow as you."

Above the cab, with a click that sounded to everyone present like the closing of a book, the signal turned green.

He gave her back the cup. He did not say anything else; he did not know what it would have been. He drew in the door, and took the regulator in his hand, and the great engine began, with a long sigh, to move; and at the end of the platform a woman with a yellow handkerchief did not wave it, but pressed it to her mouth, and stood.

And then, as the train drew out into the evening, for the first time in eleven years, the horn did not say *two short, one long.* It said something else: a new sentence, entirely unrehearsed, a long, rising, trembling blast that went on far longer than regulations allow, and was heard, it is reported, at the signal cabin, at the school, and in a small kitchen two streets away, where an old woman put down a ladle.

*Mark this, reader. It was not in the code.*

---

>
> *Entry 0032, Nikolai Ivanov, of Sofia, thirty-eight.*
>
> *I will set this down plainly, for I have promised the Register an honest keeper. He served nine weeks. In the ninth, in the infirmary of the prison, the heart he had never told anyone about, because a guard may not be ill, stopped on a Tuesday afternoon, while he was reading a letter aloud to a man in the next bed who had never been taught to read. It was a letter from Entry 0534, in her fourth language. The man in the next bed said afterwards that it was the first letter anyone had ever read to him, and that he had understood every word, though it was in French.*
>
> *I did not foresee that the truth could cost a man his post. I foresaw only that it might cost him his sleep. I have been wrong in forty-five years about a number of things, and I would like it understood that I know the number.*

---
