## Chapter 39
### Brass and Mud

> *"The band is folding and you are the only thing I would keep."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0542

---

*Enter the Chorus, in a raincoat, which in Manchester is the only costume that never goes out of fashion.*

> Two things this city lost and could not mend:
> A ground whose grass has run its final mile,
> A band whose brass must lay its music down.
> Yet one small note, held faithful to the end,
> May outlast stand and bandroom, turf and town.

---

### SCENE I
*Marsden Road Ground, Manchester. Dawn, the last Saturday of the season. Drizzle, as ordered.*

There are two kinds of grass in Manchester: the kind that is grown, and the kind that is *kept*. The first needs only rain, of which the city has a surplus. The second needs a man.

William Hartley was that man. He was thirty, he had been at Marsden Road since the age of sixteen, when he had been handed a roller as big as a bus and told to make the world flat, and he knew every blade of the pitch the way a shepherd knows a flock: by temperament. The left wing sulked in October. The penalty spot drank water like a Methodist at a wedding. The centre circle, which he had painted ten thousand times with a chalk-wheel and a steady hand, had a slight tilt to the east, as though even the middle of things were leaning toward something else.

This morning he mowed it for the last time.

He did it slowly, as a man eats the last of anything. Up the length of the pitch, a stripe dark where the grass bent away; back again, a stripe pale where it bent toward him. Behind him the stands rose, grey and empty and a little rusted, like the ribs of some patient animal that had been told it was to be put down and had decided to be dignified about it. On the east gate a banner, already tired, said: **MARSDEN GARDENS: 214 LUXURY APARTMENTS. COMING SOON.**

"Coming soon," William told the roller. "They always say *soon*. Nobody says *sorry*."

"I say it!" cried a voice from the tunnel. "Sorry! Sorry! Terribly sorry! I have been trying to say it for a week and it keeps coming out as a whistle."

It was true. It generally did.

Out of the tunnel, with a bunch of keys the size of a small bagpipe and a flat cap that had seen three decades of Saturdays, came Mr. George Lowe, forty-five, caretaker of the Marsden Town Silver Band's rehearsal room beneath the east stand, known to every living soul in the district as **Mr. Pennywhistle**, because he could not walk, think, grieve or be afraid without whistling, and because no one had ever heard him whistle a recognisable tune. He had been writing the Great Salford Novel for nineteen years. It was, by his own account, "nearly there"; its first chapter had been nearly there since 2006.

"Pennywhistle."

"Will! A word. Two words. Three, if you will pay for them." He leaned on the rail, panting, all anxious elbows. "I have news. Poppy Ashworth has been seen in the bandroom at six in the morning, *alone*, playing the one piece she says she has not played since Easter. A woman who plays by herself at dawn, William, is a woman with a thing on her mind."

"She practises."

"She practises *you*."

"Pennywhistle."

"A groundsman and a cornetist," said Mr. Pennywhistle, with the air of a man unveiling a statue. "One keeps the pitch; the other hits it. If that is not Providence, I do not know what is, and I have read the Bible twice and a great deal of the Yellow Pages."

"It is not Providence. It is a pun."

"Providence *is* a pun, William. It is the pun God makes when He is too tired to explain." He wagged a finger. "You have been mowing round that centre circle as though you were afraid of it. Mark me. If a man will not look at his own middle, he will not look at anything."

William did look at it. The circle sat in the green, pale and perfect, a whole round O, and for a moment he thought that it looked like nothing so much as a note.

He put the thought away. A groundsman does not entertain thoughts that cannot be rolled.

---

### SCENE II
*The same night. The pitch, empty. A single floodlight, the last still working, throws his shadow a hundred yards.*

He had told no one about the letters.

There were two. The first, from the club, offered him a place at the *new* ground, four miles east and shining like a new tooth, where the grass was plastic, and the man who looked after it was called a *surface technician*, and the work consisted of sweeping rubber crumbs from one end of a carpet to the other. The second came from an academy in Southampton, three hundred miles away, where they grew real turf under real sky and wanted a head groundsman who knew the difference.

He had folded both in his breast pocket. He had carried them to the pitch. And now, in the one remaining light, with the rain thinned to a mist and the stands dark as a sleeping choir, William Hartley did what the lonely do when they are certain that nobody is listening: he spoke it out.

> *Good ground, old ground, that held me up so long,
> I never learned to stand on anything else,
> Forgive the man who leaves you to the diggers.
> I fed you, and you fed me back in silence:
> Each autumn's mud, each summer's patient green,
> The hush before the whistle when ten thousand
> Held in a single breath. I knew you, ground.
> I knew you by your moods, and by your drains.
> And yet it is not you I cannot leave.
> It is a girl who plays a cornet badly
> At six a.m., on purpose, so I'll hear.
> She thinks I do not know. I know. I know.
> And she is going, too — to Leeds, they say;
> A school, a salary, an end to brass.
> So both of us are leaving, and the grass
> Will keep the footprints longer than the feet.*

He stopped. The floodlight buzzed. Somewhere beyond the wall a late bus coughed up Marsden Road and went on without anyone.

"That was very good," said a small voice.

William nearly left his own skin on the turf.

At the touchline stood a girl of thirteen in a school coat three sizes too wide, holding a torch like a sword. It was Hannah Hughes, the neighbour's daughter, who had climbed the back fence nightly for two years to count the foxes and who had never once, to anyone's knowledge, been where she was supposed to be.

"How long have you been there?"

"Since *good ground, old ground.*" She considered. "It doesn't rhyme."

"It is not meant to rhyme."

"Then it's a speech. You should say it to her. Poppy. Not to the grass. The grass can't say anything back."

"Hannah, go home."

"I am *going*." She turned. Then she said, with the withering patience of the very young, "Grown-ups always say things to the wrong thing. My nan says things to the cat." And she was over the fence and gone, and William was left alone with the floodlight and the unpleasant sensation of having been correctly judged by somebody who still had a primary-school timetable.

---

### SCENE III
*Kisumu, on Lake Victoria. The same hour of the clock, which in Kenya is three hours further into the day. The beach at Dunga, before sunrise. The lake the colour of weak tea; the sky preparing something larger.*

*Mark this, reader, for we must cross a continent between two paragraphs. Pack lightly.*

A woman in a green anorak stood among the moored boats, with a notebook she had decided not to open.

Her name was Wanjiru Kamau. She was twenty-seven, she was a technology journalist of the exact and unflattering kind, and four months ago she had written an article that had begun, *The man who calls himself Captain Kali has never caught a Nile perch heavier than his own ego.* It had been true in every particular. It had also cost a fisherman from Kisumu four hundred thousand followers and, as far as she could judge, a good deal of sleep. It had cost her the same sleep, on the other side of the ledger, and she had not yet worked out the exchange rate.

She had taken the first flight from Nairobi. She had not told him. She had come to correct the record, which is what she told herself, and which was what the notebook was for.

"You are standing in my light," said a voice from a boat.

Otieno Odhiambo, twenty-nine, was sitting in the stern of a wooden boat called *Mama Akinyi* (after his grandmother, who had fished this gulf for sixty years and had never once worn a cape). He was untangling a net. He did not wear the cape either. He wore a torn grey sweater and the expression of a man who had been very loud for a long time and had recently discovered how pleasant it is to be quiet.

"Wanjiru."

"Otieno."

"You came to fact-check my net?"

"I came," said Wanjiru, "to say that I wrote a true thing and I am not sorry I wrote it, and that I have been sorry every day since. Both are the case. I could not find an article that fits both. So I came to say it aloud."

He looked at her for a long moment, and the sun, which had been waiting politely behind Kit Mikayi, put one pink finger on the lake.

"Get in," said Otieno. "The omena do not run for apologies."

They went out. He rowed first, and then ran the little motor, and the gulf opened round them, wide as a held breath, papyrus along the margin and water hyacinth drifting in green islands, with egrets standing on them like waiters who had not been told the party was over. He told her he had posted nothing in four months. He told her the truth about the persona, which was that Captain Kali had begun as a joke to sell dried fish, and then the joke had begun to sell *him*, and then there was a day he could not find where the Captain stopped and he began.

"The hippo story?" said Wanjiru.

"Never met a hippo. They frighten me."

"And the sixty-kilo perch?"

"I bought it from Mama Njeri in the market. She gave me a discount on the *story.*"

"Otieno."

"I know."

"Why?"

"Because a fisherman who catches tilapia is a fisherman," he said, "and a fisherman who wrestles a perch is *content*, and nobody would pay for the truth, which is that I am good at a quiet job and was afraid of that." He cut the engine. The silence that came was enormous and full of water. "You wrote it was a lie. It was. But you also wrote, in the last paragraph, *the man has real talent, and I would rather watch him use it honestly.* I have read that line four hundred times. I am not sure you meant to put it in."

Wanjiru, who had never in her career been caught by her own sentences, looked at the water.

"I did not mean to," she said. "It was the only true thing I could not edit out."

Then, thirty yards off the starboard bow, the lake bulged. A grey back the size of a wardrobe rose, blew a plume of spray into the dawn, and opened a mouth that could have comfortably accommodated a family saloon.

Otieno screamed.

It was not the scream of Captain Kali. It was a long, high, honest scream, the scream of a boy, and it went on until he ran out of lungs, whereupon he clapped both hands over his mouth, and Wanjiru, who had begun to laugh somewhere around the second second, was laughing so hard that the boat rocked.

"Never met a hippo," she wheezed.

"I *have* now!"

"You are not filming it."

"I forgot the camera!" said Otieno, wide-eyed. "I forgot to *perform!* Did you see? I was only frightened!"

"I saw." She wiped her eyes. "That. That man. He was very good."

"He has fewer followers."

Wanjiru Kamau looked at him in the first true light, a fisherman in a torn sweater, afraid of hippos, with the whole bright lake around him like a verdict.

"He has one," she said.

The hippo sank. The omena ran. Neither of them noticed.

---

### SCENE IV
*Marsden Road. The following Saturday. Last match, last whistle, last light. The ground full for the first time in a decade, and every seat damp.*

They lost two–one in the ninety-third minute, which the crowd agreed was the only fitting way to end, as the club had never in its history been on time for anything.

Then, as the referee's whistle died, the old tunnel doors swung open and out marched the Marsden Town Silver Band, twenty-six strong, in their maroon jackets gone to the colour of old wine, with Poppy Ashworth at the front.

She was twenty-nine, she was loud in every sense a woman can be, and her cornet was dented from a fall off a coach in 2019 and played all the better for it. She marched with her chin up and her eyes straight ahead, which is how you march when you are afraid to look at the thing you most want to see.

Behind her came Callum Brown, the euphonium, forty and shy as a clam, who was William's best friend and who had once spent an entire wedding trying to ask a bridesmaid to dance and had asked the cake instead. Behind him came the basses, the trombones, the old man on the bass drum who had played at the Cup final in a blizzard and had never let anyone forget it.

They marched into the middle of the mud.

For it was mud now, a century of drainage in the rain, black and sticking, up to the ankle, and the bandsmen's polished shoes went into it with a noise like a sigh. They did not stop. Brass bands, as Mr. Pennywhistle would tell you, do not stop for weather; they stop for *death*, and then only after the last verse.

"Have you looked at the pitch, Poppy?" hissed Callum.

"I am not looking at the pitch."

"You should look at the pitch."

"*I am not looking at the pitch, Callum.*"

But in the press box, high on the roof of the west stand, Mr. Pennywhistle, who had climbed up there with a thermos and a notebook and had been writing nothing at all for forty minutes, had seen it. He was the only man in the ground who could. And when he realised what it was he stood up so fast that the thermos went over the edge, bounced three times, and landed in the executive car park to a sound that has been described in the literature as *a terrible gong*.

"Look!" he shrieked, to no one. "*Look at the grass!*"

For this is what William Hartley had done on the last morning of his craft. He had not mown it in stripes. He had mown it in *lines*: five long bands, straight as rails, down the whole length of the ground, dark and pale and dark and pale and dark, until, seen from above, the pitch was a great musical stave laid across the earth. And in the very middle of it, on the third line, where the centre circle sat in its tilt toward the east, there was a single round, hollow, perfect mark.

A whole note. A semibreve. The longest thing in music, the one you hold until the conductor lets you go. And on a stave in the treble clef, the third line is **B**.

It was the note Poppy had been practising, alone, at six every morning since Easter. It was the note that began the piece the band had never played in public because she said it was too private. And only one man in the whole of Manchester knew that she played it, because only one man had been standing outside the bandroom window at dawn every day for seven months pretending to check the drains.

The band reached the centre. They turned. Callum lifted his baton, because the conductor had gone home with a cold, and nodded to Poppy.

She stood in the mud with her cornet at her lip, and for the first time in her life did not know whether she could breathe. She looked up. Not at the stands. At the grass. Across the field, stripe after stripe, she followed it, and found at the end of it all the one round O at her feet, and, standing in the technical area with his cap in his hand, soaked to the skin, the man who had made it.

William did not wave. He did not smile. He only nodded, very slightly, the way you nod to someone across a railway platform when you have decided not to be a coward.

She played.

Mark this, reader, if you have never heard a cornet in the rain. It is not a sweet sound. It is a *bright* one, a bright hard thread pulled through the wet air, and it climbed out of the old ground in one long note that held and held and would not let go, past the rusted stands, past the banner, past the cranes already waiting beyond the wall; and when she ran out of breath and had to lift her lip, the whole band took it up beneath her, twenty-six brass voices in the mud, and the crowd who had come to bury a football ground found that it had been given instead a hymn.

Nobody left. Ten thousand people stood in the rain and sang a tune they had known all their lives, and the groundsman stood at the edge of the grass he had made and wept, very quietly, into his cap.

---

### SCENE V
*After. The tunnel. A bucket of water, a towel, a cornet case with the lid open, and two people who had both been very brave and are now very tired.*

"You mowed a stave," said Poppy.

"I mowed a stave."

"On purpose."

"A groundsman does nothing by accident. We do not have the budget."

"William." She turned the cornet in her hands. "I'm going to Leeds. There is a school. They offered me the music department. The band is folding, and I thought—" she laughed, one short crack—"I thought, well, if I cannot keep the band I may as well keep the *pay.* I wrote to say yes. I have not posted it."

"I am going to Southampton," said William. "There's an academy. They want a head groundsman. I wrote to say yes. I have not posted it."

They looked at each other.

"We have *both* got letters in our pockets," said Poppy.

"That is the most Manchester thing I have ever heard."

"You were going to leave me at the same time I was going to leave you, and neither of us said."

"I said it to the grass."

"I heard," said Poppy. "Hannah Hughes told me. She told me in the chip shop. She said you said it wrong."

"Hannah Hughes has no respect for privacy."

"She's *thirteen*, William. She is the only honest person in Salford."

He laughed, and it came out of him like a held breath. Then, because it was the sort of evening on which everyone had said too much, he said a little more.

"I'm not going to Southampton," said William. "I tore it in two on the way down the tunnel. There's a vacancy with the city parks. Seven playing fields and a bowling green. It's not Wembley. It's got a lot of mud. I'd be good at it."

"I'm not going to Leeds," said Poppy. "I wrote to the school across the road from the park. They've an empty music room. They have, I'm told, *nine* unplayed cornets in a cupboard, and nobody to tell the children which end to blow."

"The band's still folding."

"The band's folded," said Poppy. "It's what we do. We fold, and then we're a very good *shape*." She put the cornet in its case and snapped it shut. "Mr. Pennywhistle says the room under the east stand is mine till the diggers come. After that, I'm told, we may rehearse in his flat. He has promised us biscuits. Which means we shall have none."

"Poppy."

"Yes?"

"The band is folding, and—" He faltered. A man may mow a stave in perfect straight lines and still be unable to finish a sentence. "And I would keep *you*. If that is a thing a person can say. In a tunnel. Wet."

She did not say *love.* She was Mancunian; she had her pride. She said, "I know. You mowed it in B."

And then, in the cold smell of the tunnel, among the buckets and the wet boots and the last of the Marsden brass, Poppy Ashworth kissed him once on the cheek, as one stamps a letter, and walked out into the floodlit rain with her dented cornet and her head very high. William stood quite still, with his cap in his hand, and the whole ground hummed.

From the shadows came a small, sniffling, delighted whistle, tuneless as ever.

"Pennywhistle," said William, without turning.

"I was not here."

"You have been here all night."

"I am the *caretaker*," said Mr. Pennywhistle, with immense dignity, wiping his nose on the Great Salford Novel. "It is my duty to take care. And I'll have you know that I left that door unlocked on purpose."

---

*Margin note, in pencil, in the hand of S.W.R.:*

> *Entry 0542 and Entry 0639. A ground is a promise made to the earth that it will be kept. A band is a promise made to the air that it will be heard. Both are broken, in time. But a note, once held by two people at the same moment, is not broken; it merely passes into the walls.*
>
> *Entry 0483 and Entry 0826. The lake forgave him before the woman did. She, however, was not slow.*

---

*End of Chapter 39.*


---

## Chapter 40
### The Calligrapher's Ink

> *"I would teach you every letter, if you asked."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0502

---

### SCENE I
*Marrakech. The spice souk, near the old square of the apothecaries. Noon, and a heat with opinions.*

A man who cannot read must be a very good liar, a very good listener, or a very good nose. Youssef Benali was all three, and handsome besides, which helps.

He was thirty, and he sold spices from a stall the width of a wardrobe, in a lane so crowded with cones of saffron-gold and cumin-brown and paprika-red that the sun came down into it already tinted. He could tell ras el hanout from its imitators with his eyes shut. He knew forty prices by heart and eleven languages of haggling. He had a voice like warm honey poured slowly over a very hot spoon, and tourists from Lyon to Lagos would stand and listen to him describe a pinch of turmeric as though he were reading them a love poem.

He was not reading. He had never read anything in his life. He had, since the age of ten, *remembered* it.

His jars carried no labels. They carried small, careful drawings: a crocus for saffron, a seed with a tail for cumin, a flame for chilli. The tourists thought this was charming branding. His customers thought it was eccentric. His accountant, a bookish clockmender named Mehdi Bennani from the next stall, who had once told him that he had "the most *visual* ledger in Morocco," thought it was a sign of genius, and was quite sincere.

"I have found," said Mehdi that noon, appearing between the saffron and the sumac with a ledger under his arm, "an error in your invoice from Fez."

"I do not see an error."

"You will, when I read it out." Mehdi, who trusted everyone and was wrong about most of them, adored reading aloud, and did so in three voices: a gruff merchant, a prim clerk, and a tragic widow. "*'Seventy kilos of cumin, at forty dirhams—'*"

"I have left my glasses at home."

"You do not wear glasses."

"Then I have left my *eyes* at home," said Youssef smoothly. "It is a hot day. Read on."

Mehdi read on. The lie passed over them as it had passed over every day for twenty years, like a small, tame cloud. It was a good lie. It had a beautiful voice. It had never once been found out, and Youssef loved it and hated it, as one loves and hates a very old coat that has come to fit exactly the shape of one's shame.

"Do you know what the trouble with you is?" said Mehdi, closing the ledger.

"I am sure you will tell me."

"You are *too* clever. A man like you could do anything, if he would only sit down and learn something."

Youssef smiled at him, and it was a very good smile, and behind it a door in his chest shut as softly as a drawer.

"A fool speaks wisdom by accident," he said, "so they say. You are the proof."

"I take that as a compliment."

"Naturally," said Youssef Benali. "You are an optimist."

---

### SCENE II
*An atelier in a lane behind the old madrasa. A window on a courtyard with a lemon tree. A long table, a row of reed pens, a smell of soot, honey and gum arabic.*

His shop sign had been commissioned in May. He had to collect it in June. That was the whole misfortune, and he had known for a month that it would end in this lane.

The woman at the table did not look up when he came in. She was finishing a stroke, and one does not interrupt a stroke any more than one interrupts a prayer. She was twenty-eight, with her hair wrapped in a plain indigo scarf, ink on the second finger of her right hand, and a way of holding her breath while the reed was on the paper that made the whole room seem to hold it with her.

Salma Idrissi lifted the pen. She let out the breath.

"You are the spice man."

"I am the spice man."

"Youssef Benali, *Épices*, two lines, one in the Maghrebi hand, one in French for the tourists. It is nearly done." She turned the board toward him. "Tell me if the proportions please you."

He looked at the board.

On it, in black ink as deep as the pupil of an eye, ran a line of Arabic so graceful that it seemed less written than *grown*, curling across a ground of faded saffron paper, the letters leaning against one another like a family on a sofa. He looked at it for a long time. He did it well; he had had twenty years of practice at looking at pages.

"It is beautiful," said Youssef.

"Thank you. And the words?"

"The words are what I asked for."

"Which is the second word?"

It was said so quietly, and so gently, that for a moment he did not understand it was a question. Then he understood, and the room tilted a little, as a boat tilts when the weight of the cargo is suddenly found.

"I would prefer," said Youssef, honey-voiced, hand steady, "to hear you read it. It is rude to read your own sign aloud. A man should hear his name in a woman's mouth."

"That is a very handsome evasion."

"I have had practice."

"I know," said Salma. "I know exactly how much."

She did not say it unkindly. She laid down the reed and wiped her finger on a cloth, and she looked at him full on, as one looks at a letter one has been trying to place for months.

"Forgive me, Monsieur Benali. I have a bad habit. I read the Register of Black Stars at night when I cannot sleep. There was an entry from Casablanca." She said it as if she were handing him something very fragile. "Number four hundred and thirty-nine. It said that a man could not read well, and had hidden it for twenty years. I do not know who wrote it. I never will, unless he tells me. But when you walked in, and looked at my work as a man looks at a closed door in a house he knows very well—"

"I do not know what you mean."

"No," said Salma. "Of course you don't."

Silence. Outside, in the courtyard, a lemon dropped from the tree and rolled across the stone, in no hurry, like a small yellow thought.

"I wrote one, too," said Salma. "It is the five hundred and second. I will not tell you what it says. It is not a thing to be *read* to someone. It is a thing to be *asked* for."

Youssef looked at his hands, which had never shaken, even in a bargain with a rival or a scorpion.

They were shaking.

"I do not ask for things," he said.

"I know. It is the same with me."

"I have lived twenty years behind this smile."

"It is a good smile."

"It is a *wall* with a good smile on it."

"Then," said Salma, with the very slightest tilt of the mouth, "we have the same architect."

He sat. It was the first time he had sat in somebody else's shop without a bargain in his head.

"I did not learn," said Youssef Benali. "The letters moved. The teacher said I was lazy. The teacher hit me, and then said I was stupid. After that I did not need a teacher to say it. I said it to myself so well." He breathed out. "The *ba* looks like the *ta* and the *ta* looks like the *nun*, and when I stare they dance. So I learned the rest. I learned the world with my nose and my tongue and my memory, and I became very, very rich in everything but the one thing every child is born into."

"Do you want to learn?"

"Yes," said Youssef.

It was the word he had not said in twenty years, and it came out of him smaller than he expected and a great deal heavier, like a stone from a well.

"Say it again," said Salma, "and mean the whole sentence."

"I am asking you," said Youssef, "if you would teach me every letter."

"I would."

---

### SCENE III
*The atelier. Many afternoons. The reeds, the ink, the lemon tree changing its mind about being green.*

She began not with letters but with ink.

"You will make your own," said Salma, "so you will know what you are asking it to carry." There was soot, scraped from a lamp; there was gum arabic, in amber tears; there was water in which a pinch of saffron had steeped, which was the only part he could have done blind. She stirred it for an hour. "Honey," she said, "to keep it from cracking. Everything that endures needs a little sweetness."

"You have been waiting to say that."

"I say it every time. It is a very good sentence." She put a reed in his hand. It had been cut on a slant, with a split at the nib, and it sat in his fingers as awkwardly as a stranger's child. "Now. The *nuqta*. The dot. Press the pen flat and make one."

He made one. A rhombus, small and clean and black.

"That," said Salma, "is your ruler. Every letter in this alphabet is measured by the dot of your own pen. The *alif* is five of them, stacked, one on the other." She drew it: a single upright stroke, plain and tall. "The circle that holds all the other letters has the *alif* for a diameter. Nothing is by eye. Nothing is *guessed.* Do you understand? This is not a thing the clever are born knowing. It is a thing you may *measure.*"

He stared at the line. He did not say anything. He had been measured all his life, and found short, by people with rulers who had never given him a reed.

She taught him by his own trade, because a teacher who ignores the pupil's gifts is a fool, and she was exacting but never foolish. The *ba*, she said, was a small boat, and in its hold a single seed. "A seed *beneath.* You know the cumin seed. Put it in the boat." The *ta* was the same boat with two gulls above. "Two gulls." The *tha*: three cloves, set above like a crown. The *nun* was not a boat at all but a bowl, deep, with one fly floating on the top.

"Ba, a seed in the hold," said Youssef slowly, and made the stroke. The reed squeaked. The line wobbled and sat on the page like a drunk on a pavement. "Ta, two gulls. Tha—three cloves. Nun, a bowl, with one fly."

"The fly is above."

"The fly is *above*," said Youssef, "and may he drown."

She laughed. It was the first time he had heard it, and it was not the tin roof or the bell or the cascade of other people's laughter. It was a short, surprised sound, as of a bird that had not meant to sing. He wrote it down in his head with the other things he was keeping, alongside the smell of the ink and the lemon tree's light on the table, and he thought: *whatever else happens, I have this.*

They had many afternoons. He cried over the second week, not noisily; he wiped his eyes with the heel of his hand, and she looked at the window until he was done, and no one mentioned it. In the third week he confused the *dal* and the *ra*, and she did not correct him; she drew a very small camel and a very small tree, and he fixed it himself.

On the fortieth day he read a word.

It was a short one. He did not read it with his eyes, as other children do. He read it with his hand: he felt the stroke before he saw it, the boat, the seed, the little gulls. It rose up out of the page as the first star rises out of the dark, a thing that had been there all along waiting for the lamps to go out.

"*Salma,*" read Youssef Benali.

"That is my name."

"It is on your door. I have walked past it for six weeks, and I did not know that it was *you.*"

"You have never read my door."

"I have read it now," said Youssef. "Now it is the only thing in Marrakech I can read."

She turned her face aside. The scarf had slipped, a little. She put it right.

"Come," said Salma. "You've earned a walk. The square is waking up."

They walked, in the long copper evening, through Jemaa el-Fna, where the snake-charmers were packing and the storytellers were beginning, each in his circle of listeners like a pebble in still water. A hakawati with a voice like an old drum was telling the story of a merchant who lost his ship and found his wife, and Youssef stood at the edge of the ring, as he had stood a thousand evenings, and listened with his whole body.

"You see?" said Salma softly. "There is more than one way to hold a story. The ears are very old. The eyes are only a *recent* arrival. My grandfather, who copied the Book in this hand sixty years, used to say that a letter well made is a courtesy to God and to the reader, but that the courtesy was first learned by those who *listened.* You are not behind, Youssef. You are *early.*"

He did not answer. He did not trust the honey in his voice. He had spent twenty years making it sweet and now it only wanted to be true.

At the end of the story the storyteller held out his cap, and Youssef dropped in a hundred-dirham note, and the old man looked at him, and said, "God make your page the colour of your heart."

"Which colour is that?" asked Youssef.

"Ask your teacher," said the hakawati, and winked.

That night, when the lane had gone to sleep and the jars stood in their rows like a congregation of small saints, Youssef sat alone at his stall under one bare bulb, with a reed, a pot of ink, and a sheet of cheap paper, and did what he had never done: he spoke to himself without a smile.

> *Twenty years I wore my silence as a coat
> And called it style. I sold the world its saffron
> And bought myself one thing: the fear of paper.
> It is a small thing, on a table, white,
> Which cannot hurt me. Yet I would have crossed
> The desert twice to dodge it. Here it lies.
> I have a seed, a boat, a bowl, a fly.
> I have a woman who will wait while I
> Make crooked letters, and who does not laugh
> Except in the right places. Is that love?
> I will not say so. I will say: the ink
> Is warm. The line is wrong. I'll draw it twice.*

He drew it twice. Then, because the *ba* has a seed beneath it, he drew the seed, and put the date under it, and the first line in his own hand that he had ever shown to nobody: a name, four letters long, with the dot where the dot belongs.

---

### SCENE IV
*Mexico City. Coyoacán. A Saturday, eleven in the morning, and a church bell with no sense of time.*

At the other side of the world, where the same sun was just climbing into an enormous blue sky, a man in a black wedding suit was standing on a ladder with a brush.

This was not, strictly, how the programme had been planned.

"Rafael!" shouted Camila Reyes, from the foot of the ladder, in a white dress and fury. "You are *married!* You have been married for forty-five minutes! There is a *mariachi!*"

"I know," said Rafael Ortega, twenty-six, painter, romantic, a man who had once in his youth painted the same woman's face on a hundred walls without knowing her name. "I will be a minute."

"You said that at the altar."

"I *was* a minute at the altar."

"You were eleven. Father Anselmo timed you."

For they had been wed at the church of San Juan Bautista at ten o'clock, in the old Coyoacán way: the *lazo*, a great looped rosary of white flowers laid round the shoulders of both in a figure eight, binding them to one another; the thirteen gold *arras* coins poured from his hands into hers, a promise to keep a house, which she received with a look that said she would be checking the accounts. Her mother, Paloma, a hairdresser who had been happy once and not noticed, had wept through the entire Mass and ruined four handkerchiefs and an uncle's tie. Rafael's father, Ignacio, retired vendor of anything, had wept into a tamale.

And now the whole party had spilled out into the lane behind the house, where an old wall of lime plaster, prepared that week by the stonemason Ximena Salazar, a woman of sixty-three with forearms like cables and the severity of an Inca queen, stood white and waiting.

"It is the hundred-and-first," said Rafael, not coming down. "I could not marry you and leave you on a hundred walls like a lost umbrella. There has to be one that is *finished.*"

"You have painted me a hundred times!"

"I painted a *face.* An idea. The girl in the pictures is a stranger. She is kind and tall and she has never once lost her temper in court."

"I lose my temper in court every day."

"I know," said Rafael. "I am going to paint *that.*"

He turned back to the wall. And the street, which had been squabbling and eating and tuning guitars, went quiet in the way crowds go quiet for a thing they have not been told to watch.

It was not the Camila of the hundred walls. It was the one who stood at the foot of the ladder in a white dress with her hair coming down: sharp-jawed, a little cross, one eyebrow raised in indictment, and in the crook of her arm a thick law book with a broken spine. She was laughing at somebody off the edge of the picture. Behind her he painted marigold petals in orange flame, the *cempasúchil* of the dead and of the living; and the thirteen coins like small suns; and, in the lower corner, very small, a street full of people who had come to a wedding and stayed to be remembered.

"Is that me?" said Officer Alejandro Hernández, forty-five, of the Coyoacán police, who had come to direct the traffic and had been standing at the edge of the mural for twenty minutes stroking his moustache.

"It is a policeman," said Rafael. "Anyone's."

"It has my moustache."

"All policemen have your moustache, Alejandro."

"I do not think that is *true,*" said Officer Hernández, deeply wounded, and went to look at his own reflection in the patrol car, saving money, as he often said, to disappear, and meanwhile appearing at every public occasion in the district.

Camila said nothing for a long time.

Then, in her wedding dress, in front of the whole of Coyoacán, she took the ladder in both hands and began to climb.

"What are you doing?" said Rafael.

"I walked to every wall," said Camila. "Ninety-nine walls, in four years, in the heat, in my good shoes, to find the hand that painted me. I found him. And I have never once held the brush." She reached the top, took it from his fingers, and dipped it in black. "Move."

"What are you going to paint?"

"Your hand," she said.

And there, at the edge of the plaster, beside her painted self, a little crooked and a little too thick, with a lawyer's confidence and no training whatsoever, Camila Reyes painted the five long fingers of the man who had painted her: the left hand, the hand that held the brush, reaching up out of the corner of the wall as though to lift her down.

The mariachi, who had been waiting since eleven, took it as a cue.

"*¡Que vivan los novios!*" cried Ignacio Salazar, with tears running into his moustache.

"*¡Que vivan!*" shouted forty neighbours; and a nine-year-old flower girl named Renata Vargas, who had been told to scatter petals and had thrown them all at the policeman, threw the basket as well.

---

*Margin note, in pencil, in the hand of S.W.R.:*

> *Entry 0439 and Entry 0502. Learning to read at thirty is not a defeat. It is a second birth, with the added advantage that one can already speak.*
>
> *Entry 0299 and Entry 0121. Observe that a hundred walls could not do for them what one hour did: the day the painted woman climbed the ladder and took the brush.*
>
> *Observe also: the heart is a very poor reader and a very good calligrapher. It spells nothing correctly, and yet is always understood.*

---

*End of Chapter 40.*


---

## Chapter 41
### The Ship's Log

> *"My captain wants me; so does the sea. You are third."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0991

---

*Enter the Chorus, in an oilskin, with a lantern, a compass and a very small violin.*

> A ship has but two mistresses: the shore
> She leaves, the sea she goes to. Let it be
> That one small heart, which neither's, wants her more
> Than either, and is told to wait. For she
> Is owned by tides; he, by a harbour wall;
> And log-books keep what lovers cannot say.
> Here is the log. We read it, one and all,
> And mark the hour where each one lost the way.

---

### SCENE I
*Split, Croatia. The Riva, the long stone promenade under the walls of Diocletian's palace. The last evening of the month. A hot, heavy wind from the south, the* jugo*, which makes the dogs bite and the philosophers weep.*

> **LOG OF THE M/V *MARJAN*, bulk carrier, Split. Entry in the hand of Ivan Horvat, deck rating.**
> *1900. All stores aboard. Crew complete but for the cook, who is late and is, he says, "not late, merely *anticipated.*" Wind S, force 4, jugo. Barometer falling. Spirits: high. Heart: not recorded; the form has no column.*

The Dalmatians have a word, *fjaka*, for the blessed state in which a man, on a warm afternoon, is neither working nor resting nor thinking, but simply *being,* as an olive is being on a branch. The jugo brings it. It lay now over the whole Riva like a damp, sweet blanket, and the palm trees stood in it motionless, and the old men on the benches argued about football in the unhurried way of men who have been wrong together for sixty years.

Through it, at a rapid, determined pace, strode Marija Kovač, thirty, second officer of the *Sveti Duje*, in her blue shore-uniform and a face from which no emotion had ever been permitted to escape without a pass.

"You are late," said Ivan Horvat.

"I am nine minutes early."

"For the *sea,*" said Ivan. "For me, a woman who is nine minutes early is nine minutes *late* in a better coat."

He was thirty-three, brown as a walnut, with the loose, windblown look of a man whose smile had been rubbed smooth by weather, like a stone at the foot of a quay. He sat on the sea wall with his legs swinging, an enormous canvas bag at his feet, and a paper bag of fritule in his lap, and he held it out to her, and she took one, because refusing him anything was a thing she had never learned to do properly.

"Six months," said Ivan.

"One hundred and eighty-two days."

"I have counted too. I make it one hundred and eighty-*three*, with the leap of my heart."

"You are not a mathematician."

"I am a *deck rating,*" said Ivan, "which is the same thing with less pay." He licked sugar off his thumb. "Marija. You said you had something to tell me. You said it four times this week. Each time you said it, you said it was nothing. A thing that is *nothing* does not need to be said four times."

She looked out at the water. Beyond the harbour, low and violet in the haze, lay the island of Brač, steady as a lie.

"Captain Šimić," she said, "has offered me a post."

"The Captain wants you."

"As chief officer. On the *Sveti Duje.* Twenty-four months. Rijeka, Suez, Busan, Shanghai, and back. There is no shore leave for the first year. The pay is—" she named it, and Ivan whistled. "I have until eight o'clock tomorrow morning to answer him."

"Well," said Ivan, "that is wonderful."

"Yes."

"That is *magnificent.* You will be the youngest chief officer in the Adriatic fleet."

"I know."

"Then why," said Ivan, and he did not stop smiling, because he was the kind of man who smiled as a ship keeps its lights on in a gale, "why are you looking at me like a woman reading out a sentence?"

"Because," said Marija, "I wrote to an astronomer in England, three winters ago, and it was the only honest sentence I have ever written. It is in the Register. I will not tell you which number."

"You do not have to."

"I know. I am going to tell you, anyway, what it says." She took a breath, as one takes a bearing. "*My captain wants me; so does the sea. You are third.*"

There was a very long silence. "Third," said Ivan Horvat.

"I am sorry."

"Third." He turned the word over like a coin. "Do you know, Marija, that on a ship the third mate is the officer who stands the watch from midnight until four? When the Captain is in his bunk, and the chief is in his, and the sea is at her blackest and every other soul aboard has gone to sleep. It is the *third* who is awake. Who holds the ship. Who sees the dawn before any of them." He grinned, wide, with an effort that cost him something. "I have always thought it the most honourable post afloat. I would be glad of it."

"Ivan, that is not—"

"I will take the dog watch, then. Gladly. Somebody should be up."

"I did not want you to be *glad.*"

"What did you want?"

She said, very low, "I wanted you to be angry. I wanted you to *ask me to stay.*"

"Ah," said Ivan, and for once he did not smile. "That is the difficulty. If I ask you to stay, you will; and if you stay, you will be a woman who stayed. I knew a girl at school who never forgave a man for a thing he did not ask. I would rather be third than be the reason."

---

### SCENE II
*The same night. A quay, a hundred paces down the harbour. A tall gangway, a large man, and a very large supper.*

> *2130. Cook arrived. Reports he was "detained by destiny." Destiny, on inquiry, turned out to be a barmaid in Kaštela. Wind backing SW, force 5. Visibility moderate. Cook says it is the first time in thirty years he has been seasick *before* sailing.*

The ship's cook of the *Marjan* was a man called Luka Matić, fifty-five, from Zagreb, who had never in his life been outdone in vanity by anyone but his own moustache. He was a chef of great and terrible talent. He had once, he claimed, been dismissed from a presidential luncheon for "being too delicious," and had taken to the sea at fifty because "a man who will not be a legend on land must be one at sea, where no one can check."

He stood now at the foot of the gangway with a stockpot in his arms, regarding the departing deck rating with a long, shrewd, meddling eye.

"You have *told* her."

"I have said nothing, Luka."

"You have said *nothing,* in the loud way. Nothing, with the shoulders." He put down the pot. "There is a technique. You do not say 'I love you.' That is for the amateurs. You say, 'I have made you a stew.' You see? It means the same, and nobody can sue."

"Luka. She has been offered the sea."

"The sea!" Luka threw up his hands. "The sea is a *brute.* The sea has no manners. It will not remember her birthday. It has never once thanked me for a meal." He lowered his voice; his hand, Ivan noticed, went briefly to his side, below the ribs, and came away again, in the quick way of a man brushing off a crumb. "The truth is, boy, that most people spend their whole lives choosing between two things they love, and the thing they *lose* is whichever they were too busy to hold. Do not stand there like a bollard. Go and *do* something."

"What?"

"Something stupid!" said Luka. "That is the only kind of thing that has ever worked!"

He picked up the pot and went up the gangway, humming, a little unsteadily.

Ivan stood alone on the dark quay. Above him the *Marjan* creaked at her lines. Along the Riva, a klapa of six old men in white shirts had begun to sing in the close harmony of that coast, about a girl who waited by the sea and a sailor who could not say when he would come. He listened. Then he walked to the waterfront bar, borrowed a pen, and did a stupid thing.

---

### SCENE III
*Dawn. The* Sveti Duje*, at her berth. A steel ship, a steel sky, and a steel-grey woman at the head of the gangway, with a piece of paper in each hand.*

> **LOG OF THE M/V *SVETI DUJE.* Entry in the hand of M. Kovač, Second Officer.**
> *0540. Wind NE, force 3, the* bura *arriving, cold and clean. The jugo has gone. Decision outstanding.*
> *0610. Received, delivered by hand by a deckhand of another vessel, a small package, no name. Contents: a paper bag of fritule, now cold; and on the back of the paper bag, in pencil, a note.*

She had read it eleven times.

It said: *I did not ask you to stay. I am asking you, instead, to come back. It is the only question I know how to ask of a person who is going away. — I.*

And under it, smaller: *P.S. The third mate takes the watch you cannot. I will be awake.*

Marija did not weep; it was against regulations. But her chin did something it had never done on duty: it *trembled,* once, like the needle of an instrument finding north.

At 0745, Captain Vlaho Šimić came down the gangway, sixty-one, a large grey walrus of a man in a cap that had survived four ships and two marriages.

"Well, Kovač?" he said gruffly. "I will have your answer."

She looked at him. She looked at the sea beyond him, wide and cold and bright, and at the harbour mouth where, even now, a bulk carrier with a white funnel was easing out under the shadow of Marjan hill, with a small figure at the stern, a long way off, who was too far to be seen and who she knew, without any evidence whatever, was waving.

"I will take the post, Captain."

"Ha!" said the Captain, and clapped her on the shoulder so hard that she very nearly went into the harbour.

"For six months."

"For *six* months?"

"For one rotation. At the end of it I will tell you if I stay."

The Captain's eyebrows travelled up his forehead like two caterpillars discovering a new leaf.

"Is it a man?"

"It is a rotation," said Marija Kovač, with the flat, unarguable calm of an officer at the end of an argument. "That is the whole of the answer. And I will take the watch from midnight until four, whoever is on the roster."

"That is the *third* mate's watch."

"Yes," said Marija. "I know."

He looked at her for a long time, and then, being a man who had been in love twice and wrong only once, he grunted and went up the gangway.

---

### SCENE IV
*Cairo. A Thursday evening, under a sky the colour of a ripe apricot. The Khan el-Khalili, drums, lanterns, and a family trying to get through a door at once.*

Elsewhere, where the Nile slides under the old bridges like a slow brown thought, a wedding was beginning.

I must be brief, reader, for it was a very long wedding. The *zaffa* began at six: drums, tambourines, a reed pipe that could weep and make you dance in the same bar, forty cousins with candles; and in front of them, in a cream-coloured jacket cut by a tailor who had not been paid and was only attending to see he would be, walked **Omar Haddad,** thirty-five, antiques dealer, and the finest liar in the whole of Egypt, with the look of a man who had, for the first time in his life, nothing to sell.

The *katb el-kitab,* the signing of the contract, was done in the courtyard of the bride's family house, beneath a trellis hung with jasmine. The officiant was a venerable sheikh with a beard like a cloud. The witnesses were Karim, a potter, built like a wardrobe and weeping like a fountain, and Tarek Hassan, a librarian of forty-one, who drank tea at every hour and had read too many contracts to trust any of them.

"Read the conditions," said the sheikh kindly.

Tarek unrolled the paper. Layla Mansour, thirty-two, the bride, in a gown of ivory silk, sat beneath her veil with a back as straight as an argument. For she was a restorer of antiquities, and the Islamic law, in its wisdom, permits a bride to add her own conditions to the contract; and this one had added her own with the exactness of one cataloguing a tomb.

"*'The first,'*" read Tarek, with a quiver, "*'that the husband shall never sell the wife anything without a receipt.'*"

"*'The second: that if the husband should at any time describe an object as "genuine," he shall provide a certificate; and if there is none, he shall provide a confession.'*"

"Third," read Tarek, who had begun to enjoy himself and so had begun to sweat. "*'That the husband shall come home on time on Fridays; and that, should he be late, he shall say plainly that the clock was wrong, and not that he was detained by an Italian count.'*"

"That," said Omar, "was *one time.*"

"*'Fourth: that the bride was not deceived.'*" Tarek read slowly, and the courtyard fell still. "*'She knew it was false. She kept it because it was his.'*" He cleared his throat. His eyes had gone suddenly very bright. "I do not think," he said, "that I have read a contract before in which the *clauses* made me want to cry."

They proceeded. The bride said yes. The bridegroom said yes, a little louder than needed, as a man says yes who has had much practice saying no to himself. And the women in the courtyard let loose the *zaghareet,* that long, high, trembling trill of joy that goes up from the throat of Egypt like a flock of white birds, and for one long minute the whole of Cairo seemed to be ululating.

There was a gift. Omar's was a small clay lamp from the Fayoum, plain, chipped, entirely genuine, with a certificate of provenance signed by three experts and a customs officer.

"It is *real,*" said Omar. "I swear it on every receipt I ever lost."

"I believe you," said Layla.

"Truly?"

"I have tested it." She smiled, behind the veil, for the first time. "Now. Mine."

She gave him a flat package wrapped in a newspaper. He opened it. Inside, in a frame of plain wood, restored with infinite care to its own original imperfection, was the forgery, the little false scarab he had sold her six years ago and never confessed to, with a typed card beneath: **GENUINE FAKE. Circa six years ago. Provenance: the heart.**

Omar Haddad, who had once sold a pyramid to a Dutchman, stood for a long time with his mouth open, and said nothing at all.

At the back of the courtyard, among the aunts, a fourteen-year-old girl named Dina Shaker went very pink and very still. For she had told no one that it was she, one wet afternoon last year, who had posted a certain small, anonymous note through a certain shop door, and the thing had grown and grown, as these things will, until here it was, in jasmine, with drums.

"Why are you smiling like a cat in a dairy?" asked her aunt.

"It is the blush of the wicked," said Tarek, passing with fresh tea. "A child who has done good in secret and cannot bear it. I am a librarian. I know where the bodies are shelved."

---

### SCENE V
*Naples. The Via dei Tribunali. A pizzeria older than the street's last three governments. A Saturday night, queue to the door, and a baker in a state.*

I promised a third wedding, did I not? It is not a wedding. It is the thing before: the question.

> **Alessandro Greco** was thirty-three and had spent six years in a war with a pastry chef. It had involved a stolen recipe, a rigged contest, and one very memorable incident with a hundred kilos of flour and a Vespa.

Now he stood in his own pizzeria, with a clean white apron, a hand that was not quite steady, and a calzone.

"A calzone," said Paolo Ricci, thirty, choir director, his oldest friend and his worst gossip, from the end of the counter. "You are going to propose with a *folded pizza.*"

"It is a *symbol.*"

"Of what?"

"A pizza," said Alessandro, "is open. A pizza is a thing that shows you everything. A *calzone* is a pizza that has closed its heart and is only waiting for the right person to cut it."

Paolo wiped an eye. "It is almost *sacred.* Shall I sing? I have composed a short aria."

"Paolo, if you sing, I will bake you."

The door chimed. In came Chiara Esposito, thirty-one, pastry chef, with flour in her hair and a smile on her face that was not entirely trustworthy, because she had been told by seven separate people that she was needed urgently at the pizzeria and had worked out why by the fourth.

"You have summoned me," she said, "in front of everyone."

"I have not summoned you."

"Matteo Ricci told me there was a fire."

"He is a welder, he sees fire everywhere."

"Alessandro." She came up to the counter and looked at what lay on it: a golden half-moon, crimped at the edge, sleek with oil. "What is this?"

"I stole your recipe," said Alessandro, in a tremendous rush. "Six years ago. The one for the dough. I told myself it was *competition*. It was not competition. It was that it was the most beautiful thing I had ever read, in the most beautiful handwriting, and it said at the bottom, *for whoever finds this,* and I thought, *that is me,* and then I was too proud to say so. I made it every day. I have never once said sorry, and I am sorry. This is made from it. Cut it."

"Cut what?"

"The *calzone.*"

Chiara looked at him, and at the whole queue, which had stopped breathing.

"I wrote that recipe," she said slowly, "for you to find."

"I *know,*" said Alessandro. "I worked it out in the fourth year. I am slow. I am a pizzaiolo. We are a patient people."

"You are an *idiot.*"

"I am a *closed calzone,*" said Alessandro. "Cut me."

She took the knife. She cut it, and the steam rose, and out of the ricotta and the ham and the heat tumbled a small gold ring, which rolled across the marble and came to rest against her wrist, and stopped.

"Your dough," said Chiara, picking up the ring and wiping it on her apron, "is too thick."

"That is *not an answer.*"

"It is the beginning of one," said Chiara Esposito, and put the ring on her finger, and the whole of the Via dei Tribunali, which had heard nothing in the last four minutes but its own heart, burst into noise. Paolo Ricci began his aria, which was dreadful. Nobody stopped him. Alessandro, at last, was crying into a bowl of flour, and being kissed, once, on the forehead, by a woman who tasted of cinnamon and fury.

"*Ué, guagliò,*" breathed the lottery man, wiping his eyes. "Now *that* is a Saturday."

---

### SCENE VI
*Night. The open Adriatic, a hundred miles from any shore. Two ships, a mile apart, on opposite courses. The VHF radio on the bridge of the* Sveti Duje*, in the dark.*

> *0140. Wind NW, force 4. Sea slight. The* Marjan *has just been raised on the radar, bearing 232, range 1.4 miles, steering a reciprocal course.*
> *0141. I have not slept since Wednesday.*
> *0142. Hailed her on Channel 16. For operational purposes only.*

"*Marjan, Marjan, Marjan.* This is *Sveti Duje.* *Sveti Duje.* Over."

There was a crackle. The sea hissed along the hull. A long, very long, ten seconds went by, in which the whole Adriatic seemed to lean in.

"*Sveti Duje, Sveti Duje.* This is *Marjan.* Receiving you, strength five. Over." A pause. "Is that the *chief officer?*"

"It is the officer of the watch. Over."

"The *third* watch?"

"The third watch," said Marija, and her voice shook very slightly, and she cursed it. "Over."

"I am on watch also. Over."

"Understood. Over."

"It is a fine night. Over."

"Affirmative. Over."

Another long, hissing silence. On the *Marjan,* a hundred miles from anywhere, a deck rating who ought to have been asleep stood on the wing of a dark bridge with a radio in his hand and a cook breathing down his neck. "*Say it!*" whispered Luka, from the shadow of the funnel. "*Say anything stupid!*"

"*Sveti Duje.*" Ivan's voice was careful as a man crossing a plank. "I have a message. Did you receive my paper bag? Over."

"Received. Over."

"Did you eat the fritule? Over."

"Negative. Over."

"Did you read the message? Over."

"Affirmative. Over."

"And?"

"Say again, *Marjan.* You did not say 'over.'"

"*And—over.*"

There was a very long silence. Marija Kovač stood alone in the glow of the radar, with the stars uncountable above her and a boy in a canvas coat a mile away across the dark. She lifted the handset.

"*Marjan,*" she said. "I have revised the order of priority."

"Say again?" said Ivan, hoarsely.

"Negative," said Marija. "I will say it in port. Over."

"Which port?"

"The first one," said Marija, "that either of us arrives at. Out."

The radio clicked. The two ships slid past one another in the dark, a mile apart, their running lights red and green like two small questions, and went each their way.

On the *Marjan,* a deck rating sat down very suddenly on a coil of rope.

On the *Sveti Duje,* a second officer wrote in her log, in her small, level hand, the one entry that for twelve years she had never made. It was a single line. It was not a position. It was not a bearing. It said:

> *0151. Course steady. Heart: recorded.*

---

*Margin note, in pencil, in the hand of S.W.R.:*

> *Entry 0603 and Entry 0991. A sea captain once told me that the best navigators are not those who know where they are going but those who know, to the minute, where they have been. Mark the hour. It will be asked for.*
>
> *Entry 0353 and Entry 0486. A closed calzone is, in my experience, a very sound proposal. Open ones tend to cool.*

---

*End of Chapter 41.*
