## Chapter 46
### The Weaver's Promise

> *"I promised to wait and I am weaving the promise."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0281

---

*Enter the Chorus, trailing a loose thread, a loose wire, and a loose bicycle chain.*

> Three promises, each made of different stuff:
> One thread, one wave, one wheel. The thread is slow,
> The wave is quick, the wheel goes round and round;
> And none may say which one will hold the longest.
> But mark: the thread is longer than it looks.

---

### SCENE I
*Bonwire, outside Kumasi, in the hills of Asante. A weaving shed with a tin roof, four looms, and a smell of cotton, dust and groundnut soup. August; the long rains drumming overhead like a hundred small fists.*

The loom said *clack*, and then it said *clack* again.

It is a narrow thing, the kente loom, and an ancient one: a frame of wood, a weight of stone, two pedals worked by the feet, and a warp of thread stretched away into the dark of the shed like a road that had decided to be a rumour. The weaver sits at the near end and throws the shuttle through the shed with his right hand and beats the weft with his left, and his feet, meanwhile, go up and down like a man pedalling steadily toward a place he has not told anyone about. What comes out is not cloth. It is a *strip*, four fingers wide, no more; and a hundred strips sewn edge to edge make the cloth that kings are buried in, and the cloth a girl wears to be named, and the cloth that a young man, in his thirtieth year, is weaving now, with a promise in it.

Kofi Boateng sat at the loom. He had sat there since four o'clock. He was thirty and patient, which in Asante is an old and honoured combination, and proud, which in Asante is a young man's one acknowledged vice. Beside him, on a stool, with her handbag on her knee and her glasses at the end of her nose, sat his mother, Akosua Asante, sixty-one, a lawyer. She was reading a contract. It was his.

"Paragraph three," said Akosua.

"There is no paragraph three. I did not write a contract."

"I have written one for you. Paragraph three says, *The party of the first part, being a weaver, undertakes to wait.* It does not say how long." She looked at him over the glasses. "A promise with no term, Kofi, is not a promise. It is a rumour with a heartbeat."

"It is not a contract. It is a cloth."

"It is a *warp*," said his mother, with the air of a woman who has cross-examined a hundred thieves, and found her son the most elusive. "I counted it. Do not think I did not. One hundred and forty yards. You wound that warp on Monday. A man does not wind a warp of one hundred and forty yards for a market stall; he winds it for a *term*. Twenty-four months. That is how long her scholarship runs."

Kofi's hands did not stop. *Clack.* "You have been in my shed."

"I stay where the evidence is."

"I have not asked her to wait for me."

"You have not asked her to *go*, either." Akosua folded the paper. "I stayed in this town thirty-six years when I should have gone to Accra and been a judge. Nobody asked me to stay. Nobody asked me to go. I have had a very long time to consider the difference." She stood. "Weave the cloth. But tell the girl, or the cloth will tell her, and cloth has a poor sense of timing."

Overhead, a ladder creaked. Kwabena Quaye, fifty, electrician, who had been summoned from Tema to fix the shed's single wire and had been fixing it since breakfast, put his head down through the rafters. He was a punctual man, and a bitter one, and he had never forgotten that, twenty-six years ago, a weaver had told him his shirt did not match his trousers.

"The light is ready," said Kwabena. "I want it noted that I could have done it in an hour if I had not been *judged.*"

"Nobody judged you."

"Your uncle looked at my sleeve."

"Kwabena. It is *twenty-six years.*"

"I have a good memory," said Kwabena darkly, and threw the switch. A single bulb came on above the loom and showed, in the strip that lay unrolling from the cloth-beam, a pattern of gold and green and black: broad blocks and narrow, in the order the old weavers call *Emaa Da*, which means, *it has never happened before.*

"There," said Kwabena, relenting, because the light was beautiful. "Now it has."

---

### SCENE II
*A classroom in Kumasi, after the last bell. A blackboard, thirty small chairs, a letter on a teacher's desk, and a window through which a tea-seller is shouting up the price of sugar.*

Esi Appiah, twenty-nine, schoolteacher, held a letter in both hands and had not read it for the third time that afternoon.

She did not need to. It said what it had said on Monday: that she, Esi Appiah of Kumasi, had been awarded a two-year scholarship to study education at a university in Scotland, where it rained, she had been told, as it rained here, but colder, and with opinions. It said she must reply by the end of the month. It said *Congratulations.* It was the first word on the page, and she had spent four days looking at the other ones.

"You have not said yes," said a voice from the window.

Below, with a thermos on his hip and a tray of sugar bread on his head, stood Kojo Asante, thirty-three, tea-seller, her oldest friend, and a deeply devout man who had a habit of spending money that was not his on things that were holy. He had been, that week, a hundred cedis into the church building fund on borrowed sugar, and he had asked God for a decision on the matter, and God, so far, had been silent.

"I have not said anything," said Esi.

"Not even to Kofi?"

"*Especially* not to Kofi."

"Then you are *both* very quiet." Kojo clasped his hands. "Madam. I will tell you what my grandmother told me, and then I will sell you a tea. She said, there are two things you cannot do to a person: you cannot ask them to stay, and you cannot tell them to go. You can only stand in the door and hold it open for whichever way they walk."

"That is very profound."

"It is also why she lost three husbands," said Kojo. "Tea?"

She laughed in spite of herself. And then, when the laugh was done, she turned to the empty blackboard, and spoke, as people speak who are alone with the thirty small chairs of a school:

> *I have been brave in every way but this.
> I crossed the river when the bridge was down;
> I taught a hundred children how to read,
> And stood before a minister and said
> That girls should have the books. I have not feared.
> And now, a letter, and a name, and a door,
> And on the other side of it a man
> Who has not asked, who will not ask, who sits
> At his slow loom and weaves while I decide.
> If I go, I shall not know what he weaves.
> If I stay, I shall not know what I have been.
> O Time, who carries one of us away,
> How shall I say a yes I cannot spell?*

She did not hear the shed door open, nor the footsteps on the damp laterite. She only looked up, when the poem was done, and found Kofi Boateng standing at the classroom door in his weaving clothes, with a thing wrapped in brown paper under his arm, and a tea-seller behind him pretending to count loaves.

"I came about the warp," said Kofi.

"The warp."

"It is a hundred and forty yards. It is wound for twenty-four months. I did not mean you to know until the cloth was finished." He put the parcel on her desk. His hands, which had never trembled at a loom in his life, trembled at the string. "It is a strip. It is the first. It is the width of one month. I thought, if you go, I would weave one every month you are away, and send you a hand's breadth, and at the end of two years, there is a cloth. And if you stay—" His voice caught on the word, like a shuttle on a snagged thread. "If you stay, I will cut the warp and burn it, and you will never need to know."

She opened the paper. The strip lay in her hands, four fingers wide, gold and green and black. In the weave, very small, there was a pattern she had not seen before, and he named it, as weavers do, in the old way, with a proverb.

"It is called *Emaa Da*," said Kofi.

"*It has never happened before.*"

"It has been done before. A weaver cannot make a thing that is new." He smiled, a little ruefully. "But I think it has never been done for this."

"Kofi," said Esi.

"Do not say it. Do not say yes or no, not to me. I do not ask you for a promise. I am only telling you that the thread is long. It is longer than it looks."

She stood very still with the strip lying across her palms. She was a woman who had never in her life failed to answer a direct question, and she found that she had no answer except to put one hand, lightly, over his, where it lay on the desk.

"I will write to Scotland on Friday," said Esi.

"And?"

"And I will tell you on Friday," said Esi Appiah, "which letter I wrote."

Down at the window the tea-seller dropped the entire tray of sugar bread, and said *Amen.*

---

### SCENE III
*Soweto, Johannesburg. A Sunday afternoon in the church hall of a street whose name every schoolchild knows. The roof is corrugated; the floor is polished like a wish; and on a trestle table by the door sits a radio microphone wrapped in a ribbon.*

It is a fact, known to every taxi driver in the province of Gauteng, that there was no wedding in the history of Johannesburg that the whole city heard at once.

There was one now. The radio station, whose night show had begun as a joke between a woman and a microphone and grown into the bedtime ritual of eight hundred thousand people, had parked an outside-broadcast van beside the church hall, and run a cable under the door, and informed the city that at four o'clock, on the frequency that had carried a woman's voice into the dark for four years, the woman would be married, live, to the man who had played saxophone to her through that same dark and not once been seen.

"I am not nervous," said Jabu Mokoena, twenty-nine, shopkeeper, best man, and master of ceremonies by popular misunderstanding.

"You have put the ring in your shoe," said a voice at his elbow.

"That is *tradition.*"

"It is *pain,* Jabu." This was Thandi Zulu, thirty, who sold fat-cakes from a barrow in Pretoria and had come to the wedding with forty dozen, in the belief that a hall full of the hopeful is also, by the laws of arithmetic, a hall full of the hungry. She was gleaming with oil and good intentions. She had never in her life met a stranger. "I will tell you what it is. It is that you hide behind jokes. I do too. I am a fat-cake woman; nobody asks a fat-cake woman if she is afraid. They say, *Madam, a dozen.* And I say, *Right away, sir,* and I think, *I never thanked the woman who first sold me bread.*"

"Who was she?"

"I don't know!" wailed Thandi. "That is the *problem.*"

At the front of the hall, in a dress of blue shweshwe the colour of a deep pool, with a gold necklace from her landlady Palesa Zulu round her throat, Naledi Khumalo stood in the hush of two hundred guests and one microphone. She was twenty-nine. She was warm, and wry, and a radio host, and she had never in her life been at a loss for a word.

Beside her stood Thabo Dlamini, thirty-one, saxophonist, shy offstage as a deer, in a black suit with a thin gold tie and a saxophone slung at his hip.

Neither of them had a speech. That was the arrangement. In the pause before the priest began, an old man in the second row, very thin, in a grey coat too heavy for the heat, rose up unbidden and said, in the quavering voice of eighty winters, "Excuse me. Before it starts. I wish to say that I have listened every night. I cannot read. Never learned. The radio was my newspaper and my church and my friend. I wish to thank the lady." He sat down. Tshepo Radebe, sixty-six, retired newsagent, had been listening for four years, and had come to the front on the arm of a taxi-driver, and it was observed that the bride wept before the ceremony began.

It was a short ceremony and a loud one, as Soweto weddings are: with the ululation going up from the aunts at the vows like a flock of birds that had been waiting all year to be asked, and a choir in the corner singing in three languages at once. The vows were not long. Naledi went first, because she was the voice, and said them to the microphone and the man and the city, in the plain measure that the heart finds when it has been practising for years:

> *For four years I have sent a song into the dark
> And never known the one who heard it best.
> I called you stranger. Now I call you mine,
> Not as a thing possessed, but as a hand
> Is held: because it fits, and will not tire.
> I am a voice. You are the sound I wished for.
> Be with me when the radio goes quiet.*

Then Thabo, who had no voice for it, lifted the saxophone to his mouth.

He did not speak. He played. It was a slow, warm, impossible tune, the one that had come down the wires to her on a hundred nights, and it went up through the corrugated roof and through the open door and down the length of the street, where people had stopped; and down the length of the city, where cars had pulled over, and minibus-taxis had turned off their engines in the middle of the road with the driver's hand still on the wheel, and a hundred thousand people were listening to a stranger propose, in the one language that has no accent, to a woman he had never failed to know.

When the last note went out, the hall was entirely silent.

Then Jabu Mokoena took out the ring from his shoe, with an expression of great suffering, and a cheer rose that could be heard in Pretoria. *Mark this, reader.* They say that at a taxi rank on Bree Street the whole thing was played from a single car radio, and a hundred people stood with their heads bare in the sun, and no one, afterwards, could remember who had taken up the collection, or for what.

---

### SCENE IV
*Medellín, Colombia. The Feria de las Flores, the Sunday of the great parade. A mountain road at dawn above the city; a cyclist, a farm, and a wheelbarrow.*

Meanwhile, on another continent, a man was riding downhill with forty buckets of carnations strapped to a racing bicycle.

It was the most expensive delivery van in Antioquia. Sebastián Torres, twenty-nine, professional cyclist, lately of a crash and a long plaster, stood on the pedals as the road dropped away beneath him in a series of hairpins that gave onto cloud. He had not yet been told by any doctor that this was permitted. He had been told it by Daniela Ruiz, which was a good deal more binding.

"You are carrying the Pinzón order," she had said, at dawn, on the porch of the farm that was dying. "Forty buckets. Carnations and a few spray roses for the florist. If they arrive wilted I am finished."

"They will not wilt."

"They will *wilt*, because you will ride like a lunatic."

"I will ride like a man who has been told to ride *carefully* by a woman who is afraid," said Sebastián, "which is the most dangerous kind of careful there is."

Daniela Ruiz was twenty-eight and a flower farmer, and she was bright, and proud, and in debt. In the greenhouse behind the house the roses had a blight, and in the bank in town a man named Julián Gómez, fifty-one, a notary's scribe, loyal to the point of agony and quite unable to say goodbye, held a paper from a buyer that would take the whole farm, house and ground and mountain, for a sum that was both fair and a catastrophe. He had brought it up the hill on Thursday. He had stood on the porch for an hour holding it, and gone down again without handing it over, and returned on Friday, and done the same.

"It is a very *hard* paper to deliver," Julián had explained, nearly weeping.

"Give it to me."

"I cannot. It is *heavy.*"

"It is two pages."

"It is the weight of the thing it *says,*" said Julián, "and I have been a scribe for thirty years, and nothing else has ever weighed anything."

Now, on the Sunday of the parade, the farm's last silleta, a great wooden chair of flowers strapped upon the back of a bearer, stood on the porch waiting. It had been made by Daniela's grandmother, and her grandmother's mother, and by every woman of the line for ninety years: seventy kilos of orchids, and lilies, and carnations, bound in the shape of the mountain itself, and carried down into the city once a year on a human back, in the old way, in front of five hundred thousand people. Her sister, Mariana Rojas, forty-four, a butcher, who had a cleaver for every occasion and a joke for every cleaver, had inspected it that morning with great suspicion.

"It is very heavy," said Mariana. "I will say this for it. It will never be accused of being *silly.*"

"Silleta."

"That is what I said. Silly."

"Mariana."

"I am a butcher. I carry the whole side of a cow and nobody gives me flowers." She sniffed. "Who is going to carry it? Not you; you have a bad knee. Not *him*; he has a bad *spine.*"

"I will," said Daniela.

"You will *die.*"

"Then I will die with an orchid." She put her hand on the carved arm of the chair. It was the kind of line that could be said in a house that is about to be sold. "Sebastián will ride behind me down the mountain, and every kilometre I will think: *I have not lost it yet.*"

He did, in the end. All the way down, past the roadside shrines and the vultures and the little tin kiosks selling *arepas*, behind a woman with a seventy-kilo mountain on her back, he rode at walking pace, a bicycle at the speed of a funeral; and she never once stopped, nor spoke, nor looked back, and the sun came up over the whole green valley and caught the petals, so that she seemed to walk into the city carried by a small blazing garden. Somewhere at the bottom of the hill a team manager from Spain stood waiting with a contract that would send Sebastián across an ocean for four years, and somewhere on the same hill a notary's scribe sat on a rock with his two pages, weeping at last, because he had finally decided to deliver them.

"Don't read it yet," said Daniela, over her shoulder, not knowing which paper she meant, and not turning. "Ride with me to the end of the parade. Whatever they say, we will decide it at the bottom."

"Together?"

"At the same time," said Daniela. "I'm not proud enough to say *together.*"

It was, said the Keeper later, a very good answer.

---

*Margin note, in pencil, in the hand of S.W.R.:*

> *Entry 0281 and Entry 0532. A weaver measures a promise in yards. A radio host measures it in frequencies. A cyclist measures it in kilometres, and a farmer in the weight of a flower on her back. They are all the same unit. It is called: how far are you willing to go with your hand still open?*
>
> *Entry 0586 and Entry 0360. The wheel is still turning. I will not say which way.*

---

*End of Chapter 46.*

## Chapter 47
### Tiles of Isfahan

> *"A pattern that never repeats is the closest thing to you."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0228

---

### SCENE I
*Isfahan, Iran. A ruined madrasa behind the great square, in the last gold hour of an August day. Scaffolding, a bucket of lime, a dome the colour of a turquoise someone has dropped into the sky, and a wall that is missing one corner of its own face.*

There is a legend in Isfahan, told by every tea-seller to every tourist, that the old masters made one mistake on purpose in every panel they ever laid. *Only God is perfect,* they said, and set one tile crooked, so as not to be presumptuous.

Ali Rezaei, thirty-six, tile master, did not believe the legend. He believed in measurement. But he had been kneeling since noon in front of a panel a thousand years too old for its own good, with a bucket of lime at one elbow and a stub of pencil behind one ear, and he was beginning to suspect that God had taken the legend personally.

"It is not a repeat," said a voice behind him.

"I know it is not a repeat."

"I mean that I have checked every unit in the field. It *looks* like a repeat. It looks like the five-fold stars that the masters used everywhere. But you set one star beside the next and the next one is turned a hair, and the one after, a hair more. The whole panel is made of a rule that does not close." Parisa Karimi, thirty-one, architect and restorer, had come up the scaffold with a clipboard held as carefully as a baby and the expression of a woman who has found, in a ruin, a handwriting she cannot copy. "I do not know how to restore a thing that has no template. Every other panel I have mended, I took one tile, I made forty."

"Then do not make forty."

"What do you mean?"

"I mean," said Ali, sitting back on his heels, "that you make *one.* And then you look at it, and you listen, and you make the next."

Parisa lowered the clipboard. "That is the worst building method I have ever heard."

"It is the only method that is true to the panel."

"It is *slow.*"

"It is the only speed I have." He took a glass of tea from the ledge beside him, because she had brought it, and had not said so, and he had not said thank you, which in their long habit of exactness was a form of understanding. He bit the sugar-cube between his front teeth and drank through it, the old way, and for a while the two of them looked at the wall.

"A man from Shiraz is selling a carpet in the lane," said Ali, "to a woman who does not want it. I can hear him from here."

"He has been selling it since morning."

"He will go on until she buys it, or one of them dies."

This was Reza Jafari, fifty-seven, trader, a man of such profound stubbornness that he had once sold a Shirazi rug to the husband of a woman who had come in to return the same rug. He had been conducting his business in the lane below the madrasa for three days, and had acquired an audience of tourists, pigeons, and two municipal inspectors. Now he stood at the foot of the scaffold, shouting up with great politeness.

"Master Ali! Madam Architect! I have heard everything!"

"You have heard *nothing,* Reza," said Parisa.

"I have heard that the pattern does not repeat, and the man must listen to each tile before he lays the next. I am a trader. Do you know what that is called in trade? It is called a *relationship.* And may I recommend, for the sake of your own *lives—*"

"Reza," said Parisa, going the colour of a pomegranate.

"—that a pattern which never repeats is the best a man can sit down to, because it is never boring, and never finished, and nobody can say you have done it *wrong.*" Reza bowed with great dignity, tripped over the carpet, and sat down in the lime.

Ali did not laugh. He turned very slowly towards her. He had not planned it; he had planned, for eight months, to say it on some day in the autumn, with proper notice and a proper bunch of flowers. But the light was going gold, and the dome behind her was the colour of a thing that does not last, and a man will be forgiven for the one sentence he has never been able to carve.

> *I have laid the same star ten thousand times,
> And every star was perfect, and was dead.
> The masters knew: one crooked tile, no more,
> Lets in the breath of someone who is living.
> You are the tile that will not lie like others.
> You turn a hair. You turn again. You fail
> To close the pattern. And I find, to my
> Considerable alarm, I would not have it
> Closed. I would rather listen all my life.*

Parisa Karimi, who restored ruins because she did not know how to restore herself, said nothing for so long that the muezzin, in some tower beyond the square, began the evening prayer. Then she took off her glove.

"My mother is in Shiraz," she said. "She prefers that a man's uncle call. With flowers. And sweets. It is a very old, very silly custom."

"I have an uncle."

"The tailor?"

"The tailor. He has been waiting for the call since I was nineteen. He has kept a suit."

"Tell him Friday," said Parisa. "Tell him to bring the *gaz.* Not the sugar one. The one with the pistachios."

"I will tell him."

"And Ali."

"Yes?"

"Do not make forty."

Below them, in the lime, Reza Jafari wept softly, and said it was the dust.

---

### SCENE II
*Baghdad. The new footbridge over the Tigris. Evening of the same week. A flock of pigeons, a ribbon, and a plaque.*

The new bridge was a thing of steel and glass and cable, and people had been walking on it since noon, to be sure it would hold.

It had been built in two halves, from either bank, as the best bridges are, so that it should meet in the middle, in the middle of the river, in the middle of the sky. The engineers had reckoned a tolerance of fifteen millimetres. When the two halves came together on the thirty-first of May, they had met with a gap of three.

"Three millimetres," said Mustafa Karim, thirty-four, civil engineer, to a crowd of two hundred and a television camera. "In a river that is a kilometre wide. I would like it noted that nobody has ever done better, and that I am not at all pleased."

There was applause. In the third row, a young woman in a long grey coat and a green scarf did not applaud. Noor Hashim, thirty, architect, ambitious, eloquent, stood with her arms folded and her eyes on the cables. She had not said a word to him in three weeks. She had also not left his side at any public function, and the two phenomena were beginning to confuse the neighbours.

The ribbon was cut. A poet named Huda Al-Saadi, twenty-five, devout and best friend of the engineer, climbed the little podium and began an ode of two hundred and eleven lines, each ending in the same rhyme, which was *Tigris.* The crowd, which had its principles and its supper, began to drift down the ramps. On the parapet a young stonemason named Shaimaa Al-Obaidi, twenty-eight, who had spent a month carving the plaque in the dry heat and was the wryest woman in Baghdad, stood with her chisel in her belt and her face turned carefully to the river.

"Shaimaa," said Mustafa. "The plaque says *Mustafa Kareem.* My name is spelled *Karim.*"

"I know how your name is spelled." Shaimaa did not turn. "I carved it correctly. Then a flake of limestone came off the *i,* and in fixing it I made it, in every sense but spelling, a *better* name. You may be wrong in the particular, Mustafa, but you are right in spirit."

"Nobody who builds a bridge," she added with great dignity, as he opened his mouth, "is *entirely* himself."

By the time the ode had reached its hundred-and-fortieth line, the footbridge was nearly empty. The lights came on along the cables, white and blue, and on the water below the long, slow lanterns of the fish-grillers began to glow along the bank, with the smell of *masgouf* and woodsmoke rising up to the rail. The heat that had stood on the city since June had finally drawn a little back; a hot wind from the desert went down the river like a hand smoothing a cloth.

In the middle of the bridge, where the two halves had met, a seam of three millimetres ran across the walkway like a very small, very polished scar. Noor was standing on it.

"You are standing on my error," said Mustafa, coming up.

"I wanted to see it."

"It is not a big error."

"It is the only thing on the whole bridge that is *honest.*" She looked at him, and then at the river. "Mustafa. I answered the university."

"I know."

"You know?"

"Huda told me. She was drunk on her own ode." He had put his hands behind his back, which is a thing an engineer does when he does not trust them. "You go in three weeks. Two years. Copenhagen. A studio on a canal. They want you to design a thing that has not been built."

"Yes."

"I am glad."

"You are not," said Noor, "glad."

"I am extremely glad, and also not glad, and I would like the two to stand on the bridge together without a fight." He drew a breath. "Noor, I wrote once that I was building this for you to come back to. I wrote it in the dark, and I should like to correct it. A bridge you can only *come back* over is not a bridge. It is a leash. I built it to go both ways. That is the engineering of it. A bridge lets you go, and lets you come, and does not mind which."

She was silent a long time. The call to prayer from a nearby mosque drew itself out over the water, and from the Rusafa bank a late firework spilled a thin red thread across the dark.

"I do not know if I will come back," said Noor, "to the city. Or to *you.* I want to be honest."

"I know that also."

"And you are not going to ask me to say."

"I am going to ask you," said Mustafa Karim, slowly, "to walk with me to the east end of the bridge, and back to the west, and then, if there is time before your tea gets cold, to the east again. And we will see how far that is. And I will not say another word about it."

Noor took her hands out of her coat pockets. She looked down at the seam. Then, carefully, she stepped across it, off the error, into the sky on the other side; and he stepped across beside her, a respectful two feet away; and they walked, without touching, the length of a bridge that did not need to be anyone's leash, and she did not say *yes,* and he did not say *wait.* It was the open sort of ending, and the Keeper, who disliked a closed door, let it be.

---

### SCENE III
*Mirpur, Dhaka. A Friday in the high monsoon. The lane under water to the ankle; the sky the colour of wet slate. A third-floor flat, a tea stall, and a parcel in brown paper tied with a string that has been to Rotterdam.*

It had arrived on a Thursday in the arms of a courier who stood at the foot of the stairs in the rain and refused to go up.

"One thousand eight hundred taka," said the courier. "Customs. For *cloth.*"

"It is a gift," said Fayaz.

"Gifts are taxed at the rate of generosity."

"That is not a rate."

"It is in the *regulations,*" said the courier, who had never read them. Fayaz Rahman, twenty-six, had in his pocket two hundred taka, and in his head the grey arithmetic of nine lakh still owing to a man his father had trusted. The Singapore contract worked him from midnight until eight, and was kind, but not that kind.

"Bhaiya," said a voice from the doorway of the tea stall, "I will lend it."

Bunny had come across the flooded lane with his trousers rolled to the knee and a tin in his hand. In the tin was the stall's takings of three days. He put it into the courier's hand without being asked. "It is a *loan,*" said Bunny, with the gravity of a banker. "At two spoons of sugar, one of condensed milk, repayable at tea."

"I cannot take your money."

"It is not *my* money. It is the *stall's* money. I am only its guardian." He looked at the parcel, and at the brown paper, and at the Dutch stamp, and at the neat handwriting, and made a judgement on it that would have done credit to a high court. "A parcel that comes from so far *behind* you, Bhaiya, should be paid for in advance."

Upstairs, in the third-floor flat, they opened it at the table. Tithi cut the string. Their mother sat with her hands in her lap, breathing carefully, on a cushion that Tithi had put there, and their father, home since June from the hospital, thinner, slower, and unusually quiet, sat in his chair by the window with a stick across his knees and watched without saying a word. On the table under the lamp lay a letter in a Dutch envelope, which Fayaz kept inside *Thinking in Systems,* and had read eleven times, and had never shown anyone.

The paper came away. Inside was a smell: wax, and woodsmoke, and indigo. Folded in the middle lay a note that said, in careful Latin letters, *Do not iron. — E.* And on the corner of the wrapping, chewed, was a single green feather.

"She says," said Tithi, looking at the note, "that you must *not iron* it."

"A cloth that cannot be ironed," said Bunny from the door, dripping, "is a cloth with a plan."

Fayaz unfolded it.

It was a great length of indigo, as deep as the river at midnight, and across the whole of it, in rows, were dots. They were black. They were so black that at first the eye took them for nothing, a shadow on the weave, a stain of some darker blue. Only when he turned the cloth to the lamp, and the light came across it at a slant, did they rise up out of the dye, one by one by one, each with five small points, each a star, each bright with the dull gloss of wax-resisted ink, like a thing you could see only at the edge of your attention. They were *bintang.* They were black. They went on to the end of the cloth.

"It is *beautiful,*" breathed Tithi.

"It is a *star-field,*" said their mother.

Their father got up. It took him a long time. He crossed the room with his stick and put out one hand and touched the cloth, as a man touches a thing he has no business touching, and held it to the window, and looked at the weave against the grey light.

"The dye is true," he said. "It does not run." And then, after a pause, to no one: "Tell her thank you."

Fayaz could not speak. Their mother, who had coughed twice and recovered, looked at him with eyes bright from the effort of looking, and asked, in the voice of a woman who has been waiting a year to ask: "This girl. The Java one. Is she kind?"

"She is," said Fayaz, "extremely punctual."

His mother laughed. It cost her a minute's breath. It was worth it.

---

At ten that night, which in Rotterdam was six, he propped the laptop on two textbooks, lit a candle in case, and pressed the green button. Behind the screen the room came into being: a long bare studio with steel windows, a harbour under cloud, a tall drying-rack hung with a dozen unfinished cloths, and a young woman with her hair pinned up by a pencil.

"You are four hours *behind* me," said Fayaz.

"I know. It is a demotion." Ermis Larasati put her chin on her fist. Her face was thinner, a little, in the Dutch light, and the tin roof of her laugh was exactly the same. "I have been looking at the clock since April. I have been awake in your yesterday for four months. It is *very* strange, Fayaz. I used to know what would happen to you. Now I must wait."

"You were never in my future. You were only an hour early."

"It is the same thing."

"It is not." He lifted a corner of the cloth to the camera. In the dark, the black stars did not show. He tilted it. They rose, one by one. "I have counted them."

"Of course you have."

"There are nine hundred and ninety-nine."

She did not answer. In the studio behind her a kettle, which was a Dutch one, began to whistle, and went on whistling, and she did not get up.

"The last is bare," said Fayaz. "In the corner. A star the shape of the others, but not dyed. Just the cloth. It is the only one you can see without the light."

"Yes."

"Is it a mistake?"

"I do not make mistakes in wax," said Ermis. "I make decisions."

"What is it for?"

"It is for when the sky is clear," she said. "I do not know what for. I only know that it is for *then.*"

For some time neither of them spoke. A tin roof, in the monsoon, in Mirpur, beat out the long drum of the rain. In Rotterdam the kettle shrieked and, at last, stopped, as a thing stops when somebody turns it off, because nobody else will.

"Fayaz," said Ermis.

"Yes."

"Do not say it."

"I was not going to."

"You were going to say that you would tell me everything, if you were free to."

"I was going to say," said Fayaz, "that you were kind."

It was not what she had expected. He saw it in her face. She had been braced, as people are, for the thing that has no name. And what he had given her was the other thing: the sentence she had once handed to him on the other end of a candle, and which he had been carrying since, folded very small, inside a book.

"I have seen it," he said. "I am four hours ahead of you tonight, and in that time I have already lived this Friday, and I can report that it was *very* good, and that you were kind in it. The studio, the harbour, the kettle. You were kind." He stopped, because his voice had done the thing it did when she laughed, only the other way. "I thought you ought to hear it from the future."

Ermis said nothing at all. She put her hand over her mouth. On the screen, the pencil in her hair slid, and her hair came down, and behind her, in the grey Dutch window, a gull went by like a thrown stone. At last she took her hand away and said, in a small and entirely ordinary voice: "It is the first thing anyone has told me from the future that I wanted to hear."

"Then I will tell you more next week."

"Fridays."

"Fridays," said Fayaz. "Ten, mine. Six, yours."

"I am *not* going to say *eleven,*" said Ermis, and wept, and was laughing in the same breath, so that the whole feeble connection shook.

---

When she had gone he did not sleep. The power failed at midnight, and he lit the candle, and laid the cloth across his knees; and being a man who could not leave a question alone, he began, with a pencil and the back of an old bill from the electricity board, to measure it.

It took him till two. The stars were in rows; he had known that. But the rows were not level. Each lay, by the smallest degree, at a different angle from the row above, so that the whole cloth, from first row to last, was twisted by one steady turn. He drew it, and drew it again, and worked out the angle. It came to fifteen degrees, to the width of a thread.

He sat very still with the pencil in his hand.

Fifteen degrees. It is what the sky turns, in one hour.

Outside, the rain was slackening. Somewhere in the lane a boy was singing a song from a film, with the wrong words. The candle burned straight. And in a rented flat on the third floor, a man with an ironed shirt and nine lakh of debt held a cloth made of nine hundred and ninety-nine black stars and one clear space, and thought, as a man does who has been given a very long sentence in a very small hand, that it would take him a lifetime to finish reading it, and that he had, he found, no objection at all.

---

>
> *Entry 0076 and Entry 0165. A bridge goes both ways. That is the only reason it was built.*
>
> *Entry 0713 and Entry 0714. Nine hundred and ninety-nine. The thousandth is a place kept. I know something about those. I have kept one myself.*

## Chapter 48
### The Fish Market Fire

> *"I may have started the fire with one cigarette."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0316

---

### SCENE I
*Marseille. The quay of the Old Port at six in the morning, the day after the worst night in the history of the fish market. Smoke, steam, and ten thousand gulls, all of whom feel personally addressed.*

There is nothing so ridiculous, or so sad, as a fire in a fish market.

It is a place built entirely of ice and water. Every stall has its tank, every table its drain, every crate its little coffin of crushed cold. And yet, at ten to four in the morning, with the mistral blowing down the quay like a drunk with a grudge, the polystyrene boxes at the north wall had caught, and the whole thing had gone up in nine minutes, and the fire brigade, arriving to find that it had been put out chiefly by its own stock, had been obliged to stand in a lake of sea bass with their hoses idle and their dignity at about knee level.

Nobody was hurt. That was the miracle, and the one thing that nobody in Marseille knew how to say, because every one of them was too busy telling everybody else what had caused it.

"Electrical," announced Mathieu Vidal, fifty-eight, librarian, who classified scandal as he classified books, by subject, author, and date, and who had been at the barrier since half past four with a notebook. "A short in the compressor of the number six freezer. I had it from the *fireman's cousin.*"

"It was the mistral," said a fishwife.

"It was the *Spanish*," said another. "Who were in bed. Which is exactly what they *wanted* us to think."

In the middle of the blackened aisle, in what had been, till midnight, the stall called *La Daurade Joyeuse,* stood Hugo Martin. He was thirty-five, built like a door, and he was laughing. He had been laughing since five o'clock. The stall was a skeleton of tin; the awning was a blackened sail; the family scales, three generations old, had melted into a small bronze puddle on the slab. And Hugo Martin, fish seller, boisterous, loyal, loud enough to be heard from the Panier to the Prado, stood in the wet ash in rubber boots with his arms spread wide and announced, to a quay of staring people, that the first round of pastis was on the house.

"At six in the morning?" said a policeman.

"A fire is a *festival,* monsieur! Nobody died! The fish went out *gloriously!*"

There is a kind of laughter that is a shout, and a kind that is a shield. Only the second cannot be turned off. At the barrier at the end of the aisle, in the navy jersey and cap of the Old Port ferry, a woman stood very still with her hands in her pockets and did not laugh at all.

Camille Bernard was thirty-three, a ferry pilot, calm and dry as a biscuit, and she had piloted the little boat that crosses the harbour from the Town Hall quay to the Place aux Huiles every day for nine years without once being rattled by weather, or tourists, or the Marseillais. She was not rattled now. She was stone. At ten to four that morning she had been standing at the north wall of the market, in the dark, waiting for the five o'clock crossing, with a cigarette between her fingers that she had told every person she knew, in March, she would never touch again.

She had not seen where it fell.

"Madame Bernard," said a young inspector, taking off his cap. "I understand you were on the quay."

"I am always on the quay. I drive a ferry."

"Did you see anything? Smell smoke?"

She thought of the red dot, small as a seed, going out over the dark water on the edge of the wind. She thought, *I looked. I looked at the water.*

"I don't recall," said Camille Bernard.

Behind her, with a hose coiled round one shoulder like a sea-serpent and a wrench in each pocket, came Colette Lefèvre, thirty-one, plumber, a woman so patient that fishermen came to her to be taught to wait. She had been called in at dawn to inspect the water-mains and had spent the morning defending them from accusation.

"It was not the pipes," said Colette to the inspector, with immense gentleness. "A fire is only a pipe whose water has gone the wrong way. It wants to be somewhere. Tell me where it wanted to be, and I will tell you why it left." She turned, and her eyes, which were kind and slow, rested a moment on Camille's pale face, and she added, to nobody, in the voice of one remarking on the weather: "Funny how often it is a small thing. A washer. A spark. A bit of cold. A little cigarette."

Camille went the colour of the ash.

"What did you say?" said the inspector.

"Nothing," said Colette placidly. "I said it is going to rain."

---

### SCENE II
*The following night. The burnt market, under a clean sharp moon and a ribbon of police tape. The wind has dropped. The smell is smoke, salt and wet char. A single stall light, run off a car battery, shows a broad man sitting on an upturned crate.*

He had sent them all home. That was the mark of Hugo: at midnight he had given every fish-wife a hug and every fireman a bass, and told the crowd to go to bed, and then he had sat down alone in the ruin and stopped smiling, like a man putting down a very heavy sack he has been carrying for a mile uphill.

He spoke to the dark, as the cheerful do, when nobody is in a position to be cheered:

> *They said I laughed. I did. The way you laugh
> When someone's handed you a thing too large
> To hold in just one pair of hands, so you
> Hold up the other side with joking. Father,
> This was your stall, and his, and his before.
> I took it with the scales; I took the name.
> I never learned to lose a thing. I learned
> To make the losing sound like a good story,
> And put the story on the slab, and sell it.
> Tonight I have no story. I have ash.
> If someone came now, quiet, with no joke,
> And sat beside me while the ash went cold,
> I think I'd tell them how it really was:
> I smiled so none should see me not know how.*

"I have brought coffee," said a voice at the tape.

He did not jump. He knew the voice; he had known it for nine years, across a stretch of green water, in every weather. She ducked under the ribbon and came across the wet floor with two paper cups, and put one into his hand, and sat down beside him on a second crate, not close, not far, as a ferry lies against a quay.

"It is terrible coffee," said Camille.

"It is the best I have had all day."

"That is not the praise you think."

He laughed, and it was a real laugh this time, small and cracked, and neither of them said anything for a while. A gull walked the length of the ruined slab and inspected the ash for unreasonable hopes. Across the black water the lights of Notre-Dame de la Garde burned on her hill, small and gold, like a stub of candle somebody had set on a very high shelf.

"You didn't laugh this morning," said Hugo.

"No."

"Everybody else did. They think I'm mad. I let them. It is easier."

"I know." She turned the cup in her hands. "That's why I came. I have been sitting in my kitchen since noon trying to think of a way to say it that was better than the way I'm going to say it, and there is none, so I will say it the poor way. Hugo, there is something I must tell you. About the night of the fire."

He went very still.

"I told you in March that I had stopped smoking," said Camille. "I said it on the quay. You were selling oysters. You said, *Good, a woman who can stop a thing can stop a boat,* and I was—I was so pleased, Hugo, I have never been so pleased by a thing a man said to me about boats." She breathed in. "I hadn't stopped. I had told everyone I had, because I wanted it to be true, and it is very easy to tell people things you want. On Tuesday night I was on the quay at ten to four. By your north wall. I was waiting for the first crossing. And I had one. It was the last one in the packet. I stood there in the wind, with my back to your stall, and I smoked it, and when the wind came round I

*Here the page is torn.*

---

### SCENE III
*Buenos Aires. La Boca, in the damp middle of July, which here is the middle of winter. A social club of corrugated tin painted the colours of a parrot's wing; a wooden floor worn pale by sixty years of shoes; and a hall full of people who have all agreed not to look at the dance floor.*

It was the night of the anniversary, and no one was dancing.

In Buenos Aires a milonga has laws more binding than any parliament's. The men sit on one side of the hall, the women on the other. A man who wishes to dance does not cross the floor. He looks. He catches the eye of the woman he wants, and nods, once, the smallest of nods, and if she nods back, he comes; and if she looks at her shoes, he has been refused, and nobody in the hall has seen a thing. It is called the *cabeceo.* It is the most merciful form of rejection ever devised by the human race.

Mateo Fernández, thirty-five, tango dancer, arrogant and graceful, had sat on the men's side since nine o'clock. For a year he had danced with nobody. He had danced alone in the dark of his flat with a chair, and at the corner of a rehearsal studio with a mirror, and once, in a moment he did not care to remember, with a coat-stand. But on the floor of a milonga, among the living, he had not taken a woman in his arms since the night his partner died.

"You are staring at the ceiling," said Ramiro Romero, sixty-seven, retired choir director, blunt as a brick and the evening's DJ, from the tiny booth behind the bar.

"I'm resting."

"You are resting with your whole *face.* She is over there. She has been looking at you since the second tanda." He put on the next record. "I choose the music for this room, Mateo, and I will tell you what I have chosen: three tangos and a waltz and a cortina. After the cortina, it is the last tanda. I have put in the one you used to dance to. And I have put it *last.*"

"You are cruel."

"I am a choirmaster. We believe in resolution."

On the opposite wall, in a black dress with a plain neckline and her hair drawn back like a closed fan, sat Valentina Cruz, thirty-three, tango teacher, proud and guarded, with her hands folded in her lap. She had taught him for a year. She had taught him to lead, in a studio where the sunlight came in at an angle, and she had hated every minute of it, and she had not missed a lesson. She did not look at him. She looked, instead, with great care, at an old woman in the corner who had begun, quite without hurry, to pour mate from a thermos into a gourd.

This was Agustina Benítez, fifty-four, a tea-seller from Rosario who had come three hours by bus because someone ought to. She was gentle, rather deaf, and believed the temperature of water to be the foundation of civilisation.

"It is too hot," said Agustina, to nobody, tasting. "Water at the boil is a *scream.* A person is not scalded into a conversation. A person is *coaxed.*" She held out the gourd to Valentina, without looking at her. "Take it."

"I don't want any, Señora."

"It is not for wanting. It is for holding. A woman who is holding something is a woman who does not have to hold *herself.*"

And then, from the bench beside Valentina, came a dry old voice. Julieta Romero, eighty, retired ferry hand, who had worked the river-boats of the Riachuelo for forty years and was said to have known every secret that ever crossed it, put a small brown hand over Valentina's.

"I took them across," said Julieta. "Your sister and him. Twice a week, when they were poor. They danced on the deck. Nobody asked them to; they did it as other people breathe." Her eyes, pale with age, did not leave the floor. "She told me on that boat, the last summer. She said, *Julieta, if I go first, make him dance.*"

Valentina did not move.

"I have not told you," said Julieta, "because I thought you hated him. And then I thought: she is jealous, and that is not hate; it is only love that has been left in the rain." She patted the hand. "I took the blame once for a thing you did. A broken window. You were seven. It is the only lie I have told in my life. I should like to tell a second, to say that I did not hear her say it. But I did, child. I did."

In the corner a girl of fourteen, small and suspicious, in school shoes, who had come in from the street to watch the dancers and had not been told to leave, said, quite clearly, in the hush: "Why doesn't one of them just *nod?*"

It was Lucrecia Medina, from the next block. Nobody answered her.

The cortina came on, a thin sweet curtain of music between one set and the next, and the floor, which had been empty, emptied still further.

Mateo stood. He crossed nothing; he did not walk. He lifted his eyes, across thirty feet of polished wood, and in front of the whole hall, and the DJ, and the old women, and the girl in school shoes, and a dead woman's ghost who had come, perhaps, in the mate-steam, he nodded.

Valentina looked at her shoes.

For one long second the hall stopped breathing. Then Valentina Cruz, who had been taught from the age of six that a woman refused is a woman with her dignity intact, and a woman who accepts has surrendered something she can never get back, set down the mate-gourd, and raised her head, and nodded.

They met in the middle of the floor. They did not smile. He lifted his arm and she settled into it, the way a thing slips into the place it was always cut for, and the old record began, the one he used to dance to, a slow tango, with a bandoneon that breathed in and out like an animal that had been asleep; and they walked.

Mark this, reader: they did not dance *well.* That is the thing the Keeper would have you know. He was stiff. She was angry. Every step was a negotiation. For the first minute there were two of them and a ghost, and for the second minute there were two of them, and the ghost was only a shape of warmth at the edge of the lamp; and by the third there was only a man and a woman crossing a floor, and the dead sister's name unspoken between them like a hand resting lightly on each of their backs. *Go,* it said. *Go on.*

The last tango ended. The cortina began. The floor, by every law of the milonga, cleared. The couples drifted away to their sides, and the men sat down and the women sat down, and Ramiro in his booth, with tears running down into his collar, put on the next tanda and did not need to.

Valentina and Mateo stood alone in the centre of the floor, in the cortina, which is the law of leaving, and did not leave. A man and a woman who stay on the floor after the curtain have declared a thing before the whole room. They stood there with her hand in his, and the music went on, thin and sweet and unfinished, and neither of them moved toward either wall.

"The girl is right," said Valentina, very quietly. "I should have nodded first."

"You are not supposed to nod first."

"I am a teacher. I have been breaking the rules for years." She looked up at him. "Mateo. Is this a thing that you can do?"

"I do not know," said Mateo. "Ask me after the next song."

"And the one after that?"

"And the one after that."

On the side wall, a girl of fourteen sniffed and said, with unconcealed superiority, "*Finally.*"

---

### SCENE IV
*New Delhi Railway Station. Platform Six. The tail of the monsoon, at twenty to six in the evening. Every train on the northern line has been halted by the flooding of the Yamuna, and the platform is crowded with the stranded, the sleeping, the praying, and a very great number of sweets.*

In nineteen years of driving trains, Ravi Chaudhary had never been late.

It was his only vanity. He was forty-one, a train driver, punctual and patient, a man who could tell a delay by the hum of the rails; and tonight, for the first time in all those years, he had nowhere to be. The Lucknow line was shut. The river had risen over the tracks at the bridge, and the 5:40 stood on Platform Six with its engine ticking as it cooled, and its driver, in his cap and his blue jacket, had stepped down from the cab and begun, for the first time in his life, to walk the whole length of the train.

At the far end of the platform, on the bench under the pillar, as she had been every evening for eleven years, sat Sunita Verma.

She was thirty-nine, a teacher, wry, resolute, with a cloth bag of exercise books on her knee and a tiffin carrier at her feet, and she did not look up as he came. She had learned, in eleven years, never to look up. It was a kind of discipline. The 5:40 went through Platform Six twice a day, and each time, as it passed her bench, the driver sounded his horn twice. It was not necessary. It was not in the regulations. It was a sort of sentence in a language that had two words and no grammar.

"You have stopped," said Sunita.

"The signal is red."

"It was green for eleven years."

"It was," said Ravi gravely, "a very reliable signal."

On the next bench an old woman, eighty-eight, in a faded cardigan, with a camera round her neck older than most of the trains, lifted her head from her chin. This was Neha Mehra, retired photographer, who had been taking one photograph a day of Platform Six for sixty years, and who now, with the air of a connoisseur, raised the camera to her eye.

"Don't mind me," said Neha. "I am furniture."

Beside her, wedged between a family of nine and a man asleep on his luggage, sat a plump young woman from Jaipur surrounded by forty tin trays. Pooja Singh, thirty-four, a baker, generous, had been on her way to a wedding in Lucknow with three hundred jalebis, and had now, in the course of a six-hour wait, given away two hundred and ninety, including a number to a policeman, who had accepted them under protest.

"Take one!" said Pooja Singh, thrusting a tray at the driver. "The syrup is melting. A jalebi that is not eaten is a tragedy, and I have been very sad all day."

"I cannot. I am on duty."

"You are on a platform in a flood, sir. The only duty you have is to be *sweet.*"

He took one, a small gold spiral, dripping. Sunita took one too, because it would have been ridiculous not to, and the two of them stood and ate in silence, before a camera and a baker and an audience of nine.

"I have a question," said Sunita, at last, licking her thumb. "I have had it for eleven years."

"Ask it."

"Why twice?"

"Twice?"

"The horn. Two blasts. Why not one? Why not three?"

Ravi Chaudhary, driver of the 5:40 to Lucknow, took off his cap. He turned it round, once, in his hands.

"One is a warning," he said. "Three is an emergency. Two is—" He looked for the word and found only the true one. "Two is *hello.* It is what a man says when he cannot stop the train."

"And now that you have?"

"Now it is the wrong number," said Ravi. "I will have to think of another."

Sunita, who had spent eleven years teaching children that there is no such thing as an impossible sum, set down her bag. "Sit," she said. "The bench is long."

"I am in uniform."

"The bench," said Sunita Verma, "does not care."

He sat. A respectful two feet of wood lay between them, and a third of a jalebi, and eleven years of platform. On the far bench, Neha Mehra took her photograph, and was heard to say softly, "*That's* the one." The rain, which had never entirely stopped since July, began again, drumming upon the great arched roof of the station like ten thousand patient fingers; and in a signal-box a mile away a man who had worked the points for forty years looked at a red light and, for reasons he could not have explained, decided to leave it red for a little longer.

# ACT V — THE TEMPEST CLEARS

### *The Chorus*

The storm is spent; the sea lies glass and grey,
And one by one the ships come home to shore;
What burned is ash, what drowned is borne away,
And what was owed is paid, and owed no more.
Now open every letter ever kept,
Now speak the word that waited, locked and still,
For here are those who laughed, and those who wept,
And those who learned at last to bend their will.
Look up: the dark is full of unseen light;
Each hidden star hath held its steadfast place;
And one, the thousandth, burning out of sight,
Was lit for you, and keeps you in its grace.
So close the book, but leave the window wide:
The dark is not a wall; it is a guide.
