## Chapter 58
### Ten Thousand Miles of Wifi

> *"My family is still there. I cannot settle until they are here."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0680

---

*Enter the Chorus, with a cable over one shoulder, like a man about to hang a picture of the sea.*

> Ten thousand miles of cable in the deep
> Now carry, at the speed of light, a word;
> Yet who was ever fed, or helped to sleep,
> By something only sent, and only heard?
> Tonight we ride the wire from shore to shore
> To hear a dozen lovers say, "I'm here,"
> And two who say it slant, and wish for more,
> And do not say it yet. Lean closer, dear.

---

### SCENE I
*Toronto. Pearson Airport, arrivals hall, 6:40 in the morning. A great many balloons.*

Idris Hakimi, twenty-seven, engineer, had once built a bridge over a river in a country he could not name without his throat doing something complicated, and he had never in his life been so afraid of a set of sliding doors.

"They are late," he said.

"They are on the ground," said Fatima Noori, twenty-five, nursing student, who had checked the board eleven times. "Customs takes an hour. It is the law of customs."

"It has been three years."

"Then an hour," said Fatima, "is a rounding error."

It had been three years, nine offices, two sponsors, a lawyer who had cried once at a hearing and apologised for it, and a file that had at one stage been mislaid on a Tuesday. His mother and his sister were in that building somewhere, in a line, holding two bags and a bundle of bread wrapped in cloth, and he had not slept since the call from Frankfurt.

Behind them, a voice rose, unsteady with joy and helium.

"*Idris bhai! The balloons!*"

Najib Sultani, twenty-five, writer, devout, and the most generous man in Scarborough with other people's money, came through the crowd with a sign in one hand and fourteen balloons in the other. The sign read WELCOME TO CANADA, HAKEEMY FAMILY. The balloons read, in curly silver, CONGRATULATIONS ON YOUR NEW BABY.

"Najib."

"They had a sale."

"Najib, we do not have a new baby."

"*They* do not know that," said Najib, with great logic. "And also they were from the baby shower, and the baby shower was in the next hall, and the supermarket was closed, and it is clearly the will of God that these balloons find a home. I used your card. I will repay you in the next book."

"You have never repaid me in the last book."

"It is a long book."

Fatima, who was shaking, laughed, and put her hand over her mouth; and the doors slid back, and out of them, pushing a trolley with a bundle in a cloth, walked a small woman in a grey headscarf and a long coat, and beside her a girl of fifteen with enormous eyes, who looked at the balloons, and the sign, and the ceiling, and the enormous gleaming country behind the glass, and said, in Dari, "Madar-jan, it is very *clean.*"

Idris did not run. He was an engineer; he walked the whole distance, at a steady load-bearing pace, and when he reached his mother he said, as he had rehearsed on the plane, "*Salaam, Madar-jan,*" and then said nothing else, for there was nothing in the engineering of language that would hold.

She put both hands on his face. She looked at it as one looks at a bridge one has been told has been rebuilt, and has not quite believed.

Then Fatima stepped forward.

She had rehearsed it for two years, on the bus, in the bath, once in a hospital cafeteria at four in the morning with a patient's grandfather correcting her vowels. Her parents had come from Herat, but they had raised her in kitchen Dari, a Dari for salt and bread and *wash your hands,* and she had needed more: a Dari for this.

"*Madar-jan,*" said Fatima, slowly, setting each word down like a cup on a tray. "*Khosh āmadid.*"

*Welcome.* Then, in the same careful hand, a second sentence, longer, in a language that had taken her two winters to learn, and which the page, for once, will not translate, except to say that it was about how a person does not have to be carried alone any more. Idris stood very still beside her; for the first time in his life he did not translate; he could not have.

The old woman said nothing. She took Fatima's face in both hands, as she had taken her son's, and kissed her once on the forehead, and began, without any dignity at all, to weep. Beside her, the girl said, in English, "Is that a *baby* balloon?"

"It is a mistake," said Najib, "that has become a blessing."

*Mark this, reader. A man may be ten thousand miles from his mother and three years from his promise, and then a pair of doors will open, and the arithmetic will be, for once, kind.*

---

### SCENE II
*Lyon. A bakery and a florist's, side by side, with a new door cut through the wall between them. Sunday, five in the morning.*

Pierre Dubois, forty-five, baker, gruff, stooped, and a widower of eight years' standing, stood at the oven in a floury apron and lifted out two loaves.

The first was his wife's: round, dark, dusted, scored with a cross. He had baked it every Sunday for eight years, and it was the best bread in the arrondissement, and he had never once sold it.

The second was new. It was scored not with a cross but with a spray of small curved cuts, like a handful of violets thrown at a wall.

"It is crooked," said Mathieu Lefèvre, the clockmender, fifty-nine, from the doorway. He had come to oil the shop clock and had stayed, as he always stayed, for the free bread and the pleasure of being slightly wrong. "A baker's loaf should not look like a *mistake.*"

"It looks like violets."

"Which is a mistake in a loaf." Mathieu consulted his watch. "It is ten past five. No. Twenty to six. No— I believe the clock above your door is correct and my watch is a liar. Pierre. Why have you cut a door in your wall?"

"For the draught."

"You have cut a door in a wall for a draught."

"It is a *very* specific draught," said Pierre, and went through the door.

On the other side, in the dark among the buckets, stood Margaux Laurent, forty-two, florist, widow, with her sleeves rolled and a bunch of violets in her hand. She had been leaving flowers at his door for three years. Nobody was supposed to know. All of Lyon knew.

He set the loaf on her counter. He did not say anything. His hands, which were large and white with flour, were shaking, and she looked at them with the gentlest irony in France.

"It was always me," said Pierre at last, hoarsely. "The bread. On your step. Every week, when you thought it was the neighbour's boy. I could not put a note in it. A note is a thing that can be read."

"I know."

"You *know*?"

"The neighbour's boy cannot bake," said Margaux. "He has been to my kitchen. He has burned a salad."

He laughed, a sound like a heavy door on a good hinge. She put the violets in his hand, and took the loaf in hers, and they stood in the dark and held each other's offerings like two people exchanging coats on a cold platform.

Behind them, in the bakery, Mathieu's clock struck, thirteen times, and was never repaired.

---

### SCENE III
*Mirpur, Dhaka. The tea stall at the corner of the lane, a Friday, nine-fifteen at night. It does not rain. The lane has electricity. Everyone is slightly alarmed.*

"Bhaiya," said Bunny, who was fourteen now, and had been promoted from the kettle to the cash drawer, and from opinion to policy, "you have been looking at your phone for six minutes without drinking your tea."

"It is a thread. From the Register." Fayaz Rahman, twenty-seven, looked up. He had on the good shirt, ironed, and the look of a man who has for twelve months been rather more afraid of good news than of bad. "Nadeesha started it. *One year. Say where you are.* There are four hundred replies."

"Read me one."

"*Youssef, Casablanca,*" read Fayaz. "*I read this whole page myself. It took eleven minutes. Salma timed me. She says the next one may take ten.*"

"Good. Another."

"*Dr. Nusrat, Sylhet. The new autoclave is a marvel. Rahim bhai says that is because it has never met the district.*"

"I like him. He is from Chittagong?"

"He is a foreman."

"Same thing. Another."

"*Dewi, Ubud,*" read Fayaz. "*For my cousin in Rotterdam: your grandmother says Ayu has learned a new word and will not tell me which. I have my suspicions. Putu says I am not to say. I am not saying.*"

Bunny wiped the counter, which did not need it. "Bhaiya. In Rotterdam it is five hours behind us."

"You have looked it up."

"I look up everything. Last year she was one hour in front of you. Now she is five behind. At this rate, by next year she will be in yesterday and you will be in Tuesday and the only place you can meet is in the middle of the sea."

Fayaz opened his mouth, and shut it, with the face of a man who has been handed an important parcel by a child.

"That," he said, "is not very far from geographically accurate."

"I know," said Bunny, with immense dignity. "I read the map."

---

### SCENE IV
*The flat, third floor. A desk, a lamp, an Instant Power Supply the size of a small coffin, humming. On the wall above the desk, hung with four pins and tremendous care, a long cloth of dark indigo covered in black stars.*

At 9:58 by his clock, which was now correct to the second, since a man with a contract keeps the time he is paid by, Fayaz sat down and pressed the green button.

He had a contract. He wished, he found, to say it often, as one says the name of a new town. Not the night-work for the agency in Singapore, which had been a rope thrown across a river; but a contract in his own name, with a logistics firm, for the building of a system that would track containers across half the world, and a day-time salary in a currency that was, in the language of his old arrangements, *kind.* On the balcony, his father sat with the green ledger on his knee, as he had every night since the spring, and with a steel ruler and a pencil, and on the first of each month he drew a neat line through a number. There were four numbers left. They were large. They were visible, which was a different thing from large.

The Wi-Fi was called BINTANG_HITAM. Tithi had named it, and refused to rename it, on the ground that it was the only thing in the house that never dropped.

The screen woke.

It was a studio. Tall windows, the dark coming down on a wet grey city at five o'clock in the afternoon, a long table, a steaming iron, a copper canting in a brass dish, pinned cloths in rust and indigo and a white so pale it seemed to be thinking. On the wall, over the table, hung a clock whose hands said eleven.

"It is five o'clock in Rotterdam," said Fayaz.

"On Fridays," said Ermis Larasati, twenty-five now, indigo on both cheekbones and a pencil in her hair, "Rotterdam is a province of Java. I have told them the clock is broken. They find me charming and a little ill."

"You have kept it for six months."

"I have kept it for every Friday. You said *ten, yours; eleven, mine.* You did not say whose clock." She smiled. "You have a generator!"

"I have an IPS."

"It is a *generator.*"

"It is, on the right circuit," said Fayaz, "and I would like it recorded that no one was more surprised than me."

They looked at each other. A year of Fridays, he thought, is not a year of looking: it is a year of looking *at.*

"Show me," said Ermis.

He turned the laptop. She leaned toward it, the way one leans toward a small window in a very large wall, and took in the long cloth on the wall of the Dhaka flat: *Bintang Hitam,* a field of black dots on indigo, the pattern she had drawn for him in the spring.

"Tithi counted the dots," said Fayaz, "and gave up at four hundred and some. She says a pattern that wants to be counted is flirting."

"Tithi is a very dangerous girl."

"She has just been admitted to the university."

"I *know.* She told me. She told me *first.*" Ermis laughed, and her eyes were bright. "Fayaz. It is finished. Mine. The big one. It goes on the wall tomorrow."

She turned a second camera, and the screen showed a cloth three metres long, hung from the beams, in two halves. The left half was night: deep indigo, a single white star, small as a pin. The right half was dawn: the palest blue, and in the middle of it, one black star.

"*Selisih,*" said Ermis. "It means the difference. As in, *the difference between two clocks.* The director asked me what it meant and I said *an hour.* She said it was a very expensive hour. I said that is how they come."

"It is beautiful."

"I am going to cut it in half."

"You are *what?*"

"It is made to be two," said Ermis. "I have always known. I have not decided which half will be whose." She looked into the camera. "I will decide when I can see."

Something small rang in the room behind her: a phone, propped against a jar, playing a message. A voice that had been compressed through three networks and a grandmother's thumb shrieked into the studio:

"*TOO LATE! TOO LATE! FAYYAAS! BEAUTIFUL!*"

There was a very long silence.

"She learned my *name*?" said Fayaz.

"She learned it," said Ermis, in a voice of ruined dignity, "from my grandmother. Who learned it from me. Who said it, very *occasionally,* in the kitchen, to a *saucepan.*"

"She has put it in the right order."

"She says it to *everyone.*"

"She said it to me *first.*"

"Fayaz—"

"I have no complaints," said Fayaz, with the gravity of a judge who is also laughing. "I wish only to record it."

She put her face in both hands. When she took them away her cheeks had a third stripe of blue, and her mouth was trembling, not from sorrow.

"All right," said Ermis. "Now. Serious. The thing we have not said in a year. I want us to say it."

"Which thing?"

"*When.*"

He had known it was coming. He had known it for a year, as one knows the date of one's own exam; and he had come to the screen with a plan, three contingencies and a spreadsheet, and found them all, in the face of that small lit window, perfectly useless.

"I cannot say a date," said Fayaz, slowly. "My debt is four lakh from clear, and four lakh is very near, and very far. My mother's treatment has its second phase. My father is better, and I do not wish to leave while he is learning to be." He took a breath. "You have the lab until March. And a second year, if you take it. And after that the world has asked for you."

"I know."

"I would not hold a date over your head like a wet cloth."

"Nor I over yours." She picked up the canting, put it down. "So no date. I do not want a date. A date is a promise with a lid on it. I want something *looser.*"

"When both our skies are clear," said Fayaz.

The pencil in her hair slid and fell. She did not move.

"Say that again."

"When both our skies are clear. Not before. Not by plan. The way a tide comes." He smiled, a little crookedly. "I think it was something I took from my Keeper."

"Where?" said Ermis.

"*Where* is the question." He pulled up a map on the second screen, because he was, after all, a man who built systems. "Dhaka to Yogyakarta, by line, is four thousand kilometres. You cannot come here, with Rotterdam, and I cannot go there, with the embassies as they are, so we need a place *between.* Halfway. I have measured. A few hundred kilometres of unfairness in my favour. I will carry the bags." He turned the screen. "Bunny says we shall meet in the middle of the sea. I have looked for the least wet place."

The map showed the long green leg of the Malay peninsula, and, hanging off it into the blue like a pendant on a thread, an island.

"*Phuket,*" said Ermis.

"It is in the Andaman Sea."

"It is in *Thailand,* Fayaz. Thailand has a flag."

"The beach does not."

"Beaches do not have *visas.*"

"Exactly," said Fayaz. "It is halfway. It is where no flag stands. I will bring a passport that has been renewed, which in Dhaka is a pilgrimage in itself. And I will not be sick on the ferry."

"It is on my time," said Ermis, who had begun to laugh and cry in the same breath, which in a designer is called *registration.* "Phuket is on the Java hour. You will have to put your watch forward."

"I know."

"You will be in *my hour.*"

"For once," said Fayaz, "neither of us will be ahead."

She stopped laughing. In the window, her face had gone very still, and very soft, and she looked just then like the girl in the workshop in a pale first morning, with her sentence on a page, and no one to say it to.

"Then I will tell you what I will do," said Ermis. "In the spring I said that I was an hour ahead of you. Now I am five hours behind you, and it is the first time in my life that I have been behind anyone and not minded." She leaned on one hand. "From where I sit, you are in my future. Tell me what you see."

"Ermis—"

"Tell me. I saw yours, once. It is only fair."

Fayaz looked at the cloth on his wall, and at his father on the balcony, drawing a line through a number with a steel ruler, and at the lit window with the pencil-haired woman in it, five hours back in the day and a year forward in everything else.

"I see a beach," he said slowly. "I see two people who are very bad at beginning a sentence. And one of them says, *I would tell you everything.*" He breathed. "And the other waits for the *if* — and there is no *if.*"

There was a very long quiet. Rain on the Rotterdam windows. A kettle on the Dhaka stove. A parrot, in a recording, three thousand miles away, saying nothing at all, for once, as though she had understood the occasion.

"Be on time," said Ermis, finally, in a voice that was not entirely steady.

"I have never been late."

"Last Friday you were four minutes late."

"It was the *router.*"

"It was four minutes."

"By *four* minutes," said Fayaz. "A very small error, very consistently made."

She laughed, and he laughed, and the Wi-Fi, which never dropped, held them both across five time zones and ten thousand miles of cable on the floor of the sea.

"Good night," said Ermis. "Or good afternoon."

"Whichever of us is right."

She reached to end the call; and did not, quite, and he did not either; and the screen held the two of them, looking.

> *Fayaz is typing…*
>
> *Ermis is typing…*

Two sets of dots rose in two windows, five hours apart, and sank, and rose again, like two hearts in a pretended calm.

Neither of them sent.

---

*Margin note, in pencil, in the hand of S.W.R., beside Entries 0713 and 0714:*

> *One year. The debt is not paid; the work is not done. But a clock has been chosen, and it is neither of theirs, and I find that this is the correct beginning for a meeting.*
>
> *Entry 0680 and Entry 0332: a language learned in order to say a short thing well. Entry 0844 and Entry 0908: bread and violets, through a door cut for a draught.*
>
> *Observe the dots, reader. The ledger records them. It records, too, that the sending is not the sentence. The sentence is what they carry to the beach.*

---

*End of Chapter 58.*


---

## Chapter 59
### The Last Postman of Cornwall

> *"There are forty letters I never delivered."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 0266

---

**Penhallow Cove, Cornwall. 6:10 a.m. The last Saturday of October.**

The sub-post-office at Penhallow had a counter, a scale, a stamp machine that spoke only in Cornish grunts, and Mrs. Trelawny, who had the ears of a bat and the discretion of a church bell.

"It is a disgrace," said Mrs. Trelawny, to the empty shop, which agreed with her. "Forty-five years. Forty-five years the man has walked that round, in hail and fog and the great snow of eighty-seven, and now they will send a van from Truro with a boy in it who cannot tell a Trevithick from a Tregenza. *And* they are shutting the counter. By the New Year I shall be selling stamps from a *bucket.*"

"Morning, Ruth," said Harry Whitcombe.

He stood in the doorway in the red jacket he had worn for forty-five years, with the bag across his chest and a shortbread tin under his arm. The tin was tartan, dented, decorated with a Highland cow whose expression had worn thin from handling.

Harry was seventy, with the stoop of a man who has been bowing to letterboxes since the days of decimalisation, a face as creased and kind as a well-used envelope, and the largest store of other people's secrets in the county, which he had never, in all his years, spent.

"Last round, Harry," said Mrs. Trelawny, with tears in her eyes and a saffron bun in her fist. "Eat. You will need it."

"Thank you, Ruth."

"What's in the tin?"

"Biscuits."

"It does not rattle like biscuits."

"It is a very quiet biscuit."

"I have known you since you were twenty-five," said Mrs. Trelawny, "and in forty-five years you have never carried a tin. You have carried a *face.* That tin is *something.*" She leaned across the counter, with the entire small village behind her eyes. "Harry Whitcombe. Is it a *woman?*"

"It is," said Harry, going red from the collar up, "a matter for the Royal Mail."

"Which is no longer in this building," said Mrs. Trelawny, with satisfaction, and handed him the sorting list, and a second bun.

---

**The round.**

It was a morning of the colour of slate. The lanes of Penhallow ran down the hill to the harbour like loose threads, and Harry walked them, as he had walked them for forty-five years, in a particular rhythm that his feet knew and he did not, letterbox, gate, step, letterbox, until it felt less like a job than a prayer in a language of doors.

At Trevean Farm, a collie came round the barn at a low run, with his ears flat and the light of an old and sacred purpose in his eye.

"Not today, Boscawen," said Harry. "It is my last."

The dog, the fourth Boscawen of that name, who had inherited from his father, his grandfather and his great-grandfather a settled determination to bite the left cuff of the postman's trousers every Tuesday and most Saturdays, paused, consulted his conscience, and bit it.

"Thank you," said Harry. "I would have been disappointed."

At Mrs. Penhale's he left a catalogue of seeds, at the fishmonger's, Tamsin Trevithick, a postcard from her sister in Perth, at the Methodist chapel a bill, and, at every door along the way, an item of news, for he was the last man in the district who could be trusted with it. "She's had a girl." "He's got the job." "It's from the hospital, but it's good." They came out to say goodbye with their hands in their sleeves and their eyes on his tin, and Harry said goodbye to forty-three houses, and did not once look up the hill at Chapel Row.

For he had spent forty years not looking at Chapel Row. He had grown so skilled at it that he could walk past number three with his eyes on the gutter and know, through the soles of his boots, whether the light in the window was on.

It was always on. It was a window in which a woman sat to sew, for the light, she told the village. The light was very good. It was the best light in Penhallow.

At the head of the lane he stopped, and, for the first time in his life, looked in his tin.

There were forty letters inside, each in a cream envelope, each addressed in the same neat upright hand to *Miss D. Penrose, 3 Chapel Row, Penhallow,* each stamped, not one posted. They lay in the tin like a stack of small, patient, folded doves.

He had written one every year, on the night before the fourteenth of March, which was her birthday. He had never sent a single one. A postman knows better than any man alive the size of the gap between a letter and its door: it is eleven paces and a flap of tin, and it can last a lifetime.

He stood, and spoke, and the wind took the words, as it takes most things in Cornwall:

> Forty times the winter, forty times
> The primrose, and I carried every word
> To every door in Penhallow but one.
> I knew the weight of what she'd had from banks;
> I knew her bills, her birthday cards, the lilt
> Her sister's handwriting took when she was well.
> I did not know what I should say to her.
> There is no form for it. No pre-paid slip.
> A man may carry love through all the weather
> That God sends down on Cornwall, and not once
> Contrive to lay it on a mat and leave.
> And now the round is done, and I am retired,
> And what is left to carry? Forty envelopes.
> Forty. And one more street. I'll try the cliff.

He turned the other way, up the long road to the headland, and left Chapel Row, as he had for forty years, for later.

---

**Lantern House. 10:05 a.m.**

"Mr. Whitcombe," said Nadeesha Fernando. "You are in time for the tea, and for the world."

"Miss Fernando."

"Korea, India, Zambia, Japan." She held the door. "I have been waiting for you all week. Everyone has been writing to the Keeper, and the Keeper, as you know, has not been in a position to reply. I have four of the letters, and I have not read them aloud, because they did not seem like letters to be read alone, and you are the nearest thing in this county to a *postman,* and I thought you should hear them, since you carried the first thousand."

He had. He had carried every one of the thousand letters up the cliff path to the oak cabinet in this house, over forty-five years: letters in a hundred languages, with stamps from places he had to look up. He had never opened one. He had known, though, as a postman knows, from the weight of the paper and the hesitation of the handwriting, that they were a different kind of mail. They were not for the post. They were for the thing the post was for.

She made him tea in the kitchen, in a cup the size of a small bucket. And then, at the long table, among the wool and the seagull feathers and the great cold plain of the Atlantic in the window, she opened them, one by one, and read.

> **Seoul.** *Dear Keeper: I have now measured everyone in this city, and one man twice. Daniel has resigned from his team and sits in my shop in the afternoons, folding silk and complaining that it is quiet. I have sewn him a coat. It fits. I enclose the lining; it is the colour of the quiet he asked for. — Ji-woo Han (#0351). P.S. He says to tell you that he has stopped checking the score of things.*

> **Delhi.** *Dear Madam: Platform six. 5:40. For twenty years the train has not stopped there, and the woman in the blue sari has stood there anyway. On the fourteenth, I stopped it. I have received a letter of warning from the Railways, which I have framed. It is the best letter I have ever received. — Ravi Chaudhary (#0363). We are to be married at the new year. She says I should apologise to the signalman. I shall.*

> **Lusaka.** *Dear Keeper: We were married on Saturday in the school yard, with two hundred children singing in four keys and none of them ours. Grace sold maize to the wedding guests. She says a wedding is no reason to close a stall. My children call her "Mama Grace-and-the-Maize." She does not mind. — Joseph Tembo (#0133).*

> **Sapporo.** *Dear Madam: He built me a sculpture that would not melt, from a kind of resin. I made him take it down. I told him I prefer the ones that melt, because then he has to come and make another. He says that is the most sensible thing anyone has said about art. I have kept the first one in a bottle: it says "Takumi, February." — Yuki Nakamura (#0556).*

Harry sat with his tea going cold. He had the look of a man who has been hit very gently with a very large object.

"They are good," he said at last, "at saying."

"They are," said Nadeesha. "They had a thousand letters before them, and they learned from them."

"Miss Fernando." He cleared his throat. "I have a tin."

"I know you do."

"How—"

"Mrs. Trelawny telephoned at six." She smiled, and her eyes were tired and bright. "She says it is a matter for the Royal Mail. And Mr. Whitcombe, I have read Entry 0266. I read all of them. I read it on the first night." She reached over, very gently, and put her hand for a second on his. "I read another one, too, in the same county. It is Entry 0918. I am not at liberty to say what it says. The Keeper would not allow it. But I will say that it has been *waiting,* and I will say that you know the street."

Harry looked at the great grey window.

"Eleven paces," he said. "And a flap of tin."

"It is generally less far than the heart supposes," said Nadeesha. "One more thing. If you are going out again—" She put an envelope in his bag. "Would you deliver this to Mr. Ashby, at the old coastguard cottage? It is an invitation. For the night of the new moon, a fortnight on. He has not answered the last three."

"He does not read his post," said Harry. "In forty-five years I have taken that man nothing but a seed catalogue and the council tax. He sits in the garden at night with a telescope he can no longer see through." He tucked it in. "I will take it. It is my last day. I will take it *dreckly.*"

"*Dreckly,*" said Nadeesha, "in Cornwall, I understand, means *not in this life.*"

"Not at all," said Harry Whitcombe, rising, with a great new dignity, and the shortbread tin in both hands. "It means *directly.* It is only that the sense of the word has taken a long road."

---

**Chapel Row. Noon.**

Number three had a green door, a brass knocker in the shape of a fish, and a window.

In that window, at a Singer machine of 1951 with a treadle worn pale by sixty years of feet, sat Dorothy Penrose, sixty-eight, retired seamstress, with a mouth like a taut thread, spectacles on a chain, and a back as straight as a ruler.

She was not sewing. She had been not-sewing since ten.

Forty years she had sat in that window. She had taken in wedding dresses, funeral black, christening gowns, a surplice for the vicar and a kilt for a Cornishman who claimed ancestry; and she had told the village it was for the light. It was a good light. It was also, from that chair, the only one that fell exactly on the lane, where, at ten-fifteen every weekday morning, there walked past, with his eyes on the gutter, a postman.

She had never once called him in. She did not know the sentence for it. A woman could take in a hem for a stranger, and put the pins in her mouth, and hold a man's trouser leg and look him in the eye; but there was no regulation, in the great book of what is done, that permitted a woman to say, *Come in and stay.* So she had said instead, forty times, with her mouth full of pins, *That will be one first-class stamp.*

She spoke now to the lane. She did not know she was speaking aloud.

> The light is very good. I tell them so.
> I tell them it's the light. It is, in part.
> And part of it is that a woman who waits
> Should wait at something: wheel, or thread, or glass.
> A woman needs a thing to hold, to do,
> While all the clocks of Cornwall go the long way round.
> Today he comes the last time down the lane.
> They've told me at the shop. The last. The last.
> And I shall hem a seam, and say good morning,
> And watch him walk away with his eyes on the gutter,
> Forty years of Tuesdays. And I shall say—
> What shall I say? I have had forty years.
> I have a jar of stamps and not one letter.

Then she did a thing that she had never done: she stood up from the machine.

She walked the four steps to the front door. She stood with her hand on the latch, and took it off, and put it back. She was, at that moment, in her private estimation, a fool of the first water, in a cardigan.

Outside, in the lane, a number of persons had unexpectedly discovered that the day was fine for hanging washing. Mrs. Trelawny was weighing a sack of potatoes on the pavement, for lack of any other excuse. Tamsin Trevithick, at the fishmonger's, had come to her door with a mackerel in each hand. At the end of the row, with his ears flat and the light of an old and sacred purpose in his eye, sat Boscawen the collie, who had followed the postman into the village for reasons of his own.

And up the lane, in the red jacket, with a shortbread tin held before him like a man bearing a small, delicate casket, came Harry Whitcombe.

He did not look at the gutter.

He walked straight up to the green door, to the brass fish, and he knocked. It was three small knocks, in an old, polite rhythm: the knock of a man who is accustomed to knocking on a door to ask whether the door is open.

Dorothy opened it.

For a moment neither said anything. Behind them the lane held its breath, in every window, in every stoop, with a thoroughness that would have been the envy of the Admiralty.

"Mr. Whitcombe," said Dorothy.

"Miss Penrose."

"You are not delivering."

"I am," said Harry. "A little late."

"How late?"

"Forty years, give or take a Tuesday."

She looked at the tin. She looked at the cow on the lid. She looked, for the first time in forty years, straight into his face without a trouser-leg between them, and found it to be much like her own: lined, and tired, and not at all ready.

"Is that the whole of it?"

"There are forty," said Harry. "One a year. On the night before your birthday. I put on a stamp every time, so they would be correct. I never posted one. I have no excuse. I am a postman. It was the one regulation I could not break."

He held out the tin. She took it. Her hands were quite steady; it was her breath that was not.

She took off the lid. She lifted from the top the last of them, in the cream envelope, and held it, and then, because she was a woman of method, set it back, and reached all the way to the bottom of the pile for the first. The paper had gone the colour of tea. It had the fold of forty years of waiting to be opened.

She read it standing on her own step, in front of the whole of Penhallow:

> *Dear Miss Penrose,*
>
> *I hope you will pardon a postman writing to you, which is not in the regulations. I have delivered to your door six hundred and twelve items since I began the round, and I know the weight of every one. I do not know the weight of what I should like to say, so I am sending only this. Your light is very good. I notice it when I pass. — H. Whitcombe.*

Dorothy lowered the page. Her glasses had misted.

"That is a very short letter," she said, "for forty years."

"I did not want to be a nuisance."

"You were a *postman,*" said Dorothy Penrose, "in a village of three hundred people, and you were forty years walking past a woman who could see you from her window. You were not a nuisance, Harry Whitcombe. You were a *stile.* I climbed over you for forty years, to look at the field."

"I am sorry."

"I will tell you what you are. You are the most expensive pair of trousers I have ever hemmed." She held up the first, and with her other hand, from the pocket of her cardigan, drew out a small glass jar, in which lay, flat and dry and in perfect order, forty first-class stamps. "I charged you a stamp every time. I did not use one. I kept every one. A woman with forty stamps and no one to write to is a woman who knows exactly what she is waiting for."

Harry looked at the jar. He looked at the cuff of his left trouser leg, bitten that morning, as ever.

"There is a thing," he said, "I ought to confess."

"There is nothing else *to* confess. You have confessed a tin."

"The dog."

She paused.

"On the first Tuesday," said Harry, to the pavement, in a very small voice, "I put a sausage in the cuff. In 1986. The first Boscawen never forgot it. He told his sons."

There was a silence the length of Chapel Row.

"A *sausage,*" said Dorothy.

"A small one."

"For forty years."

"The other leg has never had a hole in it."

"I am aware," said Dorothy. "I am a seamstress. I *noticed.*" Her mouth was doing something very difficult. "Forty years I mended a trouser leg that a man had loaded with pork. You, Harry Whitcombe, are the only man alive who has stuffed a collie in order to get a hem."

Behind them Mrs. Trelawny gave a sound like a kettle going off. Tamsin Trevithick dropped a mackerel. Boscawen, who had heard his own name and the word *sausage,* sat up with great expectation.

Dorothy Penrose laughed.

It was a startling sound, because it had been so long coming, and it went up the lane like a bird out of a shut room. She laughed until she had to hold the door; and then, in the middle of it, she was crying, with her glasses off and one hand over her eyes; and Harry Whitcombe, who had been standing at the door of that house for forty years in the only way he knew, put down the tin on her step, quite gently, and held out his two arms, with no regulation whatever.

She walked into them.

"You are forty years late," said Dorothy into the red jacket.

"I know."

"You are not dead. It puts you ahead of most of my customers."

"I try to keep up."

She stepped back. She was crisp again; she dried her face with the back of a hand and looked at him with the eye of one pricing a lining.

"Now," said Dorothy. "I want these done properly. Not all at once; I am sixty-eight, and I will not have forty years of feeling in an afternoon, I should expire on the mat. I want them delivered. By *you.* To this address. One a day. You shall put them through the box at ten-fifteen, in the red jacket, and I shall read each at the machine, and you shall wait on the step for the answer."

"I am retired, Dorothy."

"Then you shall deliver them out of the goodness of your heart. It is a perfectly respectable way to travel." She tucked the jar of stamps into his hand. "These are for the postage. I shall not be using them. The Royal Mail is to be paid."

"It will be a pleasure."

"It will take forty days."

"I have forty days," said Harry Whitcombe, and found, to his great surprise, that he had a great deal more than that.

"Then come in," said Dorothy Penrose, and opened the green door, and for the first time in forty years, did not shut the window of that house on the lane. "The kettle is hot. And we shall see about that sausage."

*In the lane the whole village, as one soul, discovered that it had urgent business elsewhere, and went to it extremely slowly. Mrs. Trelawny took the potatoes, and, by dint of repeating the story, the rest of the day. The dog, who had been given a sausage at last, in public, by a woman with a seamstress's eye, was never heard to bite another cuff.*

---

*Margin note, in pencil, in the hand of S.W.R., beside Entries 0266 and 0918:*

> *The Royal Mail has no category for letters delivered forty years late. I have taken the liberty of inventing one: "Arrived."*
>
> *Observe, reader: they were never apart by anything but eleven paces and a flap of tin. It is generally less far than the heart supposes, and a great deal further than the post can carry.*
>
> *Entries 0351 and 0254, 0363 and 0292, 0133 and 0662, 0296 and 0556: four letters received at the last hour, in four languages, saying the same sentence. The sentence is "We are still here." It is the whole of the Register, and it fits on a stamp.*

---

*End of Chapter 59.*


---

## Chapter 60
### The Sixty-First Letter

> *"I have kept a thousand secrets and never said my own."*
> — Register of Black Stars, Entry 1000

---

*Enter the Chorus, alone, with a lantern. It is, this once, of use.*

> A year to the night. The wind is at the door.
> The sea and sky have once again agreed
> To be one colour. In an upper floor,
> A lamp is lit. It is the lamp we need.

---

### SCENE I
*Lantern House, Cornwall. The new moon. Nine o'clock at night, a year to the hour. The wind knocks at every window as though it, too, had a letter to deliver.*

"It is not a good moon," said Mrs. Grace Lowe, sixty, baker, lately of Liverpool, devout, and constitutionally incapable of praise. "I am not saying it is a *bad* moon. I am saying that it is a moon, and that it exists."

The cake stood on the long kitchen table: a round, white, enormous disc of sponge, cratered with almonds, on which the baker had piped, in blue icing, the single word *Entry.* It was, as even the severest critic present would have admitted, the finest cake in Cornwall.

"It is a very handsome moon," said Nadeesha Fernando.

"It is a *plausible* moon."

"Mrs. Lowe, I have never loved a cake so much."

"You will not say that when you've cut it," said Mrs. Lowe, with the satisfaction of one who has been given what she was fishing for.

At the end of the table sat Mrs. Hannah Clarke, sixty-six, retired barrister, from the cottage by the gate, who had been asked to witness the evening on the ground that she disapproved of everything equally and could therefore be relied upon.

"For the record," said Mrs. Clarke, "I should like it noted that, in law, a letter is not delivered until it is received. This one was never posted. It is therefore, technically, a thought."

"It is a letter," said Nadeesha.

"It is a very *well-documented* thought," said Mrs. Clarke, and took a slice.

It had been a year. A year since a girl of twenty-nine put a trembling finger on a key. In that year the Register had been read, as Nadeesha, who was a nurse and refused on principle to round a number, put it, *by a very large number of people, most of whom were kind.* There had been weddings, and funerals, and apologies sent by post and by satellite, and a rather alarming proportion of lost umbrellas. She had answered hundreds by hand. She had a blister on her second finger that she regarded as a decoration. Of the thousand entries, one pair, 0713 and 0714, drew a curious number of return visits, always on Friday nights, always at about the same hour; she did not look into it. A nurse knows which charts one does not read.

Upstairs, in the lantern room at the very top of the house, where the glass looked on the sea, a man was on his knees, with a spanner and a tin of oil and a set of old brass fittings laid in a row on a clean cloth.

"Anil?" Nadeesha stood in the doorway, with her cardigan wrapped round her.

"One moment." Anil Perera, thirty-two, lighthouse keeper's son, steady, quiet, in the third week of being her husband, set the last fitting in place. He had married her in Galle in the spring, with the old lighthouse on the point lit for the guests for the first time in eleven years, and he had learned, in the months since, that it is possible to be entirely happy and to carry a spanner at the same time. "The lamp in this room has been dark for a year," he said. "It is a Fresnel, from the nineteen-thirties. Her mother's mother's, I think. It needs only oil, and a wick, and a hand that knows how."

"Aunty lit it every night."

"For thirty years. I found the log." He struck a match. The flame took, and caught the old glass, and the whole lantern room blossomed gold. "She wrote one line each evening. *Lit. Ships safe. He is at the window.*"

Nadeesha did not say anything.

"I do not know who *he* is," said Anil. "I think it is the reason I came up here to fix it. I have kept lamps all my life for ships. I thought, tonight: one for him."

On the black rim of the sea, two miles round the bay, a very small window went yellow, and a very small figure moved across it.

"He's there," said Anil softly.

"He has been there for thirty years."

"Then," said Anil Perera, "I am afraid the lamp is going to have to burn a great deal longer."

---

### SCENE II
*The kitchen. A laptop, a cake, a router in the pantry which is loved by no one and obeyed by fewer. Half past nine.*

"*Can you see us?*"

"We can see you."

"*Can you see us now?*"

"We can see the *ceiling.*"

"*That is Despina,*" said a woman's voice. "*She is standing on the table. Despina, get down from the table, you are going to be famous!*"

The screen showed a courtyard in Crete in the light of a lamp: a long table, a vine over it, a great quantity of olives in bowls, a woman of forty-eight leaning out of the corner of the picture and shouting at somebody off-stage about a donkey. In the middle, side by side on a bench, sat two people in their late fifties: a broad grey man with the hands of a tree, and a thin, straight woman dressed head to toe in black.

"George Papadakis, Eleni Stavrou," said Nadeesha, to the room. "Entries 0208 and 0078. Crete. It is half past eleven there."

"*We do not sleep,*" said Eleni Stavrou, fifty-eight, widow, shopkeeper, in the voice of one who has been disapproving of sleep since 1974. "*We have been reading.*"

"*She has read them all,*" said George Papadakis, sixty, olive grower, with the pride of a man whose letters have been, after thirty years, collected. "*Thirty springs. Thirty letters. She opened the whole pile in one week. She would not come out of the kitchen.*"

"*It was unbearable,*" said Eleni.

"*It was—*"

"*It was unbearable,*" said Eleni, with a severity that went all the way down, "*because they were kind. All of them. I kept them shut for thirty years because I was afraid they would be kind, and I opened them and they were. Every one. I have not been the same woman since.*" She looked into the camera. "*I recommend it. I advise every person in the world to open their post.*"

"I have practised at the Bar for forty years," said Hannah Clarke, unexpectedly, "and I endorse the advice."

"*We are to be married,*" said George. "*In spring. After the pruning.*"

"*In black,*" said Eleni.

"*In black?*" said Nadeesha.

"*In case he changes his mind,*" said Eleni. "*I shall already be dressed for it.*"

"*She will wear black,*" said George, quite gently, with thirty years in his voice, "*and I shall wear my father's jacket, and the whole island will weep, and the olives will not care.*" He put his large hand over her small one on the bench. She did not move it. She looked at it with the air of a woman reviewing evidence.

"*Tell her about the donkey!*" shouted Despina.

"*Nobody is telling anybody about the donkey!*"

The window shivered, and a second window opened beside it: a room with a high ceiling and a ceiling fan, and a long bench strewn with brown leaves, a smell of tobacco that came, one almost believed, through the glass. A broad, laughing man in an apron had his hand on the shoulder of a neat woman in a white blouse, sitting very upright, with a classroom pointer in her lap.

"*Héctor Álvarez, Rosa Hernández,*" said Nadeesha. "Havana. It is half past four in the afternoon there. Entries 0207 and 0364."

"*Hola, Cornwall,*" said Héctor Álvarez, forty-four, cigar roller, with the voice of a man who has been telling the truth with a flourish for twenty years. "*Is it raining?*"

"It is always raining."

"*Then it is a little like home.*" He beamed. "*I have a thing to report. Rosa will not let me say it. I will say it. Rosa has read the replies.*"

"*Héctor.*"

"*She has read them aloud, to the class, as a lesson in correspondence.*"

Rosa Hernández, forty-one, schoolteacher, practical, secretly poetic, laid her pointer on the bench with a certain decision and unfolded a sheet of airmail paper.

"For nine years," she said, "Señor Álvarez put a note into every box of cigars that left his bench. One note. *For Rosa.* A different one each time. I did not know. Nobody did. The boxes went to Germany, to Spain, to Canada, to Dubai." She cleared her throat. "In the spring, the first replies began to arrive. The customers had been finding them. I will read one."

> *"Dear Mr. Álvarez. I am a retired dentist in Hamburg. I have smoked your cigars for eleven years and I have found eleven notes. I am not Rosa, and I confess that on the fourth note I wept in a restaurant. I should be most grateful to know how the matter ended. Please tell her I said yes. — Dr. K."*

"*He is not Rosa,*" said Héctor, to the camera, in great sorrow.

"*I told him,*" said Rosa, "*that the matter had not ended. I told him it was proceeding.*" She looked, all at once, very young. "*My sister is in Madrid. I have been deciding for seven years whether I might follow. I am going in the spring. For a month. To look. And then I am coming home.*"

"*To roll the cigars,*" said Héctor, "*somebody must.*"

"*To teach the class,*" said Rosa. "*Somebody must.*"

"*And to see,*" said Héctor, "*whether there is a note in the next box.*"

"*There is not,*" said Rosa Hernández, and, with great dignity and a quiver that she did not manage to conceal, drew a small slip of paper from her blouse. "*It is here.*"

The three women round the Cornish table said "*Oh*" at once. Mrs. Lowe said, "I am not saying it is touching." She did not look at anybody.

"*The post is a very slow thing,*" said Eleni Stavrou, from Crete, with great satisfaction. "*It teaches us patience.*"

The clock in the hall struck the half past ten.

---

### SCENE III
*The doorbell, which has not rung for a year. Two persons in the door: a postman in a red jacket, off duty, and a very old man in a heavy overcoat and a tie.*

"I have brought him," said Harry Whitcombe.

"I came *myself,*" said Edmund Ashby.

"He came himself," said Harry, "on my arm, along the cliff path, in the dark, at a quarter to eleven, at the speed of a retired postman, and I wish to say that I am a good deal better at the first mile of that path than the last."

"I was not going to come," said Edmund. "I read the invitation. I have read it, I should say, in the way that a man in my condition reads: with the help of the postman, who stood on my step for forty minutes and would not leave." He lifted his chin. "And then at nine o'clock tonight the light came on."

Nadeesha, in the kitchen doorway, stood quite still.

Edmund Ashby, eighty-one, retired astronomer, Register Entry 0001, was a tall man gone narrow, with a white moustache, a stick, an old Harris tweed coat that had been good in 1974, and eyes the colour of milk. He was, by his own account, completely blind in the left, and in the right, *a rumour.* He had the manners of a man who has been polite to the universe for sixty years and expects it to reciprocate.

"Miss Fernando," he said. "I am here under protest. I have not decided what the protest is about."

"Mr. Ashby. You are sitting down."

"A technicality."

She brought him to the window, to the big chair that looked on the sea. He sat. The others, with an instinct that had nothing to do with law, withdrew to the kitchen door, and stood there, and did not speak. Harry had taken off his cap. Anil, behind them, had a hand on the wall.

Edmund turned his face to the dark of the glass. Across the water, two miles round the bay, in an upper window of his own cottage, he could not see the lamp he had left lit; but behind him, high in the house, he could feel through the soles of his shoes the other lamp, burning. He spoke, not to them, but, as the old do, to the weather:

> Thirty years I have lived a lantern's throw
> From her, and told myself it was for the dark.
> The sky was clean, the cottage cheap, the air
> Without a street-lamp in it for ten miles.
> I told them at the Observatory: *darkness.*
> A man can lie in four-syllable words
> For thirty years and never be arrested.
> And every night I saw it, in the cove:
> A little gold across the water, burning.
> I knew whose lamp it was. I never went.
> I said: she has her life. I said: I left.
> I said a great many things; and none of them
> Was *I was afraid of what I'd feel if you
> Should open the door.* And then, last winter, with no word,
> The lamp went out. And I knew, by the dark.

He stopped. "I am sorry. I did not intend to make a speech."

"It was a good speech," said Mrs. Lowe, from the door, in a strangled voice. "I am not saying it was a *good* speech."

"Mr. Ashby," said Nadeesha. It was eleven-forty-eight. In her hands, in a plain brown envelope, with the key that had been in the lamp, was a single folded sheet. "I was told that I might not read this until a year after she died, and not aloud until the proper hour, and then only to the person it was for. I was told that you would know."

"Which hour is that?"

"Eleven minutes before midnight. It is the hour she died."

"She was always a little early to her own appointments," said Edmund, in a voice with a crack in it. "Read it, please. I cannot see it. But I can hear. I have always been able to hear her."

---

### SCENE IV
*The window. The wind. The lamp upstairs. Eleven minutes before midnight.*

Nadeesha unfolded the page. It was a single sheet of grey airmail paper, closely written in a small, steady, old-fashioned hand, and, as she held it to the light, she saw that the lower edge was ragged, as though it had been torn from a longer sheet, a long time ago, by someone in a hurry or by someone who had very much wished not to be.

She began to read, in the voice of a nurse reading a chart at a bedside, a plain, level, tender voice, which shook only once.

> **ENTRY 1000 — Colombo / Cornwall.**
>
> *Dear Edmund,*
>
> *You will say I am late. I have been late once before, in nineteen seventy-seven, on a railway platform, when I did not say what I should have said while the train was still in the station. So let me say it first, before the clocks, and before the wind, and before you have the chance to be honourable at me.*
>
> *You were the first. You wrote to me from a ship, and said you were sorry, and did not say for what. I read it a hundred times. On the hundredth I understood that it was not an apology at all. It was an address. It said, in the only language a frightened man possesses, I am here and I cannot come to you. And I thought: if one man is carrying a sentence like that, how many more? And so I began a book, and the book became a life, and the life, I find, was an answer to a letter I had not the courage to write back.*
>
> *I kept a thousand. I did not reply to one. I thought it was a vow. It was a hiding place, with a very fine lock.*
>
> *I knew where you lived. I will confess it, since the dead are, I am told, permitted. You took the cottage at the cove thirty years ago, and on the first night I saw your window come alight across the water, and I lit the lantern, so that you should have, at the least, something to look at. I told myself it was for ships. It was for one ship. You have never once, in thirty years, run aground upon my door, and I have loved you for the discipline of it, and hated you for the same.*
>
> *We were two astronomers, you and I. That is to say, two persons capable of spending a lifetime observing a thing from a great distance and calling it devotion.*
>
> *I was not angry. I was not ever angry. I was only afraid, as you were afraid, and for the same reason, which is that we were both of us certain we would love the other too much, and neither of us could bear to be the one who*

*Here the page is torn.*

---

## The Chorus Speaks the Epilogue

> The page is torn. We do not know the rest;
> It was the Keeper's, and the Keeper's gone.
> Yet you are not by silence dispossessed:
> You have the stars that wait before the dawn.
> Some loves were crowned, and some were laid in earth,
> And some broke off mid-word and were not mended;
> And some, half-lit, in lands of different birth,
> Sit patiently until the night is ended.
> For out in Phuket, on a beach of white,
> Where neither flag nor creed nor country stands,
> A girl stained blue by dye and lamp and night
> Meets one who walks the world with open hands.
> What then they said, the Keeper will not tell.
> The sixty-first is yours. Go. Write it well.

---

*Margin note, in pencil, beside Entries 0713 and 0714, in the Keeper's hand, added in the final week of her life and read by Nadeesha one year later:*

> **"Met. See the next ledger."**

---

*THE END*

*(of this book. The Register of Black Stars is closed at one thousand — but the dark is never full.)*
